News.title: Hotel migrant who police believed was ‘on the run’ after attacking 2 female cops was already in jail for drug dealing
News.content:
COP BLUNDER Hotel migrant who police believed was ‘on the run’ after attacking 2 female cops was already in jail for drug dealing







Next

A HOTEL migrant who police believed to be on the run after attacking two female officers was already in jail for drug dealing.

It had been assumed that “fugitive” Kenson Noel, 31, was at large after he failed to show up for a court case after assaulting two cops.



His solicitor had been unable to contact him as he was no longer living at the Roundhouse Hotel in Bournemouth, Dorset.

Enquiries revealed he had been moved to a different “facility” although nobody involved in the case knew where.



The trial went ahead in Noel’s absence and defendant was found guilty of the assaults and a warrant was issued for his arrest

But it has now emerged that Noel was in jail all along after he was arrested by another force and remanded into custody for a separate drug dealing matter.

The court heard he didn’t tell prison staff about his trial on August 19 and his whereabouts weren’t apparently disclosed to the courts by the Home Office.

Noel has now appeared in court via prison video link to be sentenced for the assault on two officers at the Roundhouse Hotel.

He was an illegal immigrant from Trinidad and Tobago and came to the UK in 2024 after fleeing drug gangs there.

He was sent to live on the Bibby Stockholm migrant barge in Portland, Dorset, but when he boarded he was found to have 6.5g of cannabis on him along with a set of scales, bags and £800 of cash.



As he was being arrested he bit the police officer on the elbow – Noel was let off with a community order.

After the barge was scrapped in 2025 he was sent to live at the migrant hotel in Bournemouth.

On June 26, 2025 he was arrested in Bournemouth Lower Gardens, which was a known drug dealing spot.

He jumped into a stream to evade police officers but when he was caught he was found to have 9.5g of cocaine on him.

His mobile phone was recovered after he threw it into the water but the damage meant police couldn’t analyse it.



Noel was released on bail and carried on living at the Roundhouse.

On October 27 last year police were called to arrest Noel after he became aggressive and locked himself in his room.

As he was being detained he tried to headbutt PC Maddie Duncanson and then attempted to bite her and PC Sinead Sheath – he also spat at PC Duncanson.

Noel appeared before magistrates in November 2025 for two charges of assault which he denied and his trial was listed for August 19.

Charles Nightingale, prosecuting, said: “He was on unconditional bail. On the day of the trial he didn’t attend and the matter proceeded in his absence.



“In the meantime between November 2025 and August 19 the defendant had been arrested and remanded in respect of other matters. He was in custody as of August 19.”

But Mr Nightingale said the defendant was fully aware of his trial date and it was his responsibility to have informed prison staff.

By not doing so he had absented himself from the trial, Mr Nightingale said.

Noel was jailed at Bristol Crown Court to three years and three months for possessing cocaine with intent to supply.

Ewa Russell, defending, accepted Noel could have been proactive and informed the court he was in prison but the case had slipped his mind after being arrested and remanded into custody for drug dealing.



She said: “These are two assaults where no contact was made and luckily no injury was suffered by either of the two officers.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

In relation to the drug possession charge, which Noel admitted, she said the cocaine was for his own personal use.

He was sentenced to a total of eight months for the assault on the two officers and these will run concurrently with the three years and three months he is already serving.

News.title: Moment balaclava-clad thugs smash up farm shop while stealing safe that had been left empty after business went cashless
News.content:
Next

THIS is the moment balaclava-clad thugs smash up a farm shop while stealing a safe that had been left empty after the business went cashless.

Two men targeted the rural premises in Haughley, Suffolk, in an attempted late-night smash and grab.



In shocking footage, they attempt to smash the safe off the wall with a pick axe, having ignored a sign stating the business had stopped accepting cash in August.

As the alarm is blaring, one of men initially misses the safe and puts a hole through the wooden cabin.



He swings at the safe three more times with no success before the pair tie a rope around the safe to pull it off using a motor parked outside.

The force of them yanking out the safe destroyed the farm shop and stock inside.

Despite the motion cameras and alarms alerting the owners, the thieves were gone in the three minutes it took them to get to the shop on their farm.

They have been forced to shut the business and are considering whether it’s viable to continue.



Olivia Colton, who runs the farm with her partner, said: “We set up the little shop about four years ago and sold eggs, honey and a few other things like wax candles.

“We used to take cash but went cashless about two months ago. There was a sign on the top of the safe that said ‘no cash accepted since August’.

“In hindsight maybe we should have just removed it or left it open but you don’t really think about that. Even if we had still taken cash there would have only been about £30 in it.

“We’ve got motion detecting cameras and then we heard the alarms from the farm.

“My partner went down there, it took him about three minutes to get to the shed and the police were maybe a minute behind him and they were gone by then.



“They tied a rope around the safe and pulled it out with a vehicle, the shed followed it, it was totally destroyed.

“There was about £500 worth of stock. It was about £2,500 of damage in total, for an empty safe.

“It’s been a bit of a nightmare. It’s frustrating. The farm doesn’t pay enough, we both have separate jobs.

“The shop helps pay for the day-to-day ticking along of the farm, animal feed and things like that.

“So we are out of pocket with the cost of the damage but also can’t make the money selling our produce as we can’t reopen the shop.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We have got a lot of eggs and honey but nowhere to sell them and we are so busy. We do sell them at a few outlets locally so we’ve tried to direct people there.”

The couple have nearly 100 hives on the farm and produce a couple of tonnes of honey a year.

News.title: I witnessed Christa Pike’s failed execution by lethal injection – the surreal moment we knew it had gone horribly wrong
News.content:
Next

AN EYEWITNESS to Christa Pike’s botched execution has revealed the moments he realized it was failing as she writhed, snored and remained alive after two rounds of lethal drugs.

Will Puckett was one of just seven media witnesses who watched the 50-year-old killer’s attempted execution dramatically unravel inside Tennessee’s death chamber before she was taken to hospital.



The veteran reporter described the experience as “surreal” and admitted he was left “at a loss for words” after his first time witnessing an execution ended in failure during a working day approaching 22 hours.

Puckett and the other witnesses entered the viewing area at 6.41 pm, but according to his notes the curtain did not open until 7.27 pm – far longer than the “10 minutes max” he had been told it should take.



It was during that agonizing wait that an experienced execution witness sitting alongside him issued a chilling warning.

Puckett told The U.S. Sun: “As we’re sitting in this room, and it’s now taking nearly an hour for them to open the curtain from the time that we’re sat, one of my colleagues in there, who had seen her fair share of executions, who was kind enough to kind of walk me through the process, leaned over and said, ‘It should not be taking this long for the curtains to open. Something’s going wrong.’



“And then I’m at that point expecting the Tennessee Department of Correction to say, ‘This isn’t happening. We have another execution that has not gone correctly. We’ll share more information,’ but they open the curtains.”

Puckett said he’s not surprised by the public reaction after what happened on Wednesday night at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville.

“I think if you’re a taxpayer and somebody who says the state should be transparent, I think you are justifiably feeling angry today,” he said.

“Frustrated at the minimum.”



Pike had been set to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years for the brutal 1995 torture and murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.

Pike, then 18, believed Slemmer was trying to steal her 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp, and the pair joined Shadolla Peterson in luring her from their Knoxville Job Corps center to an isolated area.

Slemmer was subjected to a prolonged attack in which Pike and Shipp beat and cut her, with Shipp carving a pentagram into her chest and Pike smashing her head with a chunk of asphalt before taking a piece of her skull as a souvenir.



Pike was sentenced to death, while Shipp received life and Peterson was given probation after pleading guilty to being an accessory after the fact.

Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, traveled around 600 miles from Florida with her husband Raul to witness Pike’s execution after waiting more than 31 years for justice.

Once the curtain opened at 7.27 pm, Pike gave her final statement, saying she was “gonna go out with love,” that it was a “happy day” and she was “ready to go.”

“It should have been 20 minutes from that moment to the state of Tennessee announcing Christa Pike’s time of death,” Puckett told The U.S. Sun.

Instead, the attempt continued until 8.53 pm without succeeding and members of the media were at times left in the dark about what was going on behind the curtains.



Puckett said Pike received two lethal doses of pentobarbital during the failed procedure.

“The first round should be enough to kill a fully grown human,” he said.

“Everybody tells me one shot should have been enough, let alone two lethal doses of it.



“That should have been more than enough.”

Instead, Puckett heard Pike begin snoring deeply as she remained strapped to the gurney.

“It is the snoring that you can imagine, someone, almost like you would see in a movie of an older person sleeping, an older man sleeping,” he said.

“That’s the snoring, that deep draw of somebody in the deepest depths of sleep was that snore sound.

“It was rhythmic. It sounded maybe labored at points.



“Her body did writhe at points, lift off the gurney, back down.”

Puckett said Pike’s legs and feet also moved back and forth, comparing the motion to a “swimming stroke,” but stressed that it did not appear to him to be a reaction to pain.

Pike also complained about a vein in her arm feeling like it was “going to bust” and questioned whether the burning sensation she was experiencing was normal.

“At no point did she scream,” Puckett said of the chilling experience.

“A couple of times did it look like it was going to be her final breath.



“It was just, this looks, this is obviously going wrong.”

The curtain was first closed at 7.46 pm and reopened at 7.49 pm before being shut again at 8.05 pm, according to Puckett’s notes.

“That was exceptionally rare,” he said.

Puckett, an Emmy Award-winning anchor and journalist at WVLT News at in Knoxville, Tennessee, said the decision meant witnesses could still hear what was happening but were no longer able to see it.

“The point of us being in there, or for observers, [is] to say, ‘Yep, the state did what it’s supposed to,’ but because they pulled the curtain, we cannot say that.”



The witnesses repeatedly turned to the Tennessee Department of Correction’s communications director for answers but they were not given updates.

Puckett recalled: “The communications director was like, ‘I don’t know anything. I can’t get you an answer. You’re seeing and hearing what I’m seeing and hearing.'”

Pike was eventually removed from the prison and taken to an off-site medical facility, where she is critically ill but is not believed to be in a coma.

She remains unconscious and unable to communicate, her lawyer told TMZ.

“Any brain damage, any possible paralyzation, no one knows,” Puckett said.



“TDOC either doesn’t know themselves or won’t share that information with us.”

Puckett said an investigation was now “the only fair move,” as Tennessee Governor Bill Lee ordered a third-party review and halted the state’s remaining scheduled execution this year.

After an exhausting day, Puckett was facing a two-and-a-half-hour journey home to Knoxville, where his wife, four-month-old baby and dog were waiting for him.

But he remained in Nashville to help other media outlets and wait for updates.

Reflecting on the night, Puckett said: “In this line of work, you try and divorce yourself from reality, almost operating like a robot.



“It was just a very surreal moment and, you know, our job is to chronicle history, right?

“And you’re in what was supposed to be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years… and then it’s failed.

“And so you’re trying to ride the line of, you know, that there are people who thought that this day would bring them closure.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I don’t like using that term, but would give them some sort of peace.

“And now it’s done anything but that.”

CONVICTED killer Christa Pike remains unresponsive but not in a coma following her botched execution, where she was pierced with seven needles, her attorney said.

Pike, 50, is still alive and in critical condition, receiving life-saving medical care after surviving two full doses of pentobarbital, a lethal drug, in a failed execution attempt on Wednesday evening.



Pike‘s attorney, Randy Spivey, slammed the state of Tennessee for its botched execution, which he called “inefficient, cruel, and torturous.”

“Christa is alive. We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health,” Spivey said during a press conference on Thursday.



Spivey said the execution team at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville attempted to find a vein for an hour.

“I counted at least seven needles used in her left arm alone,” the defense attorney said.

“One of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her left arm after an unsuccessful attempt.”

Stephen Ferrell, Pike’s other attorney, said she repeatedly assisted the execution team, instructing them on where to find IV lines.

“Ms. Pike was not just cooperative, but was trying to help instruct the people placing the IV lines of where they could find them,” Ferrell said.

“She over and over again said, ‘Please, try up on my shoulder higher. Please, try here, please try here. I think it will be Okay,’ and she thanked them, at least when they thought they had established a line.



“Ms. Pike was kind, she was cooperative, and she was at peace the whole time.”

Spivey said there was “blistering and burning” around areas of Pike’s arms where she was injected.

Prison officials repeatedly closed the window curtains to shield the death chamber from media and other witnesses, including Pike’s legal team and her spiritual advisor.

He called the botched execution predictable, saying Pike’s legal team had informed the court and the state that her medical conditions would cause her to suffer an agonizing death.

The attorney called on Tennessee Governor Bill Lee to commute Pike’s death sentence to life in prison.

Lee has halted all executions in the state for the remainder of the year and called for an independent review into Pike’s attempted execution.

However, Spivey said Lee’s actions do not go far enough.



“After having endured solitary confinement for more than 20 years and a full attempt to kill her by lethal injection, Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty,” he said.

Spivey said the ramifications of Pike’s “chemical torture” remain unclear.

“We will never know exactly what physical pain and what mental pain she was going through,” Ferrell added.

“But that was her biggest fear as a survivor of sexual abuse, that she would be pinned down, prodded, poked, cut for a prolonged period of time.”

Spivey said he saw no life-saving measures being administered to Pike after she had survived the lethal doses.



“I’m haunted by last night,” Spivey said, adding, “What I saw last night is not something that should ever, ever happen again.”

News.title: How Christa Pike BEGGED to be put to death by all-female firing squad or hanging hours before botched lethal injection
News.content:
Next

DEATH row killer Christa Pike desperately fought to avoid lethal injection, asking to be shot by an all-female firing squad or even hanged before the procedure she feared ended in chaos.

The extraordinary requests were made as Pike’s lawyers warned that putting her to death through an IV could cause a prolonged and painful execution.



Pike, 50, was due to die on Wednesday at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, Tennessee, for the savage 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.

In the weeks before her execution date, Pike asked for an all-female firing squad rather than lethal injection, according to reports on her legal battle.



Her lawyers said an execution involving male officers restraining and touching her could retraumatise Pike because of the severe sexual abuse she said she suffered as a child.

They wanted an all-woman team to carry out the death sentence and proposed a firing squad as Pike’s preferred method.

But Tennessee does not authorize executions by firing squad.

Pike’s attorneys had also proposed hanging during an August court battle, pointing out that it was the method last used by Tennessee to execute a woman.

The state pushed back, saying it did not have the equipment or legal authority to carry out a hanging.

A judge rejected that alternative but left open the possibility of an all-female team participating in Pike’s execution.



Tennessee law instead allows lethal injection, while inmates whose crimes were committed before January 1999 can also choose the electric chair.

Pike’s murder of Slemmer took place in 1995, meaning she was eligible for that option, but her legal team sought other alternatives as it challenged lethal injection.

Her fears centered partly on concerns about gaining intravenous access.

Her lawyers said Pike had small veins and a blood condition that could make inserting an IV more difficult, allegations that became especially significant after Tennessee was forced to abandon another execution earlier this year.

Officials called off Tony Carruthers’ planned May execution after they were unable to establish suitable IV access.



The case intensified existing scrutiny of lethal injection, which critic and medical ethicists have argued can cause severe suffering when drugs or IV lines do not work as intended.

Supporters of lethal injection have historically presented it as a less visibly violent execution method, while death-penalty opponents and some medical experts argue its appearance can conceal complications and pain.

Pike’s execution was first delayed after the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals issued a last-minute stay while considering claims surrounding her childhood abuse and sentencing.

The US Supreme Court later lifted the stay, allowing Tennessee officials to proceed before the death warrant expired.

Pike was then strapped to a gurney and given pentobarbital under Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol.



But the first round failed to kill her.

Officials administered a second round — also without carrying out the death sentence, as stunned media witnesses watched Pike continue breathing.

At one stage, she lifted her head and complained about pain and burning in her arm, witnesses said.

Reporters could later hear ragged breathing and snoring from inside the chamber as the procedure stretched on.

Her lawyers rushed to court, saying both syringes of lethal chemicals had been administered but Pike remained alive.



The execution was eventually abandoned and Pike was taken to an off-site medical facility.

The Tennessee Department of Correction maintained that staff had followed every step of the state’s approved protocol.

It said the lethal injection drug had “consistently been effective” and that the protocol did not permit officials to carry out any additional procedures after what had already been done.

Governor Bill Lee subsequently halted Tennessee’s remaining executions for the year and ordered an independent review into what went wrong.

The disastrous attempt came more than three decades after the crime that put Pike on death row.



Pike was 18 and attending a Job Corps program in Knoxville when she became convinced fellow student Slemmer was interested in her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp.

Prosecutors said Slemmer was lured to a secluded area on January 12, 1995, before being brutally attacked.

She was beaten and slashed during the prolonged assault, and a pentagram was carved into her chest.

Investigators also said Pike kept a piece of Slemmer’s skull after the killing.

Pike was convicted of murder and conspiracy and sentenced to death in 1996.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Shipp, who was 17 when Slemmer was killed, received a life sentence, while another woman involved in the case, Shadolla Peterson, received probation.

Pike would have become the first woman executed by Tennessee in more than 200 years.

News.title: Iran ‘involved’ in hijacking attempt on Israel-bound jet, Trump suggests – as he warns ‘they’ll be hit very hard’
News.content:
Next

DONALD Trump has suggested Iran was involved in the hijacking attempt of the Israel-bound Flydubai jet.

Standing outside the White House, the US President said that officials are still probing the incident – after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the arrested co-pilot underwent “radical Islamist indoctrination.”



When questioned whether the Islamic Republic was behind the attack, he told reporters: “I would say the answer, based on what I’m hearing, is yes, but we’re working on it right now.”

Another reporter then asked if the US would retaliate if Iran was behind the attack.



Trump replied: “Oh they’ll be hit, very hard, don’t worry. You just ask them. They know what happened. They’ll be hit very hard.”

“It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist,” he told reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday, after speaking with Netanyahu.



Two Israeli security officials said Israel‘s initial assessment was that the co-pilot was likely acting alone, ⁠though the investigation was still ongoing.

Meanwhile, Israel’s envoy to the UAE, Yossi Shelley, said ‌it was too early to draw conclusions and no motive had been determined.



So far, the only piece of information released about the assailant is that he is from Oman, but Omani authorities are yet to confirm this.

One of the major twists is his nationality.

As per security protocols agreed to by the UAE and Israel, crew members from countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel cannot work on flights to Israel.

Netanyahu told Fox: “We have constraints that say you cannot have pilots ⁠from countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with Israel.

“So obviously he was able to go through that.”



In a separate interview with Fox News, the PM said the attacker was being investigated in Saudi Arabia and that he believed that he would be taken to the UAE.

Asked if there was any indication of Iranian involvement, Netanyahu said it was “too early” to say.

The investigation is being led by the Saudi security services, which have been interrogating the co-pilot.



Meanwhile, the UAE has also formed a team to investigate the incident.

A spokesperson for Emirati Foreign Minister Afra Alhameli said: “The investigation includes examining all circumstances and motives surrounding the incident, including any possible connection to terrorist activity or intent, and whether it involved prior planning or direction.”

This comes as the Pentagon is deploying 9,000 troops aboard a group of ships to the Middle East to bolster US presence.

It includes the USS Theodore Roosevelt, which recently deployed with the cruiser USS Chosin, and the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

They are expected to arrive in the region as early as the end of October, according to a US official.



Given the personnel already in place in the Middle East, the move would bring the US naval presence to an unusually high number of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines and hundreds of aircraft.

News.title: Trafficking boss behind deaths of 27 migrants including young girl & five women when dinghy sank in Channel is jailed
News.content:
DEATH SMUGGLER Trafficking boss behind deaths of 27 migrants including young girl & five women when dinghy sank in Channel is jailed







Next

A TRAFFICKING gang ringleader behind the deaths of 27 migrants after a dinghy capsized in the English Channel has been jailed.

Only two people survived when the inflatable sank in the rough seas off Calais in November 2021 with a young girl and five women among the victims.



The death of the 27 migrants – who were mainly Iraqi Kurds – remains the biggest single loss of life in the Channel linked to small boats.

Following a French investigation into the tragedy, one of the ringleaders of the crossing was found to have smuggled themselves into the UK in the back of a lorry.



Harem Ahmed Abwbaker, 36, was tracked down by National Crime Agency investigators to a hotel in Cheltenham, Gloucestershire, and was arrested in 2022.

He has now been convicted of manslaughter in France in connection to the crossing and sentenced to eight years in prison.



A French fisherman had raised the alarm at 2pm after finding 15 ­bodies floating off Calais on November 23, 2021.

France later confirmed at least 27 migrants had died — including five women and a girl.



That evening, a grey naval rescue boat bearing the victims edged into the Port of Calais – two survivors were seen wrapped in foil blankets.

Authorities at the time said the dinghy had refused help after suffering engine trouble.

Dunkirk prosecutors opened a probe into manslaughter as a hunt for the traffickers was launched.

The gang – made up of Afghan and Kurdish members – had charged migrants a staggering 3,000 euros each to make the crossing.

After Abwbaker was tracked down in the UK, he was subsequently extradited to France to face manslaughter, human trafficking and organised crime charges in July 2023.



On September 30, at the Tribunal Judiciaire de Paris, he was one of six people convicted of manslaughter.

French prosecutors said he was a key ringleader of the people smuggling gang behind the fatal crossing.

The five other members were given sentences of between six and ten years.

Meanwhile, another seven people were convicted of other offences linked to the event.

This included facilitating illegal immigration and being members of an organised crime group.



Their sentences ranged from six months suspended to four years behind bars.

NCA Deputy Director of Investigations Craig Turner said: “This was a tragic incident which starkly demonstrated the callous nature of the gangs involved in organising Channel boat crossings.

“Abwbaker and his co-conspirators did not care about the dangers of putting an over-loaded and completely unsuitable dinghy into the sea. They just wanted to get paid.

“Sadly, many of those on board the boat ended up paying with their lives.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The NCA worked closely with our French partners on this investigation, and I pay tribute to the French police and prosecutors who have worked to get justice for the families of those whose lives were lost.



“Cases like this are exactly why tackling people smuggling remains a top priority for the NCA, and we continue to do all we can to disrupt and dismantle the cruel organised criminal networks involved.”

News.title: FlyDubai FZ1073 latest: Netanyahu says hijack pilot 'used axe' in cockpit attack
News.content:
The pilot who allegedly stabbed another pilot and tried to take over FlyDubai flight FZ1073 on Wednesday may have used an 'axe' in the attack, Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu claimed

The pilot who allegedly stabbed another pilot and tried to take over FlyDubai flight FZ1073 may have used an "axe" in the attack, according to Israel's prime minister.

Benjamin Netanyahu told CBS News yesterday: "As they approached Israel, one of the co-pilots stabbed or hit with an axe the other pilot, an Indian pilot. And the pilot that was hit, bleeding profusely, fighting for his life, managed to unlock the pilot's door." Airlines are generally required to carry crash axes in the cockpit for use in an emergency to break open a window to escape or break open a panel to access a fire.

The flight issued an emergency hijacking alert yesterday morning, around two and a half hours into its flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The injured pilot - identified as Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar - and a number of passengers bravely fought back control and regained control of the plane, which subsequently made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

One of the passengers who helped was Yaniv Hayoun, who Netanyahu described as a "great hero". Mr Hayoun said: "I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and pulled him - first and foremost - outside."

He then said he helped pull the aircraft's controls. Mr Hayoun claimed he knew how to control the plane after watching the TV show Air Crash Investigation.

Have you been involved in the FlyDubai incident? If so, please get in touch and share your story by emailing livenews@reachplc.com

News.title: Police issue stern warning after urban explorers break into former zoo Living Coasts and set fires
News.content:
Police issue stern warning after urban explorers break into former zoo Living Coasts and set fires

A Devon and Cornwall Police inspector has warned would-be urban explorers to avoid the former Living Coasts project in Torquay and not to encourage others after it was damaged in multiple incidents

View 4 Images Officials have warned explorers against entering the Torquay site (Image: DevonLive)

Urban explorers have been handed a warning by police following a "number of incidents" of trespass, damage and arson at a former zoo.

‌



‌



Devon and Cornwall Police have warned intrepid Brits against breaking into the site of the former Living Coasts project on Beacon Quay in Torquay. The service said it had investigated "a number of incidents in recent weeks" at the site, which was owned by South West Environmental Parks and closed in 2020 over income losses caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

‌



Incidents at the site led to damage, trespass and arson, investigators said, and would-be explorers have been handed a stern warning by a local inspector.

‌



View 4 Images Police and site administrators have warned the site is not abandoned (Image: DevonLive)

Rob Harvey, the neighbourhood inspector for Torquay, warned people to stay out of the site and not encourage anyone to enter. He said: "Stay out of the site, do not encourage others to enter, and think carefully before following social media trends that could put you in danger or leave you with a criminal record."

‌



While Living Coasts officially closed in 2020 and is expected to remain shuttered, it was announced in 2025 that marine habitat restoration firm ARC Marine would be taking over the site.

Wild Planet Trust said it would be turned into a "state-of-the-art marine restoration centre", with ARC Marine's founder and CEO saying the firms were looking forward to bringing their vision "to life". Tom Birbeck said at the time: "We are glad to work alongside Torbay Council and the Wild Planet Trust to bring this vision to life."

View 4 Images Urban explorers have captured themselves entering the site in Torquay and posted the videos online (Image: DevonLive)

‌



Inspector Harvey hit out against a "misconception" that the site is completely abandoned and available to urban explorers.

He said: "There is a misconception amongst some that this site has been abandoned and is there to be explored; that is simply not the case. The recent incidents of trespass, vandalism and fire setting at the Beacon Quay site are unacceptable.

"They divert emergency services from genuine emergencies, place those involved at risk and cause unnecessary costs and disruption."

‌



View 4 Images The Beacon Quay site manager has said they were forced to fix cut netting and fire damage (Image: DevonLive)

Beacon Quay has been the subject of a number of social media videos taken by urban explorers. Searching through platforms like TikTok reveal at least half a dozen attempts to comb through the site. ARC Marine's facilities manager Eunice Godinho, said explorers have gone beyond "harmless curiosity".

The manager said netting was cut open on the site, and that it had sustained fire damage which had taken time to repair.

Article continues below

Ms Godinho said: "We completely understand why the former Living Coasts site attracts curiosity, but what we are experiencing goes far beyond harmless curiosity. We're asking people to respect the site, stay out and not encourage others to enter for the sake of social media content."

News.title: Manchester City tax questions put to HMRC after club found guilty of financial breaches
News.content:
Manchester City tax questions put to HMRC after club found guilty of financial breaches

The Premier League said the club arranged “sham contracts” with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830million

View 3 Images Man City tax questions put to HMRC (Image: Getty Images)

The House of Commons Treasury Committee has written to HMRC to ask about any tax implications of the Premier League’s investigation into Manchester City.

‌



‌



The league this week said the club arranged “sham contracts” with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830million.

‌



They confirmed that City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

‌



7 future England stars aiming to prove Thomas Tuchel wrong and become the next Harry Kane READ MORE :

View 3 Images Man City were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules (Image: Getty Images)

An independent commission found that, during that time period, the club arranged the “sham contracts” as well as “relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs”.

The club continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until October 2 to submit an appeal.

‌



Now, the powerful Treasury committee has sent a letter to HMRC in relation to the findings.

Chair Dame Meg Hillier MP has asked for reassurance that the department is “seized of the importance” of the case and poses a number of questions to Permanent Secretary John-Paul Marks.

These include whether HMRC is aware of the findings and if an unredacted copy of the report had been requested by the department.

‌



The Chair also asked for an overview of HMRC work around the taxation of remuneration and any other potential tax avoidance within football clubs.

The letter states: “While I acknowledge that taxpayer confidentiality may inhibit what you can disclose, I would welcome reassurance from HMRC that you are seized of the importance of these issues and the public interest in the case.”

Tax expert Dan Needle has also asked on the Tax Policy Associates website, did Manchester City cheat HMRC out of £12 million?

‌



He wrote: “Manchester City’s rule-breaking may go beyond football. The independent Commission found that the club inflated its income, concealed expenses and paid a key individual through a sham consultancy.

“Leaked documents identify him as City’s manager, Roberto Mancini, with payments routed to his company, Sparkleglow Holdings Ltd.

“We believe the evidence points to £12m in unpaid UK tax. The consequences could include a much larger tax bill and a criminal investigation.”

‌



View 3 Images Treasury committee has written to HMRC about Man City (Image: Getty Images)

He states his report is a preliminary assessment based on the evidence currently available - acknowledging that City maintain their innocence.

Based on this he concluded: “Roberto Mancini received large payments under a consultancy contract with Al Jazira Sports and Cultural Club.

‌



“On the basis of the Commission’s findings and leaked documents, the contract was a sham, and in reality represented remuneration for Mr Mancini’s employment with Manchester City.

“Manchester City should therefore have applied UK PAYE income tax and National Insurance in the usual way – but the evidence suggests the club unlawfully failed to do so. We expect around £12m of tax went unpaid.

“We don’t know whether HMRC has commenced an investigation into these arrangements and, if it has, whether it has been resolved – but there’s no sign of any settlement payments in Manchester City’s accounts.

‌



“The highly irregular nature of the arrangement, and the Commission’s findings of sham and intentional concealment, suggest to us that there should be a criminal investigation into whether tax evasion offences were committed.

“The Commission’s finding that Manchester City knowingly filed false accounts suggest that Companies Act criminal offences may have been committed.”

In full, Manchester City said: "Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission, that has been published today.

‌



"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The Club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

"The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence. The Club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete."

Article continues below

Mancini said, in response: "I don't think Manchester City were found guilty, quite the opposite. It's not a problem that concerns me, and it isn't anything new. Manchester City are not guilty, and on the double contract it isn't my problem, theirs if anything."

News.title: Christa Pike victim's family left furious after death row murderer survives two executions
News.content:
Christa Pike victim's family left furious after death row murderer survives two executions

May Martinez, the mum of Christa Pike victim Colleen Slemmer, was left fuming after the convicted murderer escaped with her life following two lethal injection attempts

View 5 Images Christa Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19 (Image: Tennessee Department of Correction/AFP via Getty Images)

The mum of Christa Pike's victim has been left furious with prison authorities after the death row murderer survived two execution attempts.

‌



‌



Pike, 50, "lost consciousness" and was "audibly snoring " when officials in Tennessee, in the US, administered the second of two lethal injections, with her legal representatives forced to file an emergency motion to stop the attempt. She has since been rushed to hospital, where she is "being provided life-saving measures", and her future is now up in smoke due to the state's execution protocols.

‌



The mum of twisted Pike's victim has come out swinging against state officials, saying "they f***** up" after she was let in the dark about the state of the execution.

‌



View 5 Images The mother of Pike's victim was left furious by the failure to carry out a successful execution (Image: WVLT 8)

Speaking to US outlet NBC news, May Martinez, the mum of Colleen Slemmer, who 19 when she was tortured and brutally killed by Pike in 1995, said she wanted the execution to be carried out. But, she added: "They went to try to execute her, and she didn’t die."

She was left furious with the state's Republican governor Bill Lee, its Department of Correction and attorney general after her daughter's murderer was rushed to hospital.

‌



The mum said the killer had never expressed remorse during the attempted execution on Wednesday, and since the twin attempts has received little communication from officials. She said: "They didn’t say anything, and then, all of a sudden, they asked all the victims to leave. And we left."

View 5 Images Pike murdered Colleen Slemmer in 1995 (Image: WVLT 8)

“We didn’t know anything until we got up to the office and saw the commissioner. And he said that it didn’t work ... and she’s on her way to the hospital.”

‌



When asked what her message to the governor and attorney general was by NBC, furious Martinez replied: "They f----- up." Pike has never denied killing Ms Slemmer, who died more than 30 years ago when she was tortued by the murderer, then 18, and her 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp.

Shipp and Pike used boxcutters and a rock to carry out the brutal torture, with the former of the pair carving a pentagram into their victim's chest. Pike is said to have taken a fragment of Ms Slemmer's skull, which she later showed to a friend.

View 5 Images An ambulance was seen presumably carrying Christa Pike to the hospital (Image: AP Photo/George Walker IV)

‌



Pike, who was later diagnosed with mental health disorders, was convicted of murder in 1996, and placed on Tennessee's death row. Pike's execution took place at the Riverbend maximum security institution on Thursday, in the presence of a gallery, including seven journalists.

Officials administered the lethal poison pentobarbital, which is meant to induce unconsciousness before quickly causing death. Pike was still awake and snoring around 40 minutes after the drug was administered.

Journalists in attendance described seeing Pike start to snore before corrections officials escorted them and Pike's victims out of the room. John North, a reporter at WBIR, an affiliate of ABC News, said following the execution attempt: "It appears this did not go how this was supposed to go."

Article continues below

View 5 Images Media witnesses recount the horror events (Image: AP Photo/George Walker IV)

"When we left the building, so far as we knew, she was probably still alive.” Pike's legal team released a statement following their client's botched execution saying their concerns were vindicated.

They said in a statement to the Tennessean: "Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution. We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy."

News.title: Vladimir Putin's 'Professor Doomsday' warns 'millions will die' in Europe nuclear strike
News.content:
Vladimir Putin's 'Professor Doomsday' warns 'millions will die' in Europe nuclear strike

One of Vladimir Putin's former advisers, Sergei Karaganov, warned that Russia will go nuclear if NATO sends troops to Ukraine or touches Kaliningrad

View Image Putin has reportedly said a nuclear war against Europe would be 'short' (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

A former adviser to Russian president Vladimir Putin has warned "millions of innocent people would perish" in a nuclear war.

‌



‌



Russia has once again warned NATO of a "very short" nuclear war, which has led to the chilling claims by "Professor Doomsday" Sergei Karaganov. He also said Russia is ready to go nuclear if the West sends troops into Ukraine or touches the Kremlin’s Baltic Sea outpost Kaliningrad or other territory.

‌



He added: "I hope it does not come to that, but Russia would be forced to launch a nuclear strike if NATO countries deployed troops to Ukrainian territory or if there were a direct threat to Russian territory.

‌



"Fortunately, both the foreign minister [Sergei Lavrov] and the president [Vladimir Putin] himself have stated that if the situation escalates - for instance, if NATO were to act directly on our soil, specifically in Kaliningrad - the war would be short."

He gave a chilling smile as he said: "It is absolutely clear that such a war would be nuclear." Karaganov claimed: "I do not want that, and I am actively working to prevent such a scenario."

‌



Yet he boasted: "A nuclear war in Europe could easily be won. But it would inflict terrible moral damage on us, and millions of innocent people would perish." The deaths, he implied, would be in Europe.

He did not mention the prospect of a reprisal strike by NATO. An interviewer then reminded him that he had earlier proposed "launching a pre-emptive nuclear strike", to which Karaganov replied: "It’s not too late. It’s never too late."

He added: "I hope things won’t come to that, but I am very pleased that both the Russian president and the foreign minister have started saying that if a war were to break out, it would be very short. And that means exactly what I was saying."

Article continues below

Karaganov was an adviser to the Kremlin for 12 years and is the academic supervisor of the prestigious Faculty of World Economy and International Affairs at Moscow’s Higher School of Economics (HSE), and of its Institute for Global Military Economics and Strategy.

Moscow's Higher School of Economics lists him as a distinguished professor and member of its Academic Council. He is also chairman of the editorial board of Russia in Global Affairs.

News.title: Man repeatedly stabbed while saving hundreds from being killed by terrorist wins Mirror Pride of Britain Award
News.content:
Bleeding from three stab wounds inflicted by a murderous terrorist, Andrew Franks’ first thought was not of himself. Instead, despite injuries so serious he nearly died three times, he raced to protect the hundreds of worshippers in the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue from further harm on Yom Kippur.

Speaking for the first time ahead of the anniversary of the antisemitic attack on October 2 last year, in which Melvin Cravitz, 66, and Adrian Daulby, 53, were killed, Andrew says he doesn’t know how he managed it. He recalls: “He stabbed me three times, yelling that he was going to kill me. I shouted, ‘lock the doors’ and quickly ran inside. Everyone ­barricaded the doors while my 80-year-old dad held me as I was bleeding from my neck. I thought I was going to die.”

Carol Vorderman calls on the nation to nominate youngsters for Pride of the Playground award READ MORE :

The 53-year-old chef, from Bury, Greater Manchester, will pick up a Daily Mirror Pride of Britain Award, in partnership with P&O Cruises, at our star-studded gala, which honours the nation’s unsung heroes. He will be presented with the award for Outstanding Bravery in honour of his courage in confronting Jihad Al-Shamie, who left him with life-changing injuries to his head, neck, spine and face.

View 7 Images Andrew Franks with his daughter Tamara Franks, dad Ellis Franks, and sister Joanne Gordon (Image: Ben Borland)

‌



Andrew, who had been ­volunteering as a security guard at his family synagogue for about a year, was called in to cover at the last minute on the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. He says: “When I arrived in the morning I noticed a guy standing on his own outside the shops. It was odd because he was taking photos of the synagogue. I had a strange feeling ­something was going to happen.

“I was keeping an eye on him. ­Something wasn’t quite right. A few minutes later, the guy came over and asked the other security guards if he could park his car in the synagogue. He was told: ‘Sorry, you can’t park here, please can you go.’ Then they said he started shouting about Jews and stumbled off. I told the security guards to dial 999.”

A few minutes later, at around 9.30am, there was a loud bang as the attacker rammed his car into the gate and Andrew rushed to help. Andrew says: “He was shouting and I didn’t realise at this point that he’d already killed someone and had a knife on him. I went to grab him and thought he stabbed me once, although I found out it was three times.

It felt like my ear was hanging off. He was wearing what looked like a suicide belt, but it turned out to be false. He shouted ‘I’m going to f***ing kill you, you Jewish…’. Then I managed to trip him up as he was running towards the ­synagogue and trying to get inside. Then I got up, I still don’t know how, and shouted ‘lock the doors!’”

‌



View 7 Images Mourners pay tribute to the victims of the attack at the synagogue in Manchester (Image: William Lailey / SWNS)

Andrew was chased by the knifeman and attacked again, but he escaped and was let into the synagogue by one of the congregation. His heroic intervention delayed the attacker long enough for hundreds of people inside the building, which has a capacity of 850, to barricade the doors.

Al-Shamie, 35, pounded on the windows and smashed pots against the doors trying to get in, but he was shot dead by firearms officers who had raced to the scene. Sadly, a stray round passed through the doors and killed Adrian, an old school friend of Andrew, as well as injuring Yoni Finlay, who was bravely hanging on to the door.

Melvin had been fatally stabbed outside the gates, while security guard Bernard Agyemang was injured after being struck by the car. Inside the synagogue, Andrew’s father Ellis Franks held his son’s wounds until medics arrived. Andrew, who has one teenage daughter Tamara, recalls: “I was in and out of consciousness. I kept saying: ‘Dad, I’m going to die, I’m going to die, I can’t leave Tamara.’

‌



“He kept telling me: ‘Everything will be fine, just take a deep breath.’ I could hear the man banging on the doors trying to get in. It was really scary. After that, I heard the gunshots. I tried to stand up but I collapsed. Then it was all over and he was dead. There were bomb experts because he had a vest on and they didn’t know if it was a real suicide vest. I had a blood ­transfusion on the street before I was taken to hospital.”

View 7 Images Forensic teams arrive at Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue, Manchester (Image: William Lailey / SWNS)

Ellis, now 81, from Salford, Greater Manchester, says: “I was already in the synagogue when someone called me to say Andrew was injured. Blood was pouring and pouring out, it was a flood. I got some tissues and I pressed against his ear. I didn’t know he’d been stabbed in the neck.

“I held it there until the bleeding slowed, then he started going in and out of consciousness. Later, the consultant said I’d saved his life. The attacker was trying to get in. I can still picture his face pressing up against the windows. He was screaming about killing the Jews.

‌



“Andrew kept saying ‘I’m going to die’. I was really calm at that point, but afterwards I started shaking. As we left the synagogue ­afterwards we could see the attacker lying dead on the floor and poor Melvin. At the hospital, Andrew was crying to Tamara, saying, ‘I’m sorry, I’m sorry’. We were told that Andrew nearly died three times as he lost so much blood. We are both seeing a counsellor, it’s been awful.

“I just get upset when I see Andrew because he’s not going to recover 100%. It’s heartbreaking. When we were at synagogue for Yom Kippur this year, Andrew was called up to receive a blessing during the service and I cried.”

View 7 Images Worshippers Adrian Daulby (left) and Melvin Cravitz were killed during the terror attack

Andrew, whose wife Rama died last March after battling cancer for 15 years, has been part of the synagogue community his whole life, celebrating his wedding and Bar Mitzvah there. He has not yet been able to return to work for the NHS Greater Manchester Mental Health Unit and is still receiving treatment for his injuries.

‌



Andrew says: “When I arrived at the hospital, the surgeon took one look at me and said: ‘I’m going to take you to theatre right now.’ I said to him: ‘Please save me. I have a daughter.’”

The attacker had cut through Andrew’s facial and eye nerves, leaving him with difficulty eating. He also had a skull and spinal fracture. Andrew adds: “I was in theatre for nine-and-a-half hours and I was in hospital for a fortnight. I was told I nearly died three times on the ­operating table. I’m still having ­nightmares and I’m seeing a trauma psychologist. My eyesight is OK, but my eye will not shut properly.

“I’ve seen a stroke team because my injuries are a bit like what happens to stroke victims. They are helping me learn how to eat a bit better. I drool occasionally when I eat – I feel like a two-year-old and I’m very self-conscious. I hope it will improve but there’s no guarantee.”

View 7 Images Armed Police officers stand by emergency vehicles outside Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation synagogue in Crumpsall (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Inquests were opened after the atrocity, but the Chief Coroner for England and Wales, Judge Alexia Durran, has recommended that they are converted into a public inquiry because there is classified MI5 ­intelligence to review. Sir Stephen Watson, Chief Constable for Greater Manchester Police, says: “Andrew Franks was very bravely seeking to fend off the attacker and prevent him from entering the synagogue and ­committing further acts of terrorism.

“Thank goodness he was there because despite the fact that he sustained those awful injuries, it was his actions that undoubtedly prevented further loss of life. He confronted him, grappled with him, tripped him up and was shouting at people to lock the doors. Despite his injuries, he continued in seeking to protect those inside.

“I have no doubt that had this ­radicalised terrorist got into that synagogue, he would have committed mass murder. There is absolutely no question that the motive of the attacker was purely to attack these people simply because they were Jewish.”

View 7 Images Jihad Al-Shamie, the terrorist who killed two Jewish people on Yom Kippur in the suburb he grew up

‌



Andrew’s sister Joanne Gordon, 56, an animal talent booker from Altrincham, Cheshire, says: “I couldn’t be prouder of my little brother Andrew. When it mattered most, he showed incredible courage, putting himself in danger to protect others. He stepped forward when others needed him.”

Andrew’s daughter Tamara adds: “I was so scared and just wanted to know my dad was safe. He put himself at risk to help save others and I couldn’t be prouder.” Sara Stanger, Andrew’s solicitor from JMW, adds: “This award is not only for him, but the families who lost loved ones and the Jewish community in Manchester and beyond.”

*Don’t miss The Daily Mirror Pride of Britain Awards coming soon to ITV1 and ITVX.

News.title: Prince William consoles residents of 'forgotten' flood-hit village ahead of storm season
News.content:
Prince William consoles residents of 'forgotten' flood-hit village ahead of storm season

Prince William travelled to Skenfrith in Monmouthshire, Wales, today to meet residents who have been flooded out of their homes four times in the last six years

Prince William declines Diana documentary offer to avoid ‘being pitted against’ Prince Harry

Prince William consoled residents of a "forgotten" Welsh village as they prepared to batten down the hatches for storm season.

‌



‌



The Prince of Wales travelled to Skenfrith, Monmouthshire, where some locals have been flooded out of their homes four times in the last six years. He also visited the nearby White Castle Farm, where he hopped over a fence to meet Stump Up For Trees - an environmental charity working to restore native woodland as a sustainable way of helping to prevent flooding.

‌



Last year in Skenfrith, firemen had to rescue locals from their cottages by boat during last winter's Storm Claudia as water levels reached waist-height when the River Monnow burst its banks.

‌



View 5 Images Prince William chats to Andrew Hooper and Ginette Lee to hear about the impact of flooding on Skenfrith (Image: Getty Images)

Today, William praised villagers' resilience and sympathised with them as they prepared for this winter’s storms predicted to be worse than ever due to the El Niño effect.

The prince wanted to visit the community fighting back against the floods, which saw a five-foot-deep torrent of water gush through the village. He told villager Jeanette Lee, 70: “It must be demoralising. There can be nothing worse than large volumes of water coming into your house.”

‌



Some locals have sold up and moved out after seeing the value of their properties plummet and finding they could no longer get insurance.

View 5 Images The prince chats to Rod and Helen Wyatt, who had been flooded out of their home (Image: Mathieu Willcocks/PA Wire)

But Jacqueline Brown, 79, said she is staying put even though she has her belongings packed in boxes ready to move upstairs when the next flood hits. She has lived in Skenfrith for the last 60 years and has a memory of the village being flooded in the distant past.

‌



But she told William that her cottage in the village has been flooded four times in the last six years. The prince then called into the village hall to meet members of Monmouthshire County Council and Natural Resources Wales who have been part of a formal inquiry into flood risk management in the area.

Dr Catrin Maybe, Monmouthshire Council’s cabinet member for climate change and environment, told him: “It is harrowing for people who live in the Monnow Valley - there is a sense of real fear and anxiety as we are coming up to storm season.”

View 5 Images William climbs over a wire fence during a visit to White Castle Farm today (Image: Chris Jackson/PA Wire)

‌



The village of 24 houses was also hit by Storm Dennis six years ago, and after getting itself back on its feet, Storm Claudia hit last year.

William walked past a three-bedroomed cottage opposite the church, on the market for £155,000, about half its marked value pre-floods. One villager joked: “If someone buys it they should turn the upstairs into a flat and the downstairs into a dock to keep a boat.” Villager Helen Wyatt, 57, welcomed the Prince’s visit saying Skenfrith was a “forgotten village” and needed all the help it can get in fighting the floods.

After at Great Tre Rhew Farm, William got his hands dirty planting a tree and joked that “a pint of cider a day keeps the doctor away”.

‌



There he planted a Welsh Oak and heard told how local farmers had reinstated a historic cider orchard as part of a project to plant one million native trees across the region.

View 5 Images William helps collect seeds from a Field Maple (Image: Chris Jackson/PA Wire)

Farmers Jim and Kate Beavan told him how they had replanted apple trees on a north-facing slope which meant they flowered later and missed the last frost, producing better fruit.

‌



Cider fan William clearly approved of their efforts, but insisted he would only ever stick to one pint of their homemade Great Tre Rhew cider because “it’s eight per cent!”

He visited the farm near White Castle, Monmouthshire, to see how the charity Stump Up For Trees is planting shelter belts on hillsides - strips of forestry to provide shelter for livestock and improve soil infiltration, helping to keep water in the ground to prevent flooding, but also to serve as a firebreak.

View 5 Images William said seed collecting was 'therapeutic' (Image: Chris Jackson/PA Wire)

‌



Last year, Storm Claudia caused the nearby River Monnow to burst its banks, causing significant damage to the local area. Over the summer wildfires devastated hillsides around nearby Blaenavon, making the charity's work more relevant than ever.

William planted his own tree in the strip of land, joking as he approached a pre-dug hole, “Here’s one I made earlier”. Lowering the sapling into the ground, he got his hands dirty, scattering soil around the base.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Article continues below

“Hopefully that will be nice and tall. It’s in a good spot, it’s got lots of space,” he said. Earlier, William helped collect seeds from a Field Maple, reaching into the branches to harvest them to be added to the nursery.

“There’s nothing more calming and therapeutic,” he said as he helped volunteers to pick them off. "I’m a bit taller than the rest of you so I should be reaching up here for some of these higher ones.”

News.title: 'Suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford is test for Burnham and UK security'
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has confirmed what many believed was likely from the start of the RAF Fairford mystery.

That the Government believed Iran "played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford", which prompted the arrest and then bailing of five men seized close to the mainly US airbase on Sunday.

It has promoted a further storm of confusion and hysteria cast by right-wing commentators, furious that the five suspects arrested have been released under conditions.

But there are two likelihoods, that whoever is really behind this mystery is a serious entity like Iranian intelligence and whoever was seized on the ground may be far less seriously involved in an international plot. Or so they may have thought.

It is possible that intelligence agencies have been probing an Iranian attempt to do something against the Gloucestershire air base, housing US bombers.

These are warplanes that have been repeatedly involved in operations against Iran.

View 3 Images US bomber on the tarmac at RAF Fairford (Image: Ben Birchall/PA Wire)

Interestingly PM Burnham has paid tribute to counter-terror police and anyone involved in the investigation, which will include our own intelligence agencies.

And it is also possible Iran, if it is involved in this, was probing security arrangements at RAF Fairford with a view to launching a future mission against the complex or another one elsewhere in the UK.

Tehran’s intelligence agencies are known to have hired at arms length groups for money to carry out activities against the UK in the past.

It is possible to do this via social media or gaming apps in such a way that whoever has been contacted will never know who they are really being employed by and why.

We do not know what these men thought they were doing but it is also possible they were duped into approaching the base, whilst Iran watched, able to take notes on the reaction.

An Iranian intelligence agency will have gleaned information on armed police response times, vulnerabilities in the security system and the reaction of the British authorities.

US President Donald Trump stated as a fact that “we” have been watching them, immediately giving away the possibility that there was an intelligence operation underway.

This does not mean the men are guilty of anything, just that he believes there was a surveillance operation already underway relating to RAF Fairford.

There is an outside chance the FBI or CIA has tipped off UK officials within MI5 that a suspected plot against Fairford was underway.

This may have been picked up in intercepted conversations by the National Security Agency, the US version of our GCHQ..

Or it could be that this was a British-led operation which the US authorities had been made aware of and which Trump has exposed.

But we do not know if an intelligence operation was underway, how long it had been running for and how serious it was.

It has also been suggested one of the men made a ‘999 call’ to police an hour before the farmer who reported their behaviour to police.

This would fit with the idea that the group was acting on someone else’s behalf but he had rumbled that the real reason they were there was more suspicious than he thought.

This may well have been a test, one that if bungled still had a positive effect for Iran, embarrassing the authorities, all the way up to the US President.

Even if it was a test that has been bungled by the 999 call and the farmer’s tip-off it may not matter to Iran, if it is indeed behind the alleged plot.

This very bungle has caused more confusion and insecurity for ordinary British citizens, embarrassed the authorities and unfairly made the UK look weak.

View 3 Images US B-1 Lancer Bomber at RAF Fairford (Image: NEIL HALL/EPA/Shutterstock)

It has also sparked fury amongst the increasingly suggestible and gullible far-right groups who appear to be doing the work for Iran and other enemies of the UK such as Russia.

Division, confusion, aggression and degrading respect for the police and other authorities is exactly what Britain’s enemies want.

And every time something like this involving a counter-terror probe and the suggestion a foreign group is involved happens the far-right falls for it.

Instead of directing their ire at the state or group doing it, they target the very UK authorities who are trying to keep them safe and have to obey legal parameters, screaming about incompetence and two-tier policing.

This is a pretty good result for Iran and its anti-UK allies, assisted as is often the case, by right-wing critics of the government and police.

News.title: UK-Iranian dual national arrested over RAF Fairford incident, police say
News.content:
A UK-Iranian dual national has been arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with the incident at RAF Fairford, counter-terror police have said.

The 25-year-old man was arrested in Westminster, London. Two properties in the area have been searched.

Five men in their twenties who were arrested near the Gloucestershire airbase on Sunday remain on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London.

Counter-terror police are considering "all possible angles - including foreign state involvement", the force's senior national coordinator Vicki Evans said.

"The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry," she said.

"I'd like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this investigation."

Police had initially given the dual UK-Iranian national's age as 27 and said a second man had been questioned under caution, but in a later update said that this was not the case.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday there were "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident. He did not provide further details, and Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

The five men were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning after "three suspicious vehicles" were reported travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident.

The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

Police said a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of vans near the site.

The group were aged between 23 and 25. Four live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes were carried out.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that "the hands of a foreign actor" had clearly been involved in the incident at the base, which has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades.

In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the airbase for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

News.title: HMRC urged to scrutinise tax implications of Man City case
News.content:
Findings from the Premier League's case against Manchester City require scrutiny from His Majesty's Revenue and Customs, the chair of a cross-party group of MPs has told the tax authority.

It was confirmed on Tuesday that an independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

City have repeatedly denied guilt, and have signalled an intent to lodge an appeal by Friday.

The club were found to have artificially inflated revenue through "sham" sponsorship agreements with the help of their owners.

The independent commission which studied the case found City "utilised devices" to "disguise the true extent of certain club liabilities".

The Treasury Committee, which is responsible for overseeing policies and administration of HMRC, has therefore asked whether the government department has requested the redacted documents contained within the commission's report.

Dame Meg Hillier, chair of the Treasury Committee, said she would "welcome reassurance from HMRC that you are seized of the importance of these issues and the public interest in this case".

The letter follows a report from the Tax Policy Associates, external which claims City failed to pay as much as Â£12m in unpaid tax because of a "sham" contract with former manager Roberto Mancini.

In addition to unpaid income tax and National Insurance, the report claims City could face a penalty charge that would take their liabilities to Â£24m.

News.title: Man City not 'above the rules', says No 10 after backlash to Burnham remarks
News.content:
Downing Street has said Manchester City are not "above the rules" after Andy Burnham was criticised for his comments about the club's breaches of Premier League financial rules.

The prime minister said on Wednesday he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners decide to sell up after City were found guilty by an independent commission of most of the 115 charges they faced.

His remarks were branded "completely out of touch" and "extraordinary" by the Tories and took many in the football community by surprise.

In a statement following the backlash, Downing Street said the PM had made clear "the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules".

In an attempt to clarify the PM's position, a No 10 spokesperson added: "He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected.

"Wherever wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."

Man City deny any wrongdoing and have until Friday to submit an appeal.

Sources told BBC Sport that City are expected to claim that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners, as part of an appeal.

Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than Â£830m.

The Premier League said City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

In an interview on Wednesday with the BBC's political editor Chris Mason, Burnham - who was mayor of Greater Manchester until June - said he was "not getting directly involved in the process", saying it must be undertaken independently by the Premier League.

He said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and it would be "wrong" to "jump to a conclusion".

Asked if he was worried the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, a royal and the United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister - might sell up, Burnham said: "I would be really concerned to lose them.

"They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.

"I can't intervene more in the process, it would be wrong for me to do that."

In response, the Tories accused Burnham of "publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues" and questioned whether "political pressure" was being applied.

News.title: UK in talks with EU partners to release strategic fuel reserves if needed, BBC understands
News.content:
Britain is in talks with EU partners to release additional strategic fuel reserves, including diesel, if needed, the BBC understands.

The talks come after President Donald Trump threatened to ban diesel exports from the US in a bid to reduce record prices at the pumps for Americans.

Diesel prices in the UK also hit record highs this week and are hovering just under 200p per litre, according to motoring organisation the RAC.

The US is a vital supplier of diesel to the world, exporting between 1.2 and 1.5 million barrels per day, with experts warning a ban on shipments abroad could put further pressure on prices in other countries.

"We're thinking about it very seriously," Trump said of an export ban at the weekend.

Energy Minister Martin McCluskey was on a call with European counterparts on Thursday to discuss the potential ban.

A source familiar with the discussions told the BBC it was prudent to prepare a co-ordinated response with other countries, including those across EU, but added that there were still European reserves left from a coordinated release of strategic fuel stocks earlier in the year.

"We have a diverse and resilient supply.â¯We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry," a government spokesperson said. The government has stressed that there is no cause for concern about potential diesel shortages, though prices are expected to rise further.

News.title: Fires break out at French schools as students protest over funding
News.content:
Fires have broken out at several schools in France, as students protest by blockading education institutions nationwide over school funding and studying conditions.

Blazes were reported at two high schools in Nantes, western France, while another was filmed engulfing the entrance of a school in the northern city of Rouen.

Students are protesting about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined the demonstrations on Thursday, citing similar demands.

The interior ministry said 1,949 people had been arrested on Thursday, with 305 police officers injured. Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu held a crisis meeting on Thursday to discuss the unrest.

The government said afterwards that the student-led demonstrations had descended into "urban violence".

Both fires in Nantes spread after a bin was set alight. The blaze at the Nelson Mandela high school, in the city centre, then spread to the front of the building, damaging the entrance hall.

In the southern city of Marseille, staff at Victor Hugo high school were splashed with petrol as protesters reportedly filled containers.

While in the north, a headteacher at Degrugillier high school, in the village of Auchel, was injured in the ear by a wayward firework.

The blockades and protests at French lycÃ©es - for 15-18 year olds and equivalent to sixth forms in the UK or high schools in the US - began last week before spreading to hundreds of schools across the country.

So far, 1,027 lycees have been affected by demonstrations, with blockades at 222 of them, according to the interior ministry.

At least 30 universities have also reportedly been blockaded, including campuses in Rennes and Paris.

On Thursday, public transport services in Marseille and Strasbourg were halted due vandalism, threats of violence and to hinder protesters from moving around.

News.title: PM warned Rosebank oil field could breach West Bank sanctions
News.content:
The prime minister has been warned that approving a controversial oil field risks contravening his own sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

The government will soon have to make a long-awaited decision on whether to go ahead with Rosebank, Britain's largest untapped oil field, which sits off Shetland.

Environmental campaigners and Green Party leader Zack Polanski have both separately written to Andy Burnham and the foreign secretary to raise concerns about Rosebank's links to an Israeli company, Delek Group.

Last year Delek Group was included in a UN database of firms which allegedly provide services or utilities to support settlements in occupied Palestinian territories.

A spokesman for the company told the Daily Telegraph, external it no longer had any involvement in Israeli settlements and was wrongly included in the database.

Delek Group controls Ithaca Energy, which holds a 20% stake in Rosebank.

The campaign group Uplift, whose legal challenge against the Rosebank project in 2023 led to the ongoing delay over a decision on exploration, has helped organise a letter to Burnham and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.

In a letter seen by BBC News, campaigners from Stop Rosebank and Greenpeace, with assistance from Uplift, have asked the government to clarify whether Delek will fall foul of the sanctions announced last month.

Separately, Polanski has also written to Miliband, asking what steps the government would take to make sure revenue from UK oil and gas production did not finance illegal settlements.

He said: "Rosebank is a test of whether Labour's proposed sanctions regime is fit for purpose.

"Companies blacklisted by the UN for operating in the illegal settlements should not be financed by oil and gas revenues from the North Sea."

News.title: Hundreds of criminals start leaving prison under new early release scheme
News.content:
Hundreds of criminals are being released early from prisons in England and Wales under new rules introduced to prevent facilities reaching capacity.

The first 700 of an expected 4,500 inmates eligible under the scheme were due to be let out on Thursday.

The government has stressed they will remain subject to strict monitoring arrangements, including the expanded use of electronic tagging, and has said action was needed to prevent prisons from becoming full.

But the plan has been strongly criticised by victims and questions have been raised over whether the Probation Service has sufficient resources to monitor thousands more criminals in the community.

Prisons in England and Wales are a matter of months away from reaching capacity, with Ministry of Justice data showing as of Monday 87,499 people were incarcerated, taking prison population levels up to 98.2%.

Thursday's release is the first of 10 scheduled to take place, with the final slated for June 2027.

Prisoners released initially were serving sentences of up to 19 months, with the most serious offenders - serving fixed sentences of more than 12 years - leaving in later waves.

News.title: What we know about Cornell University frat house rape investigation
News.content:
