The county's top prosecutor said on Monday that his office would reopen a criminal inquiry into the alleged rape.

Once appropriate charges were determined, the case would be prosecuted "in the most objective and impartial means possible" through a grand jury, said Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten.

In the US legal system, prosecutors convene grand juries to weigh evidence and testimony, and eventually vote on whether they merit criminal charges.

The prosecutor said that at the time of the assault two years ago, his office concluded that evidence from the woman's statement to authorities did not meet the legal bar to bring charges.

He said he contacted Doe and her lawyers for more information as he prepared to bring the case to a grand jury.

In his statement, Van Houten included a summary of what Doe told the Cornell University Police Department in 2024 after the alleged attack, noting it differed from the allegations laid out in the lawsuit.

"Jane Doe's sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped," Van Houten said in a statement on Monday.

"On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual."

A Cornell University spokesperson told the BBC that its police department shared a "lengthy police investigation report" with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office.

New reports have detailed what Doe reported to Cornell University's police following the incident.

CBS News New York, external obtained a transcript of Doe's interviews with campus police that began on 14 November - more than three weeks after the incident.

She tells police of the initial sexual encounter: "I was pretty OK with all of this."

But the outlet reports that she said of what happened later: "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."

ABC News, external also obtained a police report from 15 November, in which Doe said in a statement that during one of the later encounters that night, "I felt like I was unable to make any decision because of how intoxicated I was".

"To me, that felt like coercion," she said in her statement. "Also I felt like due to my intoxication, they should have known how intoxicated I was based on how I was slurring my words."

The BBC has contacted Van Houten's office and Doe's attorney.

Van Houten told CBS News he had never seen the transcript of the interview with campus police.

He also told the New York Times on Wednesday that he hoped to speak to Doe "to discuss new evidence that exists"., external

Van Houten told the Times he did not believe the allegations in the civil lawsuit meet the legal bar to bring charges.

He did note that "the significance of it means that she believes that crimes were committed, and we want to get to the bottom of that".

News.title: Body of baby girl found in Wales may have been in the water for weeks, police say
News.content:
The body of a baby girl found along a north Wales shoreline may have been in the water for up to a few weeks, according to initial indications.

A member of the public found the body on the Menai Strait shoreline near Siliwen Road in Bangor, Gwynedd, on Sunday shortly before 17:00 BST.

In an update on Thursday, North Wales Police said a post-mortem examination revealed the newborn was a girl.

The force is continuing the search for the girl's mother and urged her to make contact with police.

Further tests to find more about the baby are under way, North Wales Police said.

"We understand that the mother may be fearful of coming forward but we urge her to make contact with us," Supt Llinos Davies said, adding that she wanted to reassure her that her welfare and safety was their "utmost concern".

"Anyone with concerns about a girl or a woman you think may have been pregnant or whose behaviour has been unusual or out of character over the past few months including withdrawing from friends, family or social ties, please contact us," Davies said.

She said all names received would be treated with the utmost discretion and can be eliminated as the mother, without delay.

"I understand that this is a terribly sad incident for the community and I am grateful for the overwhelming support and assistance that we have received so far," Davies said.

Fiona Giraud, director of midwifery and women's services for Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board, said her priority remained with the mother.

Addressing her, she said: "Our immediate concern remains to be your health, safety and wellbeing.

"You may feel you have nowhere to turn, or that you cannot speak to anyone about what has happened. Please do not feel that you have to face this alone," she said.

"We don't yet know all the circumstances surrounding your baby's death, but what is important right now is that we find you, make sure you are safe and ensure you receive any medical attention and support you may need.

"I am asking you personally, please take the first step and contact us. There are people to help you," Giraud said.

News.title: Educating Cardiff teacher admits sexually assaulting teenage girl
News.content:
A teacher who featured in the Channel 4 documentary series Educating Cardiff has pleaded guilty to sexually assaulting a 17-year-old girl.

Gareth Ritter, 44, of Bryngwyn, in Monmouthshire, was in the middle of giving evidence in his defence when his barrister asked for the charge to be put to him again.

Ritter, who was also a prominent member of a number of brass bands, was asked to stand up and, when asked how he pleaded, he said "guilty".

He was told all of the charges he had admitted carried a custodial sentence and the court would consider immediate custody.

Ritter had previously denied intentionally touching the teenager sexually without consent when he was in his 30s.

Earlier in the trial, the jury was told that, following an event in Cardiff, Ritter offered to drive the victim home but stopped at a flat he owned in Cardiff Bay, saying he had to check it before a new tenant arrived and invited her in.

Once inside, she said he touched her bottom while they stood on a balcony overlooking the city and later kissed her in the hallway.

The woman, now in her 20s, said: "One hand went around my back, it dropped to my bum and he lent in and kissed me.

"I remember his tongue going into my mouth.

"I remember being against the wall, I couldn't step back, I remember him kissing me. I turned my face away, my hands were on him, I wasn't forceful, I held out my hands on his chest. It was a light push but not forceful."

Asked by prosecutor Andrew Davies if she said anything to him, she replied: "It might seem like a strange comment, but I said 'I'm a good girl, I don't do this. I go to a Christian school'."

The court was told Ritter then drove her home, repeatedly asking her if she was going to tell anyone about what had happened.

"I remember him saying 'Nobody needs to know about this. Are you going to tell anyone about this?'

"What do you say in that situation? Gareth was someone I really looked up to. How do you confront that? I'd never been in that situation."

She said she just wanted to "brush it under the carpet".

The court heard the woman reported the alleged incident several years later after Ritter's phone was examined by detectives following an "unrelated matter" that ended with no charges being brought.

Police had found intimate images of a young woman who was under the age of 18. When she was traced, it was the same woman who was sexually assaulted by Ritter.

The court was told the images had originally been screen grabbed with her consent during an intimate video conversation between the woman and another man.

The images had been stored on his tablet, which had been accessed and shared by the man's housemates, and were later found on Ritter's phone.

The jury were told Ritter had since pleaded guilty to the possession and distribution of unlawful images, as the woman was 17 at the time the images were taken.

The woman said when she was told her images had been found on Ritter's phone she decided to report the incident in Cardiff Bay.

The court was told that when Ritter was interviewed by police in December 2022 he denied knowing about the Cardiff Bay flat, and denied taking the woman there. He also told police he had not given her a lift home.

A year later he was interviewed by police again. When asked if he had given a truthful account in his first interview, he said no.

Ritter was granted bail until sentencing on 4 November.

News.title: Hundreds of jobs under threat at Grangemouth chemical plant
News.content:
Hundreds of jobs are under threat in Grangemouth after an agricultural chemical firm announced plans to cease operations at the site.

Syngenta said it had been unable to make its business at the plant "competitive" in the face of "increasing international competition".

A spokesperson for the company - which manufactures chemicals used for the protection of crops - said it would enter a consultation period over the move, but added a final decision has yet to be taken.

The Economy Secretary, Stephen Flynn, described the plans as "extremely disappointing".

The UK government's Reindustrialisation Minister, Blair McDougall, said they had worked with Scottish counterparts to "explore every possible avenue" for support, but Syngenta had taken the decision on a commercial basis.

A total of 377 workers are set to be affected by the move.

It comes over a year after Syngenta was awarded Â£2.2m from Scottish Enterprise to expand production at the site.

News.title: AI boom could trigger market shocks, Bank of England boss warns
News.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) could trigger financial market shocks and the UK needs to be prepared for them, the governor of the Bank of England has warned.

Andrew Bailey said the central bank is watching the huge amounts of money being invested in AI "very carefully" and cautioned that "not everybody always wins".

The money that has been spent on and loaned to AI firms over the last few years in the hope of large returns is causing markets to value some of them as multi-trillion dollar businesses.

Asked if he believed an AI bubble could burst, Bailey said: "You could see some correction of asset prices at some point."

He was speaking exclusively to the BBC about what the risks and benefits of AI could be for the UK economy.

Bailey said he believed the technology has "great potential to strengthen growth in our economies", adding that this was something the country needed.

"But it also brings with it substantial risks and so we have to be on top of both of those."

One such risk is what happens if the big bets being made on AI don't pay off.

AI chipmaker Nvidia is currently the world's most valuable listed company, with a market valuation of $5.5tn (Â£4.14tn), thanks largely to investors who believe in the big profits AI could create.

Meanwhile, tech giants Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on the technology.

And two of the largest AI companies in the world â Anthropic and OpenAI â are also preparing to sell shares in their firms on the US stock market in moves which many believe will lead to hundreds of billions of dollars more flowing into the industry.

"There is a large, very large, amount of investment going into this sector now, and of course that's natural because it's a major area of growth," said Bailey.

"And of course you see that the asset prices of the companies that are developing it have gone up a lot and that reflects the fact that there are high expectations of what it can deliver."

"Everybody is currently priced to be a winner," he added, but warned that "you look back at the past, not everybody is a winner".

"Google was not the first market leader in internet search. It was Netscape. Nobody can remember Netscape today. It doesn't exist. So not everybody always wins.

"We are prepared for the fact that there will be, I think, some shocks come along to markets and we have to deal with that. We have to make sure the system is resilient."

News.title: Prince of Wales tells villagers 'holistic' approach is needed to tackle flooding
News.content:
The Prince of Wales has said a "holistic" approach is needed to tackle severe flooding, as a small Welsh village prepares for the upcoming storm season.

Residents in Skenfrith, Monmouthshire, have faced four major floods in the past six years.

An extreme flood last winter had a devastating impact on the village, when the River Monnow burst its banks after Storm Claudia brought a month's worth of rain in just 24 hours to parts of England and Wales.

Prince William was visiting the area to learn about how communities have been affected by recent flooding and what measures were being taken by local authorities and other agencies to mitigate future incidents.

Over the years, families have reported that their homes and possessions had been destroyed by the floods. In 2019, about 25 homes were evacuated in the village following flooding and a power cut after heavy rain.

The prince sympathised with residents who might be "anxious" about extreme weather events he said were no longer "one in 50-year" occurrences but instead seemed to be happening every year.

News.title: Two men jailed for raping woman in underground car park
News.content:
Two men have been jailed for raping a woman in an underground car park in County Tyrone.

Luis Dos Martins Mariano, 20, with an address of Sloan Street, and Alcino Soares, 21, with an address of Braeside, also in Dungannon, both previously pleaded guilty to rape.

Both men moved to Northern Ireland from East Timor when they were younger.

The rape took place on 10 September 2023 when both men were 17 and some of it was recorded on CCTV. The victim was 19 at the time.

At Downpatrick Crown Court on Thursday the judge sentenced both men to six years, three of those will be served in prison and three out on license.

Both men appeared in court via video link from Hydebank prison.

Judge Richard Greene said the CCTV footage of the incident "makes for disturbing viewing".

He also commended the "bravery" of the victim coming forward and said she was a "survivor".

He said her impact statement was both "eloquent and moving".

Judge Greene said the victim was subjected to a "prolonged and humiliating ordeal" with Soares and Mariano taking turns to rape her.

"It should have been obvious to both of them she was intoxicated and she was less able to recognise the danger she was in, she was not capable of resisting this cowardly attack on her and she was not able to call for help," he said.

Judge Greene said taking her to a car park at this late time showed a "significant degree of planning and foresight".

When sentencing the men Judge Greene said he took into account their young age at the time of offending, their learning difficulties, the fact they had both entered guilty pleas, delays to the case and time they had already spent in prison.

Warning: This article contains details readers may find upsetting

During an earlier sentencing hearing last month, the court heard details of the rape.

During the hearing in Dungannon Crown Court on 3 September, the prosecution outlined the victim's account.

A Tetum interpreter was present in court and stood beside Soares and Mariano translating the prosecution's account.

The court heard that the victim had been on a night out in Dungannon on 9 September 2023.

She said she had been outside a fast food shop and was "quite drunk".

She said she was approached by two males who appeared to be East Timorese.

Her next memory is then of both men walking either side of her down an alleyway which led into a car park.

The victim recalled she had difficulty standing and could not talk properly.

News.title: Travelodge failed sex assault victim 'at every stage'
News.content:
A woman who was sexually assaulted by a man given a key to her hotel room was "fundamentally failed" by Travelodge "at every stage", an independent review has found.

Barrister Paul Greaney KC said the chain's security policies at the time of the attack at its Maidenhead hotel in December 2022 were "not fit for the purpose of keeping guests safe".

He found guests were still not as safe as they should be, with room intrusions reported at nearly one-in-10 Travelodge hotels this summer, and no policy in place on violence against women and girls.

Travelodge apologised "unreservedly" to the woman. The review did credit the company with making changes since March.

Kyran Smith, who obtained the key by falsely claiming to be the woman's boyfriend, was jailed for seven-and-a-half years in January.

The review found he was handed the key less than three minutes after approaching the reception desk, by a receptionist who had received no training in key security.

News.title: Jagtar Singh Johal freed on bail after nine years in Indian prison
News.content:
A Scottish Sikh activist has been released from prison in India after being detained for almost nine years without being convicted.

Jagtar Singh Johal thanked "the almighty" as he walked free from gate three of the Tihar Prison complex in Delhi.

The 39-year-old from Dumbarton was arrested in 2017 over allegations he had a role in a series of targeted killings of religious and political figures - which he denies.

Johal was granted bail at Delhi High Court on 18 September, but has only now been released from detention.

He was embraced by his mother-in-law and father-in law after leaving the jail in Janakpuri, in the south-west of the city.

Johal was given flowers and presented with a bright orange saropau, an honorary garment given in Sikh tradition to convey respect.

His release was welcomed with shouts of "Jo hole so nihal, sat Sri Akal" or "whoever utters these words shall be fulfilled true is the eternal timeless Lord".

News.title: Canada fast-tracks oil pipeline to reduce dependence on US and mend relations with Alberta
News.content:

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday fast-tracked a proposed million-barrel-a-day oil pipeline to the Pacific Coast, moving to reduce the nation’s dependence on the United States and heal ties with oil-rich Alberta as separatists push for a referendum on leaving Canada.

Carney, appearing alongside Alberta Premier Danielle Smith in Fort McMurray at the center of Canada’s oil sands, designated the line—now named Pacific Link—a project of national interest under legislation passed by his government to accelerate major infrastructure projects.

A bid to keep Alberta in Canada

Alberta is set to hold a public vote on Oct. 19 regarding whether to hold a referendum on seceding from Canada. Smith has repeatedly argued that Carney’s predecessor, Justin Trudeau, stymied Alberta’s energy sector and stoked separatist sentiment.

Smith indicated she will vote to keep Alberta in Canada, describing the roughly 22% support for separation in a recent poll as "still too high for my liking."

"I don’t like the fact that that many of our fellow citizens have given up on Canada," Smith stated, adding that the pipeline served as proof of how "cooperative federalism can work in action."

open image in gallery Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks during a news conference in Fort McMurray, Alberta, Canada, on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, regarding the Pacific Link pipeline project ( Greg Halinda/The Canadian Press via AP )

Asked what message Albertans weighing separation ought to gather from the decision, Carney said it showed that "Canada is working" and demonstrated what the country can accomplish when acting together.

Ian Brodie, a political science professor at the University of Calgary and former chief of staff to Conservative Prime Minister Stephen Harper, suggested the announcement could still aid separatists by highlighting Alberta’s reliance on Ottawa.

"There’s no reason this pipeline couldn’t have been fast-tracked in July, so we’ve lost three months in the project," Brodie said. "It’s a reminder that Alberta has to have a sympathetic prime minister in order to grow its oil sector. We don’t control our fate."

A pipeline to loosen the US grip

"Today, 90% of Alberta’s oil goes to the United States," Carney said. "Pacific Link will materially reduce that dependence by allowing Canada to export an additional 1 million barrels a day to growing markets in Asia."

Carney framed Pacific Link as part of a wider effort to decrease Canada’s dependence on the United States and build "greater strategic autonomy, so we can continue to live our lives as we choose." Carney has outlined a target of doubling Canada’s non-U.S. exports over the next decade.

The government reported that 90.1% of Canadian crude exports were delivered to the U.S. last year, characterizing the nation’s reliance on American-bound infrastructure as a "structural vulnerability."

It noted that Pacific Link, alongside improvements to the Trans Mountain system, could lower Canada’s fixed pipeline reliance on the U.S. from roughly 82%-83% of capacity down to 65%-70%.

The push occurs as U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade conflict and threats to Canadian sovereignty have prompted Carney to reduce Canada’s longstanding economic dependence on its neighbor to the south.

The proposed 1,250-kilometer (775-mile) pipeline will extend from Bruderheim, northeast of Edmonton, Alberta, to a deepwater port near Delta, British Columbia. It will largely follow the existing Trans Mountain route and load crude onto tankers bound for global markets.

Questions remain over money and opposition

The project carries an estimated cost of $25 billion to $31 billion and continues to face major questions regarding funding and whether oil producers will commit to using it.

The special designation does not equal final approval for the project. Carney explained that proponents must still resolve engineering, cost, environmental, and other regulatory conditions before a final determination to move forward.

The federal government and Alberta government are contributing roughly US$2.8 billion upfront before the primary private investor has committed its required construction share.

Calgary-based Pembina Pipeline Corp. holds a 10% economic interest in the initiative but has not yet supplied its share of construction capital. A federal official stated Pembina would decide whether to make that investment at or prior to a final investment decision.

Asked how much federal taxpayers could ultimately contribute to the effort, Carney did not offer a figure, stating instead: "The Canadian taxpayer is going to make a lot of money off this pipeline."

An open season to determine how much capacity oil producers want to contract is scheduled for next spring. Officials noted strong interest but admitted that accelerating the process does not guarantee the pipeline will secure sufficient shippers or capital to proceed.

A senior government official suggested a faster approval process could attract additional private investment, while expanding access to Asia would give Canadian producers stronger leverage with buyers.

The official noted that the Trans Mountain expansion required 14 years from its inception in 2010 until the first crude flowed in 2024.

The pipeline also faces significant Indigenous and environmental hurdles.

The government admitted that most consulted Indigenous communities were not ready to support listing the project based on available details, citing unanswered questions regarding route design, environmental impacts, marine shipping, and treaty rights. Carney noted that the "real intensive consultation process will begin now."

Canada, Alberta, and the project developers have pledged to offer Indigenous communities at least a 10% ownership stake in the pipeline.

Carney said construction of the Pathways carbon-capture initiative would be a prerequisite for Pacific Link. The government expects Pathways and related efforts to cut oil sands emissions by 16 million metric tons annually.

However, the government acknowledged that the pipeline is expected to enable higher oil production and extra emissions.

Carney said the government wants final regulatory conditions in place by September 2027, clearing the way for construction. The pipeline is targeted to begin operating around 2032 or 2033.

News.title: Trump says AI can self-regulate. Even some top Republicans don’t trust that

For the past month, as Americans’ anxieties about artificial intelligence have increased, President Donald Trump has repeatedly said there should be no legislative guardrails, and called the panic around them a “hoax.” Rather, he’s argued that he alone can rein them in and argued that if the United States doesn’t go all-in on AI, China will win the AI race.

This week, he even attempted to re-brand AI as “super intelligence.” And he brought the nation’s leading tech giants to the White House and had them sign a “morally binding” and “self-policing” accord. Trump hosted AI leaders such as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, Google’s Sundar Pichai, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and SpaceX’s Elon Musk, saying the companies signed a “morally binding” accord to “self-police” AI.

But amid all of these declarations, even the most MAGA of Republicans are saying that the voluntary regulations are not enough and that there needs to be oversight of AI, SI, or whatever they want to call it, beyond Trump and the tech titans themselves.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), for example, convened a Senate Homeland Security Subcommittee on Disaster Management on rogue AI and cyber threats. Hawley, perhaps the foremost critic of big tech on the Republican side, has had to walk a fine line between his criticism of AI and the fact that Trump has said the only guardrail AI needs is a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.”

“He brought the leaders of these companies together for the first time to sign some voluntary commitments, which is a heck of a lot more than Congress has done,” Hawley told The Independent.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump has feted AI executives as capable of self-regulation. But even some Republican senators are not so sure. ( Getty )

“So I think that it's good to have, No. 1, the companies acknowledge that they have some responsibility here,” Hawley said. “This is really the first time that they've done that, and I think Congress needs to do something.” But the Missouri Republican also said incentives needed to be put in place to force AI companies to pay if they develop models that misbehave.

This comes after OpenAI had to apologize after an autonomous AI agent the Services Australia Medicare Statistics Reporting Service, a public health care data portal in Australia.

Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), an ally of the president who is retiring, also said the self-regulation could only be temporary.

“For now, they can choose to self-regulate, but it’s all voluntary,” she told The Independent after the subcommittee hearing.

So far, no major legislation has passed on reining in AI yet, but there are some trial balloon pieces of legislation in the House of Representatives. Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) has his own piece of legislation called the Make AI Work for Americans Act, which would set up a federal trust fund to support workers amid major changes AI could make to the global economy.

open image in gallery Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO) held a Senate Homeland Security Subcommittee hearing on AI earlier this week ( Getty(Photo by Finn Gomez/Getty Images) )

“In my prior career, when you're flying something like the space shuttle, there's like catastrophic things that could happen,” Kelly, a former pilot and astronaut, told The Independent. “They might be low probability, but you still try to deal with it.”

He also cast doubt on Trump saying earlier this month in an interview with GB News that humans will have a “little gear” to prevent AI from running rampant.

“I don't even know what that is,” Kelly said. “I don't think he knows what that is. We have to put guardrails in place, and it's always better to do that sooner rather than later.”

Earlier this month, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon set off alarms when he announced his resignation and said that people working on AI genuinely fear it “could kill us all by the end of the decade.” In response, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and former Trump adviser Steve Bannon participated in a summit focused on human-centered AI.

“Yes, I have absolute confidence that the wealthiest, most greedy people in the world, who are out to make trillions of dollars, will regulate themselves,” Sanders told The Independent. “I don't think so.”

But Trump has proven allergic to any safety measures around rogue AI agents, instead focusing on rebranding it “Super Intelligence.”

Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.), who is leaving the Senate to run for governor, said AI companies will will have to do some self-regulation.

open image in gallery Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) said Trump was not being serious about AI oversight ( Reuters )

“At the end of the day, we're going to there's going to be something done up here,” he told The Independent. “But everybody's got to take care of their own business. I mean, they'll self-destruct if they don't do their self-regulation to a certain point.”

But Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) the youngest senator who is running for re-election, said the president has a vested interest in opposing guardrails on AI, pointing out the president has a financial stake in many companies working on AI.

“The first family is so heavily invested in the industry, the conflicts are so immense, and the president's judgment is so poor that the American people are rightly concerned that Donald Trump has neither the capacity nor the incentive to protect them from the risks arising from this technology,” he told The Independent.

But despite the concerns, there is little likelihood the Senate will take up any action of AI by the end of this year. The Senate left late on Wednesday evening and will not return after the midterm election. After which time, it will be in for a limited amount of weeks because of the holiday season before the new Congress convenes at the beginning of the year.

Starting October 1, millions of additional Amazon Prime customers could receive automatic payments as part of an expanded federal settlement over billing and cancellation practices.

The upcoming distribution phase expands eligibility to consumers who used between 11 and 20 Prime benefits during a single year, a group excluded from earlier distributions, according to the Federal Trade Commission.

The payments are part of a landmark $2.5 billion agreement resolving government allegations that Amazon enrolled consumers in Prime without explicit consent and created complex digital processes that hindered efforts to cancel memberships. Under the resolution, Amazon agreed to pay a $1 billion civil penalty and set aside $1.5 billion for direct consumer restitution.

Subscribers qualify for restitution if they are based in the U.S. and either enrolled through specific disputed checkout screens or attempted unsuccessfully to cancel their membership between June 23, 2019, and June 23, 2025.

Qualifying subscribers must also have used no more than 20 Prime benefits, such as Prime Video or Prime Music, in any 12-month period following enrollment.

open image in gallery Millions of additional Amazon Prime members could automatically receive settlement money starting October 1 under a broadening federal agreement targeting disputed sign-ups and cancellations ( Getty Images )

A federal court recently approved modifications to the settlement terms that increased the maximum total payout per eligible customer from $51 to $200. Consumers who previously received the lower capped amount may receive supplemental payments of up to $149 to reach the revised cap, according to the FTC.

Eligible customers do not need to fill out forms, submit claims or respond to notices to receive compensation. Amazon will issue funds directly through PayPal, Venmo or mailed paper checks.

Recipients must cash or redeem checks or electronic payments within 60 days of issuance.

open image in gallery Amazon, founded by Jeff Bezos, has already issued more than $845 million in direct restitution as part of its landmark $2.5 billion resolution with federal regulators ( PA Archive )

Amazon had already issued more than $845 million in refunds to affected customers as of September, FTC officials said in a news release. The full payment schedule under the modified agreement is set to conclude by April 2027.

Federal regulators are also urging consumers to remain alert for fraudulent activity related to the payouts. Neither the FTC nor Amazon will contact consumers demanding money, requesting personal details or requiring payment to release funds.

Officials warned that any third party promising expedited distribution or guaranteed access in exchange for a fee is attempting a scam.

President Vladimir Putin on Thursday reiterated Moscow's long-held position that Russia is not planning to attack European countries but will respond to aggression with “all weapons" in its arsenal.

In remarks at a foreign policy forum, Putin accused the West and Europe of escalating tensions by talking about preparing for a war with Moscow in the coming years, conducting military drills in the Baltic Sea, and seizing Russian vessels.

His remarks followed Moscow's warning to NATO that it would not hesitate to use nuclear weapons to defend Kaliningrad should any members of the military alliance try to cut off the Baltic exclave from the rest of Russia.

Several Russian embassies in Europe this week issued statements that said Moscow has “information that NATO is preparing (an) air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and (the) Kaliningrad region.”

They accused European leaders of “playing a dangerous game” by saying Russia might attack another country or ramp up a campaign of destabilizing attacks with drones and sabotage. Moscow has called the allegations absurd.

“There should be no mistake — Russia would be ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO countries try to isolate (the) Kaliningrad region from the rest of the country,” the Russian Embassy in Ireland said in its statement on Tuesday.

Asked at the Valdai Club forum Thursday whether Russia was on the cusp of a war with NATO or whether both were trying to intimidate each other, Putin said: “It's not intimidation, it’s a response to an attempt to intimidate us.”

Putin said that “everything is written correctly” in the earlier warning to NATO.

“If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation — in this case we mean Kaliningrad, or maybe some other territories — of course, inevitably and immediately the question of Russian Federation using all weapons at the disposal of our country will appear on the agenda,” he said.

Putin didn’t specify whether Moscow would use nuclear weapons but said it has arms that “no one else has” and would determine which to use in case of an attack.

NATO pushed back against Russian nuclear rhetoric

NATO spokesperson Allison Hart confirmed Wednesday that Russia had sent a written message to the U.S.-led military alliance. “We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric,” she said in a statement.

Hart insisted NATO is not targeting Kaliningrad and had sent a reply noting that “NATO is a defensive alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia.”

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said Wednesday the bloc's response to the message was “short and concise."

“Basically what we said is, ‘Hey, listen, we are defensive alliance, and stop the nuclear threat. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful,’” Rutte told Euronews.

NATO's response also urged Russia to stop its “unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine,” now in its fifth year.

The Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad sits between NATO members Poland and Lithuania. It is home to Russia’s main Baltic navy base and other military assets, and nuclear-capable Iskander missiles are deployed there.

Western military officers have said that key military installations in Kaliningrad would be a likely first target should Russia ever attack any NATO ally.

NATO allies have conducted military exercises in the Baltic Sea region in recent months. More are planned in October. It launched Operation Baltic Sentry there last year to protect communication cables and pipelines.

On Aug. 18, NATO held an exercise over northern Poland and the Baltic region involving several aircraft, including an EA-37B Compass Call — a sophisticated American plane that can jam communications and radar, the U.S. Air Forces in Europe said.

Defense analysts believe the unannounced, large-scale exercise would not have been welcomed by the Kremlin.

Rutte urges continued focus on supporting Ukraine

European leaders and intelligence services have warned that Russia could be ready to strike at another country within a few years, especially if it wins its war on Ukraine.

Rutte told Euronews that Russia is trying “to divide us and lose the focus” on defending Ukraine.

“We will not,” he said, adding that the best way to respond is to provide Kyiv with more support.

“That’s the message. Calm, carry on, keep the support for Ukraine going. That’s how we deal with it," Rutte said.

——

Associated Press reporter Lorne Cook in Brussels contributed.

Consumer spending through buy now, pay later options reached over $160 billion last year, according to new study from Federal Reserve economists.

Industry specialists report that individuals are frequently turning to these financing models for basic essentials, such as groceries, utility bills, transit, and even rent.

"It has been very hard out there for a lot of people," said Sara Rathner, NerdWallet’s credit card expert. "It’s a tough job market, and it’s a rough economy, and the cost of the things that we buy every day has been going up, in some cases more than people’s incomes."

Pay-in-four programs, which let buyers split transactions into four installments over six weeks, represented nearly half the total expenditure. Usage of this setup has surged by almost 80 percent since 2023.

Other transactions were divided between shorter- and longer-term credit structures.

How consumers are using buy now pay later

When Elizabeth Brown first used buy now, pay later, she had just started living by herself and was earning a salary that made it hard to afford basic expenses. She would buy groceries and, once she got her paycheck, pay for them through buy now, pay later. Six years later, things haven’t changed much.

“I used buy now, pay later so I can have the furniture I need. I have groceries in my fridge because of it. I don’t necessarily feel shameful for using it because at the end it’s very beneficial to me at this point of my life,” said Brown, 26, of Columbia, South Carolina, who works as a clinical service member at an optical store.

Buy now, pay later products have evolved. Rent now, pay later services are one form, which break rent into multiple payments.

In general, if you miss a buy now, pay later payment, you can face fees, interest or the possibility of being banned from using the services in the future ( AP Photo/Aijaz Rahi )

“It isn’t really just a convenience element anymore; it really is becoming a cash flow challenge,” said Mark Elliott, chief customer officer at Happen Bank, a financial services company formerly known as Lending Club.

Jordan Williams, 28, first used buy now, pay later to get concert tickets to Hozier. Then, when she experienced financial hardship after her daughter was born, she started leaning on it to pay for some of her groceries.

“There’s just not a lot of resources, and that makes me angry because this shouldn’t be something I have to do," said Williams, a lecturer and content creator from Greensboro, North Carolina. "We should be able to just afford groceries. I feel angry and then I feel embarrassed.”

For a long time, Williams felt ashamed about having to use buy now, pay later for basic expenses. She now feels less alone after talking with other people who also have debt.

If you're going to use buy now, pay later plans, here are some expert recommendations:

Read the fine print

The most well-known buy now, pay later product is pay-in-four, where you can pay back what you owe in four payments, one every two weeks, with a 0% annual percentage rate, or APR. However, not every buy now, pay later loan has the same terms. Before you commit to buying something using buy now, pay later, Ed deHaan, a professor at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, recommends that you read your contract carefully.

“So-called buy now, pay later products are popping up that are not good deals at all," deHaan said. "Some of them charge hefty fees, both upfront and if you miss a payment."

In general, if you miss a buy now, pay later payment, you can face fees, interest or the possibility of being banned from using the services in the future.

Know how it impacts your credit score

In the past, buy now, pay later loans didn’t impact your credit score, but that has changed. Buy now, pay later agencies now report credit lending activity to one of the three major credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion.

“Entering into a buy now, pay later plan for now isn’t going to affect your credit in any way, but missing a payment can, so that’s where you really want to be careful,” Rathner said.

Credit reporting depends on the company and its policies. For example, both Affirm and Klarna report to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay does not report to any credit bureau.

Only borrow what you can pay back

Before purchasing something with buy now, pay later, deHaan recommends pausing to consider whether it’s an amount you can pay back.

“The general advice for credit is that it's very easy to spend and hard to pay off," deHaan said. “And most of us, many of us, are not good at making good predictions about what we will be able to pay in the future.”

When using buy now, pay later, Brown set herself a limit of $100 a month across payments, and she avoids signing up for payments every two weeks and instead chooses the monthly payment options.

Avoid stacking plans

As with credit cards, you can 

“Avoid multiple purchases because then it gets really hard to track, especially if they’re with different companies,” Sanchez-Adams said.

If you have to utilize multiple loans, make sure you keep track of the payment amounts and dates so you avoid late fees, she added.

Seek out additional resources

Looking into additional resources such as food banks, SNAP or hardship help programs in your area can be helpful, Rathner said.

“If you are stretched thin for affording food and going into debt to do so, it could be time to seek out additional help," she said. “So this is hopefully less of a struggle for you and your family while you’re going through this difficult time.”

Seek help from a nonprofit credit counseling agency

If you've reached a point where you have too many buy now, pay later loans and maybe some credit card debt too, it might be time to seek help from a credit counseling agency. Two well-known resources for finding nonprofit credit counseling agencies are the National Foundation for Credit Counseling and the Financial Counseling Association of America. Both can help you connect with certified agencies and counselors.

“You have financial stress, you have work stress, you have family stress," Rathner said. “Get help with the financial stress because that can help you feel more in control of this area of your life. And it can help take one step at a time toward paying down your debts and feeling more in control.”

Controversial CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss will not have a role at CNN after the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery deal is closed, according to a new report.

The two media conglomerates will officially merge on Tuesday after the deal was held up for months over antitrust concerns. On Wednesday, a federal judge approved the settlement between Skydance’s Paramount and a dozen state attorneys general who attempted to block its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.

Questions remain about how the deal will shape company leadership and impact the former rival newsrooms at CBS and CNN.

Paramount CEO David Ellison and his team have reportedly been deciding how CNN, owned by Warner Bros. Discovery, will work with Paramount’s CBS News and its embattled leader, Weiss.

open image in gallery Controversial CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss will not have a role at CNN after the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery deal is closed, according to a new report ( Getty Images for Uber, X and The Free Press )

But Weiss isn’t expected to have a role at CNN after the merger is complete, people familiar with Ellison’s thinking told The Wall Street Journal.

Weiss, founder of the media outlet The Free Press, was appointed CBS News’ editor-in-chief last October after Ellison, who has courted President Donald Trump, took over Paramount.

Weiss has faced scrutiny over her editorial decisions, particularly her choice to pull a 60 Minutes segment about Venezuelan migrants sent by the Trump administration to CECOT, an El Salvadoran prison accused of having inhumane conditions.

The segment aired nearly one month later.

open image in gallery Weiss, who was chosen to lead CBS News last October, has faced scrutiny over her editorial decisions ( Getty Images )

60 Minutes, America’s most-watched TV program, has seen a massive shakeup under Weiss’ leadership.

Executive Producer Tanya Simon was ousted in May, along with her deputy, Draggan Mihailovich, and correspondents Cecilia Vega and Sharyn Alfonsi in a single day, dubbed “Black Thursday.”

As part of Paramount’s recently approved settlement, the company will create a board of journalists to monitor editorial independence at CNN and CBS News — two networks known for different newsroom cultures.

Ellison asked Mark Thompson, the chief executive of CNN, to stay on after the merger, people familiar with the matter told the Journal.

The two are currently discussing a new contract, but terms haven’t been reached yet, according to the Journal’s sources.

Gov. Wes Moore of Maryland is forming a bipartisan group of governors to respond to mounting concerns about the threats posed by artificial intelligence as he argued that states need to fill a void left by the federal government's inaction on the issue.

In an interview, Moore, a Democrat, criticized President Donald Trump's meeting with AI executives at the White House this week as a “billionaire boys club." He was also critical of Congress for leaving Washington until after next month's midterms without addressing the rapidly evolving technology.

“The federal government has a unique leadership role that they have to play and that includes both the White House and Congress,” Moore said after speaking at an innovation conference in Baltimore. “In the absence of that, the governors cannot just sit on our hands.”

Moore is the chair of the National Governors Association this year and said his co-chair, Republican Gov. Mike Braun of Indiana, would partner with him in developing an AI framework. Other governors from both parties are planning to participate, Moore said.

Increasingly dire warnings from tech executives that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity have tested the ability of governments at all levels to respond nimbly to fast-moving developments. So far, states have been more active than the federal government, but their power is limited when it comes to dealing with a technology that spans the country and the globe.

In the past month, governors in Maryland, California, Illinois, Oregon and Virginia have issued executive orders or taken other steps intended to create some standards for the technology. Republicans have been among those taking action at the state level with governors including Spencer Cox of Utah and Greg Abbott of Texas cracking down on data center development.

However, the action has been much slower in Washington. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., hosted a briefing with lawmakers and experts last month and Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., has launched an investigation into OpenAI. There has been little agreement, however, on a legislative response.

At the White House, Trump has dismissed AI fears as a “hoax” and emphasized the need to remain competitive with technology developed in China. He is one of the few prominent leaders who continues to boost data centers.

Trump and tech leaders signed a voluntary accord this week that he called “morally binding” and will include internal and external reviews. After meeting with the leaders, the president praised the industry for engaging in “tremendous self-policing.”

“Who in the room was advocating for more transparency or more regulatory guardrails?” Moore said of the White House meeting. “What the president did in no way, shape or form made me feel like what the governors are now doing was now unnecessary.”

The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

The debate over responding to artificial intelligence could play an important role in the early stages of the next presidential campaign. Moore has said he's not running for president and is focused on this year's midterms, when he is on the ballot for reelection in Maryland.

Whoever enters the field could face scrutiny for past moves including support for data centers, which were once seen as economic booms for states but have since become broadly unpopular. Moore is among the governors who has become more critical of data centers, signing an executive order last month establishing new rules to govern them.

He has also called on state lawmakers to repeal a tax exemption that was passed before he took office.

In the interview, Moore acknowledged the “speed of this technology that is moving at such a rapid clip.” He said that elements of an AI executive order he signed in 2024 are “antiquated now.”

“The operations might move,” he said. “But my values will never move.”

News.title: FTSE 100 tumbles amid bond market sell-off
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. House prices fell unexpectedly last month as mortgage borrowers prepare for a jump in interest rates.

Typical property values declined by 0.2pc during September, reversing 0.2pc growth in August, according to the Nationwide house price index.

The figure was much worse than analysts had forecasts, with most expecting prices to remain steady.

Over the course of the year to September, the rate of house price growth halved from 1.6pc to 0.8pc, which was the weakest rate since December 2025.

The value of the average home has fallen to £274,251 over concerns the Bank of England is on the cusp of raising interest rates, making borrowing more expensive for mortgage holders.

Money markets indicate there is an 84pc chance policymakers will raise rates from 3.75pc to 4pc in November in an effort to bring down inflation caused by the Iran war energy shock.

Robert Gardner, chief economist at Nationwide, said:“Market activity and house prices have remained subdued in recent months, in part reflecting the uncertain economic backdrop.

“Geopolitical tensions remain high, with the conflict in the Middle East exerting upward pressure on energy prices, fanning inflation concerns.

“This in turn has led to mounting financial market expectations of Bank Rate increases, which has maintained upward pressure on the market interest rates which underpin mortgage pricing.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Polanski urges Miliband to block Rosebank oil field over Israel links | Green leader claims North Sea project is a test of Foreign Secretary’s proposed sanctions regime

2) Netherlands ditches wealth tax over exodus fears | Dutch PM scraps plan to target paper profits, instead introducing a more convention capital gains levy

3) Diesel crisis deepens as UK’s biggest refinery shuts for 10 weeks | Fears of squeeze on supplies after fuel costs rise higher than £2 per litre

4) Debt-ridden France branded ‘the new sick man of Europe’ | Investors hope the European Central Bank sees the struggling country as ‘too big to fail’

5) Britain blocks foreign lawyers after surge in south Asian applicants | Bar Standards Board halts scheme unless candidates have already secured a position

What happened overnight

The cost of government borrowing edged higher in Asia as soaring energy costs sparked inflation fears.

Bond yields, a benchmark for what governments pay to borrow money, surged in September as investors brace for a period where interest rates stay higher for ​longer.

The yield on benchmark US 10-year Treasury notes hit 5.31pc, the ‌highest level since mid-June 2007. The 10-year yield gained 87 basis points in the July-September quarter, the biggest quarterly rise since 1994.

Market focus has been on how long US Treasury yields stay above the psychologically important 5pc level, while some investors even contemplate the possibility of yields breaching 6pc.

Yields in Japan have climbed to multi-decade highs too, while those in Germany, France and Britain have all hit 17 to 19 year peaks.

On Thursday, the benchmark 10-year Japanese government ​bond yield was at 3.11pc, not far from the 30-year high it hit last week.

Asian technology stocks rose after a boost from AI chipmaker Micron, ​although US bonds struggled ‌after their sharpest quarterly sell-off in more than three decades as inflation risks from elevated energy prices linger.

Stalling peace talks between the US and Iran to end the seven-month-long war in the Middle East have kept crude prices aloft.Brent futures surged 42pc in the July-September quarter.

The high-stakes earnings from Micron, a key supplier to AI bellwether Nvidia, signalled strong demand for AI memory chips, with financial commitments under long-term supply agreements at $32 billion, up from $22 billion in June.

That helped push tech-heavy stock markets in Asia higher. Japan’s Nikkei jumped over 3pc, and South Korea’s Kospi reversed earlier losses to gain 1.7pc. Taiwan’s stock benchmark was 0.8pc higher.

News.title: Chewing tobacco killed 250,000 people in one year, study shows
News.content:
Chewing tobacco killed around a quarter of a million people in 2023, with use of the product remaining stubbornly high, according to research.

The smokeless tobacco is particularly popular in south Asia that is placed between the cheek and lower gum. It is flavoured and sometimes sweetened, and users often spit out unwanted juices while chewing. It is often viewed as safer than smoking but it is a major cause of stroke, as well as head and neck cancer.

Chewing tobacco is different to white snus or nicotine pouches, which contain no tobacco. These white pouches are also made up of flavourings and sometimes sweeteners, and deliver a hit of nicotine through the lining of the mouth.

Despite a successful fight against smoking over the last few decades, rates of chewing tobacco use have fallen little and it has often been overlooked in tobacco control efforts, researchers point out. In a study published in the Lancet Global Health, researchers from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation in the US estimate that 241 million people aged 15 years and older used chewing tobacco in 2023.

Researchers looked at data on use in 204 countries between 1990 and 2023 and found that there was no significant decrease in the number of users of chewing tobacco over that period. And in 24 countries there was a significant uptick in the number of people using the product. Researchers estimate that about one in five men and one in 10 women in south Asia chewed tobacco in 2023.

Bangladesh has seen the biggest increase in the number of people using the product with 15 million new users between 1990 and 2023. Nepal, Madagascar and Yemen also saw increases in the number of users.

In India 105 million people chew tobacco regularly, accounting for just over two thirds of users globally. Historically, Indians would chew paan, tobacco in its raw form which was mixed with betel leaf and areca nut, a mild stimulant. But the use of chewing tobacco exploded in the 1980s when manufacturers began grinding these into a powder and selling them in packets known as gutkha. This was banned in 2012 but is still widely available. Chewing tobacco is also popular in Pakistan, China and Vietnam.

News.title: Esther Rantzen dies aged 86
News.content:
Dame Esther was a vocal supporter of the Assisted Dying Bill, claiming in March that most people “want and need” the right to end their own lives.

When the bill was defeated in the House of Commons in September, as MPs voted 286 to 270 against the legislation, she called it a “tragic day”. The bill would have allowed those with less than six months to live to seek medical assistance to end their lives.

In 2024, she said that she had joined the Dignitas assisted-dying clinic in Switzerland.

Writing for The Telegraph at the beginning of September, Rebecca Wilcox, Dame Esther’s daughter, said her mother was “too ill now to travel to Dignitas as she had planned and paid for”.

Earlier this month, Dame Esther said in a statement that it was too late for her to “buzz off” to the clinic in Switzerland and said Britain’s current laws on assisted dying are “messy and cruel”.

In a final message shared by her family, the presenter said she had been “immensely lucky” for the support she had received from the public, which she said had enabled her “to live such a long and happy life”.

She added: “Sadly, all good things come to an end, as they say. So I particularly wanted to say goodbye and thank you so very, very much. Perhaps I will see you eventually, on the other side. I do hope so. With very good wishes, as ever, Esther.”

News.title: Laptop running slowly? These tips will improve performance (and save your sanity)
News.content:
MacBooks and Windows laptops both have modes intended to maximise battery life. Low Power Mode (Mac) and Power Saver (Windows) should be avoided if you want peak performance.

On a Mac, you’ll find the Low Power Mode switch in Settings > Battery. For the best experience, set this to Never, but remember to change it back if you need your MacBook to last longer.

On a Windows laptop, there are two controls you need to consider. Both are found in Settings > System > Power & Battery.

Energy Saver mode uses multiple tactics to reduce battery consumption, including lowering maximum power. Switch this off, and you have access to Power Mode controls.

Your options are Best Power Efficiency, Balanced and Best Performance. While Balanced is the default, I was able to unlock up to 33 per cent more power by playing around with these settings using my own laptop.

To make matters more complicated, some laptops have their own performance modes. Many Asus laptops have MyAsus or Armory Crate, for example. Lenovo has the Vantage app, Dell has MyDell, and MSI laptops have MSI Center.

3. Stop applications from opening on start-up

If your laptop is slow when it first starts up, it may be because a whole bunch of apps have been given the green light to wake up with it.

Some applications such as antivirus software are critical, but most can be toggled off. As an example, I make sure apps such as Spotify, Steam and WhatsApp don’t open on startup; I only launch them when I need them.

On a MacBook, you can see which apps have this permission in Settings > General, under Open at Login. Select an app entry and click the “minus” button to remove it.

On a Windows laptop, you’ll find the list of start-up apps in Settings > Apps > Startup. Each entry has a little on/off slider.

News.title: Why the UK medicine supply chain is dangerously exposed to global shocks
News.content:
The UK’s medicine supply chain is dangerously exposed to global shocks, experts have warned, with the NHS dependent on a system where much of the world relies on a handful of countries for its drug supplies.

India and China are the backbone of the global medicines market, manufacturing around two-thirds of the world’s active pharmaceutical ingredients. This leaves countries exposed to factory shutdowns, natural disasters, geopolitical tensions, shipping disruption and sudden changes in the price or availability of raw materials, experts told The Telegraph.

“We rely now more than ever on other countries to make sure we can get access to the medicines that the vast majority of people take,” said Dr James Davies, director of research and insights at Community Pharmacy England.

Nearly all the active ingredients in the UK’s most widely used medicines are made overseas, around 80 per cent of them in China and India, leaving the NHS exposed to shocks thousands of miles beyond its control.

The resilience of Britain’s medicine supply has eroded gradually in recent years, as global instability has placed growing strain on the supply chains it depends on.

“We’ve seen more global turbulence in general,” said Dr Davies. “It’s not unique to the UK, but it’s affecting countries across Europe, across the Western world, with the Iran war, with difficulties flying things over Ukraine and Russia, and challenges with shipping in the Red Sea.”

In the UK, shortages have been reported across a wide range of products, including antibiotics, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder medicines, epilepsy treatments, hormone replacement therapy, and some diabetes medicines.

The drugs most at risk are the cheapest and most widely used – statins, blood pressure pills and antibiotics – taken by millions of people and manufactured in China and India at huge scale and minimal cost.

“Some antibiotics are almost exclusively made in China,” said Dr Davies. “For some of the blood pressure medicines, they’re more likely to be made in India. But across the board, those two are where most of the raw ingredients for those active pharmaceutical ingredients come from.”

News.title: Fraudster jailed for 41 years over Pakistani nurse scam in Saudi
News.content:
A fraudster who sent 92 Pakistani nurses to Saudi Arabia on fake documents in an elaborate scam to provide workers for short-staffed Gulf hospitals has been jailed for 41 years.

Ghulam Zulfiqar Ali used forged experience certificates, created fake verification QR codes and phoney employment platform IDs.

Ali was being paid by the Saudi authorities to find staff, but also charged genuine Pakistani nurses who wanted a job overseas, in a racket that has caused major embarrassment to the Pakistan’s authorities.

Gulf nations including Saudi Arabia are experiencing a severe shortage of nurses, compounded by rapid population growth, a rising burden of chronic diseases, and heavy dependence on nurses from abroad.

The World Health Organization (WHO) forecasts a global shortfall of 4.5 million nurses by 2030, and recruiting nurses for developed countries is a lucrative trade.

The 91 women were all genuine nurses, but did not meet the criteria for the “Nurse Highly Qualified” visa category under which they were sent.

When the Saudi authorities realised the fraud they deported all the nurses.

Syed Shehzad Nadeem Bukhari, director of Pakistan’s Federal Investigation Agency, told the Telegraph: “They lost both their money and their employment, and the incident caused serious embarrassment to Pakistan internationally.”

Investigators found that between October 2022 and September 2023, a Pakistani employment firm called M/S Sahou Manpower obtained permissions for the recruitment of 108 nurses for a Saudi-based manpower company, to work in hospitals under the visa category “Nurse Highly Qualified”.

The investigation found the Saudi employer bore all recruitment costs, including visa processing fees and air tickets.

It paid the Pakistani recruiting firm between $800 (GBP 600) and $1,100 (GBP 830) per candidate. However, Ali was also demanding between $800 (GBP 600) and $1,000 (GBP 750) from each nurse.

Investigators found the candidates were genuine nurses, but did not meet experience requirements and were given fake certificates.

Meanwhile Ali had not uploaded their details to Saudi systems designed to verify and check qualifications and give each applicant a QR code. Instead he provided them with faked QR codes and verification platform IDs.

Ali was convicted of cheating, two counts of forgery and emigration offences.

He was given 41 years imprisonment by the special court in Rawalpindi. He was also fined £1,904 and ordered to pay £25,031 compensation – £272 to each of the 92 nurses.

His accomplice, Ghulam Fareed, was given three years’ imprisonment and a £544 penalty.

Nasreen Begum, one of nurses, told the Telegraph: “We are thankful to FIA for compensation. Most of us have genuine qualifications as nurse-midwives, licenced practical nurses, clinical nursing assistants and a lady health visitor but our documents weren’t verified and that landed us in a difficult situation.”

Zeenat Khan, another victim of the fraud, said she had opted to take a job in Saudi Arabia because she was jobless despite having nursing qualifications.

She said: “I have three kids and wanted to give them a good education. Now, I hope to get back my money,” she said.

Swera Ali said she had been working in a private hospital in her native Lahore, Punjab province, but received only £50 a month and performed 16 hours duty.

She said: “My parents took a loan from relatives to facilitate me, but my hope of making money from an overseas job was short-lived when they deported us after less than a month.”

Mr Bukhari added: “The investigation established that their nursing diplomas were genuine. The fake QR codes and fake [employment platform] IDs were created by the accused, and the experience certificates were forged by the visa agent without the knowledge of the nurses.”

News.title: How vaccines and antibiotics can beat some cancers
News.content:
At least one in eight cancers worldwide are caused by viruses and bacteria, according to a new study published in The Lancet.

An estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 – out of a total of 20 million recorded worldwide – were caused by common infections, almost all of which could have been prevented with treatments such as antibiotics or vaccines.

Almost half of infection-linked cancers, around 760,000 cases, were caused by H. pylori, a bacterium that infects the stomach, researchers from the International Agency for Research on Cancer found.

The pathogen, which is typically ingested through contaminated food and water and is carried by around 60 per cent of the world’s population at any given time, can remain relatively undetected in the gut for between 20 and 40 years without causing any symptoms.

If left untreated, it can trigger chronic inflammation in the stomach and cellular mutations that, in some cases, lead to gastric cancer.

Cases of stomach cancer linked to H. pylori are particularly common in East Asia, where roughly 80 per cent of the population carries the bacterium. This is due in part to the prevalence of a more aggressive strain of the pathogen, known as CagA, which is endemic to the region.

East Asian diets – which typically include salty, pickled or smoked foods – can also damage the stomach’s protective lining and accelerate the inflammatory processes that can contribute to stomach cancer, researchers have found.

While H. pylori infection is treatable with a course of antibiotics, its symptoms often mimic those of other digestive problems and can be difficult to distinguish without testing.

This means the infection can remain undetected for years, allowing inflammation and damage to progress.

Sports.title: 'Major milestone' with women to earn equal prize money at tennis events
Sports.content:
All combined WTA 1000 tournaments will award women equal ‌prize money to the men from 2027, the Women's Tennis Association ‌said on Thursday, with the Italian Open and other ​major events joining the rest of the category in offering the same pay-outs.

In 2027 - nearly six decades after Billie Jean King won the Italian Open at the Foro Italico - the Rome clay-court event will finally award women the same amount of total prize money as men as part a "major milestone" initiative.

It means that all combined WTA 1000 events will award equal prize money for the first time.

Sports.title: HMRC asked to explore tax implications of Man City case
Sports.content:
The Treasury Committee has written to the chief executive of HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) to ask about the tax implications of the Premier League's investigation into Manchester City.

HMRC could investigate whether City paid the right amount of tax and national insurance during the nine seasons they have been found guilty of financial rule breaches.

In the letter, Dame Meg Hillier MP asks JP Marks, permanent secretary of HMRC, whether the department has received an unredacted version of the Premier League's report and requests "reassurance from HMRC that you are seized of the importance of these issues and the public interest in the case".

Hillier also says she would welcome an "overview of current HMRC work around football clubs."

The letter reads: "I would be interested in any common issues around taxation (including the taxation of remuneration) that you have found in their practices and how HMRC is tackling them."

The deadline for a reply is set at Thursday October 15.

Man City continue to deny wrongdoing and plan to launch an appeal against the verdict, which they must do by Friday.

The Premier League investigation into City was triggered by the publication of hacked internal emails in the German magazine Der Spiegel in 2018.

Der Spiegel said it had evidence which appeared to show that Roberto Mancini, who was City manager from 2009 to 2013, had a secret second contract.

As well as being paid £1.45m net by City, a company connected to him in Italy was being paid £1.75m for a four-day annual coaching consultancy commitment at Abu Dhabi-based UAE Pro League club Al Jazira.

Analysis: What are the tax implications of Man City's guilty judgement?

Sky Sports News' Kaveh Solhekol:

"The Treasury Committee have written to HMRC to ask about the tax implications of the Premier League's investigation into Manchester City.

"For instance, HMRC could investigate to see if City have been paying the right amount of tax over the nine seasons when they have been found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules.

"The investigation into Manchester City was triggered by some hacked internal emails which were published by Der Speigel in 2018.

"According to Der Speigel, some of those emails appeared to show that former manager Roberto Mancini had two contracts. One for managing Manchester City, for which he was paid £1.45m, and a second contract whereby £1.75m was being paid per year to a company associated with him.

"I perhaps think what the Treasury Committe are getting at is just making sure that HMRC is going to be looking into this. Potentially, is this a case where the right amount of tax and national insurance wasn't paid?

"The Treasury Committee also ask [in their letter] for reassurances that the department has seized the importance of the case."

Sports.title: World No 979 Stewart claims share of Alfred Dunhill Links lead
Sports.content:
World No 979 Michael Stewart outscored a big-name field to share the lead at the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship after a first-round 65.

The 36-year-old has played only five DP World Tour events - the last in 2023 - and teed off less than 24 hours after finishing second in the Tartan Tour's Duddingston Classic having received a sponsor's invite earlier this week.

He had a remarkable back nine at Carnoustie, where an eagle at the par-five 12th was the catalyst to play five holes in six under par.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Piers Morgan narrowly escaped hitting some fans at the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship after topping his drive on the famous 17th Road hole

With a solitary birdie on the front nine he finished with a blemish-free seven under.

"It's easy to get yourself up for this event. I played Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday [at Duddingston] but I've played a lot here in the past," said Stewart on his lack of a practice round.

"Just delighted to be able to be part of the event. I feel right at home with links golf. I just played really nice all day."

The tournament is played over three courses - Carnoustie, Kingsbarns and St Andrews with the Old Course hosting the final day - and also incorporates a team event with a number of former sports stars and celebrities paired with the professionals.

Matt Fitzpatrick, who arrived in Scotland off the back of his fourth win of the year at the Open de France, shot a four-under 68 at Carnoustie, with Ryder Cup team-mate Tommy Fleetwood two under at the same course.

Five-time major winner Brooks Koepka was three under after a 69 at Carnoustie, while defending champion and home favourite Bob MacIntyre was one under at the same course.

Lee Westwood and Ian Poulter, on their first DP World Tour appearances in almost four years, shot one under at St Andrews and level par at Carnoustie respectively with fellow LIV golfer Bubba Watson also level at Carnoustie.
