World.title: Shadrack Sibiya court wrap: WhatsApps, witness claims and new charge
World.content:
: Suspended Deputy National Police Commissioner Lieutenant-General Shadrack Sibiya appeared in the Randburg Magistrate’s Court as his bail hearing continued, with the State placing alleged WhatsApp messages, witness interference claims and a new firearm charge before court. Image: X/Justice, Crime, Prevention and Security

Suspended Deputy National Police Commissioner Lieutenant-General Shadrack Sibiya’s bail hearing took a dramatic turn on Thursday as the State placed alleged WhatsApp messages involving a 16-year-old girl and claims of possible witness interference before the Randburg Magistrate’s Court.

Prosecutors also added a sixth charge against the 59-year-old senior police officer, relating to the alleged unlawful storage of a firearm.

Sibiya remains behind bars at Kgosi Mampuru II Correctional Centre while his Schedule 6 bail application continues.



The case returns to court on Friday.

Shadrack Sibiya bail hearing focuses on WhatsApp messages

Investigating officer Detective Sergeant Nokukhanya Ndlovu took the stand and detailed WhatsApp communication the State alleges took place between Sibiya and the 16-year-old complainant.

The court heard that investigators recovered messages and calls which prosecutors believe support the sexual grooming charges against him.



Ndlovu testified that Sibiya allegedly questioned the teenager about whether she was sexually active, told her not to date anyone else and asked her to keep their communication secret.

The State further alleges that Sibiya asked the girl to send explicit photographs and videos.

The allegations have not yet been tested at trial.



Sibiya intends to plead not guilty and has previously denied having a sexual relationship with the teenager.

State raises witness interference concerns

The investigating officer also opposed Sibiya’s release on bail, telling the court that investigators had concerns over possible interference with witnesses.

The court heard a recorded telephone conversation involving Bishop Azwihangwi Maumela, described as a close friend of Sibiya, and the father of the 16-year-old complainant.



Prosecutors alleged that Maumela asked the father about the identity of the 18-year-old complainant and discussed finding her so they could speak to her.

The State relied on the conversation as part of its argument against bail.

Sibiya’s defence rejected any suggestion that he instructed Maumela to contact witnesses.



His son, Ofentse Magwenya, submitted an affidavit stating that Maumela acted on his own and was never asked by Sibiya or his family to contact, threaten or intimidate any complainant or witness.

The alleged risk of witness interference has become one of the key issues in Sibiya’s bail application.

Sixth charge added against Shadrack Sibiya

Sibiya also returned to court facing an additional charge under the Firearms Control Act.



Prosecutors allege the charge relates to the unlawful storage of a firearm found in his vehicle around the time of his arrest.

The latest charge brings the total number of counts against him to six.

His defence questioned the timing of the new charge during Thursday’s proceedings.



Sibiya already faces rape, trafficking in persons, promoting the sexual grooming of a child and two counts of sexually grooming a child.

The charges involve an 18-year-old woman and a 16-year-old girl.

Sibiya says sex with 18-year-old was consensual

As previously reported by The South African, Sibiya admitted having sex with the 18-year-old complainant but denied raping her.



In his bail affidavit, the suspended police general described the encounter as consensual and said the pair remained in contact afterwards.

The State alleges the woman had become heavily intoxicated before the alleged rape at a Sandton hotel.

Sibiya has described the case against him as based on false allegations and told the court that he intends to plead not guilty.



He has asked the court to release him on R20 000 bail.

Because the matter falls under Schedule 6 of the Criminal Procedure Act, Sibiya must show exceptional circumstances that justify his release in the interests of justice.

Why Shadrack Sibiya remains at Kgosi Mampuru

Sibiya has remained at Kgosi Mampuru II Correctional Centre since his first court appearance on 22 September.



Prosecutors previously cited intelligence relating to a possible escape if authorities detained him at a police station.

The State has also raised concerns over possible threats and interference with witnesses.

Sibiya has denied trying to evade authorities or interfere with the investigation.



His legal team argued that he knew authorities were investigating him before his arrest but did not flee.

SAPS disciplinary hearing set for 5 October

Sibiya’s criminal case is unfolding alongside internal SAPS disciplinary proceedings.

National police spokesperson Brigadier Athlenda Mathe confirmed this week that SAPS served Sibiya with notice to appear at an expedited disciplinary hearing on 5 October.



The proceedings relate to allegations arising from the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry.

Mathe said the hearing could take place at Kgosi Mampuru if Sibiya remains in custody.

If the court grants him bail, SAPS will arrange another venue.



His lawyers also told the court that Sibiya had received further disciplinary notices.

Sibiya’s bail application continues in the Randburg Magistrate’s Court on Friday.

World.title: International Coffee Day: Who sells the best cuppa in SA?
World.content:
Millions of South Africans continue to drink coffee daily despite rising prices, with the cost of instant coffee increasing faster than broader food inflation. Image: Wikimedia Commons

Millions of South Africans continue to drink coffee daily despite rising prices, with the cost of instant coffee increasing faster than broader food inflation.

The latest consumer data comes as International Coffee Day is marked on 1 October, putting the spotlight on the cost of one of South Africa’s most popular daily beverages.

READ | Shoprite bets big on coffee with Vida e Caffè purchase



South Africa’s headline consumer inflation stood at 4.4% in August 2026, while inflation for food and non-alcoholic beverages was considerably lower at 1.1%.

However, instant coffee has increased by 62.6% since August 2022, while cappuccino sachets have risen by a reported 24.4% over the same period.

Price of 250g of instant coffee

Year Price August 2022 R47.72 August 2023 R52.70 August 2024 R67.37 August 2025 R75.34 August 2026 R77.57

Ground coffee and beans are no longer included in South Africa’s official consumer price basket, leaving instant coffee as the available measure for tracking coffee-price movements.

Millions of South Africans still drinking coffee

Higher prices have not resulted in a major collapse in coffee consumption.

Around 22 million South Africans drank some form of coffee on the day surveyed, according to the latest available MAPS data.

The figure includes instant coffee, ground beans, pods and instant cappuccino.



Tea remains more widely consumed, with approximately 26 million people drinking Ceylon, rooibos or green tea.

The figures measure the number of people consuming the beverages rather than the total number of cups consumed, meaning they do not indicate how much coffee or tea each person drinks during the day.

Coffee consumption also varies across different groups.

Ground coffee has a stronger association with higher-income households, while instant cappuccino is more prominent among students.

The data indicates that coffee drinkers have become more responsive to price increases, while tea consumption has increased over the period measured.

Ricoffy remains a popular choice

Brand preferences also highlight the distinctive nature of South Africa’s coffee market.

Ricoffy remains a major player in the instant coffee category, with previous consumer research finding that it was consumed by more people than the next five leading instant coffee brands combined.

For consumers who regularly buy coffee away from home, Mugg & Bean is the most frequently visited coffee venue among households earning more than R10 000 per month.

Seattle Coffee, Woolworths and Vida also feature prominently.

At the same time, South Africa’s speciality coffee market continues to attract interest, with consumers increasingly exploring single-origin beans, alternative brewing methods and the origins of the coffee they drink.

Could prices eventually fall?

There could be some relief for coffee drinkers further down the line.

Global coffee production is forecast to increase by 6% to a record 189.7 million bags in 2026/27.

Global consumption is also expected to remain strong, with the worldwide market forecast to reach a record 179.7 million bags.

The increase in production could eventually put downward pressure on global coffee prices and, in turn, provide some relief for South African consumers.

However, any impact on local prices is unlikely to be immediate.

For now, coffee remains a significant part of the daily routine for millions of South Africans – even as the price of that morning cup continues to climb.

Who sells the best coffee in South Africa?

World.title: JUST IN: Western Cape mayor, CFO arrested in alleged kickback bust
World.content:
The SAPS Political Killings Task Team carried out the arrests on Thursday following an investigation into alleged payments linked to a municipal contract. Image: Pexels

Police have arrested a Western Cape mayor, municipal manager and chief financial officer in a corruption probe over alleged kickbacks linked to a municipal security contract.

The SAPS Political Killings Task Team (PKTT) arrested the three senior officials on Thursday, 1 October, after investigators received information about an alleged kickback scheme at a municipality on the southern coast of the Western Cape.

SAPS has not yet named the municipality or the three officials.



Western Cape mayor arrested over alleged kickbacks

Police allege a businessman who secured a security services contract faced demands for kickbacks to keep the contract.

SAPS spokesperson Brigadier Athlenda Mathe said the businessman allegedly paid hundreds of thousands of rands because he feared officials would terminate the deal if he refused.

Investigators followed the information and arrested the mayor, municipal manager and CFO.



Police have not yet disclosed the value of the security contract or the total amount allegedly paid.

Trio face corruption charges

The three officials face corruption charges and will appear in court on Monday, 5 October 2026.

SAPS has not yet detailed the allegations against each suspect or confirmed whether investigators expect more arrests.



The identities of the officials and the municipality remain under wraps ahead of their first court appearance.

World.title: WATCH | Calls for stronger grassroot football
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Kay Motsepe Schools Championship Finals are showcasing some of South Africa's brightest young football talent.

But former Bafana Bafana player Surprise Moriri said more needs to be done to strengthen grassroots structures.

This, he said, includes creating a clear pathway from junior football to the professional game and national team.

This follows Bafana Bafana coach Pitso Mosimane’s call for football to learn from rugby and cricket by building a stronger school-based development system.

For the former internationals, competitions like the Kay Motsepe Schools Championship can help uncover the next generation of talent.

But they said a sustainable development pathway is needed to ensure that talent is nurtured and reaches the highest level.

World.title: Number Of The Day | R16,60 | 01 October 2026
World.content:
A Strong Rand Is A Buffer, Not A Shield

For much of 2026, South Africans had an unusual piece of good news sitting quietly behind some very bad global headlines: the rand was holding up.

That resilience mattered. A stronger currency cannot stop an oil shock, erase geopolitical risk or make imported goods cheap overnight, but it can soften the blow. When the rand buys more dollars, the country needs fewer rands to pay for goods priced internationally. When it weakens, that protection starts disappearing.

The move through R16.60/$ is therefore important for a reason bigger than the number itself.

The exchange rate is part of South Africa's inflation defence

The South African Reserve Bank has repeatedly pointed to the rand's resilience as one reason import-price pressure remained relatively contained during 2026. Its September Monetary Policy Committee statement noted that the currency had

helped keep import prices in check even while fuel and services inflation remained elevated.

That is the part of exchange-rate movements that can feel invisible until the direction changes.

South Africa imports large quantities of goods priced in foreign currency, including oil. When the rand weakens, the same dollar-priced barrel becomes more expensive in rand terms before it even enters the rest of the pricing chain.

The episode captures that mechanism clearly. Higher imported fuel costs can move into farming, transport and logistics before eventually reaching consumers through the prices of goods on shelves.

The Reserve Bank's latest Quarterly Bulletin makes the importance of that buffer even clearer. It found that the stronger rand had partly softened the domestic effect of sharply higher international energy prices during 2026.

A weaker currency does not automatically produce an immediate price spike. Businesses hedge currency exposure, contracts differ, inventories were bought at earlier prices, and companies do not always pass every cost increase directly to customers. But the direction of pressure changes.

Sometimes the story is happening somewhere else

It is tempting to treat every fall in the rand as a referendum on South Africa.

That can be misleading.

On 1 October, the US dollar strengthened broadly as global government bonds sold off and US Treasury yields climbed to levels not seen since 2002. Reuters reported that the pressure was not confined to South Africa, with inflation fears and higher borrowing costs driving significant moves across global markets.

That matters because investors constantly compare opportunities.

If relatively safe US government debt suddenly offers significantly higher returns, some investors have less reason to hold assets in emerging markets. The result can be pressure on currencies such as the rand even when the immediate trigger is thousands of kilometres away.

South African economic data on the day was not uniformly negative either. Reuters reported that manufacturing sentiment had improved and vehicle sales remained resilient, while the stronger dollar still weighed on the rand.

Currency movements rarely tell one clean story.

Resilience can be lost faster than it was built

This is why R16.60/$ matters without needing to become a catastrophe headline.

The episode itself makes the distinction. The rand is weaker than it was at the end of August, but Gareth Edwards and Francis Herd also note that its broader performance had remained relatively strong before the latest move.

The lesson is not that a currency has suddenly failed. It is that resilience is conditional.

A strong exchange rate can provide South Africa with breathing room against global shocks. It can reduce some import costs and soften inflation pressure. But it cannot permanently insulate an open economy from an oil shock, higher global interest rates, a stronger dollar or investors moving towards safer assets.

The number to watch is R16.60.

The bigger story is how quickly a useful economic buffer can thin when the global environment turns.

References

Number of the Day, 01 October 2026 episode transcript.

South African Reserve Bank, Statement of the Monetary Policy Committee, September 2026.

South African Reserve Bank, Quarterly Bulletin, September 2026.

Reuters, Dollar hits 17-month high versus euro as bond selloff lifts yields, 01 October 2026.

Reuters, South African rand weakens as investors assess manufacturing survey, vehicle sales, 01 October 2026.

World.title: Public Prosecutor confirms probe into Senzo Mchunu at advanced stage
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Public Protector investigations into Police Minister Senzo Mchunu have reached an advanced stage.

According to the Public Protector's chief operating officer, Nelisiwe Nkabinde, they are following up on new information that keeps coming to light.

“We have received full cooperation from everyone, and that has led to us getting more and more information and evidence as we continue with the various consultations," she said.

Investigations stem from allegations against Mchunu, including political interference and abuse of power.

The Public Protector's office is, however, stressed that it's not running a parallel Madlanga Commission.
