In a statement to Fox News Digital, a spokesperson for Hillsboro School District said the district cannot comment on pending litigation.

World.title: Reporter's Notebook: Congress dodged a fall shutdown, but the real fight looms
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

"And all at once, summer collapsed into fall…" – Oscar Wilde

Congress certainly collapsed into fall this year. It lacked the usual mayhem of an imminent government shutdown for the first time in years. The government is usually only funded through September 30, the end of the federal fiscal year. Lawmakers solved that fiscal riddle early.

So the beginning of fall in Congress is usually anything but enjoyable. Others are devouring cobbler, enjoying spiced pumpkin lattes and viewing leaves of amber. When a government shutdown looms, the infernality of summer continues to stew on Capitol Hill. Imagine simmering political temperatures mixed with boiling urban concrete and a soupçon of petrichor. That epitomizes the customary fall tension in the halls of Congress when lawmakers are on the precipice of a shutdown.

But this year is different.

TRUMP SIGNS GOVERNMENT FUNDING BILL, AVOIDING A SHUTDOWN AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

No shutdown. That’s a good thing, considering last year’s 43-day shutdown odyssey which crawled from October 1 into mid-November. Everything is funded through December 11. So at least members and journalists can enjoy some of those autumnal fall trappings and dash to the pumpkin patch. That’s because we don’t know what’s going to await everyone for the next spending round in mid-December.

Lawmakers are recovering from the battle scars of last fall. So with the midterms approaching, no one wanted to return to the 2025 contretemps. The sides are willing to tussle over spending. But only after the midterms.

Does that mean a shutdown in December? Unclear.

If Democrats seize control of the House or Senate — or both — that could compel House and Senate Republicans to fund the government the way they want through the fall of 2027 right away. They won’t want an interim spending bill which punts things into early next year when Democrats may have power.

That said, if Democrats capture either the House or Senate, they will argue that the voters have spoken and it’s incumbent on them to decide how to spend taxpayer money next year. Under those scenarios, Democrats will push for a stopgap bill, hoping to tangle with President Trump in the early days of 2027.

The only thing which is known is that President Trump will in fact still be in office come January. This scenario could spark a shut down next year – if not December.

The reason? You still need 60 votes to clear a filibuster (and probably two) in the U.S. Senate. That means Republicans just can’t ram through whatever spending package they want. That may work in the House. And the GOP could even test the willingness of Reps. Jared Golden, D-Maine, and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., to buck their party and assist passing a GOP-favored spending measure in the lame duck.

FETTERMAN STRONGLY SUPPORTS THE FILIBUSTER AS TRUMP URGES SENATE REPUBLICANS TO SCRAP IT

But in the Senate, Republicans will certainly need the cooperation of at least seven Democrats to help them hit the 60 vote threshold. Those Democrats won’t be anxious to assist unless they won the majority and think they can apply their stamp on federal spending in the first quarter of next year.

This is the same problem which vexed the Senate during the shutdown of 2025.

The House passed a partisan spending bill to re-up all current funding on an interim basis. But Senate Republicans could never break a filibuster to lug that spending package across the finish line. The same circumstances may be true in December.

So could the 120th Congress begin in January with a shutdown?

It’s happened before. In fact, under very similar circumstances.

Democrats flipped control of the House during the 2018 midterms – two years into President Trump’s first term. But the President and outgoing House Speaker Paul Ryan, R-Wis., balked at a bipartisan spending package the Senate cleared just before Christmas that year. So the government closed. There was no way to resuscitate the Senate-approved package. So the 116th Congress began with a shutdown. It ran a then-record 35 days.

A possible government shutdown over spending disputes frankly serves as a symptom for what could be ahead if voters flip either or both bodies of Congress. Democrats will convulse at spending plans made by Republicans and the President. Plus, House Democrats likely add several progressives and Democratic Socialists to their ranks in November in solidly blue districts. Granted, those left-wing politicians won’t take office until January. But House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., must court the support of candidates Melat Kiros in Colorado along with Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez in New York to win the Speaker’s gavel. Any missteps by the Democratic brain trust in the lame duck could ignite an internecine firestorm – before Democrats potentially seize the majority in January.

Republicans could face their own issues, too.

SCHUMER PREACHES AFFORDABILITY IN DEM MIDTERM PITCH WHILE SABOTAGING GOP FIXES FOR SOARING COSTS

Some rank-and-file Republicans are ready to move on from House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA). Granted, it is said that Johnson is Speaker as long as President Trump wants him in the job. But what’s not clear is what happens if Republicans lose control of the House. Will the President and others support Johnson for Minority Leader? Does Johnson want that job? What happens to House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-LA) and House Minority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn.?

There are signals that House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, is interested in moving into leadership. Especially if the GOP loses the majority. Jordan is tight with President Trump. He lost a bid to become Speaker three years ago after Republicans unceremoniously ousted former Speaker Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif.

If Republicans lose the majority, it’s not clear that some Republicans will back Johnson for the top GOP job in the House – regardless of what President Trump says. Some House Republicans will blame the President if the party loses the House. Especially since they believe he’s responsible for the toxic political climate they face right now. It’s unknown if a Republican party out of power might begin pushing back against President Trump, frustrated by the economy, tariffs, the price of gasoline and the war in Iran. Most GOPers have shown a reluctance to break with the President so far. But that could change if voters hand Congressional Republicans their head in the midterms.

We haven’t even raised the question about the future of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. – although the New York Democrat insists he isn’t going anywhere. But questions would emerge if Democrats don’t flip the Senate, considering that progressives and younger activists want to move on from the 75-year-old Schumer.

The same with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D. President Trump and Thune have never been close. If Republicans lose the Senate, would the President use that as a reason to call for the removal of the South Dakota Republican?

All of this will color those questions about spending bills, maybe renewing FISA – or even getting the House to sync up with the Senate on the college sports bill during the lame duck Congress.

Summer collapsed into fall. Capitol Hill was bereft of the usual autumnal mayhem.

So go pick out some pumpkins. Sip a cinnamon spice latte. Prepare for trick or treating. Fall is here.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

But that autumn Congressional bedlam is only delayed. It will hit Capitol Hill after the election.

World.title: Make unknown callers explain why they're calling
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

You know the feeling. Your phone rings, you look down and see a number you do not recognize. Now you have to decide whether to answer or let it go to voicemail. That choice gets harder when you are expecting a call from a doctor, repair person or someone else who may not be in your contacts.

Fortunately, your phone can now help figure out who is on the other end before you get involved. With iOS 27, your iPhone can ask an unknown caller for their name and why they are calling. Google Pixel phones have their own Call Screen feature. Compatible Samsung Galaxy phones can also use AI-powered call screening. Here is how each one works on the latest software.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare With AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com

ANDROID FAKE CALL DETECTION WARNS YOU ABOUT SCAMS

How to screen unknown callers on iPhone

Apple's Call Screening feature can automatically answer calls from unknown numbers without interrupting you. The caller gets asked for their name and the reason for the call. After they respond, your iPhone rings and shows you what they said. That gives you a little more information before deciding whether to answer.

How to turn on Call Screening on iPhone

Open Settings

Scroll down and tap Apps

Tap Phone

Scroll to Screen Unknown Callers

Select Ask Reason for Calling

Once you turn it on, calls from unknown numbers are asked for more information before your iPhone rings. Apple also gives you two other options in the same section. Never turn Call Screening off. Silence sends calls from unsaved numbers directly to voicemail and keeps them in your Recents list. For many people, Ask Reason for Calling may offer a useful middle ground. You can still hear from someone important without immediately answering every unfamiliar number.

You can filter suspected spam calls too

While you are in the Phone settings, you can also review Apple's call filtering options. Go to Settings → Apps → Phone, then scroll to the call filtering section. Turning on Spam lets your carrier identify potential spam or fraud calls. Those calls can then be silenced, sent to voicemail and moved into the Spam list. You can also turn on Unknown Callers. That moves calls from unknown numbers out of your main Recents list and into a separate Unknown Callers list.

FAKE VERIZON FRAUD CALL NEARLY STOLE HIS ACCOUNT

How Samsung Galaxy screens unknown calls

Samsung has also brought call screening to compatible Galaxy phones. Samsung says the feature is available on supported Galaxy phones running One UI 8.5 or later. However, feature availability can still vary by Galaxy model, carrier and region. Galaxy Call screening can answer the caller and ask why they are calling. You can then read the caller's response as a live transcription.

How to turn on Call screening on Samsung Galaxy

Open the Phone app

Tap the three vertical dots

Tap Settings

Tap Call screening

Turn on Call screening

Turn on Auto screen calls if you want unknown calls screened automatically

Samsung also lets you choose a transcription language and customize the assistant's voice. If you prefer to decide which calls get screened, you can do that manually. When an incoming call appears, tap Call assist, then tap Call screening. The AI assistant answers for you and asks the caller to state the purpose of the call. Their response then appears as text on your screen. If you do not see Call screening, check for the latest Galaxy software update. You should also make sure the Samsung Phone app is current. Some Galaxy models may not support the feature.

How to screen unknown calls on a Google Pixel

Google Pixel phones take a slightly different approach with Call Screen. The feature can answer certain calls for you and ask the caller why they are calling. Depending on your Pixel and settings, Google can also screen some calls automatically.

How to turn on Call Screen on Pixel

Open the Phone app

Tap the three dots

Tap Settings

Tap Spam and Call Screen or Call Screen

Tap Call Screen

Turn on Automatic Call Screen

Choose your preferred protection level

On newer Pixel phones, you may see Maximum protection, Medium protection and Basic protection. Medium protection is Google's recommended setting and screens suspicious calls while declining known spam. Maximum protection screens unknown numbers more aggressively, while Basic protection mainly declines known spam. You can still screen a call manually. When an unfamiliar number comes in, tap Screen call. Call Assist will ask who is calling and why while you watch the response appear as a live transcript. From there, you can answer the call, hang up or use one of the suggested responses.

Why screening can beat automatically silencing every unknown caller

Sending every unfamiliar number straight to voicemail certainly cuts down on interruptions. However, it can also send legitimate callers there. Maybe you are waiting for a medical office to call from a number you have never seen. Perhaps a service technician needs to reach you from a work phone. Call screening gives that person a chance to explain why they are trying to reach you. You can then make the call about whether to answer.

There is also a security benefit. Scam callers often count on getting someone on the phone quickly. Screening puts another step between the caller and you. However, do not assume someone is legitimate simply because they answered the screening question. Scammers can still lie about who they are. Caller ID can also be spoofed.

Do not let a convincing answer lower your guard

Call screening gives you information. It does not verify someone's identity. If a caller claims to represent your bank or another company and suddenly asks for money or login information, end the call. The same advice applies if someone asks for a one-time security code. Instead, contact the organization yourself through its official app or website. For financial accounts, you can also use the phone number printed on your card or statement. This is especially important because phone scams continue to get more convincing. Scammers can spoof familiar numbers and create a sense of urgency to push you into acting quickly.

Kurt's key takeaways

I like the idea of making an unknown caller explain themselves before they get my attention. With iOS 27, iPhone owners can have unfamiliar callers provide a name and reason before the phone rings. Pixel owners can use Google's Call Screen, while compatible Galaxy phones offer their own call screening feature. For me, screening makes more sense than automatically silencing every unfamiliar number. There are plenty of legitimate reasons someone outside your contacts may need to reach you. Still, treat the screening response as information rather than proof. If the conversation turns to passwords, money or account access, hang up and contact the company yourself.

Would you rather have your phone screen every unknown caller first, or do you still prefer sending unfamiliar numbers straight to voicemail? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

World.title: Joe Burrow's girlfriend shares cheating hot take, woman's sister hooked up with her date & regaining the spark
World.content:
Welcome to the latest edition of True Romance. For whatever reason, this week we're being hit from all sorts of angles with tales of cheating.

I don't know if that's the type of mood fall sets or what, but it's everywhere. I try my best to steer us back towards hope. I don't know that I'm successful.

I take a deep dive into why it's time for a woman to forgive her sister for hooking up with a guy she went on a date with, and we bring the spark back before all is said and done this week.

MAN IN TROUBLE FOR USING ROBOT VACUUM TO RECORD WIFE'S AFFAIR, FRIENDS WITH BENEFITS LEASE UP & HALL PASS WINS

Is that enough? I can't say. I put it out there, hope for the best and let you decide. I don't look to the stars for answers.

Unfortunately for Tom Brady, that's what Gisele Bundchen did, according to a new book about the legendary quarterback, reports Page Six. The stars allegedly told her they weren’t compatible.

From one quarterback and model relationship to another. As far as we know, the stars haven't told Olivia Ponton that she and Joe Burrow aren't compatible. Although, she's had other relationships that didn’t work out.

In fact, she revealed during a recent episode of her Booked, Blonde & Busy podcast that she had been cheated on in all of her past relationships. But she finally realized after the third time it happened that she wasn't the problem.

Forget that common denominator nonsense. Ponton has it figured out.

"I think cheating is a sign of insecurity," she said. "If you feel the need to be in a happy, healthy relationship with somebody, and go to get outside validation that you are attractive, that is not a reflection of this perfectly great person that could be in your life. That is a reflection on them. That’s my hot take."

She's the perfectly great person that you're now missing out on. Well, not the Cincinnati Bengals quarterback. He presumably isn't seeking outside validation that he's attractive. Good for him.

INNOCENT WRESTLING WITH SISTER OF WIFE'S BEST FRIEND REVEALS CHEATING WITH A TWIST, MCDONALD'S WEDDING & SIGNS

Go follow True Romance on Twitter and Facebook and keep sending your emails here: sean.joseph@outkick.com (anonymously if you prefer).

If you can believe it, Brooke Hogan says her dad sleeping with her friend changed their relationship

I think you're just going to have to trust me on this one. Call me crazy, but I believe Brooke Hogan when she says her relationship with Hulk Hogan changed after she says he slept with her friend.

She's a forgiving person, so that wasn’t the issue. She forgave her dad, but the relationship they had prior to him sleeping with one of her best friends was gone. How you ask? It's one of life's mysteries.

"A major turning point came after he slept with my friend Christiane [Plante]," Brooke told Us Magazine. "I forgive people very easily — sometimes probably too easily — and I forgave him, but something between us changed afterward. I don’t think he ever related to me in quite the same way again."

The Hulkster was known to run wild on occasion. This relationship with her friend might have been one of those times. But all wasn’t lost.

Hooking up with her friend, her parent's divorce, and everything that went along with it, didn’t mean she didn’t still care for Hulk.

"I can love my father profoundly and still tell the truth about where he hurt me," Brooke added. "I can acknowledge the wonderful things my family gave me while also acknowledging that eventually the dynamic became something I could no longer live inside. Both things can be true."

Exactly. It's all about forgiveness. I think this is a lesson that a lot of us can learn from, including another of the stories we're going to get into.



This Week In True Romance

Follow True Romance on Twitter and Facebook .

Woman's sister hooked up with a guy she went on a date with

How long is too long to hold a grudge with your sister just because she slept with a guy that you went on a date with? A week? A month? A year? How about six years?

This wasn’t a guy that she was in a serious relationship with. This was a guy she really liked is all. Yet she still hasn't gotten over it.

"My sister and I lived together and I went on a date with a guy I really liked. I introduced them before he and I went out and I thought we had a great time. She wasn't home when I got back but we texted a little and I told her I had the best time, etc. She told me not to wait up for her so I didn't," she wrote on Reddit.

"The next morning I was making breakfast when I heard her coming in and I saw my date from the day before with her. He ran away once he saw me but she couldn't hide what they did. She was giggling and it was clear she had been with someone. I made breakfast and then hid in my room from her for the rest of the day and texted my brothers."

She's off to a decent start. She sees her sister coming in after a night out and her date is there. She knows by the look on her sister's face that they slept together and instead of a confrontation right there, she stuffs her feelings deep inside and hides out in her room.

"When I was still avoiding her the next day she barged into my room and asked me what was wrong and why I was avoiding her and I broke down and told her she hurt me when she slept with my date. Her whole demeanor changed and it was like she had no idea that might have hurt my feelings," she continued.

"She apologized but I didn't want to hear it and I told her to leave me alone. She asked me what she could do and she promised she'd never sleep with him again and she'd tell him to take me out again but that made it worse. I stayed a few more days but moved in with my brother when I realized I couldn't keep living with her and I didn't forgive her just because she said she was sorry."

Since then, she's been "civil" with her sister, but they’re not hanging out or doing anything together. Those days are gone.

Things came to a head recently when one of their brothers told the sister's boyfriend, who she was in a serious relationship with, about the incident. The sister thinks it's time to get over it.

"She was upset with our brother but then she told me I needed to get over what she did because it was one stupid decision and she is too damn good of a sister to let one thing ruin us," she added.

"She also defended what she did because she doesn't think what she did was bad, which honestly was what I suspected all along."

The reason she suspected it all along is because that's the truth. This wasn’t a guy she was planning to marry. It was one date, and sure the timing wasn't great, but better to find out what this guy is all about immediately.

She should be thanking her sister, not dragging this out for this long.

Couples who have been together 10–20+ years: what brought the spark back?

This one proves there's not a single way that couples who have put time in together keep the spark going or bring it back. You really have to find what works for you. I think that's the lesson here.

There are things like losing weight and trying to stay healthy that work for some. Others point to communication. Hormones do the trick for couples too. And so does swinging and presenting divorce papers.

As I said, find what works for you. Here's what some couples on Reddit found that worked for them.

Staying healthy, hyping one another up, and just accepting that sometimes slumps happen, and we don’t need to shame/guilt ourselves or one another when we go through phases of not feeling super intimate. If we have a dry spell, it’s not the end of the world, it doesn’t mean we don’t love one another.

Time away from the kids

Clear open and honest communication

All sorts of stuff become way more interesting if we put our insecurities aside.

World.title: Supreme Court to decide lawfulness of Trump’s immigrant detention policy
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court said Thursday it will consider whether immigrants subject to deportation can be held in detention indefinitely while their cases are adjudicated.

The eventual ruling could endorse or end a key feature of President Donald Trump’s hard-line immigration crackdown.

The case was among three the court took up ahead of the justices’ return to action Monday for a new nine-month term following a summer break. Rulings in all three are due by the end of June.

The focus in the first case is whether such immigrants should have a chance to argue at a bond hearing that they can be released while the deportation process moves forward, which was standard practice under previous presidents.

The justices will hear a Trump administration appeal in the case of Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a man from Brazil who originally entered the United States in the mid-2000s.

He was detained following a traffic stop in Norwood, Massachusetts, in September 2025. He sued, and a federal district judge ordered that he be released. The New York-based 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld that decision on appeal.

Lower courts have been divided on the issue, although the majority have sided with immigrants who have argued that the federal law the Trump administration cites to hold them without a bond hearing only applies to people detained near the border.

Since last summer, the Trump administration has sought to apply that federal law to anyone deemed to have entered the United States illegally, even if they are nowhere near the border and have lived in the country for years.

Several cases on the issue are pending at the Supreme Court.

“Try as it might, the government cannot twist the law to detain immigrants for months or even years on end without a bond hearing. Not only is it cruel and inhumane; it is unlawful,” Michael Tan, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union representing various detainees, said in a statement.

In court papers, Solicitor General D. John Sauer, representing the Trump administration, called the issue a “critically important question of immigration law.” The policy removes a “perverse incentive” whereby people who evade detention when they enter the United States get treated more leniently than those detained at the border, he added.

The litigation, Sauer said, is “disrupting the orderly administration of immigration law.”

Thousands of people have already been detained under the policy, which could apply to millions of immigrants if expanded, and many of them have contested it. The case does not concern immigrants who have been convicted of certain crimes. Under federal law, they can be detained until they are deported, although separate lawsuits have raised questions about whether they should be eligible for bond hearings, too.

ACLU lawyers said in court papers that the Trump administration policy is a “radical reinterpretation” of immigration law, pointing out that some of those being detained were young children when they crossed the border.

Those challenging their confinement are not a flight risk or a potential danger to the public, ACLU lawyers say.

World.title: Diddy placed in solitary following NBC News report on his VIP prison life
World.content:
Sean “Diddy” Combs has been placed in solitary confinement following an NBC News report on his VIP lifestyle inside prison, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.

The disgraced hip hop mogul arrived at the Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey in October after he was sentenced to 50 months behind bars for transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters.

Since then, he has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his high-end lifestyle to the low-security prison, NBC News reported Tuesday in a story based on interviews with four men who spent time in the same unit as Combs.

They said he had no trouble acquiring contraband items such as cellphones and premium liquor, including Hennessy. He also pays several inmates who cook special meals for him, clean the toilet and shower areas before he uses them, do his laundry, make his bed and even give him Chinese-style massages.

“This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” one of the sources said. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”

NBC News also obtained photos and videos inside the prison, which includes footage of Combs appearing to use a contraband cellphone.

00:17 Diddy appears to use cellphone in prison 00:00 00:00

After the report was published, Combs was removed from his dormitory-style quarters and placed in a special housing unit, better known as solitary confinement or the SHU, according to the source.

A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson would neither confirm nor deny that Combs was moved.

“For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including quarters assignment or whether a particular individual is the subject of allegations, investigations, or sanctions,” the spokesperson said.

TMZ was first to report that the Bad Boy Records founder was moved to solitary.

Federal prisons often transfer inmates to the special housing unit when they are the subjects of an investigation, experts say.

“We’d put people in the SHU while we were gathering evidence,” said Vito Maraviglia, a retired special investigator for the Bureau of Prisons who worked at Fort Dix in the late 1990s.

Maraviglia said the New Jersey prison is known as one of the cushiest in the federal prison system. It has segmented housing areas that are more difficult to monitor than at other facilities, making it easier for inmates to hide and use contraband items like cellphones.

“A high-profile guy like that, with all that money, I’m surprised they put him at a place like Fort Dix,” Maraviglia said.

Food that was prepared at Fort Dix federal prison, in New Jersey, by inmates who were cooking special meals for Sean "Diddy" Combs and others. Obtained by NBC News

Inmates placed in the SHU are locked in a cell with one other person for at least 23 hours a day, according to two men who spent time at Fort Dix. Inmates are allowed a book or two and a wind-up radio, the sources said, and they must wear an orange jumpsuit instead of the regular khaki uniform or grey sweatpants and shirts.

Meals are delivered in trays but commissary access is restricted, and they are permitted to shower only a few days a week. The sources said they must otherwise wash up in a sink.

“It’s nasty down there,” one of the sources said.

It isn’t Combs’ first time in solitary confinement at Fort Dix. Last summer, he was placed in the special housing unit after he got into a fight with another inmate.

He was later kicked out of a drug treatment program at the prison but continued paying inmates to do a range of services for him, NBC News reported Tuesday.

The story prompted responses from people as varied as Combs’ longtime nemesis 50 Cent and the prominent attorney Gloria Allred, who represents a woman suing him for allegedly raping her more than 20 years ago. (Combs has denied the allegations, and the case is ongoing.)

“These serious allegations against Mr. Combs cry out for an immediate federal investigation and appropriate federal action including a prosecution if the allegations of having and using a cell phone while incarcerated can be proven beyond a reasonable doubt,” Allred said in a statement.

Other famous people have also received perks in prison, including Martha Stewart and Harvey Weinstein.

Combs’ trial last year centered on drug-fueled orgies he organized called “freak offs.” They involved male sex workers and his former girlfriends – including the singer Cassie – who filed a lawsuit against Combs alleging years of physical and sexual abuse. (The case was settled, with Combs denying any wrongdoing.)

The trial ended in a split verdict, with a New York jury finding him not guilty on the more serious charges of sex trafficking and racketeering charges that could have put him in prison for life.

World.title: What we know about the pilot hailed as a hero for averting crash of Israel-bound plane
World.content:
He is being hailed around the world as a hero for helping stop a passenger plane bound for Israel from plunging into the ground, despite his own severe injuries.

Images of Capt. Smit Machchhar covered in blood have gone viral after he fought his fellow pilot, who, according to Israeli officials, stabbed him and attempted to nose-dive the plane carrying 174 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv.

While bleeding profusely, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing other passengers and the Emirati crew to overpower the other pilot and take control of the aircraft. The flight was diverted to an airport in Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely.

The Mumbai native’s actions have “shown the world the highest form of courage” and “prevented another 9/11 like attack from happening,” Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Thursday, after speaking with Machchhar’s family. “The whole world is proud of him,” he added.

Machchhar spoke previously of getting the “aviation bug” at 19 while pursuing a management course to grow his family’s textile business.

He worked for years at a low-cost Indian airline before joining Flydubai, and had nearly 10,000 hours of flying experience before Wednesday’s incident.

Machchhar is being treated in a hospital in Tabuk city in northwest Saudi Arabia, with his condition described as “stable” on Wednesday by the Indian Embassy in Riyadh. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News he was “very badly wounded.”

Deepak Mittal, India’s ambassador to the United Arab Emirates, said on X he met with Machhar’s family on Thursday in Dubai and “conveyed full support of the Government of India in ensuring welfare and wellbeing of the Indian Hero.”

Flydubai Capt. Smit Machchhar. via Israel Foreign Ministry

A still image taken from video verified by NBC News shows a chaotic scene aboard the Flydubai plane as a man covered in blood receives treatment. via Telegram

Netanyahu called Machchhar “a true hero.”

“Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster,” he said.

Machchhar’s former employer, the Indian budget carrier SpiceJet, said on X that he flew for the airline for 10 years. According to his LinkedIn profile, Machchhar joined the Emirati low-cost carrier Flydubai in 2022 after flying for SpiceJet since 2011.

On Wednesday, the veteran captain was flying a Boeing 737 Max 8, the newer variant of the 737 plane that Machchhar had nearly 10,000 hours of experience flying, according to his profile and a YouTube podcast interview he gave last year.

“My first aircraft was a Boeing, and it’s always been that aircraft all my life,” he said.

Machchhar said he had flown challenging routes, dodged bad weather, and handled medical emergencies in the air before.

Passengers from the Flydubai flight arrive at Ben Gurion International Airport near Tel Aviv on Wednesday. Ariel Schalit / AP

His mother was “scared” when he first told her of his plan to become a pilot, he said in the 2025 interview, but his supportive father agreed to cover the steep fees for aviation training.

Between 2008 and 2009, Machchhar trained for 18 months at an aviation college in New Zealand. It was the first time he had been outside India, he said, and he had only been on a “couple of flights” as a passenger before learning to fly.

He “stood out” among those training and did well with his studies, Mainland Air chief executive Philip Kean told New Zealand’s 1News, adding: “We’re all very proud of him here.”

In his early days as a qualified pilot, he took whatever flight routes he was assigned.

“When I started flying ... the only thing I wanted to do then was fly,” Machchhar told the podcast. “I didn’t want to sleep, I didn’t want to go anywhere, and they loved me for it.”

“For a pilot to gain that experience and to refine your skills is what a pilot is,” he added.

But his attitude changed when he got married and started a family, he said.

“Now I would say I try when I get out of the cockpit or the aircraft, I don’t want the other guy to know that I’m a pilot. I don’t want to discuss aviation,” he said.

“Now the kids are there,” he said. “They want to play with you.”

In the interview, Machchhar also spoke about the “rigorous training” that pilots and cabin crew undergo, which includes safety and emergency procedures.

“When we are up there and if something happens, who is going to save you? You’ll be lucky enough to have a doctor on board,” he said.

“They can save your life,” he said, referring to the cabin crew.

World.title: Screaming, panicking, blood: Passengers detail horrifying Israel-bound flight
World.content:
TEL AVIV — A stabbing, an emergency alert, a terrifying mid-air plunge.

Details are still emerging after an Israel-bound flight carrying some 180 people emitted a distress signal Wednesday, raising fears of a possible hijacking when one pilot stabbed the other in the cockpit.

Aviatar Alevi, who was onboard the Flydubai flight Wednesday, described people “screaming, running, panicking, blood.”

“At the start I thought it was a plane malfunction, but then I started hearing screaming about the stabbings,” Alevi, 17, told NBC News. “Then I understood the weight of the actual situation.”

“We didn’t know what was going to happen,” he said, adding that the possibility of death “was definitely an option.”

Aviatar Alevi. NBC News

The plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, one of its rudders damaged, apparently by the force of its descent.

The passengers, who had been flying from Dubai before the crisis, were mobbed by media and flag-waving fellow Israelis after finally arriving at Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport.

They said they had feared for their lives after the plane plunged more than 14,000 feet in the span of 29 seconds at one point, according to FlightRadar24.

“Imagine sitting on the plane, all scared after you fell down five kilometers. You don’t understand anything,” 16-year-old Peleg Itali told NBC News.

Captain Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, was recovering in a hospital in Saudi Arabia on Thursday as the other pilot, so far identified only as an Omani citizen, was being interrogated elsewhere in the country. Machchhar was widely praised for his efforts to prevent the plane from crashing, opening the cockpit door and allowing passengers and crew to rush in.

Few details had emerged about the pilot as of Thursday morning. Questions about a possible motive, including whether it was terrorism-related, hang over the attack.

“I don’t think it was a hijacking. It looks like a suicide attempt, simply because of what this hero, Yaniv, has described,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on “CBS Evening News,” as he praised Yaniv Hayun, who rushed into the cockpit and subdued the attacker.

Hayun, who was pictured with his shirt spattered with blood sitting next to Netanyahu, said that he had confronted the pilot who had initiated the attack, according to the Israeli government press office.

“I grabbed the attacker, and choked him, pulled him out first,” Hayun said. “I started pulling the controls.”

“Thank God, we pulled it off. We really put our heads together and worked as a team,” Hayun said, adding: “It was between fear and a sense of a do-or-die situation.”

“We had to win. We had to pull through and come out on top,” he said. Hayun told Netanyahu that he had acted based on what he’d seen on a TV show and helped stabilize the plane.

Flydubai said on-duty crew who were onboard the flight were able to land the plane.

Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu and Yaniv Hayun, a flyDubai passenger who helped subdue the attacker during the incident on Wednesday. GPO via Reuters

Motive under investigation

Netanyahu said it was still too early to determine why the pilot apparently stabbed his colleague and appeared to try to take over the Flydubai flight, and whether there was any Iranian involvement.

“We’ve had signs that Iran, in particular through its proxies, was intending to heighten terrorist attacks against Israel and Israeli nationals abroad,” he said. “But I think it’s too early to say whether there was Iranian collusion here.”

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, meanwhile, branded the incident a “jihadist terrorist attack attempt,” without expanding on how he reached that conclusion.

President Donald Trump also weighed in, calling it “an incredible story.”

“It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job, and he stabbed the pilot,” Trump told reporters.

All the passengers were Israeli, according to Netanyahu’s office. Four were dual American-Israeli citizens, two U.S. officials told NBC News.

With few details on the suspect or on any potential motive surrounding the incident, Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for Netanyahu’s office said there was a “strong opinion” that the incident was a terror attack “but we can’t be sure until we debrief everybody.”

A still image taken from video verified by NBC News shows a chaotic scene on the Flydubai plane as a man covered in blood receives treatment. via Telegram

An investigation by Saudi authorities is ongoing, David Mencer, a spokesperson for the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office, separately said.

A senior U.S. official briefed on the Israeli investigation and a Saudi official also briefed on the probe said the stabbing increasingly looks like an act of terrorism based on early findings.

The United Arab Emirates’ Attorney-General, Dr. Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, separately ordered an investigation into the incident.

His office said the probe would seek to “gather information and evidence, establish the facts and circumstances of the incident, and determine the underlying motives,” in addition to examining “whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose, or involved any prior planning or direction.”

Hessa Alyahya, spokesperson for the Saudi Embassy in the U.S., said authorities were waiting to determine whether the attack was a dispute between the pilots or whether it was an act sponsored by Iran or the Houthis.

Israel and Saudi Arabia do not have official diplomatic relations.

World.title: How 16 undecided voters are weighing their 2026 election options
World.content:
James Morton isn’t sure which party he’s going to support in November’s elections, and he doesn’t like his options.

Morton, a 67-year-old retired truck driver in Colorado, said Democrats have “gone too far to the left towards socialism,” while Republicans are “globalists” who “don’t care about the working-class people in this country.”

Morton, an independent who voted for Donald Trump in 2024, is leaning toward backing third-party candidates in races for the House and the Senate this year. But he said his decision will come down to the high cost of living.

“The No. 1 thing is getting the cost of things back down, inflation under control, and pretty much that’s it,” Morton said. He noted that he and his wife have been buying different groceries as they navigate high prices.

Morton is among the 5% of voters surveyed last month in a national NBC News poll who said they weren’t sure which party they wanted to see controlling Congress after this year’s elections. NBC News spoke with 16 of those undecided voters as they weigh their votes this fall, some of whom declined to share their full names discussing politics.

These voters feel little loyalty to either party — and many of them said that’s in part because they aren’t sure either party understands what’s important to them. Almost every one said high costs are top of mind.

In the NBC News poll, 50% of voters said they wanted Democrats to win control of Congress in the midterms, while 45% said they wanted Republicans to have control. How the undecided voters in between resolve their strong, sometimes conflicting feelings could ultimately decide what Congress looks like in 2027, from who controls the majority to how many seats that party holds.

Costs dominate

Voters’ focus on making ends meet has been standing out in recent polling. In the latest NBC News survey, voters ranked cost of living and inflation as the most important issues facing the country, followed by government corruption and threats to democracy.

“I don’t like how expensive things are, and I don’t think anyone does,” said Aidan Valenzuela, a 19-year-old security worker in Texas, who said he hasn’t decided whom to support in his state’s hotly contested races for governor and the Senate.

Joanne, a 72-year-old Vermont independent who works for a heating company, said she plans to sit out her state’s governor’s race, and she hasn’t decided whom she’ll support farther down the ballot.

“I just want somebody to bring some of these prices back down,” she said. Joanne said her husband relies on multiple medications, including insulin. “It’s pretty expensive and leaves nothing for anything else.”

Luke Melanson, 49, of Louisiana, who is retired from construction work, said the rising cost of groceries has changed how he shops.

“I’m not eating as much. I’m eating less food because I can only afford so much,” he said.

Melanson doesn’t identify with either political party, instead considering himself a libertarian, and he declined to say where he was leaning in the midterm election. But he is frustrated with both parties and wants to see new candidates emerge who can personally relate to his financial position.

“I want a plumber. I want someone that ran a smaller business, like a Kroger’s,” he said. “A teacher. I take anybody that isn’t a lawyer or someone so ultra-rich that the pay gap is so far they would never understand what I’m going through.”

Meanwhile, South Carolinian Darien Thompson, a 25-year-old unarmed security guard at a mall, sees gas as the biggest financial woe of the moment. The cost of his commute is only going up.

“It does take a mental load when it’s like, well, it’s going to cost this much to get to work and back, and I’m only making this much,” Thompson said.

It doesn’t bode well for his long-term hopes of owning a home, and he doesn’t see any current politicians stepping up to tackle the issues in a way that has earned his support.

“Politicians are getting into these petty squabbles,” he said. “But it’s, like, none of us can afford houses.”

Thompson doesn’t see himself voting for a Republican in November, but he’s still undecided. He has leaned Democratic before, voting for then-Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, but his vote this year will depend entirely on the specific candidate Democrats run in his area.

Ibraham, a 42-year-old truck driver in Ohio who isn’t registered with either party, said he plans to back Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown in the Senate race in his state. Ibraham supported Harris in 2024 and said his vote this year is driven almost entirely by the surging price of diesel and a higher cost of living.

“I’ve been driving for nine years. I’ve never seen anything like it. Never. Never, ever. Even during Covid, it didn’t get that high,” Ibraham said, noting that his weekly diesel costs have jumped from $2,000 to $3,500 or $3,700.

“I’m spending an extra $1,500 on diesel every week. Just think about it — it’s a fortune,” he said.

Down on both parties and Trump

Ibraham described his support for Brown as more about opposing Republicans than endorsing Democrats, blaming the GOP-controlled White House and Congress for the current economic struggles.

“It’s not about Brown,” Ibraham said of his Senate vote. “It’s just voting against the Republicans for what they’re doing. That’s it.”

Other voters who were undecided but leaning toward Democrats expressed similar views, expressing caution and saying their potential support for Democrats was motivated more by reining in Trump and Republicans.

Several voters — including those who backed Trump two years ago — specifically voiced concerns about Trump’s handling of the economy and the war in Iran.

“I will probably support [a] Democrat this time around just so there’s some check and balances in place,” said Aaron L., a 30-year-old California independent who works in tech. He didn’t vote in 2024 while he was moving, but he said he most likely would have voted for Trump. But nearly two years into Trump’s second term, Aaron said, the economy is “a mess.”

“It seems like the party, the Republican Party, just follow whatever Donald Trump says,” Aaron said.

Like other undecided voters, Aaron said the economy and the war in Iran were among his top issues. Dissatisfaction with the war was high, including among Trump voters.

“One of his platforms was no more useless wars, and here we are — we’re back,” said Kevin, a 35-year-old civil engineer in Massachusetts. Kevin, a Democrat, voted for Trump in 2024 hoping he would boost the economy.

This year, he said, he is leaning toward supporting Republican Mike Minogue in the Massachusetts governor’s race, hoping he could shake up the state, and leaning toward backing Democratic Sen. Ed Markey for re-election.

“It goes back to the checks and balances,” Kevin said of the possibility that he could split his ticket, saying he wants to see a Democratic-controlled Congress end the war in Iran.

Kaleb Saracino, 21, of Nevada, doesn’t like how many resources are being poured into the Iran war or the idea that the U.S. is fighting there in behalf of Israel. He said he wants the government to cut off support for Israel, bring down costs and refocus on issues affecting everyday Americans.

“The cost of groceries, the cost of gas, the cost of living have all gone up because of these endless wars,” Saracino said.

Saracino knows he doesn’t want to support Trump, so he’s leaning toward the Democrats this year. But he doesn’t have warm feelings for either party.

“They’re looking out for themselves, their careers, because they’re career politicians, not so much the betterment of the American people,” Saracino said about both Republicans and Democrats.

Alexis, a 20-year-old college student in Florida, also expressed frustration with both parties in Washington.

“They’ve made a bunch of promises that haven’t been fulfilled, and you know why? It’s because people cannot talk to each other these days. Congress is so divided,” she said.

Alexis, an independent who voted for Harris in 2024, isn’t sure whom she’ll support in the Florida Senate race. She said more could get done “when we start allowing younger candidates who are more open-minded to vouching for the American people as a whole, rather than their own specific party.”

Essen Zali, a 46-year-old IT consultant from Texas, voted for Joe Biden in 2020 but backed Trump in 2024 after he became frustrated with Biden during the conflict in Gaza. Now, the Iran war has again left him frustrated.

“He went two steps forward with the whole war thing, and now we are all over the place,” he said. On top of that, Zali said, Trump seems focused on the wrong things.

“All the construction work that was going on in Washington, that was not ever required. All the beautifications and everything, that’s secondary. The tariff war without a reason,” Zali said. “It seems like he is burning all the ships.”

Connor Woodring, a 22-year-old independent from Colorado, also supported Trump in 2024. He was another voter who felt disdain for both parties.

“They’re one on the same side of the same coin, basically. Republicans are the warmongering side of it. Democrats are the side that try to pull at your heartstrings,” he said. “Either way, they’re going to vote and do the same thing they’ve done for the last 50 years, so it doesn’t matter which side you vote in.”

Woodring is a registered independent and doesn’t like any candidates in his area. His preference is to vote for someone not in either major party.

But, he said, “there’s a lot that can happen between now and November.”

World.title: Judge bars U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro from charging ex-Olympian in Reflecting Pool case
World.content:
WASHINGTON — A Superior Court judge in the District of Columbia has permanently banned U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office from bringing charges against a former Olympic canoeist over damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

Judge Todd Edelman entered an order on Thursday that dismissed the case with prejudice. Edelman cited the “exceptional circumstances” of the case and said the government’s “own representations make plain” that bringing another indictment against David “Davey” Hearn “is theoretical at best, and more likely, is simply fanciful.”

Trump, Edelman wrote, “has criticized the decision of the Office of the United States Attorney to drop the case in the most vituperative terms; demanded that the government reinstitute the prosecution, in part because of Mr. Hearn’s political activity and the identity of one of his attorneys; and publicly entertained the possibility of firing the United States Attorney as a result of the dismissal.”

Hearn, Edelman wrote, “faces the unique possibility that the government will revive this case — one that it has already announced to be meritless — based on political pressure brought by the President of the United States upon his subordinate officers.” The government “has no right to retain the ability to compound the errors it has already made, or even to threaten to do so, at Mr. Hearn’s expense,” Edelman wrote.

Trump had lashed out at Hearn over political donations and because one of his lawyers, Norm Eisen, has been a longtime Trump critic involved in many legal battles against the administration.

Eisen and Hearn’s other attorneys — Mary Dohrmann, Steve Levin and Michael Bromwich — said in a joint statement that the decision “is a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice” and said the case never should have been brought in the first place.

“This was a miscarriage of justice, and what happened to Mr. Hearn is an outrage that should shock every American,” they wrote. “This administration chose to pursue an unjust prosecution against Mr. Hearn. It should not get repeated chances to wield the power of criminal prosecution against someone who should never have been prosecuted. Today’s decision protects Mr. Hearn from that threat, allowing him to move forward with his life as he deserves.”

Pirro’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Attorneys for Hearn and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia sparred in court last month over whether Hearn’s Reflecting Pool case should be dismissed with prejudice, meaning prosecutors would be barred from bringing another case against him. At the center of much of the discussion: Donald Trump’s pressure campaign on Pirro’s office and his decision to link his desire for prosecution to the political beliefs of Hearn and one of his attorneys, Norm Eisen.

Pirro’s office dropped the case in late July after evidence showed the area was already damaged, and Hearn’s team moved to ban the office from bringing another case in August.

At an unrelated press conference last month, Pirro declined to answer several questions from reporters about her handling of the Reflecting Pool case.

Former Olympian David Hearn outside D.C. Superior Court in July. Daniel Heuer / Bloomberg via Getty Images file

Pirro’s office wanted to maintain its ability to bring a theoretical case, even though its own evidence — that the section of the Reflecting Pool that Hearn allegedly touched was already damaged, and they can’t prove more than $1,000 in damage — would make bringing another felony case impossible.

“What future prosecution could even occur?” Edelman asked at the hearing.

“That I don’t know,” said Michael Spence, a career official in the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia.

“Give me an example of one possible thing that could happen” to change the fundamentally flawed case, the judge asked. “Even theoretically, what could there be?”

Spence conceded he had no satisfactory answer. He added that the U.S. Attorney’s Office had no investigation going into Hearn “as of this second” but said that could change.

Edelman noted that it was going to be pretty difficult to find a case with similar circumstances to Hearn’s case, and asked Spence how he was supposed to look at Trump’s statements calling for a prosecution that Pirro’s office admits was meritless. The president’s statements, Spence said, “speak for themselves.”

Steve Levin, an attorney for Hearn, said prosecutors “had no case” and that the government abused its prosecutorial discretion by rushing to indict Hearn to please the president, misleading a grand jury along the way.

“That’s where the bad faith comes into play,” Levin said. How is Hearn supposed to trust the grand jury process, Levin asked, given that the case got through before? “There’s no confidence that Mr. Hearn has that the grand jury will do the right thing” if another case was presented,” he said.

Jeanine Pirro is U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia. Anna Moneymaker / Getty Images file

Pirro’s office, Levin argued, is trying to keep a “discredited felony accusation on life support,” and doing so served no public interest.

“There is nothing that can save the case they dismissed,” Levin said. “The government has basically acknowledged there is nothing that can revive this case.”

But Spence said the grand jury process would still give Hearn protection from a bad faith prosecution.

“The government did act in good faith in this case,” Spence argued.

World.title: Whale sinks yacht in South Pacific, sailors rescued alive 18 hours later
World.content:
A sperm whale cracked the hull of a yacht sailing in the remote South Pacific, forcing four sailors into a day-and-night fight for survival on the high seas.

Crew members on the 52-foot Tai Tam told AFP on Thursday of their weekend encounter with a pod of sperm whales 250 nautical miles north of tiny Norfolk Island.

"There was sort of a loud thud. The whole boat was pushed sideways," said Australian Jemma Cooper, who was thrown from the steering wheel by the force of the blow.

Not knowing at first what had happened, she noticed a brown discoloration in the water and a sperm whale.

"We looked out to our port side, and there were six to eight, a pod, of whales there. So then it became clear that that's what it was," she told AFP.

Her husband Jeremy Cooper said he was sleeping below deck when the impact woke him.

"It was pretty immediately evident it was very serious," he said.

"All the steering gear was smashed on the starboard side, and there was a significant amount of water coming in," Jeremy told AFP.

A sperm whale cracked the hull of a yacht sailing in the remote South Pacific. New Zealand Defence Force

At 1 p.m. New Zealand time on Saturday — about 30 minutes after the whale collision — they activated an emergency beacon.

"We declared a full mayday," said New Zealand crew member Terry Hetherington, adding they spent the next few hours bailing out as much water as they could.



"Terrible ending"

The Royal New Zealand Air Force flew a P-8A Poseidon patrol plane to the area to establish radio communications and coordinate the rescue, the military said in a news release, which included images of the rescue.

French crew member Martin Jaffre said the whale collision left several gashes in the hull and cracked the fiberglass structure, as well as breaking the steering.

"We could no longer steer the boat, and a boat with no steering quickly becomes a problem," he told AFP.

Jaffre battled to slow the incoming water with anything to hand, including expansion foam, and swam below the boat to inspect the hull, his crewmates said.

The sailors tried to stay aboard as long as possible, struggling to stop the engine getting clogged and bailing by hand.

Late at night, they abandoned the boat and transferred to a life raft in calm seas and under a full moon.

In the early hours of Sunday morning, they cut the tether to the yacht, fearing it might drag them down. Soon after, it slipped beneath the waves.

The New Zealand military released dramatic drone video of the yacht plunging below the water's surface and the crew ultimately being rescued.

A 470-foot container ship, the MV Sofrana Surville, rescued the sailors at 6 a.m. on Sunday, the New Zealand military said — about 18 hours after their encounter with the sperm whale.

Even the rescue was scary as the giant ship approached their tiny life raft, recalled Jeremy Cooper.

But within half an hour they had scaled a ladder to join their rescuers, have a cup of coffee and chat with the captain, he said, ruing the end of their Pacific holiday voyage.

"It was wonderful, wonderful, and just a terrible, terrible ending — but luckily no loss of life."

A sperm whale cracked the hull of a yacht sailing in the remote South Pacific. The four sailors were rescued about 18 hours later. New Zealand Defence Force

Rescue Coordination Centre Operations Manager Mike Clulow praised the efforts of the rescue team and the yacht's crew.

"This was a well-coordinated and executed rescue," Clulow said. "The crew of the yacht did all the right things, and it was unfortunate to have struck a whale in open water. They were well prepared and the early activation of their EPIRB (Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacon) was key to helping get them to safety. It is an excellent reminder that being prepared when going to sea can save your life."

Adult male sperm whales measure between 50 and 60 feet. They are considered a "vulnerable" species by the nonprofit International Union for Conservation of Nature. Sperm whales reproduce once every five to seven years and have experienced significant population decline. The species is under threat from noise pollution, plastic consumption and ship strikes.

The incident in New Zealand marks at least the second time in less than two months that a whale has sunk a boat. In July, a whale that surfaced for air slammed into a New Jersey fire department's boat, sinking the ship with firefighters on board. Someone on a personal watercraft nearby and a boater helped rescue the firefighters from the water.

World.title: Who qualifies for credit card debt forgiveness?
World.content:
We may receive commissions from some links to products on this page. Promotions are subject to availability and retailer terms.

You don't have to live with overwhelming credit card debt. You have options. Getty Images

Inflation is surging again. That's according to a new report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, showing the rate at 3.3%, the highest it has been in multiple years. That's left food prices, as well as other basic living expenses, running substantially higher than they were just a year ago. That combination of issues has left millions of Americans leaning harder on credit cards just to cover the basics. So, while carrying a balance used to be an occasional inconvenience, it's increasingly becoming a way of life for many borrowers. With credit card interest rates over 20%, however, and interest compounding daily, this can be a financially risky approach to take.

But there's a point at which carrying a balance tips from manageable to genuinely dangerous — typically when minimum payments start to feel out of reach, and interest charges are outrunning any real progress on the principal. That's when borrowers often start asking about credit card debt forgiveness, which is a process that involves negotiating directly with a creditor or debt collector to settle an account for less than what's owed. If successful, a reduced lump-sum payment closes out the debt entirely.

That can sound like a lifeline, and for some people it is. But debt forgiveness isn't without consequences. It can damage your credit score and complicate future borrowing. So, before you decide on this path, it's worth understanding both what it offers and whether you're the right type of borrower to take advantage of it.

Get access to the credit card debt relief you need now.

Who qualifies for credit card debt forgiveness?

When it comes to credit card debt relief, it's important to dispel a common misconception: There are no government-sponsored programs specifically designed to eliminate credit card debt. So, you should be wary of any offers claiming to represent such government initiatives, as they may be misleading or fraudulent.

However, this doesn't mean that credit card debt forgiveness is entirely out of reach. While not backed by the government, certain types of credit card debt forgiveness do exist. While it's highly improbable that a credit card issuer would completely erase your debt outside of bankruptcy proceedings, you might have the option to negotiate with your creditors for a partial reduction of your outstanding balance. In fact, nearly anyone who is having a hard time making their credit card payments could qualify for forgiveness.

How to get your credit card debt forgiven

There are a couple of ways to get your debt forgiven by credit card companies. Those include:

Debt settlement programs

Debt settlement programs are a type of debt relief service. At the start of the program, a debt relief expert will typically analyze your debts and financial position. Using this information, the expert will create an affordable, effective payment plan.

When you make your payments to the debt settlement company, they generally hold the money in a special-purpose savings account. Once you've saved enough money to settle your debts, the debt settlement company starts negotiating with your creditors in hopes of reducing your principal balance. These negotiations are often successful, resulting in significant long-term savings.

But there are some potential disadvantages to think about before signing up for one of these services. For starters, debt settlement companies do not make payments to your creditors as you save for your settlement. That will likely hurt your credit score and impact the ability to borrow for some time.

Moreover, there's no guarantee that your credit card company will accept the settlement. If they don't accept it, you could end up with a larger debt burden than you started with, and if they do, you'll likely need to pay income taxes on the amount of debt that was forgiven.

Find out how a debt relief service can help you now.

Bankruptcy

If credit card debt settlement doesn't provide enough relief, it may be time to reach out to a bankruptcy attorney. Sure, bankruptcy will likely harm your credit score and ability to borrow in the near term, but as a last resort, it's often an effective way to get out of overwhelming credit card debt. You may be able to get your debt 100% forgiven through bankruptcy, giving you the ability to restart on a clean financial slate.

Debt forgiveness may not be your only option

Debt settlement programs and bankruptcy both have the potential to result in forgiven debt, but they're also likely to have a significant impact on your credit score and your ability to borrow. But there are other options to consider, too, including:

The bottom line

Credit card debt can be overwhelming, but you don't have to deal with it forever. If debt consolidation loans are unavailable and debt management programs don't offer enough relief, it may be wise to use a debt settlement company to try and get a percentage of your debt forgiven. But if debt settlement doesn't provide enough relief, it may be time to file bankruptcy and restart on a clean financial slate.

This story has been updated to clarify the difference between debt management and debt consolidation programs.

World.title: Alleged Cornell gang rape victim said "I had so much ketamine ... and you still had sex with me," roommate claims
World.content:
CBS News New York has been combing through records that take us inside Cornell University's Title IX investigation into an alleged gang rape at a fraternity.

The records offer a closer look at how Jane Doe described what she says happened to her that night and in the days that followed, as well as how people around her remembered it.

The records include interviews with Doe, six of the seven men named in Doe's bombshell civil lawsuit, and 20 witnesses.

Some of the information in the records is graphic and disturbing.

One roommate recalls Doe saying "Oh my goodness, isn't that crazy?" the morning after the alleged incident at Cornell's Chi Phi house in October 2024.

The roommate said Doe was laughing as she recounted it, but seemed to be in shock. The roommate said Doe did not call it rape or assault that next morning.

A second roommate said Jane Doe did tell her "I wasn't comfortable."

About a week later, that second roommate said she heard Doe tell one of the men "You had penetrative sex with me. I had so much ketamine, my eyes were crossed, and you still had sex with me."

Those accounts are in transcripts of Cornell's Title IX investigation, distributed to the parties in January 2025. CBS News New York obtained them from a source. The documents are part of the record but do not include the Title IX panel's hearing minutes, reasoning or final findings.

In her Title IX interview in November, Doe said she didn't show "excitement and enthusiasm, which is kinda the basis of consent."

She said she told the men she was tired and didn't want to continue, and that she was sometimes encouraged to take more substances.

Doe could not pinpoint when she lost the ability to make decisions. She said she whispered to one man that she was uncomfortable.

The men, now accused of rape and assault, gave their accounts, too.

One said he asked Jane Doe if he could take ketamine from her body. He said she agreed.

Another, Scott Kretzschmar, said he was in the room for "tops, five minutes," did not see her naked, and did not do drugs.

Kretzschmar told a Title IX investigator he asked Doe if she was OK. He said her response was "I'm good" and that "she didn't seem inebriated at all."

The lawsuit names seven men and makes different allegations against them. Four are specifically accused of rape. The allegation against Kretzschmar is that he snorted ketamine from Doe's body, something his attorney Jeremy Saland denies.

"The process that Cornell had was absolutely biased in my personal experience ... biased in favor of her, not these young boys," Saland said.

Cornell said its Title IX process lasted months, included a hearing before a panel of trained faculty and staff, and resulted in sanctions, including expulsions and suspensions.

The allegations of a gang rape sparked outrage and questions about how Cornell University and its police handled the case.

The district attorney initially declined to bring charges, but has now reopened the investigation.

CBS News New York's investigative unit is continuing to work its way through the record.

World.title: Christa Pike's botched execution follows a pattern of issues with lethal drugs
World.content:
Christa Pike, the only woman on Tennessee's death row, received two doses of a lethal drug in a Nashville execution chamber Wednesday night. But she didn't die.

Although her survival was "unparalleled," as one expert said, it was the latest example of a botched execution attempt involving lethal injections in Tennessee and elsewhere around the United States.

"All of this was predicted, and the court did nothing," said Steve Ferrell, an attorney for Pike, at a news conference Thursday, referencing the state's history of problems with its lethal drug protocol.

Pike, 50, was condemned for the 1995 murder of her former classmate Colleen Slemmer, then 19, whom she and two others tortured and killed in a manner widely described as gruesome, horrific and disturbing. Eighteen at the time of the attack and 20 at her sentencing, Pike was the youngest woman sent to death row in the country's modern capital punishment era.

The extent of Pike's injuries after the failed execution was unclear, but her attorneys said Thursday that she was still alive and receiving "lifesaving medical care" at a hospital. A doctor told CBS partner BBC News that Pike would have likely suffered traumatic brain injury.

Her legal team had said in an emergency motion to halt the execution Wednesday night that she had not lost consciousness, retained a heartbeat and could be heard audibly snoring on the gurney, despite correctional staff administering two syringes' worth of the drug pentobarbital to her through an IV. At one point, Associated Press reporter Kim Chandler, who witnessed the execution, said Pike "looked toward prison officials and asked if it was supposed to feel that way."

"The case of Christa Pike lays bare multiple reasons why the death penalty should be abolished," United Nations human rights chief Volker Turk said in a statement on Thursday. "The prolonged suffering — physical and mental — arising from multiple failed execution attempts is abhorrent, and cruel. And there are key fair trial questions still unresolved."

Emergency vehicles arrive at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution after the execution of Christa Pike was halted Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, in Nashville, Tennessee. AP Photo/George Walker IV

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee, whose denial of Pike's clemency petition this week allowed the execution to move forward, has since announced the state will cancel the one remaining execution scheduled to take place this year, so that "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred" on Wednesday night could be conducted.

A problematic history

Pike's bungled injection wasn't a first for Tennessee. Earlier this year, in May, the state halted the planned execution of death row inmate Tony Carruthers when officers failed to establish an IV line through which to administer his lethal injection, after trying to do so for more than an hour.

At the time, Carruthers' attorney said he had been "tortured," telling CBS News that he groaned and bled from multiple attempted injection sites as staff tasked with handling the execution repeatedly punctured him in his chest, arms, feet and neck.

The defense team representing Carruthers had asked a Tennessee district court to stop the execution, alleging the ordeal "constituted cruel and unusual punishment," in violation of his constitutional rights, but the request was denied on the grounds that a burden of proof to demonstrate the state's actions were "cruel and unusual" hadn't been met.

Lee ultimately granted Carruthers a yearlong reprieve from execution, meaning that he'll return to the chamber a second time to be put to death after that. The governor said he wouldn't reconsider Carruthers' clemency petition, even as gaps in forensic evidence sparked public doubt over the legitimacy of the murder conviction for which he was sentenced to death.

Carruthers was among seven U.S. inmates whose executions by lethal injection failed because of issues establishing an IV line in the modern death penalty era, although researchers say other instances may exist. His attorneys' allegations of torture and unconstitutionally cruel punishment also echoed similar accusations from representatives of other inmates who've experienced botched execution attempts due to this problem.

In addition to Tennessee, these incidents have happened in Alabama, Arizona, Florida, Oklahoma and Texas, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, an organization that provides data on capital punishment but doesn't take a position on it.

Pike's survival was "singular and unparalleled," marking the first execution where an inmate remained alive after receiving lethal drugs, versus other instances where failure to locate a vein ultimately prevented the drugs from being administered, Robin Maher, the Death Penalty Information Center's executive director, told the AP. In a statement, her organization drew connections between Pike's execution and that of Clayton Lockett in Oklahoma in 2014, where Lockett appeared to survive the procedure but died of a heart attack while still in the execution chamber.

Media witnesses recount the moments before the execution of Christa Pike was halted Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, in Nashville, Tennessee. AP Photo/George Walker IV

Tennessee resumed executions in 2025 after a three-year hiatus, triggered by controversy and criticism surrounding its execution protocol. Lee, in 2022, said the pause would allow for an investigation into its lethal injection process after it was determined that corrections officials didn't test the lethal drugs they'd planned to use for that year's execution of Oscar Smith for bacteria. That review led Tennessee to alter its lethal injection protocol, shifting from a procedure involving three different drugs to the current one used in Pike's case, consisting solely of pentobarbital.

The Tennessee Department of Correction said it "followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol" in a statement released after Pike's procedure.

"The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening," the statement said.

"Veiled in secrecy"

Experts and groups advocating against the death penalty have sounded alarms for years about issues with lethal drugs used in executions. Declining support for capital punishment nationwide and skepticism over how executions were being carried out led pharmaceutical companies over the last decade or so to cut ties with state corrections departments, which, in turn, struggled to acquire lethal drugs.

Advocates have said this shift has contributed to increased incidents of lethal injections gone awry, accusing states of putting inmates to death with expired or untested chemicals. Because the details of execution protocols, within and outside of Tennessee, are frequently allowed to be kept secret, contesting them, legally, is difficult.

Pike's lawyers had raised concerns about Tennessee's protocol in appeals leading up to the execution, and Pike herself said she was "nervous" about how the procedure would play out in a letter that CBS News obtained from her spiritual adviser this week.

"I am not afraid to die. I'm only nervous about the process," said Pike in the letter, written Monday, before she learned Lee had denied her petition for clemency.

Her attorneys said the circumstances around Pike's execution proved their concerns had been valid.

"Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution," they said in a statement. "We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms. Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy."

World.title: More details emerge about FlyDubai co-pilot who tried to crash plane
World.content:
One day after a FlyDubai co-pilot made a violent attempt to crash the passenger aircraft and was subdued by passengers and other crew members, questions about his identity and motive continued to swirl Thursday.

The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was approaching Israel when the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the flight captain and attempted to crash the aircraft, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said. The captain was able to fight off the co-pilot long enough to unlock the cockpit door. Passengers then overpowered the co-pilot, and two off-duty pilots who were on the flight managed to gain control of the aircraft and make an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

There were 174 people aboard the plane. No passengers were seriously injured in the incident. The pilot sustained stab wounds in the attack. Saudi authorities said two crew members were hospitalized with unspecified injuries, and the co-pilot remained in custody on Thursday.

Who was the FlyDubai co-pilot?

The co-pilot of the flight has not yet been publicly identified.
