World.title: Two years in, Sheinbaum touts approval ratings of up to 75%: Thursday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🇲🇽 Sheinbaum marks two years in office: Speaking on the second anniversary of her swearing-in as Mexico’s first female president, Sheinbaum acknowledged the milestone at the start of the mañanera, noting that her government has now been in office for two years.

📖 Sheinbaum thanks AMLO for his book dedication: Asked about López Obrador’s 80-minute video message on Wednesday launching his new book, “Pueblo” (People), which he dedicated to her, Sheinbaum called his words “very moving.” She said she hasn’t yet got a copy but hopes to get one today.

👧🏽👦🏽 Sheinbaum says girls and boys now know ‘it’s possible’ for a woman to govern: Asked what has changed for women since she took office, the president said her election changes children’s “mentality” about who can lead a country. She cited the pension scheme for women aged 60 to 64, the constitutional enshrinement of women’s rights and a new anti-femicide law as government achievements, and said there is now “a before and an after” for women in Mexico.

📊 Sheinbaum cites strong approval ratings at the two-year mark: She asked for recent poll results to be displayed, showing a 74.9% approval rating in a FactoMétrica survey and 70% in an El Financiero poll. Sheinbaum attributed her popularity to her “principles,” including “not betraying the people.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

Claudia Sheinbaum held her Thursday morning press conference exactly two years after she was sworn in as Mexico’s first female president. She acknowledged the milestone at the start of the mañanera, noting that the government she leads has now been in office for two years.

Sheinbaum noted that her predecessor, Andrés Manuel López Obrador, spoke about her during an 80-minute video message on Wednesday, during which he launched his new book — a political history of Mexico called “Pueblo” (People).

🚨AMLO dedica su nuevo libro a Claudia Sheinbaum Andrés Manuel López Obrador anunció que dedica su nuevo libro, “Pueblo”, a la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum, a quien calificó como un “orgullo” y un ejemplo de trabajo, honestidad, rectitud y lealtad al pueblo. El expresidente… pic.twitter.com/eckb8HamNq — Azucena Uresti (@azucenau) October 1, 2026

Speaking from his home in Palenque, Chiapas, AMLO noted that he had dedicated the book to his successor.

“I dedicate it to Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo, our president and great pride, example of hard work, honesty, rectitude and loyalty to the people,” López Obrador said, reading from a page at the start of his book.

He subsequently described Sheinbaum as “the best president in the world, including men and women.”

While an assertion that Sheinbaum is the best president in the world is, of course, subjective, it is a fact that she is Mexico’s first female president.

Now two years into her six-year term, Sheinbaum spoke about the significance of her election to Mexico’s top job and also highlighted that she has broad support from the Mexican people, per opinion poll results.

Sheinbaum thanks AMLO for book dedication

Sheinbaum noted that López Obrador launched his new book on Wednesday.

“President López Obrador surprised us yesterday with his new book. I don’t have it yet. I hope to go and buy it today,” she said.

Sheinbaum described AMLO’s video message as “very moving.”

“I really appreciate his words,” she said.

“The whole message is very good. He puts what we’re going through in context,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum: Girls and boys now know ‘it’s possible’ for a woman to govern Mexico

A reporter reminded Sheinbaum that she said “It’s time for women” in her inaugural speech as president, and asked her what has changed for women in Mexico in the two years since she took office.

Sheinbaum first spoke about the significance of having a female president for the first time in Mexico and what that means for “the new generations.”

She said that girls and boys now know it’s possible for a woman to lead the country. Consequently, children’s “mentality” changes, Sheinbaum said.

She said that when she was growing up it seemed “impossible” that Mexico would have a female president because all the presidents were men. Sheinbaum then noted that in addition to having a woman president, Mexico now has a significant number of female governors.

She highlighted some of her government’s achievements for women, including the establishment of a pension scheme for women aged 60 to 64, the enshrinement of a range of women’s rights in the Mexican Constitution and the formulation of a new anti-femicide law.

World.title: MND Local CDMX: From a new theater to a crackdown on counterfeit games
World.content:
Mexico City is seeing new developments across its cultural, environmental and commercial landscapes this week. A new artistic hub opened in Santa María la Ribera, 10 significant trees received formal protections, and authorities seized more than 470 counterfeit gaming products in the Historic Center. Let’s get into it.

Santa María la Ribera gets a new theatre experience

A new artistic hub has officially set up shop in Mexico City’s Santa María la Ribera neighborhood. Dubbed Centro Cultural Casa Hechale, the new space occupies a 110-year-old home that was transformed into a multidisciplinary facility, hosting everything from artist residencies and theatre performances to sonic explorations and community events.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by CASA HECHALE (@casahechale)

The project, Hechale Productions, is the brainchild of Héctor Zavala, a seasoned bilingual theatre director and performer with deep roots in California’s San Francisco Bay Area.

“This is not simply about opening a venue in another city,” Zavala said, per Broadway World. “It is about creating the conditions for artists to stay with a question long enough for it to become a piece of work — and to encounter people, languages and histories that may change the direction of that work.”

Centro Cultural Casa Hechale will serve as a “working cultural center and a place of exchange.” Its flagship program is AWAKEN YOUR ARTIST, a weeklong residency for artists from Mexico City and abroad to “examine not only how they make work, but also where their artistic instincts come from and what experiences have shaped their voices,” according to industry outlet Broadway World.

“Artists often move between cities because the work requires it, but the structures that support that movement are not always there,” Zavala said. “Casa Hechale is our attempt to build one of those structures: a place with memory, but also a place where something not yet known can begin.”

Mexico City issues protective orders for 10 trees

Mexico City’s Environment Ministry issued nine decrees on Sept. 28, formally protecting 10 trees across six boroughs and recognizing their environmental and symbolic importance.

The decrees include special protections that limit development in the immediate vicinity of the trees, such as infrastructure work, excavations and installations, or anything else that could threaten their trunks, roots, crowns or branches.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by LJA.MX Noticias México | Historias para ti 💫 (@somoslja)

The trees, located in Benito Juárez, Coyoacán, La Magdalena Contreras, Azcapotzalco, Xochimilco and Tlalpan, include seven Montezuma cypress trees, one white cedar, one olive tree and one oak tree.

These trees are so important, both ecologically and symbolically, that some of them even have names:

“Ahuehuetlán” in Parque de las Américas

“Atlahuitl” in Coyoacán

“Cedro de Padierna” in La Magdalena Contreras

“Los Gemelos de San Álvaro” in Azcapotzalco

“Molotla,” “Teuhtli,” “San Cristóbal Xallan,” and “Tlalnahuac” in Xochimilco

“Diamante Tepeximilpa,” a roughly 400-year-old oak tree in Tlalpan

“Beyond their physical characteristics, some of these trees are linked to ancient settlements, agricultural traditions, and territorial landmarks that have given identity to neighborhoods and Indigenous communities,” the Environment Ministry noted in a news release. “Their continued existence allows the connection between these communities and the natural environment that has accompanied them throughout history to remain alive.”

Corn producers also receive protections

It’s not just trees that are being protected. Mexico City Mayor Clara Brugada recently announced 10 actions to protect the region’s corn producers, as well as the crop’s diversity and availability.

“These ten actions form a single public policy for the defense of corn,” Brugada said Sept. 29 during the opening day of a corn festival in Mexico City’s Historic Center. “We support those who plant it, we protect the seed, we care for its diversity, we bring producers closer to consumers, and we take native corn from the milpa to the tortilla and from the tortilla to the table.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Clara Brugada (@clara_brugada_m)

Brugada added, “Defending corn is defending a chain of life: the seed, the land, the producer, our food, our sovereignty, our culture.”

‘Operation Limpieza’ spells game over for some CDMX vendors

Authorities in Mexico City recovered more than 470 counterfeit products from three shopping centers that cater to gamers and other fandoms, totaling more than 1.2 million pesos (roughly US $70,000).

Authorities raided Friki Plaza, Fan Center and Plaza Meave, all located in the Historic Center and serving the capital’s gaming, anime and manga communities, on Sept. 29 in a sting known as “Operación Limpieza.”

According to El Universal, the enforcement action targeted 15 stores across the three plazas and netted 477 products valued at more than 1.2 million pesos, including video games, consoles, accessories and collectible figures.

The operation was carried out by the Naval Ministry (SEMAR), the Citizen Security Ministry (SSC) and the Mexican Institute of Industrial Property (IMPI).

Aside from the obvious copyright infringement and intellectual property rights issues, authorities warned that some counterfeit products could carry health and safety risks, since they don’t undergo the same quality assurance processes as commercial products.

“The commercialization of counterfeit products can affect those who develop and produce original goods, distort competitive conditions, and create risks for consumers, who may purchase products without guarantees of origin, quality or safety,” IMPI said in a statement. “Therefore, monitoring and verification actions are part of the institutional work to promote respect for intellectual property rights and contribute to a legal commercial environment.”

Operation Limpieza is something of a catch-all term for the Mexican government’s attempts at combating counterfeit goods and piracy. A similar operation was carried out in Coahuila in December 2024, while several more targeted Mexico City and the state of México in May 2025.

Drew Pittock serves as Mexico News Daily’s features director. He is based in Mexico City. Have an idea for a feature story or unique event in CDMX? Send an email to drew.pittock@mexiconewsdaily.com.

World.title: Mexico and My Money: What to know about working with Mexican builders and contractors
World.content:
As a homeowner in Guadalajara for the past four years, I’ve hired my share of tradespeople, including plumbers, painters, electricians, furniture makers and general contractors.

It didn’t always go well, to put it mildly.

But it turns out I am not unique. Many of our readers who are property owners and responded to the recent Mexico and My Money financial survey shared details about their own contractor engagements that went sideways.

Below is a sample of the reader feedback we received when we asked for details about contractor experiences in Mexico that did not go well:

“I’ve had contractors not use the materials they said they did.”

“Disagreements over what was included with certain construction costs arose from familiarity with what is typical in the U.S. versus what is typical in Mexico.”

“Terrible workmanship.”

“Surprise extra costs.”

“Prepaying for construction renos, ‘to buy materials,’ and never seeing the guy again.”

“Paid up front for work that never happened.”

“Contractor would not take responsibility for subcontractor’s bad work.”

Besides outright fraud, problems can arise over project cost, timing, the quality of materials, who takes responsibility and the scope of work.

Like any industry, the trades can attract bad actors. But clients are not without responsibility and sometimes act in ways that contribute to problems.

Cultural differences could impact building work

The funniest story I’ve ever encountered about an expat’s struggle to renovate a house while living abroad was Peter Mayle’s 1989 bestseller, “A Year in Provence.”

The British author’s fixation on rigid schedules and worker efficiency was constantly at odds with his French contractors’ fluid approach to time and focus on enjoying life’s pleasures (especially food!) over work.

For Americans and Canadians living in Mexico, this cultural clash will probably sound familiar. Those of us raised in Anglo-Saxon cultures misread Latin people constantly.

But with a little effort to better understand Mexican culture, we can reduce the risk of problems when working with contractors here. Below are some common missteps expats make, and how to avoid them.

Hiring contractors without meeting them in person first

Mexican society relies heavily on personal relationships. Face-to-face interactions matter a lot more here than in Anglo-Saxon cultures. If they refuse, or your gut tells you something is off when you meet, do not hire them!

Failing to conduct due diligence and vet potential contractors

We foreigners often rely too much on social media to find workers, but these platforms (I won’t name names) are a notorious playground for scammers. While it may take more time, reach out to neighbors or friends you know and trust for recommendations instead.

Most Mexicans wouldn’t dream of hiring workers without first getting positive feedback from family, friends or neighbors. This reduces the odds of hiring a contractor who does poor work or has no idea how to do what’s being asked.

Paying most (or all) of the project cost upfront

I’ve seen expats pay a large percentage, or a project’s entire cost, up front and remotely. After doing this, they never hear from the “contractor” again. If they’d taken the time to do the two steps described above, this almost certainly wouldn’t have happened.

Not speaking Spanish

Overreliance on contractors who speak English in Mexico is a recipe for excluding the most reputable and best-qualified workers, as the vast majority of tradespeople in Mexico do not speak much, if any, English.

Also, the relief that monolingual expats feel speaking their own language in a foreign culture may inadvertently lower their guard, making them more susceptible to fraud.

If you don’t speak Spanish, find a local translator or use a translation app to help you communicate with local workers. Trust me, it’s worth the effort.

Not getting project quotes in writing , with details on what is in scope

It may feel like a hassle to get everything in writing, especially when a worker isn’t tech-savvy or struggles to write due to a lack of formal schooling. But it’s an important step that ensures you and your contractor are aligned on the work to be done. If there’s a disagreement over work scope later on, you have something concrete to refer back to.

Attempting to book a contractor far in advance

I once tried to book a painter for an outdoor job during the rainy season, telling them I’d like to begin the work in a few months when it would be drier.

Big mistake. Some of the painters ghosted me.

A Mexican friend later explained that tradespeople in Mexico don’t operate this way. Most are focused on today and this week, not next month or next year.

Plus, in an economy with high inflation and uncertain supply chains, workers aren’t sure what materials will cost a few months from now. So, they will probably avoid giving you a quote until they have a good idea when the work will happen.

Checklist for working with tradespeople and contractors in Mexico

Get recommendations from your friends and neighbors. Preferably Mexican neighbors who have personally hired the contractor for work, instead of relying on social media.

Vet contractors thoroughly . Meet them in person and ask for a copy of their ID before making a down payment. Check online reviews (if they have any) or client referrals.

Collect multiple quotes and do not accept the first quote offered . Negotiate the price.

Get your project quote in writing. This should include an outline of exactly what the deliverables are.

Set up a payment schedule aligned to work progress . Do not accept a heavily front-loaded payment plan.

Provide a budget to set expectations . While few contractors will guarantee a fixed price (unforeseen challenges do occur), creating a financial ceiling for the project is important.

Create a timeline . While deadlines generally don’t work, having no timeline increases the odds of a contractor taking longer to finish a job.

Ask for photos of the receipts if your contractor purchases supplies . Avoid being overcharged for materials or having inferior ones substituted.

Review all work . Ensure it meets your standards before making a final payment, so that you have some leverage if something needs to be corrected.

What else have you tried when working with contractors in Mexico? Please drop your ideas in the comments below.

From tipping to moving money into Mexico from abroad, check out more from MND’s “Mexico and My Money” archive.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: France woos Mexico as a stronger trade partner, citing US uncertainties
World.content:
As the two nations celebrated 200 years of economic relations, a French trade minister encouraged Mexico to deepen its ties with his country as a means to diversify its markets and supply chains, thereby reducing pressure on its strained trade relationship with the United States.

During the presentation of the France-Mexico Economic Report 2026 on Tuesday, French Minister Delegate for Foreign Trade and Economic Attraction Nicolas Forissier emphasized that France and Mexico share a commitment to multilateralism and to rules-based trade relations.

Closer modern ties between Mexico and France followed the May 22 signing of the Modernized Global Agreement between Mexico and the European Union (EU), updating an agreement that had been in effect since 2000. The aim is to expand trade and investment, eliminate most remaining tariffs, and improve access to services, investment, and public procurement. It effectively eliminates tariffs on 99% of products traded between the EU and Mexico, significantly facilitating agricultural trade.

This joint stance is fueled by global trade uncertainty, as the U.S. Trump administration continues to pressure Mexico to meet its demands as part of negotiations to conclude the review of the United States-Mexico-Canada Free Trade Agreement (USMCA).

Forissier stressed the importance of securing supply chains, especially those linked to critical minerals and rare earth elements, given the risk that these resources could be used as tools for economic pressure.

He said that France views Mexico as a gateway to the Americas, while Paris seeks to position itself as a platform for Mexican companies to access the European Union, North Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East.

Forissier urged French companies to increase their presence and investment in Mexico and called for greater investment from Mexican companies in France to solidify a mutually beneficial economic relationship.

Around 700 French companies already operate in Mexico, including 37 of France’s 40 largest companies, supporting 215,000 direct jobs, according to a report presented by the French Embassy.

Cumulative French investment in Mexico between 2006 and 2025 totaled $13.6 billion, while bilateral trade reached $7.9 billion last year.

The 2026 report indicates that over 50% of the French companies surveyed source more than half of their purchases from Mexican suppliers.

With reports from López-Dóriga Digital and Reporte Indigo

World.title: Court deals setback to controversial gas terminal on the Gulf of California
World.content:
The start of construction on a liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal in the northern state of Sonora has been temporarily halted by a federal court, even though a government port authority granted the project 36 hectares last year.

The Amigo LNG terminal — planned for Catalina Bay south of Guaymas, Sonora on the Gulf of California — would receive natural gas from the United States by pipeline, cool it into a liquid for shipment and export it by tankers to Asian markets.

A federal judge in Sonora granted a definitive suspension that temporarily bars the previously authorized construction while the court reviews an amparo (a constitutional rights challenge) filed by the environmental group Nuestro Futuro.

Last week’s ruling, which followed a Sept. 18 hearing, does not cancel the project or revoke Amigo LNG’s separate agreement with the Guaymas National Port System Administration (ASIPONA Guaymas), a federal port authority.

But the case does add to mounting opposition against LNG development in the Gulf of California, also known as the Sea of Cortez.

Dubbed the “aquarium of the world” by French ocean explorer Jacques Cousteau, the gulf is home to a rich variety of marine life and includes a UNESCO World Heritage area.

In April 2025, ASIPONA Guaymas granted Amigo LNG rights to use 36 hectares in Catalina Bay, according to documents obtained by the newspaper El País.

Awarded directly, without a public bidding process, the agreement allows the company to build and run an LNG terminal in the area.

El País reported that developers chose Mexico because similar terminals have faced stricter environmental rules and opposition on the U.S. West Coast.

The project would process at least 250,000 tonnes of LNG in its first year. That figure would rise to 3.7 million tonnes a year beginning in its 10th year — a volume equivalent to 50 to 60 large LNG carriers.

Environmental groups, citing concerns similar to those raised in a separate legal challenge that ended in a victory for whales, warn that added traffic could increase underwater noise and collision risks for marine life. The gulf is also home to the critically endangered vaquita.

They also say public documents regarding the Amigo LNG terminal did not provide enough information to fully assess risks to marine life and coastal communities.

Mexico’s Agency for Safety, Energy and Environment (ASEA) said it believes the suspension could remain in place until the court resolves the amparo.

The project cannot begin construction while the suspension remains in force.

Amigo LNG is one of several proposed projects intended to move gas from Texas’ Permian Basin through Mexico and across the Pacific to Asian markets.

With reports from El País, La Silla Rota and Global Energy.mx

World.title: 2027 midterm elections in Mexico: Who are Morena’s top picks for governor?
World.content:
An ex-chief of the federal government’s Financial Intelligence Unit and a former state attorney general are among 17 men and women selected as the ruling Morena party’s presumptive candidates for gubernatorial elections next June.

Sixteen of the 17 presumptive candidates were selected via surveys conducted by Morena, the main party of the “fourth transformation” (4T) political movement led by President Claudia Sheinbaum. The presumptive candidate in San Luis Potosí was selected by consensus.

The 10 women and seven men selected by Morena were designated as “state coordinators of the transformation and national sovereignty.”

Seven of the coordinators were announced on Monday, while 10 others were previously unveiled.

It is almost certain that the 17 coordinators will subsequently be named as Morena’s gubernatorial candidates in the 17 states where gubernatorial elections will be held on June 6, 2027.

It is likely that the Labor Party (PT) and the Green Party (PVEM) will support most, if not all, of the candidates selected by Morena. Both the PT and the PVEM are allies of Morena.

Morena’s 17 presumptive gubernatorial candidates are listed below in alphabetical order by the states they are seeking to govern. Morena already governs 12 of the states where gubernatorial elections will be held next year. MND will cover prospective candidates from other parties in future articles.

World.title: Mexican Senate passes bill holding pet owners accountable for abuse or negligence
World.content:
The Mexican Senate approved on Tuesday wide-ranging legislation that recognizes animals as sentient beings and prohibits their mistreatment and cruelty as it holds owners or caregivers accountable for their health, nutrition, living conditions and mental well-being.

Though most notably aimed at the 69% of Mexican households that include pets (totaling some 80 million animals, according to the national statistics agency INEGI), the law would apply to all animals under human care, including those used in sports and entertainment; those on exhibition in zoos, aquariums or educational farms; those used in marketing; and even animals being raised for human consumption.

The bill, formally the General Law on Animal Welfare, Care, and Protection, passed the Senate on a 115-1 vote. It amends provisions of the Federal Laws on Animal Health and on Film and Audiovisual Media, as well as the General Laws on Wildlife, Ecological Balance and Environmental Protection and Civil Protection. It is now being debated in the Chamber of Deputies.

Mexico ranks first in Latin America and third worldwide in terms of animal abuse, with more than 10,000 formal complaints of animal abuse registered between 2024 and 2026.

The Mexican Constitution prohibits animal abuse. But in recognizing animals as sentient beings with rights, the new law would go further by establishing obligations for people who have animals in their care, such as providing them food, water, veterinary care and a suitable place to live.

Failing to do so — or taking any action or making any omission that causes pain or suffering, or endangers the life and well-being of animals — will be considered a punishable offense subject to a fine, administrative arrests of up to 36 hours, confiscation of the animals, closure of establishments or the revocation of permits or concessions.

Furthermore, the bill establishes that anyone who mistreats or abandons an animal will be responsible for its veterinary care, rehabilitation and shelter costs. In addition, it supports the creation of abuse reporting mechanisms and a national registry of animal welfare violators.

PAN Senator Gina Gerardina Campuzano González said that the bill seeks to open a new chapter for animal protection, especially in Mexico, where she says seven out of 10 animals suffer abuse, “so we are not talking about an isolated problem.”

With reports from Grupo Animal and Publimetro México

World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

Rio Times Markets · Mexico

Key Facts — The release Mexico’s Finance Ministry (SHCP) reported August public finances on 30 September 2026. The January to August budget deficit came in at MXN 739 billion, about US$40.9 billion at the 30 September Banxico FIX rate of 18.0710 pesos per dollar.

— Versus plan The deficit was MXN 276 billion, about US$15.3 billion, smaller than programmed. The primary balance, which excludes debt interest, showed a surplus of MXN 83.5 billion instead of the programmed MXN 70.6 billion deficit (SHCP, 30 September 2026).

— Revenue Budget revenues reached MXN 5.66 trillion, about US$313.3 billion, up 1.3 percent in real terms from the same period of 2025. It was the third straight year of growth for the period (SHCP, 30 September 2026).

— The mix Value-added tax (IVA) rose 11.4 percent in real terms, the strongest since 2021. Oil income rose 10.5 percent. Income tax (ISR) fell 5.6 percent, and fuel-tax subsidies kept draining that line (SHCP, 30 September 2026).

— Debt Historic public-sector financing requirements stood at 51.5 percent of GDP. The five-year credit default swap, the cost of insuring against default, fell to 78 basis points at the end of August from 120 at the start of the administration (SHCP, 30 September 2026).

Mexico’s public finances beat the official plan through August 2026. A surge in value-added tax and oil money offset a weak income-tax season and kept the deficit on the path Congress approved for the year.

Mexico’s Finance Ministry closed the first eight months of 2026 with a budget deficit of MXN 739 billion, roughly US$40.9 billion. That was MXN 276 billion less red ink than the program allowed. The ministry published the figures on 30 September in its monthly report to Congress.

The budget balance measures the difference between what the public sector collects and what it spends. On the broader public balance, which adds entities under indirect budget control, August alone added about MXN 5.5 billion to the cumulative deficit, a figure calculated from the ministry’s own tables.

The report lands in a sensitive month. Rating agencies have Mexico under watch, Congress is debating the 2027 budget, and the peso just posted its weakest month in more than two years.

Where the money came from

Budget revenues reached MXN 5.66 trillion between January and August, up 1.3 percent in real terms from the same period of 2025. The ministry said tax collection has now grown for four straight years over this period.

Value-added tax, known in Mexico as IVA, did the heavy lifting. Collections reached MXN 1.19 trillion, up 11.4 percent in real terms, the strongest January to August since 2021. August alone grew 23 percent. The ministry credited strong consumer spending and tighter customs work, and said IVA ran MXN 123 billion, about US$6.8 billion, above the program.

Oil income provided the second engine. Oil revenues rose 10.5 percent in real terms to MXN 690.4 billion, about US$38.2 billion, the best for the period since 2022. The average export price was US$75.2 a barrel against US$63.3 a year earlier. Revenue at Pemex, the state oil company, rose 13.6 percent.

The weak spot was income tax, or ISR. Collections fell 5.6 percent in real terms to MXN 2.00 trillion. Taxes on imports rose 9.2 percent, but still came in MXN 39 billion below plan, which the ministry blamed on the stronger peso.

Where the money went

Spending stayed below plan too. Social development outlays rose 8.4 percent in real terms, more than three times the average pace of the past decade. Health spending rose 14.3 percent and education 7.3 percent.

Physical investment rose 1.9 percent in real terms, helped by a 22.3 percent jump in August that the ministry linked to strategic infrastructure projects. Operating spending outside payrolls fell 4.4 percent.

The interest bill is shrinking. Debt service costs fell 3.5 percent in real terms and ran MXN 122 billion below the program. The ministry credited liability management and the stronger peso.

The debt picture

The historic balance of public-sector financing requirements, the broadest Mexican debt measure, stood at 51.5 percent of GDP at the end of August. Net federal government debt was 48.4 percent of GDP. Most of the debt is in pesos, at fixed rates and long maturities, which limits currency risk.

The ministry also stressed market gauges. Mexico’s five-year credit default swap, the cost of insuring against a default, fell to 78 basis points at the end of August from 120 at the start of the current administration. The yield gap against the ten-year US Treasury bond narrowed by 30 basis points over the same period.

On 27 August the government closed its 2026 foreign issuance with a samurai bond of 282.8 billion yen, about US$1.77 billion. The Japanese rating agency JCR assigned that bond an A- grade with a stable outlook on 28 August.

Why this report matters now

The publication is the ministry’s answer to a skeptical audience. S&P placed Mexico, Pemex and the Federal Electricity Commission on negative outlook in May, citing fiscal strain. Parts of the market now price Mexican debt close to junk levels, a debate covered in Mexico Inches Toward Junk Status as Fiscal Math Unravels.

The government’s message is discipline. “At the end of August, the fiscal balances showed results favorable relative to the program, with a budget deficit lower than forecast, in line with the annual targets approved by Congress and the objectives of fiscal discipline, wellbeing and economic growth,” the ministry wrote in its statement.

Timing supports the argument. Congress is now debating the 2027 budget, which loosens the deficit goal to raise welfare spending ahead of the June 2027 mid-term elections. A clean August report strengthens the ministry’s hand in that negotiation.

What is not yet known

The September figures will not appear until around the end of October. It is too early to say whether August’s discipline held through the first month of the fourth quarter.

The report does not say how much of the IVA surge is durable and how much reflects one-off customs enforcement. Nor does it explain the income-tax decline; the ministry gave no breakdown by sector or employment type.

Finally, the report does not settle the 2027 debate. The final deficit path for next year depends on the budget Congress passes, on Pemex support costs, and on the oil price, all of which remain open.

What holds, and what could reverse

The August number is better than the plan, but worse than last year. The cumulative deficit of MXN 739 billion compares with MXN 582 billion in the same period of 2025. The ministry said 2025 benefited from extraordinary one-time revenues; this year, non-tax revenue fell 8.0 percent in real terms.

What holds is the structure: a primary surplus, rising tax revenue, a falling interest bill and a debt stock mostly in local currency. What could reverse it is also clear. Fuel subsidies kept draining the gasoline and diesel tax line, which fell 5.0 percent in real terms. The oil windfall depends on a price Mexico does not control. And a weaker peso would raise the cost of servicing whatever dollar debt remains.

For readers living in Mexico, the channel runs through the currency and interest rates. The peso ended September near 18.08 per dollar, its weakest month in more than two years, and traded past 18.26 on the morning of 1 October, as covered in Mexican Peso Hits Its Weakest Since December 2025. A credible deficit path supports the peso and keeps local borrowing costs contained. That affects mortgage rates, the price of imported goods and the value of any dollar income.

The finance ministry’s next monthly report, due in late October, will show whether the August result was a milestone or a pause.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between Mexico’s budget balance and its public balance?

The budget balance covers the federal government plus state-controlled entities such as Pemex, the CFE utility and the social security institutes. The public balance adds entities under indirect budget control. Both showed similar results through August: a deficit of about MXN 739 billion on the budget measure and MXN 737 billion on the broader public measure.

Why did VAT receipts rise while income tax fell?

Consumption stayed strong and customs enforcement improved, so IVA grew 11.4 percent in real terms. Income tax depends more on corporate profits and formal payrolls, which softened this year. The ministry did not give a detailed reason for the 5.6 percent drop in ISR.

What does the August fiscal report mean for foreigners in Mexico?

A deficit below plan supports the government’s credit story, which tends to steady the peso and contain interest rates. For expats, that feeds into mortgage costs, local prices of imported goods and the peso value of dollar income. The report is one month of data, not a verdict on the year.

Sources: Secretaría de Hacienda y Crédito Público, Comunicado No. 78, “Finanzas públicas y deuda pública a agosto de 2026”, 30 September 2026; La Jornada, 30 September 2026; Revista Fortuna, 30 September 2026; La Opinión, 30 September 2026 (Banxico FIX via the Official Gazette); the RT economic calendar. This is news, not investment advice.

World.title: Venezuela: ELN Clash With National Guard Leaves One Dead in Táchira Border Town
World.content:
Venezuela · Border Security

Key Facts —What happened. An armed clash between Venezuela’s Bolivarian National Guard and members of Colombia’s ELN guerrilla on Monday left one person dead and at least five injured in Junín, Táchira state, near the Colombian border. It is the first confrontation between Venezuelan security forces and the ELN since Colombia’s right-wing president Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August. —The backdrop. Colombian intelligence has mapped 93 clandestine ELN airstrips inside Venezuela, and the US State Department warned citizens on 29 September against travel to Norte de Santander and the border strip. —Still open. Neither Caracas nor Bogotá has officially confirmed the clash or the identity of the dead man.

A firefight between Venezuela’s National Guard and ELN guerrillas in the border town of Junín has left one dead and at least five injured — the first such clash since Colombia’s new hard-line president took office, and a sign that the porous frontier is heating up.

The roughly 2,200-kilometre border between Venezuela and Colombia is shared territory for the ELN and other armed groups.

What Happened in Junín

The clash occurred on Monday, 29 September, in Junín, a locality in Venezuela’s western state of Táchira, close to the Colombian border. Members of the Bolivarian National Guard (GNB) exchanged fire with presumed members of the National Liberation Army (ELN), Colombia’s largest remaining guerrilla group.

“We are hearing of five injured and one dead,” Javier Tarazona, director of the Venezuelan human-rights NGO Fundaredes, told AFP. The injured were moved from Junín to the nearby city of Rubio, also in Táchira, where they were treated at a local clinic.

Venezuelan outlet El Nacional identified the dead man as a National Guard member, Andry Giovanni Vela Álvarez. Neither the Venezuelan government nor the GNB had issued an official statement on the incident as of Wednesday, and Colombian authorities had not commented either.

Tarazona is a longstanding and credible witness to border violence: he spent five years in prison after denouncing, among other things, guerrilla movements in the zone. Fundaredes has documented the expansion of Colombian armed groups inside Venezuela for years.

Why the Clash Matters Now

According to AFP’s reporting, the firefight is the first between Venezuelan security forces and the ELN since Abelardo de la Espriella, Colombia’s right-wing president, came to power on 7 August. For years under Nicolás Maduro, Venezuelan forces largely tolerated — and at times, watchdogs say, abetted — ELN activity on their side of the frontier.

Tarazona told AFP the situation in the region has changed since Maduro’s capture by the United States military in January and, above all, since De la Espriella’s arrival in August. The new Colombian president has made the ELN a declared military target, ending peace talks and opening an offensive in the Catatumbo region that began with an airstrike days after his inauguration.

A direct ELN–GNB firefight on Venezuelan soil would mark a break with that old modus vivendi. Whether it signals a lasting shift in Caracas’s posture — pressure, cooperation with Bogotá, or a localised dispute over territory and contraband routes — is the question analysts will watch in the coming days.

A Border Under Scrutiny

The clash lands in the same week that Colombian intelligence, according to El Tiempo, mapped 93 clandestine airstrips used by the ELN inside Venezuela — up from about 15 points tracked at the start of the year. The same reporting linked the group’s Northeastern War Front, associated with commander Luz Amanda Payares, alias Silvana Guerrero, to positions in Zulia and Táchira, the state where Monday’s clash took place.

Washington has also tightened its posture. On 29 September the US State Department told its citizens not to travel to Norte de Santander, the Colombian department facing Táchira, or to within ten kilometres of the Venezuelan border, citing the risk of drone and explosive attacks by armed groups. The ELN, classed by Washington as a terrorist organisation, fields an estimated 6,450 members according to Colombia’s Fundación Ideas para la Paz.

The roughly 2,200-kilometre border has long been porous ground where guerrillas, dissidents, traffickers and smugglers overlap. Junín sits in a corridor where control of crossings and contraband routes has triggered violence before; Monday’s toll is a reminder that the frontier’s armed ecology is being reshaped by new governments on both sides.

What We Could Not Confirm

The identity of the dead man comes from a Venezuelan media report and has not been officially confirmed; the exact casualty count rests on Fundaredes’ account to AFP. Some regional reports mentioned captures during the incident, but no authority has confirmed any detention. We could not confirm what triggered the firefight, which ELN front was involved, or whether the clash is connected to the newly mapped airstrips. No official statement from Caracas or Bogotá had been issued at the time of publication.

More: Venezuela news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in Junín, Venezuela?

On Monday, 29 September, Venezuela’s Bolivarian National Guard clashed with presumed ELN guerrillas in Junín, Táchira state, near the Colombian border. The NGO Fundaredes told AFP one person was killed and at least five injured; the wounded were treated in nearby Rubio.

Why is Colombia’s ELN active inside Venezuela?

The ELN, Colombia’s largest remaining guerrilla group with an estimated 6,450 members, has operated for years along the porous 2,200-kilometre border. Colombian intelligence says it has mapped 93 clandestine ELN airstrips inside Venezuela, up from about 15 at the start of the year.

Is the Colombia–Venezuela border region safe to visit?

No, according to the US State Department, which on 29 September warned citizens against all travel to Norte de Santander and to within ten kilometres of the Venezuelan border, citing drone and explosive attacks by armed groups. Monday’s deadly clash in Táchira underlines that assessment.

Why does the Venezuela ELN border clash matter?

It is the first confrontation between Venezuelan security forces and the ELN since Colombia’s right-wing president Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August. Colombian intelligence has mapped 93 clandestine ELN airstrips inside Venezuela.

HEALTH · HONDURAS

Key Facts — The country Honduras, led by President Nasry Asfura since 27 January 2026. Public hospitals are run by the Secretaría de Salud (Sesal), the health ministry.

— What happened On 29 September 2026 Sesal told the Colegio Médico de Honduras (CMH), the doctors’ professional body, that 95% of doctors had been paid. It asked the CMH to end its action; the college refused.

— The numbers Sesal counts 6,850 doctors: 6,480 paid and 370 pending, of whom 359 are on contract and 11 interim (ministry letter, 29 September).

— What it means for you Outpatient appointments at public hospitals are still suspended or rescheduled. Emergency, delivery and critical care stay staffed, so call ahead before travelling.

— Still open Whether a CMH assembly votes to stand down. Both sides meet again on Friday 2 October to reconcile their lists of unpaid doctors.

The Honduras doctors strike is in its fourth week, and the government now says almost everyone is paid. The health ministry told the doctors’ college on 29 September that 95% of salaries owed are settled.

The Colegio Médico de Honduras (CMH), which every practising doctor must join, has not called off its action. It says its own records still show unpaid doctors the ministry has not counted.

What the 95% figure covers

The figure comes from letter No. 3156-SSPI-2026, signed by deputy minister José Miguel Castillo, the official handling health projects and investment. TU NOTA and Noticias 24/7 both reported its contents on 29 and 30 September.

According to the letter, the ministry has 6,850 doctors on its payroll and 6,480 have received their salaries. All 5,388 permanent doctors are paid, as are 312 of 323 interim doctors.

Doctors on the Honduran health ministry payroll, paid and still pending, as stated in the ministry's letter of 29 September 2026. Source: Secretaría de Salud letter No. 3156-SSPI-2026, reported by TU NOTA and Noticias 24/7, 29–30 Sep 2026.

That leaves 370 doctors, about 5%, still waiting. The ministry says 359 of them are contract doctors going through re-hiring paperwork, with 11 interim cases outstanding.

Castillo said a further step forward could come by Friday. The ministry says it has the budget to settle every remaining salary.

Why the Honduras doctors strike goes on

The doctors began what they call asambleas informativas, or informational assemblies, on 7 September. They gather at their workplaces and suspend outpatient clinics instead of walking out. Earlier coverage: Honduras Doctors’ Protest Hits Third Week as Hospitals Suspend Outpatient Care.

After a technical meeting on Tuesday 29 September, a CMH representative said the ministry’s database did not match the college’s. Some doctors, he said, do not know under which contract type they are registered.

Before that meeting, a CMH board member said a college survey put the share of doctors still owed at about 42%. Hondudiario reported the claim on 29 September; the data behind it has not been published.

He added that only a full CMH assembly can end the action, not the technical table. The college’s wider demands also include signed contracts, reinstatement of dismissed doctors and agreed pay adjustments, Once Noticias reported.

The cost for patients

At Hospital Escuela in Tegucigalpa, the country’s main teaching hospital, about 12,500 outpatient consultations have been suspended. El Heraldo reported the figure on 30 September, after 24 days of action.

That is roughly 520 consultations for each of those 24 days, by El Heraldo’s count. State broadcaster TNH reported that at least 25 surgeries a day are still scheduled and chronic patients collect medicines directly.

El Heraldo described a couple from Maraita who leave home at 3:00 am and travel more than 30 kilometres. Each trip costs them 400 lempiras (about US$15 at 26.85 lempiras per dollar, 1 October 2026).

Pressure for a deal from both sides

Hospital Escuela’s executive director, Darío Zúñiga, has proposed a truce. Doctors who have been paid would return to clinics, while those still owed money would stay out.

On 30 September César Chirinos, head of the public employees’ association ANDEPH, urged President Asfura to receive the CMH, Proceso Digital reported. He put the number of unpaid doctors at about 300, below the ministry’s own count.

Emergency rooms and critical care units remain staffed throughout, under the college’s own rules. Private hospitals are not part of this ministry payroll dispute. Options are set out in our guide to healthcare in Honduras for expats.

What Is Not Yet Known

It is not known when the CMH will hold the national assembly that could end the action, or how members would vote. By 1 October the college had not published a list of unpaid doctors to back its 42% estimate.

The outcome of Friday’s meeting to cross-check payroll lists, which could shorten the Honduras doctors strike, is also open. Neither side has given a date for paying the remaining 370 doctors.

Sources: TU NOTA (Sesal letter, 29 Sep 2026); Noticias 24/7 (30 Sep); Once Noticias (30 Sep); El Heraldo (30 Sep); TNH (30 Sep); Proceso Digital (30 Sep); Hondudiario (29 Sep); exchange rate open.er-api.com (1 Oct 2026).

TRADE · GUYANA

Key Facts — The country Guyana, an English-speaking Caribbean state on South America’s north coast, shares the Corentyne River border with Dutch-speaking Suriname.

— What happened On Wednesday 30 September 2026, agriculture minister Zulfikar Mustapha said he had ordered a stop to banana imports from Suriname.

— Who is involved Guyana’s Ministry of Agriculture, Guyanese banana farmers, and the traders who bring Surinamese fruit across the river. No company has been named.

— What it means for you Shoppers in Guyana should see local bananas on stalls. Surinamese growers lose an informal outlet, not a recorded export channel.

— Still open How the order will be enforced at the border, and whether Suriname’s government will respond, had not been reported by 1 October.

Guyana has ordered a stop to banana imports from neighbouring Suriname, saying its own farmers already grow enough fruit for the home market. Agriculture minister Zulfikar Mustapha announced the step on Wednesday 30 September 2026.

The move is small in trade terms but telling in tone. Mustapha said that, officially, no bananas were being imported from Suriname at all.

What the Minister Said

Mustapha told the Guyanese outlet Demerara Waves Online News that he had heard Surinamese bananas were coming in. “I told them to stop all the importation of bananas because our farmers have enough bananas to supply the system,” he said.

He added that he had received unofficial complaints from several people. “We have enough bananas in the country,” the minister said.

Surinamese media carried the report the same day. The Paramaribo news sites Dagblad Suriname and Waterkant both relayed the minister’s remarks, citing the Guyanese interview.

A Standing Rule, Not a New Tariff

Mustapha framed the step as routine policy rather than a new measure. Once local output of a fruit meets domestic demand, he said, imports of that fruit should not be allowed.

The rule cuts both ways. It shields Guyanese growers in good seasons, yet imports can return if local harvests fall short of demand.

No official notice, tariff schedule or list of affected traders had been published by 1 October. The account so far rests on the minister’s own words in a single interview.

Why the Border Matters

Guyana and Suriname are linked mainly across the Corentyne River, where small boats and a ferry carry people and goods. Much of that produce trade is informal and never shows up in customs data.

In July 2025, Surinamese police stopped a truckload of bananas bound for Guyana across the Corentyne without export permits, Suriname Herald reported. Surinamese Dutch calls sweet bananas “bacoven”, the word used in that report.

That helps explain the minister’s point about unofficial imports. Bananas that cross without paperwork compete with Guyanese fruit but are hard to count or tax.

The crossing has already been under strain this year. The Corentyne ferry was suspended in August and resumed sailing on 28 August 2026.

Who Gains and Who Loses

For Guyanese banana farmers, the order removes cheaper competition at local markets. Mustapha presented it as protection for growers who already meet demand.

For Surinamese growers and small traders, Guyana is a nearby outlet for surplus fruit. Losing it could push more bananas onto markets at home, such as the stalls in Paramaribo.

Consumers sit in the middle. Local supply may keep shelves full, but fewer sellers can also mean less pressure on prices.

What Is Not Yet Known

It is not clear how border officers will enforce the order on informal river traffic. Nor has any volume or value of Surinamese bananas entering Guyana been published.

Suriname’s government had not publicly responded by 1 October. Whether the step stays a quiet domestic rule or becomes a bilateral issue depends on that reply.

Sources: Demerara Waves Online News (interview with Zulfikar Mustapha, 30 September 2026); Dagblad Suriname (30 September 2026); Waterkant (1 October 2026); Suriname Herald (23 July 2025).

SECURITY · SURINAME

Key Facts — The country Suriname, a former Dutch colony on South America’s north coast, bordering Brazil, Guyana and French Guiana. Rainforest covers most of its thinly populated interior.

— What happened On Wednesday 30 September 2026, President Jennifer Simons departed from her annual address to say she wants no drug planes landing in the interior, Starnieuws reported.

— Who is involved Simons; the National Assembly (DNA, Suriname’s parliament), where signed agreements await approval; and partners Brazil and the United States, per GFC Nieuws.

— What it means for you No new rules or flight restrictions were announced. Closer watch on small aircraft and remote airstrips is the stated direction, pending parliament.

— Still open What the agreements before parliament contain, what data they would share, and when lawmakers will vote remain unclear as of 1 October.

Suriname’s president has said she will not tolerate drug planes landing in the country’s interior. Jennifer Simons made the remarks on Wednesday 30 September, during her annual address to parliament in Paramaribo.

The comments were not in the written speech, according to the news site Starnieuws, which published them on 1 October. Simons tied the issue to signed agreements pending in parliament and to cooperation with neighbouring Brazil.

What Simons Said Off Script

Simons spoke after outlining Suriname’s term as chair of CARICOM, the Caribbean Community, from January to June 2027. She then turned to control over national territory, Starnieuws reported.

According to the outlet, she said small aircraft land in the interior and that she had been told where they were heading. “I don’t care where they are going. I don’t want them here,” she said.

“I want no drug planes in my interior,” Simons added, in remarks also carried in a Starnieuws video. The written text of the annual address does not include these lines.

An Agreement Waiting in Parliament

Simons said Suriname has asked for international support and needs better information about movements in the interior. She argued this would let the state act on policy rather than react to incidents.

“To be in charge of our territory and run a sound border policy, we need more information,” she said, as quoted by Starnieuws. She named Brazil and referred to an already signed agreement now before the National Assembly.

She said she expected parliament to cooperate so that Suriname can obtain the information quickly. GFC Nieuws reported that she cited agreements with both Brazil and the United States.

GFC Nieuws also reported her concern over international attention to Suriname as a possible drug transit country. Neither outlet described the terms of the agreements.

The Brazil Link

The remarks build on a visit Simons paid to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Brasília in late May 2026. A joint statement then promised closer work against drug trafficking, arms smuggling and illegal mining, Waterkant reported.

The two governments also agreed to improve border and airspace surveillance, according to that report. They pledged faster information exchange between police services and closer ties between Brazil’s Federal Police and Suriname’s police force.

Simons closed the passage with her foreign-policy principles. Starnieuws quoted “peace without passivity,” “sovereignty without isolation” and “cooperation without subordination.”

Stabilisers and Risks

The tough line on drug planes comes with a cooperative frame rather than a unilateral crackdown. Shared information with a large neighbour could help a small state watch a vast, lightly policed interior.

The risk lies in the details. Data-sharing deals touch on sovereignty, and lawmakers have not yet said how they view this one.

Early party reactions reported by Suriname Herald focused on the budget, inflation and the gold sector. None of the reactions it carried addressed the drug-plane comments. The speech also set out the 2027 budget, covered in Suriname President Simons Uses Annual Address to Set 2027 Deficit at 4% of GDP, and energy plans in Suriname Power Cuts: Simons Pledges Shift From Heavy Oil to Gas and Solar.

What Is Not Yet Known

It is not known what the signed agreements with Brazil and the United States contain or what data they would share. No timetable for a parliamentary vote has been published.

The government has not announced new airstrip controls, flight rules or operations. The drug-plane quotes come from Starnieuws; GFC Nieuws carried the wider passage on the interior and drug transit, but not those lines.

Sources: Starnieuws, 1 Oct 2026 · Waterkant, 29 May 2026 · GFC Nieuws, 30 Sep 2026 · Suriname Herald, 1 Oct 2026

POLITICS · DOMINICAN REPUBLIC

Key Facts — The country The Dominican Republic, a Caribbean state of about 11 million people, is seeking to join the OECD, the Paris-based club of 38 mostly wealthy economies.

— What happened On 30 September 2026 the OECD presented its integrity study of the country at the National Palace in Santo Domingo, with President Luis Abinader present.

— The numbers The country meets 78% of OECD integrity criteria in regulation but 22% in practice, against OECD averages of 80% and 45%, an OECD official said (Diario Libre).

— What it means for you The OECD recommends a lobbying register, whistleblower protection, caps on political donations and freer access to public information, changes that would affect investors and residents.

— Still open No bill, timetable or budget has been announced. The full study and the 2026–2036 national integrity strategy have not yet been published in full.

The OECD integrity study of the Dominican Republic, presented in Santo Domingo on 30 September, finds a country with good rules that it applies only patchily. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) also says there is no regulation of lobbying at all.

The tone was not hostile. Elsa Pilichowski, the OECD’s director of public governance, praised the country’s progress and said it already uses some of the best practices in the world.

A wide gap between rules and practice

According to Diario Libre, Pilichowski said the country meets 78% of OECD criteria on regulation but only 22% on practical application. The OECD averages she cited were 80% and 45%.

She called closing that gap the most important challenge for the next phase. The difficulty is common across OECD members, she added, but the Dominican Republic has wide room to improve.

Share of OECD integrity criteria met in regulation and in practice, Dominican Republic vs OECD average. Source: OECD presentation via Diario Libre, 30 Sep 2026.

Listín Diario quoted her saying that many institutions already have “strong rules” and only need to apply them. The newspaper said work on the study began about two years ago, and the presidency says it was prepared with the government’s ethics office.

Lobbying, whistleblowers and political money

The OECD integrity review says there is no framework making lobbying transparent. Acento, another Dominican outlet, reports it recommends a mandatory lobbying register created by law, with independent oversight and sanctions.

Whistleblower channels are described as fragmented, with limited protection. The study proposes confidentiality, anonymous reporting and protection against retaliation.

On party and campaign finance, a legal framework exists, but reports are incomplete and checks are thin. The OECD suggests caps on individual donations and stronger audit powers for the Central Electoral Board (JCE), which runs elections.

Campaign money is already a live issue, as covered in Dominican Republic Business Chief Warns Early Campaigns Invite Crime Money.

Weak points inside the state

The ethics office, the Directorate General of Government Ethics and Integrity (DIGEIG), was created by decree. Acento reports the OECD finds it lacks legal guarantees of independence.

Only a limited share of officials’ asset declarations is verified, the study says. It also finds that fewer than half of citizens, on average, express trust in public institutions.

Access to information has improved considerably, the OECD acknowledges. It still wants openness by default and an independent body able to hear appeals and issue binding decisions.

How the government responded

Abinader said the country must move “from diagnosis to action”, according to the presidency. Listín Diario quoted him saying the study is “not the end” but the start of a new stage.

He linked the reforms to the bid to join the OECD, which has 38 members. Presidency minister José Ignacio Paliza said his office would help DIGEIG and other bodies apply the recommendations.

The presidency says a National Public Integrity Strategy for 2026–2036 will turn the study into targets, measures and indicators. Judicial appointments are a parallel test, as seen in Dominican Republic Judge Selection Advances: 88 Vie for Six Supreme Court Seats.

What Is Not Yet Known

The government has not announced a lobbying bill, whistleblower bill or donation cap in response to the study. It has given no date for doing so.

The 78% and 22% figures come from Pilichowski’s presentation as reported by Diario Libre. The full study text was not available to check the underlying methodology.

Sources: Diario Libre (30 Sep 2026); Listín Diario (30 Sep 2026); Acento (1 Oct 2026); Presidency of the Dominican Republic (30 Sep 2026).

ECONOMY · COSTA RICA

Key Facts — The country Costa Rica, a Central American economy of about five million people that has built its export model on foreign-owned factories in tax-incentive free zones.

— What happened Foreign direct investment reached US$2.74 billion in January–June 2026, up 23.4% from US$2.22 billion a year earlier, according to Procomer figures released on 1 October.

— The numbers Free zones drew US$1.74 billion (+35%). Companies under the ordinary tax regime drew US$569.7 million (+46.9%). The United States supplied 68.9% of the total.

— What it means for you More factory and service projects mean more formal jobs, mainly in medical devices and manufacturing. Tourism investment, by contrast, fell 27% in the half.

— Still open The figures are preliminary Central Bank data and may be revised. They exclude the Fifco sale to Heineken, which Procomer values at about US$3.2 billion.

Costa Rica FDI, the foreign direct investment that flows into companies in the country, rose 23.4% in the first half of 2026. It reached US$2.74 billion, against US$2.22 billion in January–June 2025.

The figures come from Procomer, the state export and investment agency, using preliminary Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) data. Procomer, La Nación and Revista SUMMA published them on 1 October.

Free zones carry the growth

Most of the increase came from free zones (zonas francas), a regime that offers tax breaks to mainly export-oriented companies. Investment there rose 35% to US$1.74 billion, an increase of US$452.6 million, La Nación reported.

Companies under the ordinary, or “definitive”, tax regime attracted US$569.7 million, up 46.9%. Free-zone investment outside the Greater Metropolitan Area around San José rose 37% to US$149.6 million, Procomer said.

Foreign direct investment in Costa Rica in selected sectors, January to June 2026, excluding the Fifco sale to Heineken. Source: Procomer, based on preliminary BCCR data, 1 October 2026.

By sector, manufacturing dominated with US$1.95 billion, up 9.8%, Procomer reported. Services drew US$212.5 million, up from just US$9.4 million a year earlier.

Where the money comes from

The United States supplied 68.9% of the half-year total, Procomer reported. Switzerland followed with 5.7% and Spain with 5.1%.

That concentration is the model’s strength and its exposure. Medical-device and electronics makers from the United States have anchored Costa Rica’s free zones for two decades.

Trade Minister Indiana Trejos said the results show Costa Rica remains an attractive investment destination. Procomer general manager Laura López pointed to the double-digit growth outside the capital region.

The beer deal sits outside the count

The 23.4% figure excludes one extraordinary deal: the sale of the beverage businesses of Fifco, a Costa Rican brewer, to Heineken. Procomer estimates the deal at US$3.2 billion.

Including it, first-half FDI totals US$5.94 billion, La Nación reported. The deal had already lifted the first-quarter figure, as covered in One Beer Deal Made Costa Rica an Investment Magnet Overnight.

Procomer treats the acquisition as extraordinary and reports it separately. As a change of ownership rather than new capacity, the underlying number better shows the trend.

The weak spots

Not every sector grew. Investment in tourism fell 27% to US$157.9 million from US$215 million, Procomer reported, a soft patch for one of the country’s largest employers.

The capital inflow also arrives as the external accounts loosen. The second-quarter current-account gap widened, as reported in Costa Rica Current Account Deficit Widens to US$239.8 Million as Imports Outpace Exports.

Steady Costa Rica FDI helps finance that gap. For now, the free-zone pipeline gives the economy a stable source of dollars.

What Is Not Yet Known

The Central Bank data are preliminary, and may be revised. Procomer gave growth rates for new capital (+15%) and reinvested earnings (+5%), but not the full BCCR breakdown in dollars.

It is also unclear whether the fall in tourism investment is a one-off or a trend. Third-quarter figures, due later in the year, will show whether free-zone growth holds.

Sources: Procomer, analysis of preliminary Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) data, 1 October 2026; La Nación, 1 October 2026; Revista SUMMA, 1 October 2026.

World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

ECONOMY · GUATEMALA

Key Facts — The country Guatemala is Central America’s most populous country. Its currency is the quetzal, at Q7.64 to the US dollar on 1 October 2026.

— What happened Decree 22-2026 took effect on 1 October 2026, a day after publication. It suspends value-added tax and the IDP fuel levy until 31 December 2026.

— The numbers Energy ministry reference prices from 1 October: premium Q36.24 (US$4.74), regular Q34.96 (US$4.58), diesel Q42.94 (US$5.62) a gallon, down from Q45.29, Q43.29 and Q49.39.

— What it means for you Fuel receipts should show the lower tax from 1 October. Prices vary by station and distance, and the energy ministry is publishing station prices online.

— Still open Whether Congress revives the vetoed Decree 21-2026 price cap, and how pump prices behave when both taxes return on 1 January 2027.

The Guatemala fuel tax exemption took effect on Thursday 1 October 2026, and pump prices fell by up to about Q9 a gallon overnight. Decree 22-2026 suspends two fuel taxes until 31 December.

President Bernardo Arévalo signed the law on Tuesday, and it appeared in the official gazette on Wednesday. At the same time he vetoed a rival law that would have capped pump prices.
