What the new fuel prices are

The energy ministry set reference prices of Q36.24 (about US$4.74) a gallon for premium petrol and Q34.96 (US$4.58) for regular. Diesel’s reference price is Q42.94 (US$5.62), at 7.64 quetzales to the dollar on 1 October.

Until Tuesday, pumps charged Q45.29 for premium, Q43.29 for regular and Q49.39 for diesel, Prensa Libre and Soy502 reported. That puts the saving at Q9.05, Q8.33 and Q6.45 a gallon respectively.

Guatemala pump prices per gallon until 29 September and the energy ministry's tax-free reference prices from 1 October 2026. Source: Ministry of Energy and Mines via Diario de Centro América, Prensa Libre and Soy502, 30 Sep to 1 Oct 2026.

On Thursday morning Soy502 recorded premium at Q36.19, regular at Q34.89 and diesel at Q41.69. Energy Minister Erwin Barrios said reference prices may shift with world markets and with distance from the capital.

Which taxes the decree suspends

The law lifts value-added tax (IVA), charged at 12 percent, on petrol, diesel and gas oil. It also suspends the IDP, a fixed per-gallon levy on fuel distribution.

The IDP is Q4.70 (US$0.62) a gallon on premium, Q4.14 (US$0.54) on regular and Q1.30 (US$0.17) on diesel. That is why diesel falls less than petrol.

The decree requires the tax benefit to be passed in full to the final consumer, Prensa Libre reported. Both taxes return on 1 January 2027 without any further act, according to Diario de Centro América, the state newspaper.

Why the price cap was vetoed

Arévalo refused to sign Decree 21-2026, which would have capped diesel and regular petrol at Q39 (US$5.10) and premium at Q41 (US$5.37). The state news agency AGN said it required up to Q2.5 billion (about US$327 million) in public funds.

The government argued that paying a subsidy while also cutting taxes could compromise the national budget. The cap now returns to Congress, which passed it on 8 September with 130 votes.

What it means for drivers and businesses

Congress approved the tax exemption on 22 September and sent the decree to President Bernardo Arévalo for signature. That came after fuel protests shut Mexico border crossings and hauliers blocked highways across the country.

Officials blame the price rise on conflict in the Middle East around the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for oil tankers. Cheaper diesel should ease transport and food costs over time, the government says.

Officials also admit the Guatemala fuel tax exemption does not fully offset the global price shock. The cost is lost tax revenue, and prices should rise by the tax amounts in January unless world prices ease.

Drivers can check their receipts for the missing taxes from 1 October, officials said. The energy ministry is publishing prices for every station online so buyers can compare.

What Is Not Yet Known

The regulation that implements the law is still being drafted, although officials say the discount does not depend on it. It is unclear how closely the pass-through rule will be policed at individual stations.

Congress has not said when it will debate the vetoed price cap. Nor is it known whether world oil prices will ease before both taxes return in January.

Sources: Diario de Centro América (state newspaper), 1 October 2026; Prensa Libre, 30 September 2026; Soy502, 1 October 2026; Agencia Guatemalteca de Noticias (AGN), 1 October 2026; exchange rate from open.er-api.com, 1 October 2026.

World.title: Noche de Cuentos to bring “leyendas” to life in Benque Viejo
World.content:
Noche de Cuentos to bring “leyendas” to life in Benque Viejo

By Zoila Palma: As Finados approaches, the Benque Viejo House of Culture is inviting residents to bring stories, memories and traditional cuentos to life during a special Noche de Cuenta Cuentos on October 23 at 7 p.m.

The storytelling evening will provide an opportunity for community members to share tales passed down through generations, old-time stories and personal memories that have become part of the community’s heritage.

Residents who have a story or memory to share are encouraged to come forward and help preserve these narratives for future generations.

Those interested in sharing their stories are asked to contact the House of Culture at 823-2697 or 627-1806.

The event will be held at the Benque Viejo House of Culture.

World.title: International News: Caribbean Aviation Safety symposium underway in Guyana
World.content:
International News: Caribbean Aviation Safety symposium underway in Guyana

By Zoila Palma: A Caribbean High-Level Symposium on Aviation Safety is underway in Georgetown, Guyana, bringing together regional ministers, government officials and aviation industry leaders to discuss the future of air transport in the Caribbean.

The symposium’s agenda includes the presentation of the Caribbean Aviation Safety and Security Oversight System Roadmap and Action Matrix to 2035, as well as discussions on challenges, opportunities and the future of aviation safety in the region.

Participants are also engaging with regional and international partners and industry stakeholders on strengthening aviation safety and security. The discussions are focused on improving cooperation and addressing key challenges affecting Caribbean air transport.

The symposium is expected to conclude with the Georgetown Declaration on Aviation Safety, which will outline priority actions aimed at strengthening regional cooperation and building a safer and more connected Caribbean aviation sector.

World.title: Father charged with common assault after dispute with daughter says she attacked him first
World.content:
Father charged with common assault after dispute with daughter says she attacked him first

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 59-year-old father from La Democracia is out on bail after being charged with common assault following allegations made against him by his daughter.

Paul Alexander Hyde, a cabinet maker, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he initially pleaded guilty with an explanation to assaulting his daughter, Nancy Hyde.

Hyde told the court that he was sitting inside his home drinking coffee when his daughter allegedly entered the house and began hitting him.

He claimed that he did not assault her, but instead held her by the shoulders and escorted her to the door.

Because Hyde’s explanation raised a possible defence to the charge, the Magistrate could not accept his guilty plea and instead entered an equivocal plea on his behalf, allowing the case to proceed.

There was no objection to bail, and Hyde was offered bail in the sum of $800 with one surety of the same amount.

As a condition of his bail, Hyde was ordered not to interfere with his daughter while the case remains before the court.

He met bail and is due back in court on October 30, 2026.

World.title: When Thief Thief From Thief, God Laugh: Alton Nicholson out on $2,000 bail after allegedly stealing friend’s bicycle that someone stole from him
World.content:
When Thief Thief From Thief, God Laugh: Alton Nicholson out on $2,000 bail after allegedly stealing friend’s bicycle that someone stole from him

By Breaking Belize News Staff: If the old Belizean saying, “when thief thief from thief, God laugh,” is true, then the Belize City Magistrate’s Court this week must have been a comedy, where a man accused of stealing a bicycle from his own friend claimed that the same bicycle was later stolen from him.

Alton Nicholson appeared unrepresented in court on a charge of theft after he was accused of taking a red and chrome 24-inch ladies beach cruiser from a Haulze Street residence.

The complainant reported that he had left the bicycle beside the steps of his home and went inside. About 20 minutes later, he returned and found it missing.

Nicholson was reportedly the only other person in the yard at the time and, when questioned, allegedly admitted that he had taken the bicycle to use it. The twist, however, was that Nicholson claimed someone later stole the bicycle from him.

In court, Nicholson initially pleaded guilty, telling the Magistrate, “I am sorry about that,” but then explained that he believed the owner knew he had taken the bicycle and insisted that he never intended to steal it.

That explanation amounted to a possible defence to the theft charge, prompting the Magistrate to reject his guilty plea and enter an equivocal plea instead.

Nicholson was granted bail of $2,000 with one surety in the same amount and was ordered to stay away from the complainant and prosecution witnesses.

He did not immediately regain his freedom, however, because of an outstanding court fine from a previous wounding matter. Unable to pay that fine, Nicholson was remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

His theft case was adjourned to November 9, 2026.

World.title: Cruise arrivals jump 29%, fueling growth in services sector
World.content:
Cruise arrivals jump 29%, fueling growth in services sector

By Zoila Palma: Data from the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB) shows that the services sector expanded by 3.4 percent during the second quarter of 2026, emerging as the main driver of the country’s 1.4 percent economic growth.

The tertiary sector generated $885.3 million between April and June, up $28.9 million from the same period in 2025.

Wholesale and retail trade recorded the largest increase within the sector, growing by 5.5 percent to $196.7 million. Public administration also expanded by 5.9 percent, reaching $104.1 million, with the SIB linking the increase to higher government employment and increased public expenditure.

The accommodation and food services industry grew by 1.1 percent, supported in part by a significant increase in cruise tourism.

Cruise passenger arrivals jumped 29 percent, rising from 150.9 thousand visitors in the second quarter of 2025 to 194.6 thousand in the same period of 2026. The increase was associated with 13 additional cruise calls during the quarter.

However, overnight tourism moved in the opposite direction. Overnight visitor arrivals declined by 1.2 percent, from 133.0 thousand in the second quarter of 2025 to 131.4 thousand this year.

World.title: Banana, citrus and livestock production decline in second quarter
World.content:
Banana, citrus and livestock production decline in second quarter

By Zoila Palma: Belize’s primary sector contracted by 6.1 percent during the second quarter of 2026, with declines recorded in several major agricultural industries, according to the latest Gross Domestic Product estimates from the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB).

Production in the sector was valued at an estimated $116.7 million, down $7.6 million from the same period in 2025.

Banana production declined by 15.3 percent, falling from 28.5 thousand metric tons in the second quarter of 2025 to 24.2 thousand metric tons this year.

Citrus production experienced an even sharper decline, dropping by almost two-thirds from 10.4 thousand metric tons to 3.8 thousand metric tons. Livestock production also decreased by 14.1 percent, reflecting lower output of cattle, pigs and poultry.

Petroleum extraction also fell by 3.6 percent, from 33.4 thousand barrels to 32.2 thousand barrels.

However, the declines were partially offset by stronger performances in sugarcane and fishing. Sugarcane deliveries increased by 4.4 percent, reaching 920.6 thousand metric tons, which the SIB attributed to improved management of the Fusarium fungus that had affected production in 2025.

Marine exports recorded a 33.6 percent increase during the quarter, driven mainly by higher exports of shrimp, lobster meat and whole fish.

World.title: Belize Economy grows 1.4% in second quarter, led by trade and services
World.content:
Belize Economy grows 1.4% in second quarter, led by trade and services

By Zoila Palma: Belize’s economy grew by 1.4 percent during the second quarter of 2026, with the country producing an estimated $1.388 billion in goods and services between April and June, according to preliminary figures from the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB).

This represents an increase of $18.9 million compared to the $1.369 billion recorded during the same quarter of 2025.

The growth was driven primarily by the tertiary sector, which expanded by 3.4 percent to $885.3 million.

Wholesale and retail trade was the main contributor, growing by 5.5 percent to $196.7 million. Public administration also increased by 5.9 percent, reaching $104.1 million, while accommodation and food services recorded more modest growth of 1.1 percent.

The positive performance in the services sector offset contractions in the primary and secondary sectors.

Primary sector production fell by 6.1 percent to $116.7 million, while the secondary sector contracted by 6.4 percent to $200 million.

Taxes on products, however, increased by 6.4 percent, from $175.1 million in the second quarter of 2025 to $186.3 million this year.

The SIB data shows that Belize’s economic growth during the quarter was largely supported by services, even as several goods-producing industries recorded declines.

World.title: SIB: Consumer confidence plunges in Orange Walk
World.content:
SIB: Consumer confidence plunges in Orange Walk

By Zoila Palma: Residents of Orange Walk District recorded the largest decline in consumer confidence in Belize during August 2026, according to the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB).

The district’s Consumer Confidence Index fell by 18.3 percent, from 40.6 in July to 33.1 in August, with sentiment declining across all three components of the index.

The sharpest decline in Orange Walk was recorded in the ‘Durable Goods’ component which fell by 27.8 percent.

Sentiment regarding ‘Expectations’ for future economic and household financial conditions also dropped significantly by 25.4 percent, while the ‘Present’ component declined by 2.9 percent, indicating increased pessimism about current conditions compared with the previous 12 months.

Consumer confidence also moved in opposite directions between males and females nationally.

Confidence among male consumers fell by 7.5 percent, from 43.1 in July to 39.9 in August. Their expectations component recorded the largest decline, falling 10.9 percent from 53.7 to 47.8, while sentiment toward durable goods dropped 6.2 percent and the ‘Present’ component declined by 4.0 percent.

Meanwhile, female consumer confidence increased by 5.5 percent, rising from 42.1 in July to 44.4 in August.

World.title: Water crisis deepening
World.content:
JAMAICA’S water crisis is deepening, with 107 of the National Water Commission’s 405 reserve systems dipping into drought territory, even as several parishes continue to face strict water restrictions. In the meantime, Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda has put Jamaicans on warning for even tighter water restrictions come Monday, as the country continues to grapple with worsening drought conditions.

Some communities could be getting day-on, day-off supply as the crisis deepens, with rainfall projections for drought-affected parishes looking bleak for the months ahead.

World.title: Defence raises questions about cop who was member of Kevin Smith’s flock
World.content:
Late pastor of Pathways International Restoration Ministries, Kevin Smith.

THE detective sergeant who cried repeatedly on Tuesday while giving evidence in the Andre Ruddock murder trial in the Home Circuit Court in Kingston breathed a sigh of relief on Wednesday as she was released as a witness after defence attorney Anthony Williams ended his cross-examination of her.

Ruddock is on trial for murder in relation to the October 17, 2021 throat cutting of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner at the Pathways International Restoration Ministries in Albion, St James.

On Wednesday, the witness was more composed on the stand as Williams quizzed her on the happenings at the church where Gardner and two male members were killed. One of the men was killed allegedly by the late pastor of the church, Dr Kevin Smith. The other man was shot and killed by the police after he attacked lawmen with a knife.

The detective sergeant was the initial investigator assigned to the case before it was turned over to a more senior cop.

On the day of the incident, the pastor was said to have taken a Glock pistol from a female member of the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) who was also a member of the church. The pastor used that firearm to shoot at the police.

When the incident was brought to an end, the police carted away numerous individuals, including Smith and the members of his church, to a police station where criminal charges were laid against them.

The female cop, who had a close relationship with Smith, was among those who were arrested. She was charged for breaching the Disaster Risk Management Act (DRMA) during COVID-19 lockdowns when no one, except for essential workers, was supposed to be on the road. Under the Act, large gatherings were prohibited.

Williams, who is one of two attorneys representing Ruddock, along with Venice Brown, asked the witness whether any other charges were laid against the female police member of Smith’s flock.

The attorney enquired if the cop was ever referred to the Inspectorate and Professional Standards Oversight Bureau (IPROB), which is a disciplinary unit within the JCF.

“Is this arm of the JCF responsible for complaints and investigations into the conduct of any member of the JCF?” Williams asked.

The witness told him that to the best of her knowledge that was, in fact, so.

The attorney wanted to know why the cop wasn’t referred to IPROB, but no definitive answer was given to that question.

The witness told the court that when the female constable was arrested, she was taken to an area of the church which looked like living quarters where she handed over a bag that contained her private Glock pistol, handcuffs, a video recorder, personal items, as well as her police uniform.

“As indicated to me, it was a private firearm,” the witness said.

Williams asked her if the constable’s hands were swabbed, and the witness said she personally did not swab her hands but gave instructions for that activity to be carried out; however, she could not speak to the outcome of the swabbing.

“When you first saw her on the 17th of October 2021, did she say anything to you?” Williams asked.

The witness responded in the affirmative, saying that she did speak to the cop, and that she said several things.

The lawyer sought to find out if whatever was said was indicative of her involvement at Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries.

“In light of the several utterances, did it lead you to carry out any further investigation?” the attorney asked.

“Yes, sir, certainly,” the witness said, before explaining that she was not the person who charged the constable.

She explained further that she did not know who exactly charged the constable for breaching the DRMA.

The trial continues today with a new witness. The seven members of the jury are expected to view photographs of the scene at the church as described by the six witnesses who have taken the stand so far during the trial which started two weeks ago.

World.title: Kabaka Pyramid still has lots to say
World.content:
Kabaka Pyramid.

There is still a rebel in Kabaka Pyramid. Fifteen years after the Rebel Music era first introduced audiences to that particular side of his artistry, the Kingston-born musician has chosen to revisit familiar territory — but he is not quite the same man who entered it.

Though the lyrical sharpness and the instinct to make music that says something beyond simply sounding good remains, time and a few battles of his own have added new layers to the story.

That evolution is recognisable in his latest single A Warrior’s Pain, a collaboration with American rappers R-Mean and Styles P.

The track serves as the foundation for Rebel Music 1 & 2, a new lyrics tape marking 15 years since the beginning of the entertainer’s Rebel Music chapter.

For Kabaka Pyramid, the return was not the result of an elaborate master plan. In fact, it was almost accidental.

“We knew the 15-year anniversary of Rebel Music was approaching and also the 10-year anniversary of the Accurate mixtape,” he explained. “So my team and I were floating around ideas since the start of the year. We were keeping it simple — samples and hip hop drums,” he said. “I just wanted something that inspired me to be lyrical.”

That instinct reignited something the artiste said had perhaps become dormant.

“It felt like I had suppressed a part of my craft and it needed to be reawakened,” he said outlining that the first few tracks were a hit with his manager, who remarked that they sounded like the

Rebel Music days.

“That moment was when we knew what had to be done,” he said. “Everything flowed easily from there.”

That renewed focus on lyricism sits alongside another important thread in Kabaka Pyramid’s current work — vulnerability.

On A Warrior’s Pain, the entertainer brings together reggae and hip hop through a shared appreciation for substance, storytelling, and resistance. But beneath the lyrical exchanges and musical chemistry, A Warrior’s Pain speaks to a more personal kind of battle

Kabaka Pyramid points to his own struggle with confidence in his voice and singing ability as part of the experience informing his contribution.

“I was always being told I need more melody, songs need to be more catchy, simplify the music,” he said. But, rather than resist the criticism, he used it as motivation.

“So I put in the hours to train myself and be ready for anything when called upon,” he explained. “Overcoming challenges is the best way to build confidence and strength comes from there naturally.”

That growth is perhaps one of the clearest differences between the Kabaka Pyramid of the early days and the artiste he has become.

“The message is still the same, just more mature now,” he said. “I think more people can relate to what I’m saying. It’s not music only for hip hop heads that love to dissect lyrical patterns.”

With that said, Kabaka Pyramid shared that the response to reggae and conscious music from international audiences continues to surprise him, particularly in Africa, Europe, Japan, and the United States. This is sees as not cultural appropriation, but an opportunity to observe how others interpret and conduct business around Jamaican music.

“When others incorporate our music I like to learn from them, and see what aspects they connect with and also how they conduct the business of touring,” he said.

There is, however, one boundary: “If you sample my record I want what is rightfully mine,” he said with a laugh.

World.title: Green calls for regional farmworker framework
World.content:
Belize’s Minister of Agriculture, Food Security and Enterprise, Rodwell Ferguson (left) speaking on Wednesday during a plenary session on “Unlocking private sector partnerships and expanding investments in agriculture and fisheries development” during the Caribbean Week of Agriculture 2026 conference at Ocean Coral Spring Hotel in Trelawny. Looking on is Floyd Green, Jamaica’s agriculture minister. (Photo: Horace Hines)

CORAL SPRING, Trelawny — Agriculture Minister Floyd Green is calling for a regional structure to facilitate the movement of agricultural workers across the Caribbean, pointing to Dominica as a model for easing constraints on farmers and boosting production.

“I think we need a framework, a framework that works for the movement of agricultural workers across the region,” he said.

He noted that Dominica has already established a framework for agricultural migrant workers which has enabled the country to bring in about 200 workers, benefiting roughly 80 farmers and contributing to a significant increase in productivity.

Green was speaking during Wednesday’s plenary session on “Unlocking private sector partnerships and expanding investments in agriculture and fisheries development” at the Caribbean Week of Agriculture 2026 conference. It was held at Ocean Coral Spring Hotel in Trelawny.

The session, on the fourth of the six-day conference, followed a question from the floor about region-wide difficulty finding workers for agriculture.

Green said the Caribbean should reconsider its traditionally insular approach to agricultural labour.

“If given the opportunity, just as they are given the opportunity to go to Canada and to go to America and they work and they return home…what about the region?” he asked.

He said a regional mechanism could allow workers to take up agricultural employment in neighbouring territories while providing farmers with access to people willing to work within the sector.

Green acknowledged that such an arrangement would require proper oversight, but said Dominica’s experience provides a model worth examining. He said he intends to raise the matter at the Caribbean Community’s Council for Trade and Economic Development (COTED).

At the same time, Green said the region must make greater use of technology as the profile of the agricultural workforce changes.

“One of the challenges with the young people going into agriculture now, they want to be owners. They don’t want to be workers,” he said, stressing the need to provide them with tools that can improve efficiency and productivity.

Green cited agricultural drones as one example of how technology can reduce reliance on manual tasks.

Through the Rural Agricultural Development Authority (RADA), Jamaica has invested in four drones which farmers may rent. They come with trained drone pilots. The College of Agriculture, Science and Education (CASE) is also training drone operators, while Jamaican company Sky Crop has begun assembling agricultural drones locally.

Green also pointed to the growing use of small walk-behind tractors, which can enable individual farmers to more efficiently manage their operations.

He said artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging technologies should form part of the region’s response as agriculture adapts to changing workforce patterns.

Belize’s Minister of Agriculture, Food Security and Enterprise Rodwell Ferguson said his country has experienced a similar shift.

He recalled that three to four decades ago, Belize relied on agricultural workers from neighbouring Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador. That has changed as more young Belizeans have gained access to secondary and tertiary education, including university and postgraduate studies.

“Young people are getting the opportunity to go to high school, sixth form, universities, [do] master’s degree, doctorate degree. And so maybe it is a good reason for the advent of the AI because it’s a time when we are having labour shortage, and no matter what we do, we can’t convince those young people to go and do agriculture,” he said.

Ferguson said the changing aspirations of young people are also reflected in schools.

In Belize, he said, agriculture is compulsory in first and second form but becomes an elective in third and fourth form. By then, participation can fall to about five students.

Ferguson said smart agriculture could help make the sector more attractive to young people while helping Belize meet its food production needs.

“It is critical. It is crucial because we must be able to feed ourselves,” he said.

World.title: UNITED BEHIND INFANTINO
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino (left) speaks with British Virgin Islands Football Association President Avanell Morton during the launch of the island’s new technical centre on Saturday. (Photo: FIFA Media)

The Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) will not be alone in backing FIFA President Gianni Infantino with fellow Caribbean associations of Trinidad and Tobago, British Virgin Islands, Antigua and Barbuda, and St Kitts and Nevis also on board.

Infantino recently completed his tour of the Caribbean at the weekend with many critics believing the trip was used to try to secure votes as he seeks to remain FIFA president for another four years ahead of the body’s congress in Morocco in March.

Infantino, 54, has led FIFA since 2016 and has faced increased scrutiny over the past few months after his controversial plan to sell stakes in FIFA competitions, including the men’s and women’s World Cup, to private investors. This plan was eventually scrapped last month after widespread backlash. Infantino’s recent Caribbean visit was his second in a matter of weeks after attending the Caribbean Football Union Presidents’ Meeting in the Dominican Republic. He was advised prior by his FIFA vice-president and Concacaf President Victor Montagliani to stay away from the event.

His first stop was in Kingston on Friday where he met with JFF officials, including President Michael Ricketts, and attended the Reggae Boyz’s 3-2 win over Guatemala in the Concacaf Nations League at the National Stadium.

As the Jamaica Observer reported on Sunday, the JFF will back Infantino in the upcoming elections with the board of directors in favour of him staying.

Ricketts told the Observer in August that he would support Infantino, given what he describes as massive support he’s given to football, particularly in the Caribbean.

Ricketts reiterated his support for Infantino after his one-day visit to the island.

“I think Infantino has done so very well for football globally,” he said. “I remember when I got into football as the president, the support from FIFA was medial to say the least.It has been a lot better now and we are just very grateful and we are looking forward to further improvements so that we can impact not just football but the social well-being of every boy and girl who plays the sport.”

Also in Kingston during Infantino’s visit was Trinidad and Tobago Football Association (TFFA) Kieron Edwards who also attended the game on Friday. Trinidad’s senior men’s team played Haiti at Sabina Park a day before.

In 2020, FIFA appointed a normalisation committee to manage the TTFA’s affairs due to serious financial issues. However, it was lifted in 2024 with Edwards being named president.

Edwards says FIFA has helped to reshape football in his country.

“FIFA is our largest supporter when it comes to our infrastructure,” he said. “Even our leagues, when we look at our women’s league now, [it’s a] full professional league, playing for seven months for the year, over 12 teams. That was only [possible because of] the continued support of FIFA in terms of our games. When it comes to the support of FIFA in terms of growing football, not just in Trinidad and Tobago but across the Caribbean and Concacaf, it’s been tremendous so far.”

Edwards says he has no doubts that the TTFA will be backing Infantino at the elections next year.

“We would have given President Infantino our full support and we have not wavered with that. Things do come up, changes, you have to have discussions, you have to have dialogue but the support is there 100 per cent behind the President always.”

British Virgin Islands (BVI) Football Association president Avanell Morton has also thrown his support behind Infantino.

Infantino visited BVI on Saturday and opened the new BVI Technical Centre, which was funded by FIFA.

“What more can he do? He’s doing a fantastic job already. He’s doing a fantastic job in the entire region,” Morton said.

The Antigua and Barbuda Football Association (ABFA), led by President Ickford Roberts, is also in favour of Infantino staying on as president. Infantino visited the island on Saturday and met with Roberts and Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who announced that a new football stadium would be built with FIFA support.

“[Infantino’s] transformative policies, from ground-breaking investment in grassroots infrastructure to the historic expansion of World Cup access, have elevated the aspirations of emerging football nations into attainable realities,” the ABFA said in a statement recently. “By listening with genuine humility and acting with decisive conviction, he has forged a legacy of inclusivity that transcends the sport itself, affirming that every nation, regardless of size, deserves equal voice and fair opportunity on the world stage.”

Infantino also visited St Kitts and Nevis on Saturday, where he attended the launch of a new technical centre with St Kitts and Nevis Football Association President Atiba Hattis president giving his support.

Infantino could have as many as 25 Caribbean votes behind him if all of the region’s FIFA member associations support his bid.

No one has signalled intentions to challenge Infantino with nominations closing on November 18, but it’s understood that Montagliani is seen as a credible opponent who would receive the backing of Europe (UEFA) and the Asian Football Confederation.

World.title: Dinner @ OMNIA SKY LOUNGE
World.content:
(Photo: Aceion Cunningham)

Nestled atop Parkway Plaza in Ocho Rios, Omnia Sky Lounge has quickly become more than just a dining spot — it’s the embodiment of Jamaican flavour, international influences, and vibrant nightlife. Since its grand opening in April 2024, this rooftop haven has been captivating locals and tourists alike with its unique blend of great food, lively music, and inviting ambience.

For owner Doneisha Johnson, the journey to creating Omnia Sky Lounge is rooted in her travels, taking cues from stunning rooftop lounges in Indonesia and Los Angeles. Her previous venture, a Loud Fashion store in Ocho Rios, serendipitously provided the perfect platform — the rooftop space above the store — to birth a new concept. She envisioned a place that brought together food, music, ambience, and entertainment in a seamless, memorable offering.

“It was about creating something different. A place where people don’t just come to eat, but to immerse themselves in an unforgettable experience,” Johnson said.

Omnia Sky Lounge embraces the tagline ‘Dinner With a Vibe,’ aiming to transcend the typical dining experience. Whether guests come for a celebratory occasion, a casual night out, or an exclusive event, the lounge promises an atmosphere that lingers in memory long after the night ends.

The concept is clear and intentional — a fusion where the essence of Caribbean cuisine meets international flair, showcased in a setting alive with music, thoughtfully crafted cocktails, and a welcoming environment.

The menu showcases contemporary Caribbean dishes infused with Jamaican flavours — seafood, chicken, pork, curry goat, and pastas — all prepared with Omnia’s distinctive twist. Alongside enticing bites is an impressive beverage selection featuring signature cocktails, premium spirits, wines, Champagne, and bottle service.

Feedback has been overwhelmingly positive, cementing Omnia as a destination for locals and visitors, with the lounge becoming a favoured spot for special occasions like birthdays, weddings, corporate events, and family reunions.

“Seeing customers return and recommending us has been extremely rewarding. Sometimes I stand back and remember when Omnia was simply an idea in my head. Seeing people choose us for something as important as their wedding makes the challenges of entrepreneurship feel worthwhile,” Johnson expressed.

Johnson has ambitious plans for Omnia’s growth, aiming to enhance the existing space with an additional level and dedicated event areas. An exciting new concept centred on regulated cannabis is also under consideration, pending licensing and approvals.

“Our plans include adding another upper level above the kitchen area and two dedicated event spaces at the rear of the property. The goal is to continue developing Omnia into a complete dining, entertainment, events, and lifestyle destination. Long term, I definitely see the Omnia brand expanding beyond Ocho Rios,” Johnson added.

Johnson also expressed gratitude to her loyal customers, dedicated staff and excitement for the future.

“We’re proud of what we’ve built, excited about what’s ahead, and still building. My vision is for Omnia Sky Lounge to become a must-visit destination when people come to Ocho Rios and Jamaica,” Johnson concluded.

Text & Photos: Aceion Cunningham

World.title: Post match brawl mars Vauxhall’s win over Charlie Smith in Walker Cup
World.content:
Screengrab of video showing crowd gathered on Charlie Smith High School field following alleged brawl following Walker Cup round-of-16 match on Tuesday (Original Video: andrewilliamsmedia Instagram)

Vauxhall High School’s dramatic Walker Cup round-of-16 victory over Charlie Smith High School was followed by a reported post-match disturbance, with videos circulating online appearing to show alleged stone-throwing, fighting and damage to property after the game.

Vauxhall High secured their place in the next round of the competition after overcoming the hosts in a tense penalty shootout, but the celebrations were overshadowed by events that unfolded after the final whistle.

Footage shared online appears to show chaotic scenes at the venue, with reports that students and teachers from Vauxhall High were injured during the incident. There are also reports that the Vauxhall team was unable to leave the venue for more than an hour due to difficulties accessing an exit.

In one video, a man can be heard saying that people at the venue were unable to leave because stones were being thrown.

“They are throwing stones and we cannot leave,” the man said before turning the camera towards another man behind a gate, who he said had refused to open it.

Another video appears to show two men engaged in a physical confrontation on the field, while separate footage shows a coaster bus with shattered windows as students disembarked.

Inter-secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) competition director Ewan Scott confirmed that the governing body was aware of the incidents and said a full investigation would follow.

“A thorough investigation will be conducted,” Scott said, following reports submitted by the schools.

The disturbances marred what has otherwise been an impressive campaign for Vauxhall, who have emerged as one of the competition’s surprise performers after entering the knockout phase with a 2-0 victory over Norman Manley High.

Their latest victory came in another closely contested encounter, with neither side able to find a winner after 90 minutes before Vauxhall held their nerve from the penalty spot.

The result also provided another reminder of the intensity surrounding the Walker Cup, particularly with several of Jamaica’s traditional schoolboy football powers competing in a revamped knockout format.

World.title: Sugar tax shortfall
World.content:
The new sugar sweetened drinks tax came into effect on May 1, two months into the fiscal year.

The Government collected $3 billion less than it had budgeted from the local special consumption tax (SCT) during the April-June quarter, with the Ministry of Finance pointing, in part, to non-compliance following the introduction of the sugar-sweetened drinks tax.

But the country’s fiscal watchdog, the Independent Fiscal Commission (IFC), says the explanation does not go far enough.

The IFC said information provided by the Ministry of Finance and the Public Service (MoFPS) was inadequate to determine whether the explanation for the 35.5 per cent shortfall was reasonable.

According to the IFC’s latest statement on fiscal performance that was tabled in Parliament last week, the Government collected $5.52 billion in local SCT during the first quarter of the 2026/27 financial year, well below the $8.57 billion that had been budgeted.

The resulting $3.04-billion gap was the largest shortfall recorded under the local SCT heading among the production and consumption taxes for the quarter.

The ministry attributed the underperformance to several factors, with the introduction of the new tax on non-alcoholic, sugar-sweetened beverages forming only part of its explanation.

“The shortfall reflects lower-than-expected collections from new revenue measures in Q1 (quarter one), due in part to non-compliance by some firms in remitting SCT for May 2026 following the introduction of the sweetened drinks tax. Changes in production and consumption behaviour in anticipation of the scheduled tax increases announced under the FY [financial year] 2026/27 revenue measures also contributed to the shortfall.

“Lower remittances from Petrojam Limited, together with weaker-than-expected performance in the automotive, petroleum distribution, and beverage/tobacco industries, further reduced SCT collections,” the ministry told the IFC.

However, the IFC was not satisfied that the explanation provided enough information to properly assess the reasons for the shortfall.

The new sweetened-drinks tax came into effect on May 1, two months into the fiscal year. The Government had initially proposed a charge of two cents per millilitre on non-alcoholic sweetened beverages, but subsequently changed the structure following consultations with industry. The revised measure applies SCT at 22 cents per gram of added sugar or sweetener.

The Government had said the measure was intended not only to raise revenue but also to support public-health objectives. It was originally projected to generate $10.1 billion during the fiscal year.

The implementation itself also encountered administrative challenges. Tax Administration Jamaica extended the deadline for beverage manufacturers to complete licensing under the new SCT regime to May 15, after the tax took effect.

The local SCT shortfall formed part of a wider revenue gap during the quarter. Central Government revenue and grants came in $28.7 billion, or 9.8 per cent, below budget, while tax revenue was $18.8 billion, or 6.9 per cent below target.

The IFC noted that nearly $9 billion of the overall $28.7-billion gap was related to timing differences, including tax revenue that had been projected for April but was collected in March as some companies paid early, and a $2.9-billion transfer from the National Housing Trust that was budgeted for June but was received in September.

The delayed implementation of the Environmental Protection Levy also contributed to the revenue shortfall. The IFC estimated that the delay resulted in approximately $700 million in revenue not being collected during the June quarter and projected a $1.8-billion revenue fallout for the 2026/27 FY if implementation remained delayed.

The legislation for the Environmental Protection Levy was passed by the Senate last Friday with the higher 0.85 per cent levy set to take effect on October 1.

World.title: Albania’s PM to US Democrats: Don’t use us to get revenge on Trump
World.content:
He added: “I told my Democratic friends in America: If you cannot beat Trump in America, do not come to Albania to take revenge. That is not fair.”

Kushner is linked to a multi-billion-dollar project to develop a luxury resort on the uninhabited southern Albanian island of Sazan and an adjacent strip of shoreline next to a protected area inhabited by flamingos, pelicans and diverse wetland wildlife. The plans sparked national and international protests at the end of May, with rallies ongoing every night outside Rama’s office in Tirana.

The protests drew widespread attention, with a resolution in the European Parliament, and international clothing brand Patagonia, and Kosovo-Albanian pop singer Dua Lipa getting involved.

Rama said the plans involve two projects: One on the publicly owned Sazan Island, a former Soviet military base, with only 8% to be developed, and another on a privately owned peninsula.

Protestors object to the project over environmental concerns and a lack of public consultation. Meanwhile, the country’s EU- and U.S.-backed Special Prosecutor’s Office for Organized Crime and Corruption, SPAK, is investigating whether an Albanian businessman faked ownership documents related to the private land.

The former owner has denied any wrongdoing. A spokesperson for the project’s investors, including Kushner, did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.

World.title: As Germany’s far right rises, weakened Merz looks to project strength and resolve against Putin
World.content:
Merz went on to warn of the danger of conflict in Europe with some of his most dramatic language yet.

“Would the Baltic states then become a battlefield for drone warfare, just as Donbas is today?” he said. “Which major European cities would be targeted by the ballistic missiles that Russia is currently firing at the populations of Kyiv and Kharkiv?"

“Would we Germans ultimately be targeted as well? Would we once again experience the horrors of war firsthand? Ladies and gentlemen, our most urgent European and transatlantic responsibility today is to do everything in our power to avert this.”

Merz’s comments came weeks after the far-right Alternative for Germany party recorded its best-ever election results, coming in first in two regional votes in the former East Germany, while the chancellor’s conservative Christian Democratic Union suffered historic defeats. The conservatives’ poor results were widely blamed on the deeply unpopular chancellor, prompting internal debate within his own party over whether to replace him.

The surge in popularity for the Kremlin-friendly AfD sparked concerns in Kyiv and across Europe that Germany — which under Merz has become Ukraine’s greatest military supporter — could falter in its support for Ukraine. The AfD — a party that favors ending military support for Ukraine and re-establishing economic and energy ties with Moscow — is the most popular party in the country, according to surveys, polling well above Merz’s conservatives.

Merz on Thursday took aim at the AfD, portraying the party as a conduit for Moscow’s influence and vowing that his government would continue to support Ukraine despite hybrid attacks and disinformation campaigns “orchestrated from Moscow” and spread through “the slogans of the AfD and its Russian backers.”

World.title: EU ministers explore new emergency migration measures
World.content:
Earlier this week, Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner presented plans to prevent and address sudden mass arrivals on the bloc’s borders that may be engineered and weaponized by other countries, including a ramped-up role for border agency Frontex.

The blueprint also included a European emergency response framework, which Commission President Ursula von der Leyen had included in her State of the Union address last month.

“We need to be able to react quickly to such emergencies when they come about,” Brunner said Thursday. He added that EU leaders would continue discussions at a meeting later this month, and that the Commission would make a proposal “on that basis.”

With talks Thursday not yet focused on specific proposals for the European emergency response framework, several countries were in wait-and-see mode.

Athens has proposed temporarily suspending asylum applications in emergency situations, and the German and Austrian ministers have signaled support for the idea.

Diplomats and ministers from three other countries said they’d wait for the Commission’s proposal before taking a position. Diplomats also raised concerns about the impact of suspending asylum applications — which could effectively result in large-scale pushbacks banned under international law — on fundamental rights, but agreed the EU needed to discuss it.

World.title: British-Iranian man arrested in RAF Fairford investigation
World.content:
Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said: “The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of inquiry."

“As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement. I’d like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this investigation.”

Five U.K. nationals from London were detained on Sep. 27 after receiving a report of suspicious vehicles near RAF Fairford, which is used by the U.S. Air Force.

They were arrested on suspicion of offenses under the Explosives Act and later, preparation of a terrorist act. They have since been bailed but remain under investigation.

On Wednesday, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC that Britain believes Iran “to have played a part” in the incident.

Earlier this year Britain gave permission for the U.S. Air Force to use RAF Fairford to carry out "defensive" strikes against Iran. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has previously warned the U.K. that British military bases used by the U.S. to launch strikes would be a “legitimate target.”

World.title: Un budget “réversible” ? Ce que le prochain gouvernement pourra vraiment défaire
World.content:
Le gouvernement met cet argument au cœur de son travail de conviction auprès des oppositions — en particulier du Rassemblement national — pour qu’elles ne fassent pas barrage au budget.

Le mode d’emploi

Parmi les mesures modifiables, celles de gel sont les plus faciles à rectifier. A commencer par la disposition qui pourrait être la plus urticante du budget de la Sécurité sociale : la désindexation des pensions de retraite au-delà d’un seuil fixé à 1 260 euros par mois, soit 4 milliards d’euros d’économies espérées.

Comme l’a révélé POLITICO, le mécanisme astucieux — “atypique” dans les mots du cabinet de David Amiel — propose un dispositif à trois étages permettant de revaloriser en dessous de l’inflation ou de geler les pensions par décret.

Celui-ci pourra être pris jusqu’au 31 octobre 2027 et s’appliquer rétroactivement au 1er janvier. Une sorte de clause de sauvegarde qui permet de laisser le choix au prochain exécutif, après la présidentielle, de revenir sur un gel total ou partiel.

“Ça me rend dingue, on prend une décision nécessaire et courageuse sur les retraites, et on donne la possibilité à Marine Le Pen de revenir dessus dès le premier jour”, s’étrangle un député EPR auprès de POLITICO, qui regrette que l’on dépossède le Parlement pour tenter d’éviter la censure.

Même logique pour le gel des APL, de la prime d’activité, du seuil des allègements généraux des cotisations sociales ou encore du point d’indice des fonctionnaires. “Tous les gels sont réversibles, a insisté David Amiel. Le futur gouvernement pourra revenir dessus dès sa première semaine aux affaires.”

World.title: EU, Ukraine agree to accelerate €45B loan payout in 2027
World.content:
At a recent meeting of EU defense ministers, "many called for front-loading parts of the €90 billion loan allocated for 2027," meaning disbursing part of the 2027 loan this year instead, the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas said last month.

But the Commission preferred to instead speed up the disbursement of the 2027 loan next year itself, meaning Ukraine would get that money faster, diplomats said.

"Our dialogue with the European Commission has delivered good results in addressing Ukraine's financial and defense needs for 2026 and 2027," Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. "We have agreed on the format, timeline, and steps needed to ensure full coverage," he added.

"For 2027, we have agreed to move forward swiftly with the allocation of €45 billion under the Ukraine Support Loan, subject to the established conditions," the two sides said, referring to the reforms Ukraine must carry out to receive the money. Once Ukraine meets the conditions, the funds will be immediately disbursed, according to a senior EU official.

The two sides also agreed that they will "begin work on identifying additional budgetary and defence needs" and meet monthly to coordinate their efforts.

The €90 billion EU loan was agreed by leaders last December to provide financial support to Ukraine in 2026 and 2027. It includes strict conditions for Kyiv, including adherence to the rule of law and the fight against corruption. A large share of the loan — €60 billion — is earmarked for Ukraine’s defense needs.

World.title: ‘We have not delivered’: Germany’s Wadephul criticizes slow EU enlargement progress
World.content:
“We have not delivered,” the minister said, adding: “I would really urge everybody to show them that the promise of Thessaloniki was real, that we are credible, that Europe is reliable.”

Wadephul also referred to “geopolitical adversaries and rivals” vying with the EU for influence in the region — a thinly veiled reference to Russia and China. On Wednesday, Republika Srpska Prime Minister Savo Minić and his predecessor Milorad Dodik visited Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, ahead of elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina on Sunday.

Austria’s foreign minister issued a similar warning: The EU must “understand that the clock is ticking. And the clock is ticking very quickly on a global scale. We can no longer afford to get bogged down in bureaucratic — and, until now, technocratic —processes,” Beate Meinl-Reisinger told POLITICO in an interview.

“If we give any leeway — even just a millimeter — other foreign powers will be here in a flash and will take advantage of it,” she said.

Montenegro is on the frontline of EU enlargement, aiming to become the bloc’s 28th member in 2028. EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos has praised the reform efforts of the country, saying that 18 of the 33 EU accession chapters had already been closed and that “several more” were expected to follow this month.

“There is a realistic chance that Montenegro will conclude negotiations by the end of the year or early next year,” she said, even though ratification would then take another one to two years.

Montenegro’s Foreign Affairs Minister Ervin Ibrahimović told reporters that his government had undertaken many reforms, adding that his citizens must now also be able to reap the benefits of EU membership.

“To be honest, we deserve to be admitted now,” Ibrahimović said.

World.title: ‘Thank you, Andy’: Farage gloats as Burnham reopens Brexit fight
World.content:
Polling has suggested a shift in public support towards rejoining the EU since then — but it remains a deeply divisive issue in U.K. politics.

Farage claimed that Burnham will be “in for a shock” — and tried out his arguments against trying to rejoin the bloc.

Those include a claimed £25 billion annual price tag for re-entry, a wave of immigration under freedom of movement, and a claim that Britain would be forced to join the Euro.

Each of these will doubtless be disputed by the government if Burnham does choose rejoining as one of several options he’s floated for a reboot of European ties after a general election.

But it shows the attack lines that Farage would relish fighting a campaign on.

“It’s just so contradictory,” the Reform UK boss told supporters at Doncaster racecourse.

World.title: Manchester City not 'above the rules', says Downing Street
World.content:
Downing Street said Thursday that Manchester City were not "above the rules", following criticism of British Prime Minister Andy Burnham's comments about the case.

 

In a statement, a No 10 spokesperson said: "As the prime minister made clear, the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules."

Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester and an avid supporter of Everton, told the BBC on Wednesday he did not want to see the club's Emirati owners walk away as a result of the case. "I would be really concerned to lose them," he said, highlighting the investment the club's controlling Abu Dhabi United Group had made in Manchester.

Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney at an English League Cup match between Everton and Wolverhampton Wanderers on Wednesday, Sep 2026 AP Photo/Paul Cooper

The 10-time English champions, who deny any wrongdoing, face an uncertain future after being found guilty of more than 100 breaches.

The Abu Dhabi-backed super-club were found to have arranged "sham" deals to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs by more than £900 million (€1.05 billion) between 2009 and 2018.

Downing Street said in its statement the "ongoing independent process" into the club must be "allowed to run its course and the outcome respected". "Wherever wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences," the spokesperson added.

World.title: Kyrylo Budanov: European security without the US would be ‘very dangerous’
World.content:
Russia’s intensifying aerial attacks on Ukraine are aimed at exhausting and intimidating the civilian population, Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, told Euronews in an exclusive interview.

 

“Civilians are being killed - women, children, elderly people, veterans of the Second World War,” Budanov said. “It is all truly terrible, especially when children are killed.”

Budanov described Russia’s approach as “classic terrorism”, saying its purpose was not only to inflict damage but to frighten the population.

Asked whether Moscow believed sustained attacks could exhaust Ukrainians and ultimately increase pressure on the government to make concessions, his answer was unequivocal: “Yes, they do believe that.”

But Budanov rejected the suggestion that Russia was adapting faster than Ukraine as Moscow deploys faster jet-powered drones, changes flight routes and carries out complex combined attacks.

“I don’t believe that Russia, in principle, is adapting faster than we are,” he said.

Instead, he said Ukraine was working to develop and deploy technological solutions to reduce the impact of Russia’s attacks, adding that protecting the civilian population the “number one task” in this effort.

Race to scale up new drone interceptors

One of those solutions is a new generation of Ukrainian interceptors designed to counter Russia’s faster jet-powered drones.

Budanov said the technology had moved beyond conventional testing and was already undergoing experimental use in combat.

“The issue is scaling up this technology,” he said.

“There are still engineering improvements to be made. They intercept Russian jet-powered drones in most cases, but there is still work to do. And then there is the question of mass production.”

Budanov said he believed Ukraine could reach the necessary scale before the most difficult period: the coming winter.

His confidence, he said, was based on having personally seen both the technology and its production.

“I have seen these developments, and I have seen the production,” Budanov said. “I am watching how the technological cycle is developing. They will make it in time.”

Deeper defence cooperation with Europe

Ukraine’s new defence technologies could also become part of deeper industrial partnerships with European countries.

Several countries have already signed cooperation agreements with Kyiv under Ukraine’s so-called Drone Deal framework.

Asked whether Ukraine’s latest technology for intercepting jet-powered drones could eventually form part of those agreements, Budanov said: “Anyone who has made such agreements with us has the right, so to speak, to continue negotiations on specific products.”

But he stressed that Ukraine’s own requirements would come first.

“We will be able to meet the demand of other countries when, first and foremost, we have met our own country’s needs for such products,” he said.

Budanov said future defence-industrial cooperation with European partners could take different forms, including joint ventures and, in some cases, production facilities abroad with Ukrainian engineers and shared ownership.

Such production could make sense where it offered advantages and where Ukraine remained the priority customer, he said. But some critical technologies, he argued, should remain inside the country.

Asked what Ukraine could bring to European defence partnerships that its partners could not develop as quickly themselves, Budanov pointed to two advantages: “The speed of implementing innovation, the speed of scaling production — in other words, mass production.”

‘Very dangerous’ for Europe without the US

Looking beyond defence-industrial cooperation, Budanov said it was still too early to define Ukraine’s place in Europe’s future security architecture because the framework itself had yet to take shape.

“What will the future security architecture of Europe actually be?” he said. “There is no answer to that question at the moment, but everyone is working on it.”

Once it was defined and formally agreed, he said, the role of each participating country would become clearer.

Asked whether such a system could work without the United States, Budanov was more explicit.

“I think those who will be developing this doctrine have to take absolutely different options into account,” he said. “But it seems to me that this is a bad option. A very bad one, very dangerous for Europe.”

Ukraine’s financing needs and economic future

Budanov also addressed Ukraine’s immediate financial requirements, saying Kyiv could already see how the greater part of its needs could be covered.

“We can see where the greater part can definitely be covered,” he said, pointing to ongoing negotiations between Ukraine, the International Monetary Fund and the European Commission.

He said Ukraine’s financial requirements would continue to change as the war evolved.

“Look at what is happening now with Russian missile and drone strikes,” he said. “Obviously, more is needed somewhere, but on the other hand, less is needed in other areas. All of this balances out.”

But Budanov drew a distinction between Ukraine’s immediate need to finance the war and the broader question of what its economy should eventually look like.

Longer term, he said he favoured a liberal, free economy with limited state intervention, alongside predictable tax policy and domestic stability.

“But right now, we have to survive,” Budanov said. “That is our main task - to survive here and now.”

He said the defence sector would require a different approach, particularly when it came to military-technical cooperation and arms exports.

“In any civilised country in the world, weapons are not simply sold left and right,” he said. “And Ukraine will not be an exception. There should simply be strict, transparent and understandable conditions for everyone.”

For now, he said, Ukrainian defence exports remained limited because of the country’s own wartime requirements.

Asked what success for Ukraine would look like years from now — economically, in attracting investment and bringing Ukrainians back home — Budanov offered a brief answer:

“A place in the world rankings that is not the one we have now.”

World.title: José Sevilla resigns as Unicaja chair and declines to remain at the bank
World.content:
José Sevilla, chairman of Unicaja, has announced his decision to stand down at the end of his term without seeking re-election, which is scheduled for next April. His departure, which will be formalised at the ordinary general meeting of shareholders, opens a new chapter in the leadership of the Málaga-based listed bank.

 

Sevilla took over the chairmanship on 5 April 2024 with a clear mandate: to restore calm within the institution and put behind it the turbulent governance crisis triggered by the merger with Liberbank. After two years focused on institutional stability, the executive has informed the bank’s highest governing body that he will complete his current term without aspiring to renewal.

In a market announcement filed with the Spanish National Securities Market Commission (CNMV), Unicaja has framed this handover within the usual protocols of its Succession Policy. Until the shareholders’ meeting is held, Sevilla will continue to perform all his non-executive duties at the head of the bank. The board of directors, for its part, has formally recorded its recognition and gratitude for the "valuable services" rendered by the executive throughout his tenure.

Agreed handover after internal peace

The announcement ushers in an orderly transition at the helm of the bank. According to Unicaja, Sevilla’s decision makes it possible to activate the Succession Plan ahead of time, so that the new chairman can be selected with sufficient notice and institutional safeguards.

The arrival at Unicaja of José Sevilla, the former chief executive officer of Bankia, put the finishing touch to the management reshuffle that followed the departure of Manuel Azuaga. His appointment as an independent director stabilised the command structure alongside the chief executive, Isidro Rubiales, paving the way in April 2024 for a smooth shareholders’ meeting that stood in stark contrast to the tensions of the previous year.

The turbulent episode of March 2023, when the "Málaga bloc" aligned with the Unicaja Banking Foundation voted down the ratification of two independent directors in order to regain control of the institution, now remains as the last major internal jolt.

With the tandem formed by Rubiales and Sevilla, the listed bank managed to straighten out its governance after the complex integration with Liberbank, ushering in a period of executive calm that it now hopes to prolong through this planned handover.

World.title: France: Media outlet publishes new antisemitic screenshots attributed to Jordan Bardella
World.content:
French media outlet Mediapart has published new material in the case of the antisemitic messages attributed to Jordan Bardella.

 

The investigative outlet on Thursday published screenshots of Facebook Messenger conversations involving him from 2013 and 2014, whose authenticity it says was established through a data extraction supplied by Meta and certified by a court bailiff, as Edwy Plenel, the outlet's co-founder, explained on Twitter.

Jordan Bardella's Antisemitic Writings: The Evidence of the Lie. Since our revelations, the Rassemblement National has violently challenged the work of « Mediapart ». Here are the documents at the heart of the investigation and the method used to authenticate them.

The investigation, conducted over several months, draws on dozens of written conversations and interviews with 18 people. The exchanges from 2013 and 2014 were passed on to Mediapart by two separate sources, both from Jordan Bardella's entourage. The outlet has stated the two sources are entirely separate and are not linked.

Jordan Bardella, who has denied from the very start of the affair that he is the author of these messages, filed a defamation complaint against Mediapart after the publication of the initial investigation.

The National Rally leader has so far rejected the accusations and on X denounced "crude fakes" and an operation designed to destabilise the presidential campaign. Within the RN, several senior figures have come out in support of him.

Beyond the far right, reactions have been more critical. On Wednesday, President Emmanuel Macron described the remarks attributed to Bardella as "extremely serious and unacceptable", calling on the RN to clarify the situation.

World.title: Europe went all in on soft power for too long, Belgian defence minister says
World.content:
Both when it comes to defence capabilities and industry capacities, Europe is in a very difficult position, Belgian Defence Minister Theo Francken told Euronews. He pointed to the bloc's decades-long prioritising of soft power as one reason for this.

 

His comments come as the European NATO members are ramping up defence spending and Brussels is rolling out policies to bolster the defence industry. While Francken sees progress being made, he warned Europe does not have all the capabilities it needs.

"Europe has been very good at investing in soft power, in social security, and it's beautiful to have a pension system, to have social welfare systems," Francken said in an interview at Euronews' Defence and Space Summit.

"When somebody gets sick, when somebody has lost his job, we have everything. But when there's war or when there is a hybrid threat, we don't have anything."

He noted that when it comes specifically to defence spending, Belgium has long been the bad apple.

"We neglected this for so long, we were like the worst pupil in NATO class," Francken said, again, referring to the emphasis put on soft power.

"We are the founding father of NATO; we're the founding father of the EU. I think that we always were there for diplomacy, for soft power, but when we talked hard power in Belgium, everybody was looking in the other direction."

Belgium reached NATO's 2% GDP defence spending threshold for the first time in 2025, rising from a low of 0.97% in 2014.

NATO wants that percentage to reach 3.5% by 2035; however, the country will remain at 2% until 2029 due to its challenging budgetary climate. Belgium currently has one of the worst budget deficits in the eurozone.

"Now we doubled the budget; we reached 2%. I know that we add two more, but it's quite a process. We're doing so much, but I cannot undo in 18 months of being a minister what has been neglected for 40 years."

Watch the interview with Theo Francken at the Defence and Space Summit here.

World.title: French protests over school conditions spread as students set fires and put up blockades
World.content:
A protest movement in France's high schools intensified on Thursday, with students setting fire to bins and erecting blockades outside schools in an increasing number of cities.

 

The students have been protesting overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and crumbling facilities.

Several school principals have been injured, harassed or assaulted at high schools, according to reports from regional education authorities, prefectures and union representatives.

Police have already detained hundreds of protesters at the lycées, which students aged 15 to 18 attend for their final three years of secondary education in France. There have been multiple reports of high school students being injured.

University students have now also joined the protest movement, and have blocked access to around 30 campuses across the country.

A security source said there had been 900 blockades or related incidents across the country on Thursday, with more than 160 schools shut down in Paris, Marseille and other cities.

In neighbouring Belgium, there were protests and damage at a handful of schools in the eastern city of Liege, police said.

Protesters demand better conditions

At a Paris high school where students barricaded an entrance, one 18-year-old student said protesters want to target “overloaded schedules, the system, the teachers, people who don’t listen to us, the university application process.”

High school students in France often start classes at 8 am and remain at school until late afternoon.

“Older people say, ‘Kids, go to school from 8 am to 6 pm every day.’ But you don’t know what that does mentally,” said another Paris high school student.

Clashes in Lille and Paris

In Lille, the protest led to particularly tense scenes. Bins were tipped over onto the road, projectiles were thrown and street furniture was damaged. Police intervened to disperse the demonstrators, charging into them and firing tear gas.

In Paris and in several communes in Île-de-France, clashes also broke out between young people and police. The movement had already led to several hundred arrests since the start of the week, mostly of minors.

Three investigations have also been opened by the IGPN after injuries sustained during blockades. In Tours, a student injured in the head on Wednesday was taken to hospital. According to the public prosecutor, his injuries were consistent with those of a non-lethal rubber bullet.

University students join the movement

After a first nationwide day of action on Tuesday, university students joined the movement on Thursday. Around 30 campuses were blocked, according to the France's leading students' union. Lower secondary schools were also affected in some regions.

Seconday and high school student organisations are calling above all for greater resources, replacement teachers and better teaching conditions. They say they intend to continue protesting, while the government now tries to contain the violence and keep access to schools open.

Political reactions

The government as well as far-right politician Marine Le Pen have accused the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of encouraging the protests.

But LFI's candidate for the 2027 presidential election, Jean-Luc Melenchon, said on Wednesday that his party "called for non-violent methods of struggle".

World.title: Palermo, first coffee grown and harvested in Italy: warmer climate is changing farming
World.content:
A plantation on the outskirts of Palermo has for the first time produced Arabica coffee beans grown and harvested entirely in Italy. The result, achieved on the Morettino family estate, has been made possible by climate change, which has effectively brought tropical temperatures to southern Italy.

 

While global warming had already enabled southern England to produce champagne-style sparkling wine, pushing the traditional growing areas of France and northern Italy further north, the jump made by coffee from equatorial zones to the Mediterranean is clearly even greater.

As the daily newspaper La Stampa reported on Thursday (source in Italian), the Sicilian plantation in the San Lorenzo ai Colli area, a few hundred metres above sea level, is currently producing around 100 kilograms of drupes (the fruit of the coffee plant, also known as cherries), which yield just over 15 kilograms of roasted beans.

The project, which involves the University and the Botanical Garden of Palermo (source in Italian) in studying how tropical crops adapt to the new Mediterranean climate, is still far from large-scale commercial production in terms of volume, but it already has considerable scientific and symbolic value.

Typical coffee makers used in Italy, on display at a 2013 exhibition in Milan by historic manufacturer Bialetti (AP Photo/Luca Bruno)

Where coffee is grown: the world’s main producing countries

Traditionally, coffee is grown in the planet’s tropical and equatorial regions, where high temperatures, humidity and steady rainfall favour its growth.

For this reason, the world’s main producers and exporters are largely concentrated in Latin America, Africa and Asia, with the Arabica variety, which delivers higher quality, grown at higher altitudes than Robusta.

The leading producer countries include Brazil, Colombia, Peru and Costa Rica in Latin America; Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania in Africa; and Vietnam and Indonesia in Asia.

According to the promoters of the initiative, the coffee produced in Palermo develops distinctive aromatic notes reminiscent of raisins, a feature that sets it apart from beans grown in traditional coffee-growing regions.

Before the Morettino family’s venture, a local farm had already grown coffee entirely in greenhouses (source in Italian) in Terrasini, also in the Palermo area.

Similar experiments have been attempted in various forms elsewhere in southern Europe.

In Spain, particularly in the province of Granada, experimental projects have been launched to test the resilience of the plants, with results quite different from those in Gran Canaria where, thanks to its more southerly latitude, coffee has been grown since the 19th century, taking advantage of the fertility and humidity of volcanic soils.

On the Azores islands in Portugal, where numerous private plantations have been reported that benefit from the mild climate, the archipelago marks one of the northernmost points where coffee is grown.

Former Italian prime minister and ECB president Mario Draghi sips an espresso during a break in proceedings in the Chamber of Deputies (18 February 2021) (AP Photo/Andrew Medichini)

How coffee consumption in Italy has changed

The growing interest in niche products such as the Sicilian coffee comes in a context in which Italy is the EU’s leading producer of roasted coffee, with over 400 tonnes produced in 2025.

The national coffee industry, although it relies on importing raw material from other producer countries (that is, unroasted beans, or "green coffee"), includes around a thousand roasters and generates an annual turnover of 5.9 billion euros.

The prospect of local cultivation, made possible by global warming, which is unfortunately also bringing more natural disasters, is in step with Italian consumption patterns, which remain robust and are growing, according to several studies published on 1 October to mark International Coffee Day.

According to a survey by AstraRicerche in partnership with the Segafredo brand, 82.6% of Italians consider the quality of the raw material decisive, while 71.8% pay attention to aromatic characteristics and 51.5% want to know the product’s origin and its journey along the supply chain.

Another survey, carried out by the Italian Coffee Committee of Unione Italiana Food and by Altroconsumo on more than 1,200 consumers, shows that three out of four Italians drink coffee regularly and almost one in two see it as one of the symbols of the country’s culture and lifestyle, on a par with pasta.

Among those who drink espresso, 83% have it every day, at home and at the bar, either with a moka pot or with modern capsule machines, which are now neck and neck in people’s habits.

Any commercial prospects must of course be weighed against environmental sustainability when growing coffee outside its traditional areas of origin.

Processing the beans after harvest can require between 50 and 200 litres of water for every kilogram of green coffee and produces wastewater which, if not properly treated, can affect local ecosystems.

And if, instead of the tropical rains that have always sustained coffee plantations, growing moves to areas where seasonal drought is becoming endemic, it becomes essential to match the agricultural challenge of coffee with a technological one, cutting the amount of water needed to grow and process the crop.
