World.title: Azerbaijan Agriculture University, Oklahoma State University to establish dual-degree master program
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 1. The Azerbaijan Agriculture University in Ganja, and Oklahoma State University to establish the dual-degree master program, said K. Aleks Schaefer, Director, Master of International Agriculture Program (MIAP), Department of Agricultural Economics, Oklahoma State University.

He made the remarks September 30 in a video message during the U.S.-Azerbaijan Chamber of Commerce (USACC) Members and Parters Appreciation Night in Baku.

“Our Master of International Agriculture program is a professionally designed, professionally oriented graduate program built around the idea that modern agriculture, modern food systems are inherently global. In addition to classes around agriculture, our students take classes in economics, business, trade policy, rural and community development, and international development. The fundamental question we're asking is: how do we prepare students not just to gain knowledge in the classroom, but also to solve the real-world problems that our stakeholders are facing today. And that's one of the reasons that this partnership between Oklahoma and Azerbaijan makes so much sense,” he said.

Schaefer pointed out that although those two regions are thousands and thousands of miles apart, the industry participants in Oklahoma are facing some of the same challenges that stakeholders in Azerbaijan are facing.

“How do we increase our agricultural productivity? How do we manage our water resources? How do we manage our other natural resources? How do we connect farmers to new markets? We know that all these are questions that we cannot address in any one country alone. Through this dual-degree program, Azerbaijani students are bringing their knowledge of agriculture in their region, other cultural and historical characteristics, to Oklahoma, where they can benefit from some of the cutting-edge research, cutting-edge extension practices that we're producing here in the U.S. more broadly. Ultimately, what I hope this becomes a program that's just so much more than this one little dual-degree program. I hope there are opportunities for the private sector to connect with our program through internships, applied research projects, seminar opportunities, to help students understand the real challenges facing agriculture in Azerbaijan. I'm really excited to see this partnership moving forward, and I'm looking forward to hosting the first students from Azerbaijan at Oklahoma State University,” he concluded.

World.title: USACC to help American companies evaluate Azerbaijan as base for regional engagement
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 1. The U.S.-Azerbaijan Chamber of Commerce (USACC) will focus on helping American companies evaluate Azerbaijan as a base for regional engagement, said Natig Bakhishov, Executive Director of the U.S.-Azerbaijan Chamber of Commerce (USACC).

He made the remarks September 30 during the U.S.-Azerbaijan Chamber of Commerce (USACC) Members and Parters Appreciation Night in Baku.

Bakhishov recalled that the Chamber supported commercial dialogue surrounding the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan oil pipeline and the Baku-Tbilisi-Erzurum gas pipeline, which helped establish Azerbaijan's role in international energy markets and provided a foundation for broader cooperation with American businesses.

“Since 2006, USACC has organized trade and study missions that bring companies directly into each other's markets. In agriculture, the first Illinois-Azerbaijan Agriculture Forum held in Chicago in 2019 connected agricultural businesses and institutions. Our Agriculture Export and Investment Support Initiative, developed with U.S. Government and AZPROMO, extended that cooperation to export development and investment opportunities. In finance, U.S.-Azerbaijan Banking and Finance Forum held at the Harvard Club in New York in 2015 provided a dedicated platform for financial sector engagement. That work continued through the first Azerbaijan Banking Mission to the United States in 2024, led by the Governor of the Central Bank of Azerbaijan and involving executives from 11 Azerbaijani banks. The second Azerbaijan Banking Mission in 2025 deepened professional exchanges with American financial institutions and regulatory experts,” said the USACC Executive Director.

He went on to add that regional connectivity has become another major focus.

“The 2025 U.S. business delegation to the Middle Corridor region brought American businesses across Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Georgia.

Through meetings and visits to transportation facilities, this program helped companies examine Azerbaijan's role within the wider regional market. Our Green Finance Leadership Summit, heading to COP29, held in Washington, D.C. in 2024, brought public officials, businesses, experts together to discuss sustainable climate-related investment. Our 30th anniversary conference this March continued that engagement through discussions on technology, energy, infrastructure, and finance,” said Bakhishov.

He pointed out that the USACC wants the U.S.-Azerbaijan commercial relationship to become broader, with more companies participating and more sectors producing lasting partnerships.

“Energy will remain important while we pursue opportunities in agriculture, technology, manufacturing, logistics, and services. Our regional work will focus on helping American companies evaluate Azerbaijan as a base for engagement with the South Caucasus and Central Asia. Building on our Middle Corridor missions, we intend to connect emerging routes, including opportunities associated with trade, with specific business needs in transportation, infrastructure, and trade services. We also want to strengthen the follow-up that turns our programs into commercial results,” he added.

Bakhishov noted that financial sector cooperation will remain a priority, where the USACC will build on its banking mission and compliance programs to support stronger institutional relationships and the reliable financial channel that international commerce requires.

“The next chapter will depend on our ability to work together with the same commitment that brought us here,” he said.

World.title: Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund to catalyze private investment in regional connectivity
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 1. The Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund will catalyze private investment in regional connectivity, said the U.S. Chargé d’Affaires ad interim in Azerbaijan, Amy Carlon, Trend's correspondent reports.

She made the remarks September 30 during the U.S.-Azerbaijan Chamber of Commerce (USACC) Members and Parters Appreciation Night in Baku.

“As an equity holder in the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), the United States is not just a bystander here. We have skin in the game, as we say. The recently established $201 million Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund will catalyze private sector investment in connectivity across the region. USACC has been our partner throughout this incredible journey, including this event tonight and the roundtable just last week in Washington with the State Department and the World Bank on regional connectivity,” she said.

Carlon recalled that she arrived in Azerbaijan shortly before President Trump's historic August 2025 Washington Peace Summit.

“The summit did more than create a pathway to sustainable peace. It also launched the Trump Route, and laid the groundwork for the U.S.-Azerbaijan strategic partnership. USACC has been our partner since day one. Last September, USACC led a Trans-Caspian business mission to Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Kazakhstan. This mission was one of the first major economic successes of my tenure in Azerbaijan and a signpost for what was to come. Then in February, Vice President J.D. Vance, our highest-level visitor in Azerbaijan since 2008, traveled to Baku to join President Ilham Aliyev in signing the Strategic Partnership Charter, committing both of our countries to deeper cooperation on regional connectivity, two-way investment in sectors like AI and digital technology, and security. In June, we held the first ever U.S.-Azerbaijan Economic Dialogue and we put that charter into action. We signed a critical minerals MoU, and we saw U.S. companies sign billions of dollars of deals with Azerbaijani companies that will bring mutual prosperity and jobs to both of our countries. And then just last week, at the Azerbaijan International Investment Forum, we saw ExxonMobil, Oracle, Apollo, and Comstock sign deals that could potentially revolutionize Azerbaijan's energy and digital sectors. We're just getting started. This is just the beginning of this relationship. You may have seen we also held a successful side event related to TRIPP at the UN General Assembly last week,” she said.

Carlon highlighted the role of the USACC in contributing to the development of business relations between the U.S. and Azerbaijan.

“Over the past 13 transformative months, USACC has been an incredible and consistent partner to the U.S. Embassy in Baku, and to my colleagues in Washington. Together with USACC and the government of Azerbaijan and all the partners, we have made great strides in taking the U.S.-Azerbaijan relationship to unprecedented heights.

We rely on USACC and other private sector partners to achieve our economic aims. We are focused on supporting U.S. companies in succeeding here to deliver prosperity and jobs to the American people and to bring that same prosperity here to Azerbaijan and the region,” she said.

World.title: Howard-era minister voted to outlaw offshore casinos, then co-founded one
World.content:
Howard-era minister De-Anne Kelly has been revealed as a co-founder and former part-owner of LuckyBet, an online casino registered in the Caribbean.

LuckyBet was formally warned by the communications regulator for allegedly contravening an Australian gambling law in September last year, after Ms Kelly had ceased to hold a stake in the company.

Decades earlier, Ms Kelly had voted to pass the Interactive Gambling Act (IGA).

The IGA banned certain forms of online gambling offered to Australian customers, including digital slots and the placing of bets after sports matches have started.

Ms Kelly argued in support of the bill, saying it was needed because gambling websites were "exploiting the vulnerable and susceptible in our society".

Loading...

The revelations come from newly leaked internal documents from the Curaçao Gaming Authority, the small Caribbean island's gambling regulator, which were released online last week by German activist Lilith Wittmann.

The ABC has sought to verify their contents through public sources where possible.

The files show that the former minister was both a major shareholder and the chief compliance officer of LuckyBet when it first applied for a gambling licence in March 2024, which the Curaçao regulator's staff noted was a "conflict".

Ms Kelly's son, Ian Parke, was listed as the company's director and the other major shareholder.

Documents later filed with the Curaçao regulator indicate that the Australian company, LBC Enterprises Australia Pty Ltd, through which Ms Kelly and other shareholders held a stake in LuckyBet, was removed as a shareholder on March 6, 2025.

The change left a company controlled by Mr Parke as the sole shareholder.

The Curaçao regulator revoked the casino's licence at the end of 2025. However, the LuckyBet website is still live.

Ms Kelly and Mr Parke did not respond to requests for comment.

Do you know more? Contact Julian Fell at tips@jtfell.com if you have any information about crypto casinos in Australia.

Regulator unaware of Australian ownership at time of alleged breach

In the years since the IGA was passed in 2001, the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) has been charged with investigating unlicensed online casinos that are accepting Australian customers.

On August 7, 2025, the ACMA received a complaint about LuckyBet.

Seven days on, the regulator launched its investigation. It later found LuckyBet was unlicensed in Australia and provided "a prohibited" service to customers in Australia, according to the published warning.

The LuckyBet site is still live despite losing its licence late last year. (Supplied: LuckyBet)

The leaked documents were not available to the Australian regulator at the time.

"Information available during the investigation indicated that [LuckyBet]'s owners and directors were registered in Curaçao," a spokesperson from the Australian Communications and Media Authority told the ABC.

"We will assess the new information about a possible Australian ownership connection and determine whether any further action is warranted."

Minister's founding role declared to Caribbean regulator

Ms Kelly was the federal member for Dawson from 1996 to 2007, and served as the minister for veterans' affairs for 15 months.

She was listed as a major shareholder and the chief compliance officer of LuckyBet in an early business plan, dated March 2023, submitted to the Curaçao gambling regulator.

The Australian company that originally owned LuckyBet listed Ms Kelly's investment firm, Calliope Investments, as a shareholder along with more than a dozen other individuals and companies.

The former minister was serving as a member of Australia's Administrative Appeals Tribunal when LuckyBet applied for its gambling licence with the Curaçao regulator in March 2024.

She left that role before the licence was approved and the casino commenced operation.

While Ms Kelly's involvement was not announced in the press, her son was open about his role at LuckyBet.

Ian Parke co-founded LuckyBet with his mother De-Anne Kelly. (LinkedIn: FIN-PAY)

Mr Parke was quoted in a press release announcing the sale of LuckyBet to Apple iSports in June 2025. "This partnership represents a major step forward for LuckyBet and the broader LBC ecosystem," he said.

Apple iSports later filed a notice with the US securities exchange saying this deal had fallen through.

Activist says 'public interest' drove her actions

Ms Wittmann, a Berlin-based activist and freelance journalist, says she tried "all conventional methods" to determine who owned several Curaçao-based casinos that were allegedly illegally targeting German citizens.

LuckyBet was not one of the casinos she was investigating.

Ms Wittmann says she monitored the Curaçao gambling regulator's activities and downloaded "every single regulatory document stored in the system".

She says this was in the "public interest".

Lilith Wittmann says hacking the Curaçao regulator was in the public interest. (Supplied: Lilith Wittmann)

After working with several investigative journalists in Europe, Ms Wittmann released the entire dataset on a public website.

The Curaçao Gaming Authority says it is investigating a breach of its systems and "will take any further action that may be warranted based on the findings".

World.title: School protests spread in France as fires break out and teachers injured
World.content:
French students have set fire to bins and erected blockades outside schools in several cities, protesting overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and crumbling facilities.

Several school principals were injured, harassed or assaulted during blockades at high schools on Thursday, local time, according to reports from regional education authorities, prefectures and union representatives.

Police have already detained hundreds of protesters at the lycees, which students aged 15 to 18 attend for their final three years of secondary education in France.

The interior ministry said police and gendarmes had made 1,949 arrests on Thursday, while 305 officers had been injured. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez condemned what he described as "unbridled violence".

The government said the demonstrations had become "urban violence" and cited the intelligence service to justify claims that it had been organised by the radical left.

Manuel Bompard, a leading figure in the hard-left France Unbowed party (LFI), quickly dismissed the claim, accusing the government of "sinking into conspiratorial thinking".

This latest wave of social unrest comes with tensions already running high over inflation, particularly soaring fuel prices, and just seven months away from France's presidential election where opinion polls suggest far-right leader Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner.

A students holds a board reading, "we want the BAC [high school diploma] Not the BAC [anti-criminality units]." (AP: Jean-Francois Badias)

A security source said there had been 900 blockades or related incidents across the country on Thursday, local time.

More than 160 schools were shut down, and university students joined the protests in Paris, Marseille and other cities.

And the authorities in the Paris region said around 50 schools had been "the scene of violence, clashes and damage".

School staff targeted

Since last week, pupils have staged protests outside schools over a range of grievances. They range from timetables, class sizes and a shortage of teachers to overheated classrooms during this year's heatwaves.

The protests have spread across the country from the Paris suburbs.

Riot police have lined up against the students, and the force has launched internal probes after accusations of brutality against three pupils, said Interior Minister Laurent Nunez.

University students also joined in Thursday, blocking access to around 30 campuses, a student union said.

Among reports of school staff being targeted was one incident in the southern port city of Marseille when a school principal and his deputy were splashed with petrol.

In the north-western city of Nantes firefighters had to intervene to extinguish a fire in the entrance of a high school "following a gathering marked by violence towards staff", the regional education board said.

Protests have spread across France, with authorities using tear gas to control outbreaks of rioting. (AP: Jean-Francois Badias)

Authorities reported violence near high schools, mainly in Nantes, blaming "violent individuals" who "join the students to carry out acts of vandalism".

In the north-eastern city of Strasbourg, trams were ordered to halt to "restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators", the regional prefect said.

Raphael, a 17-year-old who did not give his surname for fear of reprisals, was among the protesters outside a school in Strasbourg, where some used barriers to obstruct the nearby tramway tracks.

"There are 35 of us per classroom. With 35 [degrees Celsius] in summer it's unbearable. There aren't enough toilets and there are water leaks in some rooms," Raphael said.

" The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There's zero budget, zero resources, not enough supervisors. "

Nearby, students took photos of themselves in front of burning rubbish bins, holding up the sign with their school's name ripped off the tram stop.

Most pupils did not take part in any vandalism, instead breaking into a sprint down an avenue when the police fired tear gas.

In the southern city of Toulouse, hundreds of young people flooded the tram tracks, some toppling trash cans and starting fires, hurling projectiles or smashing bus shelters, AFP journalists said.

In the northern city of Lille, AFP reporters saw young people wearing black hoodies destroy the glass of a bus stop. Firefighters intervened to put out the flames on upturned dustbins set on fire.

The government has accused the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of encouraging the protests.

But LFI's candidate for the 2027 presidential election, Jean-Luc Melenchon, said on Wednesday that his party "called for non-violent methods of struggle".

In neighbouring Belgium, there were protests and damage at a handful of schools in the eastern city of Liege, police said.

AFP

World.title: Tasmania's alarming family violence numbers keep going up
World.content:
There are 400 known serial family violence offenders in Tasmania.

This past year Tasmania Police recorded more than 7,000 domestic and family violence incidents across the state.

That is more than double the number recorded 10 years ago.

In the past decade, according to Femicide Watch, 12 Tasmanian women have lost their lives to violence.

More than half were family or domestic violence incidents.

Every one of these women at some point had dreams and goals, they had people who loved them and left this world with a life unlived.

That is something Romany Wake knows all too well.

Romany Wake says it is alarming to hear how little understanding there is about the causes of family violence. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

Her mother Rachel was murdered by her ex-husband on Christmas Day almost five years ago.

"It's crazy to me that numbers are going up and up each day," Ms Wake said.

"It's just being normalised, like violence against women and children is something that's becoming so normalised that these numbers, while they're scary to look at, don't seem to be affecting anyone."

Vital to start conversations

Ms Wake and her mother Rachel's stories are well known in Tasmania.

In the years since her mother was murdered, Ms Wake has made it her mission to raise awareness about family violence.

Shakira Robertson and Romany Wake both lost their mothers at the hands of male family violence perpetrators in Tasmania. (ABC News: Jordan Young)

For her it's not just about sharing her mum's story, but helping others who might be living in violent homes realise that it's not normal.

"A lot of my friends, even at school and teachers and people that I grew up around, I don't think they realised the extent of what was happening," Ms Wake said.

"Being able to talk freely about what was going on behind closed doors I think has opened a lot of people's eyes.

"Being able to share my story and tell people, 'Hey, what you're actually going through isn't normal as much as you think it is, it's really not'.

" I'm hoping that one young person will be able to feel connected to and to feel heard and to realise that something's going on. "

Harmful beliefs need to be addressed

That prevention and early intervention space is something family violence advocates want to see more resourcing in.

Siobhan Mackay says the system needs more resourcing to support women. (ABC News: Jayden O'Neill)

Women's Legal Service Tasmania acting chief executive officer Siobhan Mackay said more needs to be done to change the harmful beliefs and norms that can lead to men's violence against women.

"We're continuing to see a really high level of men's violence towards women, partly because we're not doing enough around the drivers of violence, so looking at those underlying causes of gendered violence," she said.

Ms Mackay said there needs to be more investment in frontline community services.

"The whole system is so stretched," she said.

"We need significant investment in all areas of frontline services, whether that's counselling, legal services, shelters, case management, appropriate accommodation, access to emergency funding so that women and children can leave unsafe situations."

Increased disclosure of perpetrators

At the other end of the spectrum is legislative reform to deal with those who have already committed the crimes.

This year the Tasmanian government announced reforms that have been welcomed by family violence prevention advocates.

They include changing laws to better capture the patterns of behaviour that make up coercive control, a levy for family violence offenders that supports victims, and a requirement for serial family violence perpetrators to undertake behaviour change courses.

Jo Palmer says the government is progressing reforms to improve women's safety. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Minister for Family Violence Prevention Jo Palmer said a proposal that would require family violence offenders to declare new relationships on social media and dating profiles is about trying to prevent reoffending.

"People can make themselves to look as glossy and as fabulous as they want to look [online] and so this is a way of saying, if you have a history in this space, then we are going to tell you that you actually have to come clean with that," she said.

"It's also a way of saying to those offenders and those perpetrators, 'You're going to be called out publicly on this. We are not going to hide this'.

"We are going to say to our society and to our community: 'This person has done this. And here's their track record.'"

Violence extends beyond intimate relationships

But there's a key reform, raised by many experts, that it has yet to agree to — changing the definition of family violence, which is currently defined as people who are in an intimate relationship.

"How that plays out is that it's only two people who are in a more long-term relationship, a more serious relationship, maybe living together, maybe having children together," said Ms Mackay.

"But we know that the experiences of family violence go so much wider than that.

"There might be children involved, there could be in-laws, brothers and sisters, children, parents, adult children and none of those circumstances are currently covered by the act."

Law reforms are attempting to improve women's online safety, including around dating apps. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

Ms Mackay said as it stands people in very short-term relationships, or perhaps more casual ones, are not captured by the act.

The state government is working on a third tranche of reforms and has confirmed it is considering broadening the definition.

How the manosphere is changing classrooms Teachers say misogynistic behaviour from young, male students has been getting worse.

Ms Palmer said the government is also investing in early intervention and prevention, particularly in schools, teaching children about respectful relationships.

"[It] is really exciting to see the work that we are doing across our schools, and especially now, where we are just seeing what's happening with sexism and misogyny," she said.

"The department's actually providing schools with guidance on how do we support young people, and in particular, young men, to navigate online influencers, especially that awful content that we see around associated with the manosphere.

"Just really trying to get to our children when they're young to say, this is what a good relationship looks like."

They are the conversations Romany Wake would have liked to have had when she was at school.

She has been sharing her story for almost five years now, and while change is slow, she won't be letting up the fight.

"For me, personally, I don't want my mum's story to be forgotten, and … I don't want family and domestic violence to be normalised," she said.

World.title: Albanese jets off to talk climate, but interest rate pain is never far away
World.content:
Having a "Pre-COP" meeting in Fiji and Tuvalu is one of those initiatives that seemed a good idea at the time.

No doubt it still has resonance as part of Australia's wider diplomacy in the Pacific, in the battle to limit China's influence. But when Anthony Albanese, still coming down from his New York high, steps onto his plane on Monday bound for Pre-COP, it could feel more chore than opportunity.

Even COP itself, in Turkey a few weeks later and also on Albanese's itinerary, is not expected to break much ground.

Big issues have their high time, seizing public and media attention for brief or long periods. When Labor announced in 2021 that it would bid to host COP (The United Nations' annual climate meeting), climate change was still front and centre. But now — as we (with Pacific countries) are co-hosts with Turkey — global warming has slipped down the public's agenda.

This doesn't mean that objectively, climate change is any less important. It means other issues have supplanted it on the public's and the media's radar.

In terms of excitement and imagination, AI is the "big new thing". The appearance of OpenAI's representative at a parliamentary inquiry on Tuesday, questioned about the recent breach of a government site by a rogue agent and the new technology's risks and potential, will likely be of more interest to many Australians than what the PM is doing at Pre-COP, but neither will dominate their daily concerns.

In ordinary people's day-to-day thinking, the cost of living dominates, never more than this week when the Reserve Bank hiked rates for the fourth time this year, to the highest level since 2011.

Interest rate pain never far away

Albanese might fend off questions about domestic politics while he's away — as he tried to do when asked in New York about neglected Aboriginal children in Western Australia — but the home scene will remain on his mind.

The government is heading into a difficult final three months of the year.

With the latest rate rise, the argument over "blame" has intensified this week.

'Pressures bearing down' on rates Why is Australia stuck in an inflation problem that has sent interest rates to 15-year highs?

Treasurer Jim Chalmers on Monday got out in front of the Reserve Bank's announcement by laying as much responsibility as he could on the Iran war. The opposition insists the pressure on inflation and rates is mostly from government spending.

The bank on Tuesday complicated the picture. In its statement explaining the rate rise, it highlighted overseas factors. But at her lengthy news conference, RBA Governor Michele Bullock had a killer assessment in her opening statement.

"Inflation is too high and has been driven by domestic capacity pressures," Bullock said. "The inflation impulse from the Middle East conflict is in addition to this."

Domestic spending and investment have been stronger than expected, despite weak sentiment and the softening in housing market conditions. Productivity growth remains weak and the labour market remains a little tight. And outside of Australia, the global economy has also been more resilient than many expected.

Watching this, Chalmers may have, figuratively, kicked the cat.

Not only did the emphasis in Bullock's summary undercut his it's-the-war line but it also drew attention to the fact that the government's productivity agenda, a priority with Chalmers, has not yet delivered.

Obviously, a mix of factors is keeping inflation high — on Wednesday the latest annual figure rose from 3.5 per cent to 4 per cent — and driving up rates. But any differences in their ranking by key players will stoke the current fevered economic debate over blame.

Bullock speaks out

There's an irony in Bullock publicly (in effect) marking the government's homework. Her regular news conferences were part of the reforms to the Reserve Bank Chalmers and the bank made in Labor's first term.

It's a far cry from when the bank's top faces lived in the political shadows. The news conferences impose more accountability on the bank but, indirectly, on the government as well.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

For Bullock, appointed by Chalmers, the times have been testing. Asked recently about what the bank had done to help the economy navigate its challenges, she said:

"Just as an aside, I remember previous governors saying you'd be lucky to get through your term without something going badly pear-shaped. For Ian Macfarlane, that was the Asian financial crisis, for Glenn [Stevens] it was the GFC, and for Philip it [Lowe] was COVID. So I'm getting my share now."

Bullock is one of several high-profile women Chalmers appointed to key positions impacting his portfolio. They include Danielle Wood, chair of the Productivity Commission. From time to time Wood calls out the government on specific issues.

The willingness of Bullock and Wood, both of whom hold independent statutory posts, to tell it as they see it speaks to the quality of the appointments, although Chalmers mightn't relish it when it happens.

Loading

Government pulled between savings and relief

As it prepares its budget update, due in December, the government is pulled in conflicting directions: to respond to calls for fresh savings, and to spend on new cost-of-living relief.

Albanese probably misspoke when he suggested this week the update would have cost-of-living help. In a recent podcast with The Conversation Chalmers played down the prospect of new measures in the update, a position backed by other government sources.

If the government really wanted a new serious reform measure to curb spending it should consider a proposal floated by independent MP Allegra Spender this week: a return to a more general use of means testing. But restricting benefits in this era of people wanting big government and financial support is considered political suicide.

Shoebridge to woo angry voters David Shoebridge wants to hold Labor's feet to the fire. He will be a thorn in the party's side rather than a deal maker.

Among the pressures the government will face in coming months could be a more difficult Senate, where the Greens hold the balance of power. If Labor can't get a deal with the opposition on contested legislation, it has to turn to the Greens.

With Larissa Waters forced by serious ill health to stand down from the leadership, the Greens on Wednesday replaced her with David Shoebridge — a much more assertive, politically aggressive character, who gets under Labor's skin.

Shoebridge at his first news conference as leader put Labor on notice. Condemning its "rushing to the right", Shoebridge said: "We're not here to make the Labor Party any better. The Greens are here to replace them."

It's a sure bet that won't happen, but it's a good bet Shoebridge will turn the screws hard in negotiations.

Michelle Grattan is a professorial fellow at the University of Canberra and chief political correspondent at The Conversation, where this article first appeared.

World.title: Israelis recognised for landing plane with 'close to zero' survival chance
World.content:
Israel has honoured five of its citizens who helped fight off a pilot who attempted to crash a passenger plane as it flew to Israel with heroism awards.

Flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai was scheduled to land in ‌Tel Aviv on Wednesday, but was diverted and landed in Saudi Arabia after one pilot stabbed the other in the cockpit and "apparently tried to crash the plane", according to Israel's prime minister.

But passengers and crew aboard the Boeing 737 Max 8 were able to foil the co-pilot's attempt to crash the jet and managed to safely land it after it plummeted thousands of metres in a minute.

Loading...

"You put yourselves at risk to save others and prevented a terrible disaster," Israel's President Isaac Herzog said in a statement honouring those who helped.

"The whole world saw the beautiful and courageous face of Israeli society.

"I am proud of you, and I thank you on behalf of the state of Israel."

Inside the flydubai flight as Australians confirmed on board Passengers have described the terrifying plummet that saw the jet descend nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds and the cockpit scrum that helped the flydubai flight land safely.

Among the Israelis to receive the Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism was Yaniv Hayoun, a plumber who seized control of the plane, helping save all 174 people on board, including two Australians.

Mr Hayoun, still wearing a bloodied shirt, was personally greeted at Ben Gurion Airport by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu who called him "a hero who has saved many lives".

Another award recipient, Asaf Rajuan, said it was an "extraordinary incident".

Israeli passenger Asaf Rajuan will receive a heroism award. (AP: Ariel Schalit)

"We felt helpless, suspended in midair, and I didn't know who to turn to," he said.

"But it was all instinct: to survive, to save the family, the people, and the children."

Captain Smit Machchhar spoke about his aviation career and mentoring young pilots in a vodcast in 2025. (YouTube: )

Mr Herzog and Mr Netanyahu have also praised the plane's Indian pilot, Captain Smit Machchhar, who Israeli officials said managed to open the cockpit door to let passengers and crew save the plane after he was stabbed by the co-pilot.

Mr Machchhar is in a good health and recovering well in hospital, according to the the Indian embassy in the UAE.

Pilot's prophetic words Captain Smit Machchhar was stabbed while flying to Tel Aviv.

"He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals," Mr Netanyahu said in a post on X.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi called him a "hero".

"In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others. His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy," Mr Modi said.

Pilot says survival of passengers 'close to a miracle'

Pilot Gyorgy Peto, who is also a former aviation journalist, told the ABC the landing of this plane made "the landing on the Hudson like a walk in the park".

"Honestly the chances that this was survivable was pretty much close to zero," he told The World.

He said the aircraft was "close to breaking the speed of sound" when it descended so rapidly.

How flydubai plunge unfolded Passengers and crew members survived terrifying mid-air moments to save flight FZ1073 from disaster.

"There are a lot of small bits here that are close to a miracle, but this whole thing is just stunning in itself," Mr Peto said.

"Luck is a very important player in this whole equation."

He said the incident would inevitably bring changes to the aviation industry.

"The whole flying set-up, from a security point of view, was never planned that the pilots would attack each other," he said.

"I think there's a lot of changes coming, and a lot of uncomfortable changes, because of this."

Mr Peto said that should include better, more stringent background checks on pilots.

Minister calls for 'terrorist' pilot to face 'life of hell' in Israel

Mr Netanyahu claimed the flydubai co-pilot involved in the mid-air incident, identified as an Omani national, had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".

Netanyahu claims flydubai co-pilot underwent 'indoctrination' UAE, meanwhile, says it will investigate the circumstances and motives, of the incident, including whether it was linked ​to ‌any militant activity.

But the United Arab Emirates has started its own investigations seeking to establish the circumstances and motives, and determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose, or involved prior planning or direction", according to UAE state news agency.

Israeli Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir said he wanted the pilot extradited to Israel.

"I will demand in the cabinet to extradite the terrorist pilot who wanted to harm hundreds of innocent Israelis to Israel," he wrote on X.

"Here, he will encounter my policy in the prisons very well on his own flesh, a life of hell awaits him here!"

ABC/AFP/Reuters

World.title: The 10 albums we couldn't stop playing last month
World.content:
Spring has sprung, footy finals have wrecked our nerves, and Christmas decorations are already creeping in: must be September.

Here are 10 great albums released this month. Want more? Catch Shortcut on ABC listen for the full rundown.

Julia Jacklin — The Gem

Apple Music | Spotify | YouTube

The Naarm/Melbourne-based singer strips it back to the basics on her fourth album. (Supplied: 4AD/Remote Control Records)

Julia Jacklin etches herself deeper into the Australian songwriter wall of honour with her fourth album, The Gem.

Recorded in a studio above its small Collingwood pub namesake, Jacklin broke her habit of turning albums around in a fortnight, spending 11 months on this one.

The desire to be loved but also free permeates as Jacklin perfects her sound while experimenting with looped vocals and percussion.

It's stripped back to allow every instrument to shine under Melbourne's springtime sun, a time when the sweetness and warmth of nature embrace us as we emerge from hibernation, searching for our own slice of fresh-aired freedom.

For fans of: Angel Olson, Sharon Van Etten, Aldous Harding

Courtney Fry

Beck — Ride Lonesome

Spotify | Apple Music | YouTube

Ride Lonesome is the shapeshifting American musician's first album in seven years. (Supplied: Universal Music Australia)

Beck's 15th album sounds nothing like its stylish synth-pop predecessor, Hyperspace. No surprise; his discography is defined by restless creativity.

What is unusual about Ride Lonesome is that he saddles up and returns to familiar territory. Namely, the heartbroken singer-songwriter of Sea Change and Morning Phase.

Made with the same collaborators as those records, these unhurried tunes reckon with loss and failure in sublime melodies and production, orbiting wounded vocals, twangy guitars and plaintive, reverb-drenched orchestral arrangements.

Melancholy is one of the many suits hanging in the shapeshifter's musical closet. He just hasn't worn it in some time. It still fits, splendidly.

For fans of: Scott Walker, Elliott Smith, Brandi Carlile

Al Newstead

Beabadoobee — Pylon

Spotify | YouTube | Apple Music

Beabadoobee leans into heavy rock sounds on her fourth album Pylon. (Supplied: Dirty Hit)

The 90s and 2000s were a boom time for emotive rock music. Bea Laus wasn't alive for much of it, but she channels its sound and spirit with heart and precision on Pylon.

She sounds at home in noisier sonic terrain. It makes sense for a song like Sun Has Set: its guitar squalls and booming drums are a better fit for this jilted anthem than the sleeker pop of her recent records.

Pylon won't surprise fans, who already knew Bea could shapeshift. But Pylon should get her excellent songs to a whole new audience.

For fans of: Phoebe Bridgers, Hayley Williams, Olivia Rodrigo

Dan Condon

Orville Peck — Mule

Apple Music | Spotify | YouTube

Orville Peck traces the hardest years of his life through his fourth equus album, Mule. (Supplied: Gordon Nicholas)

Orville Peck's fourth equine-focused album is Mule, his most overtly personal project so far.

Across 13 career-defining tracks, the masked musician paints the picture of the last three years of his life: a major break-up, a suicide attempt, identity crises, rehab visits and his ride to sobriety. It's heavy material, delivered with the colourful camp that we've come to adore from Orville Peck.

From staying out all night, kissing NFL players, and starting bar fights to the unflinching lights and rigid routines of rehab, the album views life through the eyes of a man who sees himself as a mule; overworked, unloved and unsure of himself.

For fans of: Trixie Mattel, Johnny Blue Skies & the Dark Clouds, Charley Crockett

Courtney Fry

Tinashe — Popstar

Apple Music | Spotify | YouTube

(Supplied: A Nice Life/Atlantic/Warner)

Following a career lull, then a run of viral independent singles, Tinashe has, through pure will and grit, firmly placed herself back in the conversation around pop's "It Girls".

Now comes Popstar, her first major label release in eight years. From the 808-heavy R&B of Crashout to the Detroit techno-inspired Melatonin and early-2000s throwback Pillow Fight, it's a disparate yet addictive release from the 2 On hitmaker.

Popstar moves freely between styles while maintaining cohesion. It shines most when showcasing Tinashe's versatility, proving she's more creatively assured than ever.

For fans of: FKA Twigs, Kaytranada, Charli XCX

James Brennan

Ezra Collective — Here Because of Hope

Spotify | Apple Music | YouTube

Since forming in 2012, Ezra Collective has become the UK jazz scene's biggest success story. (Supplied: Mushroom Music)

The first jazz act to sell out Wembley Arena, this Mercury Prize-winning London quintet capitalises on their popularity with their conceptual fourth album.

Split into three movements outlining the migration of Black music across continents and eras, Here Because of Hope journeys from West Africa and the Caribbean to the UK streets, taking in Afrobeat, reggae, salsa, and more in a procession of contagious grooves.

It's a wide-ranging showcase for Ezra Collective's unbeatable synergy that hits less like a clinical music history lesson and more like a lovingly crafted celebration of culture. A cosmopolitan block party where everyone's invited.

For fans of: Kokoroko, Yussef Dayes, Surprise Chef

Al Newstead

This Is Lorelei — The Singer In My Band

Spotify | YouTube | Apple Music

When Nate Amos isn't busy with indie band Water From Your Eyes, he's making brilliant twangy folk as This Is Lorelei. (Supplied: Matador/Remote Control Records)

In a world awash with twangy storytellers, Nate Amos's point of view sets him apart.

On The Singer In My Band, he frames characters — karaoke king Billy, the sagely Sarah, the frustratingly stubborn Joey — so vividly they stop feeling fictional.

His usual shades of American twang and British folk are here, but the synth-pop of 2024's breakout Box for Buddy, Box for Star is excised. Charming as that somewhat jumbled album was, the clarity of The Singer In My Band makes it the more compelling proposition, and his finest work yet.

For fans of: MJ Lenderman, Wilco, Richard Thompson

Dan Condon

C.O.F.F.I.N. — Out In Oslo

Spotify | Apple Music | YouTube

This is the first C.O.F.F.I.N. (that’s Children of Finland Fighting In Norway) record released on King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard's p(doom) Records. (Supplied: p(doom) records)

Charging out of the gate with the title track's burly riffs, pub-punks C.O.F.F.I.N. nail the balance between accessible ferocity and explosive racket on their sixth album.

There's AC/DC worthy riffs and shout-along moments, but also splashes of surf rock, wailing harmonica and, on 13 Days, searing, slow-burning gothic splendour.

Commanding drummer-singer Ben Portnoy sounds like he's gargling razors while Abijah Rado's explosive solos are a consistent treat.

They've spent almost 20 years together refining their tinnie-crushing sound, as recent doco 10,000 Miles From Oslo chronicles. But enlisting members of Frenzal Rhomb and Amyl & The Sniffers to produce should tell you how revered C.O.F.F.I.N. has become.

For fans of: AC/DC, Amyl & The Sniffers, Private Function

Al Newstead

Big Noter — Songs In The Key Of Wrestling

Apple Music | Spotify | YouTube

Briggs leans into nu-metal on the debut Big Noter album, with a little help from Chuck D and Tom Morello. (Supplied: Island Records Australia)

Shepparton's finest, Briggs, is back with a bang with brand new project Big Noter. Missed your morning coffee? Don't worry, this will wake you up and then some.

He's swapped hip-hop production for heavy, nu-metal-inspired guitars and harsh vocals on a jam-packed record produced with Nick DiDia (Rage Against The Machine, Bruce Springsteen).

Still in the lineage of rap that's inspired Briggs, there's an interlude from Public Enemy legend Chuck D, a face-melting solo from Rage Against The Machine's Tom Morello and a verse from IDLES's Joe Tablot.

For fans of: IDLES, Limp Bizkit, Rage Against The Machine

James Brennan

AZ Chike — No Rest For The Wicked

Apple Music | Spotify | YouTube

After a high-profile spot on Kendrick Lamar's last album, AZ Chike delivers a strong debut this month. (Supplied: Warner Music)

LA rapper AZ Chike got his breakthrough moment on Kendrick Lamar's 2024 album GNX — Kendrick even performed Chike's verse from Peekaboo at the Super Bowl — and has run with the opportunity.

Known previously for his hyphy, gangster party rap, Chike has dialled in his songwriting on his major label debut. Guided by Lamar, No Rest For The Wicked carries diverse production and pockets, delivering hits, emotional moments and two stand-out features from the usually insular Tyler, The Creator.

The West has rallied around Chike; he's delivered a touchdown in return.

For fans of: YG, Nipsey Hussle, Kendrick Lamar

James Brennan

World.title: Are we in the Anthropocene Epoch? Scientists can't decide
World.content:
In 1952 the first full-yield test of a hydrogen bomb erupted not far from Naoero, mushroom cloud billowing above the Pacific Ocean.

That first test, and many more, spread plutonium-239 and -240 around the world marking the moment Earth entered a new era of humanity known as the Anthropocene.

At least that's according to a group of scientists who have spent years trying to pin down a date.

Georg Schäfer, a geoanthropologist, from the Max Planck Institute said that the Anthropocene moves from the period when "agriculture, cities, and human culture developed" into an era of "industrialised humanity".

"The particular strength of the Anthropocene is that it brings the many crises of the present into a single analytical frame," Dr Schäfer said.

"From coral reefs dying to microplastic pollution, climate change and forever chemicals."

But while the term has been used in popular culture for more than two decades, the Anthropocene is not an official geological epoch.

Crawford Lake in Canada was rejected as the "global boundary stratotype section and point" of the Anthropocene in 2024. (Flickr: Sean Marshall, CC BY-NC 2.0)

In 2024, a team of international scientists — the Anthropocene Working Group (AWG) — put forward evidence that the transition to a new epoch lay under the sludge at the bottom of a Canadian lake.

But the proposal was rejected by the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS), the peak global geosciences body, which decides what is an epoch and what is not.

"Whether it meets the criteria is not for us to judge," Dr Schäfer, an AWG member said.

"But … the evaluation by the geological institutions left too many questions open about serious procedural flaws.

" The 2024 vote was supposed to settle the scientific status of the Anthropocene. Instead, the opaque process created confusion. "

The researchers have just released a new commentary, published today in the journal Earth's Future, calling for an independent review of the IUGS's process, and for the release of more records.

"It is perfectly possible that the full record would show the process was sounder than it looks from the outside, that’s a perfectly fine outcome," Dr Schäfer said.

"This closed-door approach undermines the IUGS's own authority at a moment when society depends on sound environmental science more than ever."

Why do epochs matter?

Scott Mooney, a geographer at the University of New South Wales who was not involved in the working group, said understanding when humanity's fingerprint on Earth started was a "really big question".

Currently, according to the IUGS, we are in the Holocene epoch, which started 11,700 years ago at the end of the last glacial maximum.

This period is characterised by warmer temperatures, megafauna going extinct, and humans moving from hunter-gatherer societies to farming.

This boundary between the current Holocene and the previous epoch, the Pleistocene can be seen in an ice core from the Greenland ice sheet.

Ice cores have been used as golden spikes for certain epochs. (Supplied: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center/Ludovic Brucker)

There are dozens of these boundary markers, known as global boundary stratotype section and point or "golden spikes", around the world.

The AWG selected Crawford Lake in Canada as the "golden spike" for the start of the Anthropocene, highlighting the plutonium from nuclear testing as part of a sediment core at the location.

There was supporting evidence from 11 other sites worldwide, including Flinders Reef in Queensland.

But the IUGS resoundingly rejected the proposal.

"The outcome was a decisive rejection of the Anthropocene proposal: four votes in favour; 12 votes against; and three abstentions," they wrote in a statement at the time.

"It is clear from the comments that were made during the course of the discussion period, that many were unconvinced by the arguments in the AWG proposal, and their misgivings are clearly reflected in the decisive nature of the voting outcome."

Vote exposes rift between scientists

According to Helen Bostock, an oceanographer at the University of Queensland, the voting process felt "incredibly rushed".

Professor Bostock is a member of an IUGS subcommittee and voted on the proposal.

She was one of the four people who voted in the Anthropocene's favour, but says she felt they were "kept out of the loop" for the process.

"It was like, here's the information, you must vote by next week," she said.

She said there was a "rift" between different fields of geology — those who worked in hard rocks, and those who worked in softer rocks, and this likely was spilling over to issues such as the Anthropocene proposal.

"There's some of these old-school geologists who still think that it's too soon, [that it] needs to be a decent length of time before you can actually say something changed in the past," Professor Bostock said.

"Some of us are working on the sediments that show these human activities are having an impact on our environment. There's really no denying it when you can actually measure it and see it in your samples."

The golden spike at Enorama Creek in South Australia's Flinders Ranges which marks the boundary of the Ediacaran Period — from 635 million years ago to 542 million years ago. (Flickr: James St. John, CC BY 2.0)

Professor Bostock said that if the Anthropocene proposal was to be resubmitted, a fairer way to adjudicate would be a "broad vote" from the larger discipline rather than a small group.

"I think that would give us a much better representative, instead of a committee that might be biased in one way or another, depending on who's sitting on that committee."

Dr Mooney broadly agreed with the working group's argument about why Anthropocene should be formalised as an epoch.

"It really does highlight the impact that humanity is having on Earth," he said.

" The really good point [the group] makes is that the Anthropocene is out there — it's not just geoscientists that use [the term] — it's everyone. "

World.title: Brisbane's bid to celebrate home-grown artists ahead of Olympics
World.content:
Jarad Danby has transformed public spaces across the world with his art, and now, for the first time, he has a mural in his home city of Brisbane.

His work inside a 200-metre tunnel in the inner-city suburb of Newstead is part of a push to celebrate home-grown talent ahead of the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

A tunnel in Newstead has been transformed with a brightly coloured mural by Brisbane artist Jarad Danby. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

"When the world comes to Brisbane, it's important that we tell real Brisbane stories, and who is better to do that than our own artists?" street art curator Matthew Tervo said.

"They can give you an artwork that gives you a sense of that place, so when people come to Brisbane they leave with a sense of who we really are."

Street art curator Matthew Tervo and Brisbane artist Jarad Danby. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

In a bid to reflect the area's history in his artwork, Danby visited the local museum and selected and photographed items to incorporate into his work.

He then created a scribble grid on the wall, which gave him a reference point to be able to transfer an image he composed on his computer onto the wall at the correct scale.

"I wanted to represent the future of Brisbane and how abundant it is going to be in the lead-up to the Olympics," he said.

Artist Jarad Danby and his team carefully laid out the items on the table and photographed them before uploading the images to a computer. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

His mural features fresh fruit, and he has taken inspiration from the surrounds with a process behind each element.

"This is my first public piece in Brisbane, so that was really special, and I was able to bring my mum and dad here, and they were jubilant," he said.

A tunnel at Newstead has been transformed nto a work of art, inspired by locally sourced produce and objects from the past. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

The mural has been funded by the Brisbane City Council, with plans to do more in the next six years ahead of the Games.

"As all eyes are on Brisbane for 2032 it's important to have projects like this that showcase who we are as a city," Brisbane Councillor Julia Dixon said.

Jarad Danby says he wanted to incorporate the greenery in the surrounding area into his artwork. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Cost-effective solution

While street art is created for the public, it's also helping to offset the cost of vandalism.

It is proving to work at an underpass in Toowong, where the council was having to fork out to cover up graffiti and maintain the beige walls before it became a mural.

An underpass in Toowong has turned from beige to a piece of art, and it has proved effective in reducing graffiti. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

"The budget per square metre wasn't a lot, so we innovated and used recycled paint to achieve the outcome," Mr Tervo said.

"The metric we were given for success is if we halved the amount of spend removing vandalism, then it would be considered successful.

"So far, there's only been one instance of vandalism in six months.

"It is just proof that we are the problem as well as the solution."

Matthew Tervo says Brisbane should be on the map as a world-class street art city. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Mr Tervo said the focus should be on creating uniquely Brisbane street art as opposed to becoming "Melbourne lite".

"It's awesome for street artists but also the public because it creates a link between nature and buildings … it adds so much culture and life to a city," Danby said.

"Brisbane should be on the map as a world-class street art city because we have some of the best artists and so many blank walls as well."

World.title: ‘Islamist radical’: Israel claims horror flight co-pilot shared hate online
World.content:
Updated WorldMiddle EastAviation ‘Islamist radical’: Israel claims horror flight co-pilot shared hate online David Crowe Updated October 2, 2026 — 5:36am ,first published 3:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: The co-pilot accused of trying to crash a flight to Israel is said by government officials to have undergone an “Islamist radical indoctrination” that led him to stab the pilot and plunge the aircraft toward the ground in a horrifying ordeal for 174 passengers and crew. US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has suggested – without providing evidence – that the co-pilot may have links to Iran. Loading When asked by reporters if he had been briefed about any links between the suspect behind the attack and Tehran, he said, “I would say the answer, based on what I’m hearing, is yes, but we’re working on it right now.” Investigators have uncovered personal material that showed his Islamist tendencies, Israel’s prime minister said on Thursday, in the first formal indication of a motive for a midair emergency likened to the 9/11 attacks in the US.





Israeli government officials told the media that the co-pilot had talked on social media about killing Jews and had displayed his “jihadist ideology” online. The assertions are based on Israeli investigations into the co-pilot as well as witness statements about his actions on the aircraft, although accounts vary about what he said. Netanyahu, in an image posted on his X account, with some of the heroes of flydubai flight FZ1073: Yaniv Hayun, Or Pardilov, Dr Shota Musayev and his wife Sigalit. @IsraeliPM One witness told media in Tel Aviv, after passengers arrived safely in Israel, that he heard the co-pilot should “Allahu Akbar” as the plane plunged toward the ground. Other witnesses have not made this claim, while Netanyahu gave a different account based on his conversations with the passengers who stormed the cockpit.



Witnesses described chaos and horror as the plane plunged and the co-pilot attacked the pilot, captain Smit Machchhar, but there are no detailed accounts of anything the attacker said during the ordeal. One passenger, Tali Niss, realised the danger in the cockpit and alerted those on board. Three others – Yaniv Hayoun, Tzvika Manes and Asaf Rajuan – confronted and subdued the co-pilot in a fight that took at least 20 minutes. Another passenger, Dr Shota Musayev, treated the wounded captain. The five passengers are being honoured with presidential awards for heroism. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaking to Fox News about the flydubai incident. Fox News Netanyahu outlined some of what occurred based on his conversations with the passengers. Asked by a Fox News presenter if the co-pilot said “Allahu Akbar” before trying to crash the plane, the prime minister replied: “No, no, none of that.”



Netanyahu said the co-pilot was suicidal and appeared to be intent on smashing the aircraft before the passengers stopped him. Related Article Visual story

Aviation A terrifying plunge, loud screams, blood everywhere: How flight FZ1073 unfolded, moment by moment “They had to tie his hands, so they used the cord of the earphones in the cockpit – I mean, talk about improvisation,” he said. “And then he’s lying there now, this attacker, and he calls out to the aircrew: ‘kill me, kill me’. “So it’s clear he was suicidal. That’s not a question.



“It was clear he was going to down that plane – Oh, it’s not clear, but it looks very likely that he was going to down the plane, and with all the passengers in there. “And if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think that’ll give us a pretty good clue [about the attack].” Captain Smit Machchhar, the pilot stabbed mid-flight, received life-saving care from a dentist on board. Twitter Netanyahu added that he was not making “final conclusions” at this stage. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has described the events as a “jihadist terrorist attack” but government investigators have made no formal statements about the co-pilot’s motivations, connections to others or links to foreign states.



Trump’s suggestion of an Iranian link come as diplomatic efforts to end the war appear to have stalled. He did not elaborate why he thought Iran might be involved. Asked if the US would retaliate against Tehran if it was behind the attack, Trump said, “Oh they’ll be hit, very hard, don’t worry.” “You just ask them,” he added. “They know what happened. They’ll be hit very hard.” The investigation is expected to be led by the United Arab Emirates because flydubai flight FZ1073 originated in Dubai and was flying under the UAE flag.



The prosecutor-general in the UAE has begun the investigation. A regional official briefed on the investigation confirmed that Saudi authorities were working with countries, including Israel, to try to determine a motive. He said the UAE, the US and Oman also were involved. Saudi Arabia said on Friday morning (AEST) that the suspect had been handed over to the UAE. The injured captain was taken to hospital after the two off-duty pilots landed the aircraft at Tabuk Airport in western Saudi Arabia. He is being hailed as a hero for opening the cockpit door despite his wounds, allowing passengers to force their way in and prevent the co-pilot smashing the instrument panel. Netanyahu said it was not known how the co-pilot managed to have a knife on board, although he said he may have used an axe that was installed on the aircraft. A key concern in Israel is that flydubai, owned by an investment arm of the Dubai government, allowed an Omani citizen to fly the aircraft to Tel Aviv even when there are no diplomatic relations between Israel and Oman.



The events have raised questions about whether the Omani co-pilot would have had authority to land in Israel and should have been on the aircraft. Related Article Updated

Aviation Five passengers to be awarded for heroism during apparent attempt to crash plane Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev suspended flydubai operations to Israel while ordering a formal inquiry into potential breaches of aviation treaties. One colleague who knew the Omani co-pilot described him as a religious extremist in an article published by The Times of Israel. The colleague, who is also a pilot, told Israel’s Channel 16 that the Omani national joined flydubai eight months ago.



“He prayed excessively throughout the day and refused to shake hands with women,” the pilot said. Netanyahu expressed amazement at the way the passengers subdued the co-pilot and said one of them, Hayoun, a plumber, had told him he watched aircraft crash investigation documentaries on television. This helped the passenger know how to bring the aircraft out of its dive. “I asked him, ’How did you know how to do that? And he said, ‘Well, I watched these air disaster films’,” Netanyahu told Fox News. “This is Hollywood on steroids. You can’t make this up. You can’t believe that it actually happens in real life, but it did.” Two Australians on board, Steven and Carol Moss, are yet to comment on the events.

World.title: ASX eyes gains after rocky night on markets; Oil prices climb
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX eyes gains after rocky night on markets; Oil prices climb Stan Choe October 2, 2026 — 5:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More swings in the bond market are rattling stock markets around the world. On Wall Street, the moves were relatively modest after US bond yields cranked higher but then gave back the gains later in the day. The S&P 500 rose 0.3 per cent and was on track to break a three-day losing streak. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was virtually unchanged in mid-afternoon trade and the Nasdaq composite was 0.3 per cent higher. It has been a rollercoaster ride on global markets overnight. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to climb, with futures at 5.01am AEST pointing to a rise of 40 points or 0.5 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 2 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.24¢. The moves were more dramatic in Europe, where stock indexes tumbled 1.7 per cent in London, 1.6 per cent in Paris and 1 per cent in Frankfurt. They were hurt by sharp moves for bond yields on that side of the Atlantic. The yield on the 10-year French government bond, for example, shot to nearly 4.95 per cent and then veered toward 4.80 per cent and back up to 4.90 per cent.



Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Donald Trump’s war on the world faces a lethal blow Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist That is a punishing swing for the bond market, where moves get measured in hundredths of a percentage point. High yields slow the economy by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money, while undercutting prices for stocks and other investments. Yields are on the rise for a range of reasons, including worries about high inflation and oil prices, signals that the US economy remains solid and governments’ insistence to continue to spend much more money than they bring in. Those worries don’t look to be going away anytime soon, and oil prices climbed again Thursday to keep the pressure up on inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude leaped 4.3 per cent to $US102.24 for its latest yo-yo move on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global oil industry to return to normal.



Further reports also signalled the US economy is powering through its many challenges. Fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could mean companies are laying off fewer workers. A separate report on Thursday said growth for US manufacturing also continued in September. Potentially more concerning in that report from the Institute for Supply Management was that increases in prices accelerated, which could mean further pressure on inflation. It all sent the yield on the 10-year US Treasury briefly toward 5.34 per cent and its highest level since 2002. But the 10-year yield relented later in the day and pulled back to 5.23 per cent from 5.29 per cent late Wednesday. That helped stocks on Wall Street recover their losses and turn higher. Still, the 10-year yield remains much higher than it was last week, when it was below 5 per cent, and from before the war with Iran began, when it was below 4 per cent. High yields can hurt real-estate owners in particular. Not only do they raise the cost of borrowing, they can also make investors looking for income leave real-estate stocks and their dividends for bonds.



BXP, which owns office buildings around the country, sank 1.6 per cent. Alexandria Real Estate Equities, which owns campuses for life sciences companies, fell 2.2 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Employment Unemployment probably does need to climb … for now Millie Muroi Economics Writer Helping to counteract such losses were gains for stocks benefiting from the boom around artificial-intelligence technology. Optimism rose after Micron Technology delivered a stronger profit report for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Micron also said growth is strengthening, and it gave forecasts for upcoming profit and revenue that topped analysts’ estimates because of the AI boom. Micron’s stock rose 1.7 per cent to bring its stellar gain for the year so far to nearly 280 per cent. Elsewhere in AI, Nvidia added 1.6 per cent and was the single strongest force lifting the S&P 500, while Applied Materials rose 3.8 per cent.



Outside of tech, Accenture leaped 17 per cent after the consulting and services company reported stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It saw growth around the world, from the Americas to Asia. In stock markets abroad, Asian indexes did better than the rest of the world thanks to optimism around AI following Micron’s profit report. Japan’s Nikkei 225 jumped 3.3 per cent, and South Korea’s Kospi climbed 1.9 per cent. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
