World.title: ‘Seriously bonkers’: Inside the Knights-mania sweeping Newcastle
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘Seriously bonkers’: Inside the Knights-mania sweeping Newcastle Tom Decent October 2, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Electric Pantera Tattoo Parlour in Newcastle is buzzing. It’s been a big few weeks for body art of a certain motif in a town gearing up for Sunday’s NRL grand final. On Thursday afternoon, when most Novocastrians are hard at work, three men are sprawled across tattoo beds getting Newcastle Knights ink. Mick Sharp gets a Newcastle Knights tattoo from artist Dave Ross at Electric Pantera Tattoo Parlour in Newcastle on Thursday. Sitthixay Ditthavong One is already wearing a Knights jersey. Some tattoos are large. Others are small. The passion for the Knights is extra large.



Mick Sharp found time before his 12-hour night shift at a chemical plant to get the Knights logo that he’s wanted for years tattooed on his upper arm. He is such a Newcastle tragic that he named his first son Joey after Andrew “Joey” Johns. Loading “I was at the game on Sunday and have tickets for this Sunday, so thought why not get amongst it,” Sharp says. “It was the best rugby league moment of my life. “We talk about the Knights pretty much every time I get my tattoos. I can’t believe the way the town lifts from it.”



The first thing you see upon entering the parlour is a red and blue book on the reception desk. Our Town, Our Team: The Story of the Newcastle Knights. Newcastle Knights fans take selfies in front of a Knights mural at The Goodfriends Eatery at The Junction, Newcastle on Thursday. Sitthixay Ditthavong Owner Dave Ross has been completing about “six to seven” Knights tattoos a day of late. There were dozens in September as the team went through finals, beating the Rabbitohs, Warriors and Panthers to qualify for a grand final few expected them to make. Things got so busy Ross had to call in extra staff. The moment Newcastle edged out Penrith on Sunday in a stunning preliminary final upset, Ross heard his phone vibrating in his pocket. They were messages from prospective clients.



Beside his tattoo machine are VHS tapes of the 1997 and 2001 grand finals, Newcastle’s two premiership triumphs. Ross is wearing a corduroy hat emblazoned with an image of a shirtless Andrew Johns riding a skateboard down King Street – the famous scene after the Knights’ triumph over Manly 29 years ago. Newcastle Knights fans pose for photos with cheerleaders at a training session at McDonald Jones Stadium. Sitthixay Ditthavong After Wednesday’s open training session at McDonald Jones Stadium, where 12,000 fans turned out to watch their heroes, Thursday was supposed to be a quieter day as everyone began mentally preparing for the game ahead. It didn’t turn out that way. The young men in the tattoo parlour chat away to the artists. At times, it feels more like a therapy session – black leather couch and all – as they recall their fondest memories of Knights games from years gone by. There have been some seriously lean years along the way, too, which makes this week all the more special.



“Newcastle feels like the centre of the universe at the moment,” Ross says. “It’s truly like nothing we’ve ever experienced. “It’s never been busier. I never thought it would ever take off like this. Last week was pretty bonkers, but since the win on Sunday it’s gone seriously bonkers.” A banner supporting the Newcastle Knights is strung across the scaffolding of a house under construction at the start of the Newcastle Memorial Walk. Sitthixay Ditthavong As much as Ross would probably love the extra business, Sunday will remain sacred. No tattoos. “I need the morning and the day to mentally prepare for the Knights,” he says with a laugh.



“Everyone is the happiest I’ve seen. You can’t walk on the street without seeing a Knights shirt. It’s just the most incredible time.” To understand the Knights-mania sweeping through Newcastle, consider this: 22,000 free tickets for a grand final watch party at McDonald Jones Stadium on Sunday sold out in three minutes. Newcastle fans pack out McDonald Jones Stadium. Sitthixay Ditthavong That’s 122 a second. On Saturday, fans will line the streets of Newcastle to farewell the players as they depart for Sydney. The team bus will leave the Knights Centre of Excellence at 9.30am, travelling through the city before heading towards the M1.

World.title: The sub-tropical islands of Japan are a world away from Tokyo and Kyoto
World.content:
InspirationAsia The sub-tropical islands of Japan are a world away from Tokyo and Kyoto Catherine Marshall October 2, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The first typhoon of the season is scheduled to arrive at midday. If all goes according to plan, we will sail into its eye somewhere along Shikoku’s southern seaboard. “My question: how are your sea legs?” asks Captain Pierre-Marie Ducournau. Ponant’s Odyssey in the Heart of Japan’s Subtropical Islands alternates departures between Osaka, Japan, and Keelung, Taiwan (pictured). A nervous titter washes through Le Soleal’s auditorium, where we’ve gathered for a pre-departure briefing. But Ducournau is just teasing. Instead of sailing headfirst from Osaka into the capricious Pacific Ocean, he will instead detour through the truly pacific Seto Inland Sea. It won’t be the last calamity we thwart on this trip. “We can see Typhoon Jangmi will go fast [up] the east of Japan,” he says. “That will clear our path on the west coast of Kyushu, and thanks to this, we will be able to resume our itinerary in Kagoshima.”



We glide westwards through the night, and dock next morning at Imabari on Shikoku’s northern shore. The world outside the windows of my deluxe suite is ice blue: the millpond sea; the bridges threading together islets on their journey from Honshu; Shikoku’s mountains stacked like frozen waves against the sky. It’s hard to believe a typhoon is about to shred the coast beyond those resolute ridges. 



The sea is polished as we drift forth overnight. At dawn, the ship slips through the narrow strait separating Honshu and Kyushu and pops like a cork into the Korea Strait. Rain smudges the windows of the observation lounge. “Ah yes – the rain, the rain,” laments Yamamoto. Kurushima Kaikyo bridge in Ehime, Japan. iStock But our entreaties to the mountain god will pay multiple dividends by the end of this trip. We bump along Kyushu’s western seaboard, take refuge in Hakata Bay and make our second hastily planned stop at Fukuoka. Cherry blossom-pink buses ferry us to Kyushu National Museum in Dazaifu. “Thank you for coming in the typhoon – the typhoon!” says guide Yuko Ehara. “Usually, the typhoon season is summer time, but this [springtime] rainy season is very important for growing rice.”



Rice sprouts tremble in the flooded fields, and the glass-encased museum is spattered with raindrops. History is sealed safely inside it: earthenware vessels, sutra containers, fragile scrolls and the fossilised jaw of a Naumann’s elephant, an extinct species from the Pleistocene era. The exhibit was dredged from the Seto Inland Sea in the 19th century. “We’re just in time to see the typhoon passing,” says Ducournau, as he eases Le Soleal out of Hakata Bay and towards the East China Sea. The active volcano Sakurajima is in Kagoshima Bay on the island of Kyushu. Kagoshima Bay comes into sight right on schedule. Sakurajima, an active volcano, squats at its centre, its vent capped not with steam but with white cloud. Once an island, it’s now fastened with a collar of lava to the mainland opposite Kagoshima, from which an around-the-clock ferry service transports the residents still living in the shadow of this volatile formation named, curiously, for the graceful cherry blossom. “You want to know how many times this year it erupted?” asks guide Mayumi Uchiyama. “So far, around 30 times.”



Most eruptions are insubstantial, but some reshape the landscape: Sakurajima Visitor Centre stands on a lava field formed after an eruption in 1914. A trail skirts the volcano’s flanks; up close, it looks innocuous with its cloudy scarf and skirt of spruce. But in five days’ time it will erupt violently, blackening the sky and spewing effluvium. Mercifully, there will be no casualties. The UNESCO World Heritage-listed island of Yakushima is layered with subtropical shores, temperate slopes and sub-Arctic peaks. But we’re long gone by then, weaving our way through the Ryukyu Archipelago, which arches like a dislocated spine towards Taiwan. Until 1879, these scattered islands were part of the Ryukyu Kingdom. On their northern tip is the UNESCO World Heritage-listed Yakushima, a cupcake of an island layered with subtropical shores, temperate slopes and sub-Arctic peaks. “Botanists from all over the world come here,” says guide Yuko Ehara. “It’s a miracle island.”



Somewhere in its mountainous middle stands the 1000-plus-year-old Jomonsugi, a sugi (cedar) said to be Japan’s oldest tree. Sugis were once used to make shingles. Now protected, they provide shelter as we move through the forest’s damp, spongy epiphyte-ribbed understorey. Okinawa begins far south-west of here, a string of 160 isles anchored by the slender, elongated Okinawa Island. By the time we reach it, we’ve managed to shake off Typhoon Jangmi’s residual wisps, but the sky is still chalky, the typically radiant bays a dull turquoise. The subtropical Kerama Islands in Okinawa, Japan. iStock The ruins of Nakijin Castle at Motobu in the north seem anachronistic amid the sugar cane and pineapple plantations, the powdery beaches and shallow oyster beds. Okinawa feels more Polynesian than Japanese, like a sliver of land that’s dislodged from Hawaii and drifted into foreign waters. After Japan took over the Ryukyu Kingdom, the indigenous Okinawan language “was like a symbol of a punishment or embarrassment”, says guide Shoko Gushiken Lamb. “Okinawan language is very different to Japanese but is in danger of extinction.”



Today, an American lilt can be heard in some Okinawans’ English, a legacy of 27 years of military occupation by the US following the 1945 Battle of Okinawa, in which at least 100,000 civilians were killed. The islands were returned to Japan in 1972, but US military bases are still scattered across the island. The 50,000-odd Americans living here contribute to Okinawa’s rich cultural brew, known as champuru. “Champuru means stir fry,” says Lamb. “You know, you use some kind of meat or fish, and cook it with several vegetables, and that makes it a nice, good dish? Okinawan culture is like that.” In Naha, the island’s main city, Spam and Campbell’s soup are sold in the grocery stores beside Okinawan specialities such as beni imo, pastry shells filled with the purple sweet potato that grows plump and sticky in the subtropical heat. All night, we plough onwards through the Okinawa Trough, and in the morning find a paradise of translucent bays lapping the Miyako islands. Miyakojima’s northern spit is famed for yukishio (snow salt), so named for its powdery softness.



To the west, Irabu Ohashi, Japan’s longest non-toll bridge, rises to a pinched point before spindling downwards to tiny Irabujima and the Makiyama Observation Deck. Perched at the island’s highest point, 80 metres, it’s shaped like the open wings of the grey-faced buzzards that flock here in autumn. On the crossing, I see turtles paddling beneath the bridge in water of such an improbable hue it gave rise to the term “Miyako blue”. Related Article Japan People here live longer than anyone, but my visit shortened my lifespan “When I first visited Miyako Island, I was so surprised how beautiful the ocean is,” Lamb says. This heavenly snapshot dissolves behind us as we slide onwards to Ishigaki, our final stop before reaching Taiwan. Next morning, as I wait to join my shore excursion, an alarm shrieks through the lounge. Everyone’s phone has pinged simultaneously with an emergency alert. “Get out of the water and leave coastal regions immediately,” it says.



Ducournau’s calm voice comes over the intercom: “An 8.2-magnitude earthquake has occurred off the Philippines’ coast, and the entire Japanese archipelago is under a tsunami alert.” We sail to deeper waters; fishing vessels, small cargo ships and the coastguard follow in our wake. For hours, we anchor out there, reading, attending lectures, enjoying the fine food served in the ship’s two restaurants. Finally, we’re approved to return to shore to complete immigration procedures. Despite a slight ocean surge, Ishigaki is unscathed. Ducournau, and perhaps the mountain god, has excelled. We’ve avoided a typhoon, a volcanic eruption and a tsunami. But then, who said getting to paradise was plain sailing? DETAILS FLY

Cathay Pacific flies from Sydney and Melbourne to Osaka via Hong Kong, and return from Taipei via Hong Kong. See cathaypacific.com



CRUISE

Ponant’s 10-day Odyssey in the Heart of Japan’s Subtropical Islands alternates departures between Osaka, Japan, and Keelung, Taiwan. The next sailing departs on September 20, 2027, from $12,290 a person. See au.ponant.com The writer was a guest of Ponant.

World.title: We looked at staff salaries at Brisbane’s private schools. These pay the most
World.content:
NationalQueenslandTeaching We looked at staff salaries at Brisbane’s private schools. These pay the most Catherine Strohfeldt October 2, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of Brisbane’s most prestigious schools has inked a new pay deal for teachers, as Queensland’s private institutions set the state standard for teachers’ wages. Among the first Brisbane private schools to negotiate new deals was Brisbane Grammar School, which sent a new agreement to the Fair Work Commission for final approvals in mid-September. It would pay senior teaching staff as much as $140,000 by January next year, which Independent Education Union Queensland branch secretary Terry Burke said would match Brisbane Girls Grammar School salaries. Brisbane Grammar School is expected to finalise a new wage deal that would boost the upper limit on base salaries to $140,000. Catherine Strohfeldt “They saw the school over the other side of the lane, getting particular rates and thought that as a staff they should be getting paid those rates too,” Burke said.





The school declined to comment when contacted by this masthead. The latest Commonwealth data from the Workplace Gender Equality Agency showed the average wage for all staff across almost 40 eligible Brisbane private secondary schools sat at about $117,000 in the 2024-25 financial year. This number, which included non-teaching staff, increased from the previous year by about $4000 across all Brisbane private schools. Among the schools with the highest averages on its list was Anglican Church Grammar School (Churchie), which paid teaching and non-teaching staff an average of $149,000 across the 2024-25 financial year.



However, in 2026, the highest base salary for a teacher sat at $130,996, although teachers with additional qualifications, such as highly accomplished and lead teachers, could add another $16,000. Burke said across private institutions, independent-sector schools had an “energetic promotion” of staff to specialised roles, such as highly accomplished and lead teacher roles, which come with a several-thousand-dollar bonus. Teachers in the highest pay brackets at Brisbane Girls’ Grammar School could earn up to $135,206 this year. Catherine Strohfeldt Catholic schools, he said, were generally employing more graduate teachers, driving down salary average figures. “Even more so, the pattern of doing internships in the last year of the four-year degree – that continues to rise,” Burke said.



At the lower end of the figures, Brisbane Adventist College and Brisbane Boys’ College (BBC) paid staff, on average, less than $100,000. However, BBC’s current wage deal stipulated the school would pay its non-specialised teachers a base salary of up to $131,000 this year. Burke said the state’s public sector generally set the precedent for teachers’ pay, and private schools were “the next cab off the ranks”. “The last little while we’ve been so-so, but the big increases should have occurred in July last year for the Queensland Teachers’ Union,” he said.



The union was instead fronting arbitration in April next year, leaving the private sector to eke out its own pay deals ahead of public school teachers, Burke said. Related Article Updated

Schools State school teachers secure interim pay rise The Education Department told this masthead the current average for state school teachers – falling in the 2026-27 financial year – was about $117,000. A spokesperson said the September interim wage order bumped teachers up to base salaries between $86,600 and about $126,700. The department also offered “valuable initiates” to teachers, the spokesperson said, including incentive programs, relocation packages, and retention payments.



The Catholic sector was next to negotiate fresh pay deals. These included six agreements with Queensland’s five dioceses, and one covering religious institute schools – a group which includes St Joseph’s College Gregory Terrace (Terrace), Marist College Ashgrove and All Hallows’ School. World.title: ‘A privilege and a pleasure’: What life’s like in an award-worthy house
World.content:
PropertyNewsArchitecture ‘A privilege and a pleasure’: What life’s like in an award-worthy house Carmen Forward October 2, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When they walked into their home for the first time, Roberta Easton turned to her husband and said, “Patrick, this is it.” During her house hunt, Roberta, an interior designer, had a request. “I kept saying to the real estate agents, I have to have a wow factor… You have to show me something that is amazing … not cookie cutter,” she said. Roberta and Patrick Easton with their dog Teddy. James Brickwood In 2016, the couple bought Reeves House, designed by architects Peter Stutchbury and Sue Harper. It was commended for the Robin Boyd Award for Residential Architecture – the Australian Institute of Architects’ top award for new homes – in 2000. The tri-level property is nestled in the treetops of Clareville on Sydney’s northern beaches, with views to Pittwater, and features open spaces that maximise sun but offer shelter from the weather.



After 10 years living at 91 Hudson Parade, Roberta and Patrick, both aged 65, have decided to sell the home and make a tree change. The property is listed for sale with a $6 million price guide by private treaty. Before moving to the northern beaches, the couple were in the inner west for almost a decade and had renovated a Victorian terrace house. Patrick, a business consultant, said the difference between their current home and their prior inner west terrace was that they had felt “all enclosed.”



Roberta explained, “You walk through the front door, past the great rooms, staircase going up, and it’s not till you actually… get to the back of the house where it opens up.” “We always thought, gee, we would love to see more of the outdoors,” Patrick said. The home is set in the treetops. James Brickwood As soon as they walked into the Clareville property the empty nesters could see trees everywhere they looked. “Because I’m so interested in design and interiors … The house just stood out,” Roberta said.



She said there are “so many magnificent features, and everywhere you look in the house, it’s just another interesting moment.” They purchased the house for $2,925,000 and lived there for a while to see if they needed any changes. Residents can enjoy the outdoors. James Brickwood They added a swimming pool five years ago. “The pool is one spectacular feature. There’s no fence around the pool,” Roberta said. It was also designed by Peter Stutchbury, with edges that can’t be walked on. Updates have been minimal. Roberta added green to the colour palette to reflect more of the nature outside on the inside.



They refurbished the bathroom tiles and the splashback in the kitchen. The garden matured with the house. The use of green in the colour palette inside connects with the treetops outside. James Brickwood Day to day, they notice the impact of the architectural design detail. Patrick appreciates the house’s thoughtful orientation. “It really catches the northern sun as well as handles the western sun as well,” he said. “It’s really nestled into a little nook too, so it’s very well protected from the weather … So you might have a howling southwesterly, but you [can] still sit outside because there’ll be a deck that you can sit on that’s sheltered from that.”



The entire layout is open plan yet feels private at the same time. And while the design is primarily doorless, other than two downstairs doors, the couple didn’t mind the lack of door to their en suite. It was just the two of them. Because of the flow of the home, they haven’t felt the need to overfill the space with furniture. Each piece, Roberta said, is “limited but very considered”. The home is open plan. James Brickwood “You don’t need a lot of decor in a house like Peter Stutchbury’s house because the house is the decor, the angles, the materials,” she said. “We sit and watch the clouds roll by,” she added. They also watch the sunsets and how the light changes through the day.



A highlight of the past decade has been having Pittwater on their doorstep. They moor their Beneteau across the road. “It’s a sailors’ playground,” Roberta said, adding that Patrick is a very “keen, great sailor.” Roberta and Patrick are preparing for their next move. James Brickwood Within five minutes, they can be across the water, having lunch at Morning Bay, or sleep a few nights on the Hawkesbury River or in four hours be in Sydney Harbour. “It’s been a privilege and an absolute pleasure,” she said.



The couple will miss Clareville but are looking forward to a different experience in the Hunter Valley. Related Article Construction How Vickii transformed a higgledy-piggledy home into an entertainer’s dream “It’s a time in our life where we need to stretch out and have another adventure,” Roberta said. Roberta is going to have a pottery studio, and Patrick will continue to sail from Sydney. And their adult children look forward to visiting them in the next spot. Selling agent Marcus Lloyd-Jones from Modern House says the home stands out due to its architecture and location.



“There is a certain part of the market that truly understands great design, fantastic engineering and building,” he said. “A property of this quality is rare. It really is.”

World.title: The quiet cul-de-sac at the centre of Sydney’s newest housing debate
World.content:
NationalNSWPublic housing The quiet cul-de-sac at the centre of Sydney’s newest housing debate Anthony Segaert October 2, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There are many things that concern Louise Marchant and her son, Gary, about being forced out of their home after more than 30 years. Where will they go? How do they pack up the dozens of family photos and memories? And what do they do about the sheds overflowing with Christmas decorations in their backyard? Louise, 67, and Gary, 39, have worked with neighbours and friends to light up the quiet cul-de-sac of Indigo Way, Blacktown, in Sydney’s west, with a show-stopping display of lights and decorations ranging from snow-capped model towns to rooftop reindeer. Gary Marchant is responsible for turning Indigo Way into a Christmas wonderland. Sitthixay Ditthavong Last Christmas was their final display. Homes NSW is relocating Indigo Way’s public housing tenants, with plans to demolish 16 freestanding homes and replace them with 134 apartment blocks up to six storeys high. In being forced out, residents on the quiet cul-de-sac have found themselves at the centre of a new housing battle, stretching from the public housing centre of Waterloo to Blacktown: how, exactly, should the government increase the public supply of homes?



Homes NSW, the government agency responsible for delivering and managing public housing, is pushing in some areas to demolish and replace ageing or lower-density homes with modern and more densely packed apartments. But the Greens and other housing advocates are pushing the government to build new homes on vacant, government-owned land – and not demolish existing housing. “The delivery of these new homes could take up to 10 years,” said Greens MP Jenny Leong, the party’s housing spokesperson, who said the net effect would be a reduction in public housing numbers before construction finished. Louise Marchant has lived in her home for more than 40 years. Sitthixay Ditthavong Louise and her neighbours, most of whom declined to be interviewed, were contacted by Homes NSW on July 20 with a letter saying its staff is surveying the area for potential development and that residents may be moved in the future. Nine days later, a second letter arrived. All residents would be relocated. “We were told that they would come out here to us, to have an interview in our house, to see what we need. Not one person has had anyone come out,” Gary said. “I would have expected that within a week, you’d have a knock on the door, or a text message.



“At the end of the day, we’re happy to do it, but the way it’s being handled, the way we’re being treated – it’s not right. And we’re not standing for it.” Louise is concerned about where Homes NSW will move her, given much of her community and social life exists up and down the street. She regularly cares for her six-year-old granddaughter, who has cerebral palsy and uses her home for therapy. “We have to make it safe for her as well,” she said. Some residents of Indigo Way have already moved out of the quiet cul-de-sac. Sitthixay Ditthavong “What I can’t understand is, if they’ve got 16 empty places out there [for the residents of Indigo Way to move into], why aren’t people living [in them]? Why are they taking us out and putting us into those 16 houses … Why destroy homes that are all right and have a good community?” A similar debate has been raging in Waterloo, in inner Sydney, since the government in May announced plans to bulldoze 750 apartments built in the 1970s and put 3300 new apartments up to 33 storeys high in their place. Leong is calling on the government to build public housing on unused state-owned land.



“[The government has] confirmed under their land audit that they’ve identified unused sites that are publicly owned already that are capable of delivering 13,000 homes,” she said. “But less than 15 per cent of those are being used by the government and, of those, less than 30 per cent will be social housing.” Related Article Exclusive

City life Hundreds of inner Sydney homes to be bulldozed for 3300 units NSW Housing Minister Rose Jackson said the cost of land was a major issue in delivering housing, and “large-scale renewals on our own under-utilised land” was one method of avoiding buying more land. “I acknowledge that some families would rather stay in their existing homes and we don’t take these decisions lightly. But I have an obligation to every person on the social housing waitlist to do everything in my power to build more homes and that’s what we’re doing,” she said. “Every resident that relocates is always given a right of return, and overwhelmingly the feedback I get from residents is that they love their new homes.”



The street has garnered more than 750 signatures on a petition to the government, but hopes are fading for a Christmas display this year. “It’s going to be the worst feeling, not to be able to come and look at this house at Christmas,” Gary said. “It’s such a good little community.”

World.title: The world’s 20 last great free attractions (plus five close to home)
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As of this month, visitors to Cologne Cathedral in Germany must pay an entry fee. The colossal Gothic masterpiece has been free to visit for centuries, but that privilege ended on July 1, with tourists wanting to admire its cavernous interior now required to cough up €12 ($19.50). It is the latest in a string of attractions around the world that have introduced admission charges in recent times. The Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, for example, went from being free to costing €25 ($40) in 2024, while Rome brought in charges for both the Pantheon (in 2023) and the Trevi Fountain (in 2025). Even the great outdoors is not immune to the trend, with hikers tackling Japan’s Mount Fuji now subject to a fee. So, which of the world’s great landmarks are, for now, still completely free to visit? East Side Gallery, Berlin The famous Berlin mural depicting Leonid Brezhnev and Erich Honecker. iStock This surviving section of the Berlin Wall now stands as the world’s longest open-air gallery, featuring more than 100 paintings across almost two kilometres. The East Side Gallery has official “Denkmal” (heritage-protected) status and is open 24 hours a day, attracting more than three million visitors annually. Keep an eye out for one of its most well-known murals: the “Fraternal Kiss” depicts Erich Honecker, the East German chairman, and Leonid Brezhnev, the Soviet leader, locking lips. 



The Giant’s Causeway’s hexagonal basalt columns formed by ancient volcanic activity. iStock According to science, Northern Ireland’s first World Heritage Site owes its existence to volcanic activity and continental drift. According to legend, it owes it to a rivalry between giants. Whatever its origin story, the result was 40,000 hexagonal basalt columns and one of the UK’s most spectacular views. Book a paid visitor experience through the National Trust if you’d like to be accompanied by a storyteller, but otherwise, simply walk down to the stones on the Atlantic shore at no cost. Plaza de Espana, Seville See Seville’s charming Plaza De Espana while it’s still free. iStock With its azulejo-adorned benches and a charming canal dotted with rowing boats, the semicircle-shaped Plaza de Espana is one of Seville’s numerous architectural delights. It is also one of the few that remain free; the Royal Alcazar, the cathedral and the Giralda, as well as the Setas de Sevilla, all charge. This might change. Jose Luis Sanz, the mayor of the city, announced plans to introduce an entry fee in 2024, and it would appear that the project is still in motion despite delays. The plaza could therefore follow in the footsteps of other ticketed open-air spaces in Spain, such as Barcelona’s Park Guell, which is priced at €18 ($29). As it stands, however, the Plaza de Espana is free, even if not for much longer. Notre-Dame, Paris



You might have to queue up but visiting Notre-Dame is worth it. iStock The Parisian cathedral of Notre-Dame, overlooking the Seine, charges a fee to climb the 424 steps of one of its towers, but tourists are still able to visit the rest of the building free of charge. As with the British Museum, reserving an entry time is advised, but this is also free. The cathedral is older than Cologne’s and underwent extensive restoration following the 2019 fire that forced it to close for five years. Now, visitors can once again see its 13th-century rose windows and the Crown of Thorns relic in all their glory. The British Museum, London The British Museum’s Great Court is enclosed by a spectacular glass roof and was designed by Foster and Partners. More than 6.4 million people visited the British Museum last year, many of them probably eager to catch a glimpse of the Rosetta Stone, the treasures of Sutton Hoo or the Elgin Marbles. And if that wasn’t enough of a reason to go, viewing its impressive collection costs precisely nothing. Some temporary exhibitions do charge an entry fee; for example, standard tickets for the forthcoming loan of the Bayeux Tapestry carry a hefty price tag of £33 ($62). But fees do not apply to standard admission. That said, it is advised to book a timed slot to avoid the queues. Of course, it is just one of many excellent and free museums in London. The Natural History Museum overtook the British Museum as the UK’s premier visitor attraction last year, while the Tate Modern, the V&A and the National Gallery are home to world-class artistic collections.



St Peter’s Basilica, Vatican City Michelangelo’s Pieta can be seen free of charge at St Peter’s in Rome. iStock Although you’ll pay to see some parts of St Peter’s Basilica, such as the dome above or necropolis beneath, a general visit is free providing you’re willing to take your chances in often long queues. If you want to book a time slot, a €7 ($11) fee will apply – though you get a digital audio guide with it. The basilica is crammed with artworks; Michelangelo’s great masterpiece, Pieta, is alone worth the visit. Everywhere you look there’s something remarkable: gilded cherubs, mosaics, statues of saints, popes’ tombs, memorial tablets. Everything is on a colossal scale. Be aware that dress codes are strictly enforced, so avoid shorts, bare shoulders and skirts above the knee. Papal audiences in the square outside, held every Wednesday morning whenever the pope is in Rome, are also free. Jemaa el-Fnaa, Marrakesh Bustling Jemaa el-Fnaa square at sunset in Marrakesh, Morocco. iStock



The beating heart of Marrakesh’s medina has been drawing the city’s visitors since the 11th century, and today the square is an unmissable entry on any traveller’s itinerary. Mornings are filled with the sound of snake charmers’ pungi flutes and the smell of freshly squeezed orange juice, while evenings see it transform into a labyrinthine, lantern-lit set-up filled with food stands and fortune tellers. The Golden Temple, Amritsar The Golden Temple, in Amritsar, feeds 150,000 people daily, free of charge. iStock The Sri Harmandir Sahib complex, which houses the Golden Temple, feeds 150,000 people daily, free of charge, as a manifestation of the Sikh belief that its places of worship are open to all. Head coverings are mandatory for all visitors, but these are provided, as are foot-washing stations and shoe storage. A fee of any sort would jar with its entire ethos. The temple seems to float on the waters of the Amrit Sarovar pool and is surrounded by marble walkways where gurus read scripture and visitors rest in the shade. Dawn is often said to be the best time to visit, when the building reflects in the tranquil waters while the morning light catches on its gilded domes. Fushimi Inari Taisha, Kyoto There are 10,000 torii gates at the Fushimi Inari Shrine in Kyoto. iStock Japan’s ancient capital has no shortage of captivating Shinto shrines, but this one at the base of Mount Inari has become one of the country’s most emblematic sites. Dedicated to the harvest deity, Fushimi Inari Taisha is best known for its 10,000 densely packed torii gates.

World.title: ‘Islamist radical’: Israel claims horror flight co-pilot shared hate online
World.content:
Updated WorldMiddle EastAviation ‘Islamist radical’: Israel claims horror flight co-pilot shared hate online David Crowe Updated October 2, 2026 — 5:36am ,first published 3:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: The co-pilot accused of trying to crash a flight to Israel is said by government officials to have undergone an “Islamist radical indoctrination” that led him to stab the pilot and plunge the aircraft toward the ground in a horrifying ordeal for 174 passengers and crew. US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has suggested – without providing evidence – that the co-pilot may have links to Iran. Loading When asked by reporters if he had been briefed about any links between the suspect behind the attack and Tehran, he said, “I would say the answer, based on what I’m hearing, is yes, but we’re working on it right now.” Investigators have uncovered personal material that showed his Islamist tendencies, Israel’s prime minister said on Thursday, in the first formal indication of a motive for a midair emergency likened to the 9/11 attacks in the US.





Israeli government officials told the media that the co-pilot had talked on social media about killing Jews and had displayed his “jihadist ideology” online. The assertions are based on Israeli investigations into the co-pilot as well as witness statements about his actions on the aircraft, although accounts vary about what he said. Netanyahu, in an image posted on his X account, with some of the heroes of flydubai flight FZ1073: Yaniv Hayun, Or Pardilov, Dr Shota Musayev and his wife Sigalit. @IsraeliPM One witness told media in Tel Aviv, after passengers arrived safely in Israel, that he heard the co-pilot should “Allahu Akbar” as the plane plunged toward the ground. Other witnesses have not made this claim, while Netanyahu gave a different account based on his conversations with the passengers who stormed the cockpit.



Witnesses described chaos and horror as the plane plunged and the co-pilot attacked the pilot, captain Smit Machchhar, but there are no detailed accounts of anything the attacker said during the ordeal. One passenger, Tali Niss, realised the danger in the cockpit and alerted those on board. Three others – Yaniv Hayoun, Tzvika Manes and Asaf Rajuan – confronted and subdued the co-pilot in a fight that took at least 20 minutes. Another passenger, Dr Shota Musayev, treated the wounded captain. The five passengers are being honoured with presidential awards for heroism. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaking to Fox News about the flydubai incident. Fox News Netanyahu outlined some of what occurred based on his conversations with the passengers. Asked by a Fox News presenter if the co-pilot said “Allahu Akbar” before trying to crash the plane, the prime minister replied: “No, no, none of that.”



Netanyahu said the co-pilot was suicidal and appeared to be intent on smashing the aircraft before the passengers stopped him. Related Article Visual story

Aviation A terrifying plunge, loud screams, blood everywhere: How flight FZ1073 unfolded, moment by moment “They had to tie his hands, so they used the cord of the earphones in the cockpit – I mean, talk about improvisation,” he said. “And then he’s lying there now, this attacker, and he calls out to the aircrew: ‘kill me, kill me’. “So it’s clear he was suicidal. That’s not a question.



“It was clear he was going to down that plane – Oh, it’s not clear, but it looks very likely that he was going to down the plane, and with all the passengers in there. “And if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think that’ll give us a pretty good clue [about the attack].” Captain Smit Machchhar, the pilot stabbed mid-flight, received life-saving care from a dentist on board. Twitter Netanyahu added that he was not making “final conclusions” at this stage. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has described the events as a “jihadist terrorist attack” but government investigators have made no formal statements about the co-pilot’s motivations, connections to others or links to foreign states.



Trump’s suggestion of an Iranian link come as diplomatic efforts to end the war appear to have stalled. He did not elaborate why he thought Iran might be involved. Asked if the US would retaliate against Tehran if it was behind the attack, Trump said, “Oh they’ll be hit, very hard, don’t worry.” “You just ask them,” he added. “They know what happened. They’ll be hit very hard.” The investigation is expected to be led by the United Arab Emirates because flydubai flight FZ1073 originated in Dubai and was flying under the UAE flag.



The prosecutor-general in the UAE has begun the investigation. A regional official briefed on the investigation confirmed that Saudi authorities were working with countries, including Israel, to try to determine a motive. He said the UAE, the US and Oman also were involved. Saudi Arabia said on Friday morning (AEST) that the suspect had been handed over to the UAE. The injured captain was taken to hospital after the two off-duty pilots landed the aircraft at Tabuk Airport in western Saudi Arabia. He is being hailed as a hero for opening the cockpit door despite his wounds, allowing passengers to force their way in and prevent the co-pilot smashing the instrument panel. Netanyahu said it was not known how the co-pilot managed to have a knife on board, although he said he may have used an axe that was installed on the aircraft. A key concern in Israel is that flydubai, owned by an investment arm of the Dubai government, allowed an Omani citizen to fly the aircraft to Tel Aviv even when there are no diplomatic relations between Israel and Oman.



The events have raised questions about whether the Omani co-pilot would have had authority to land in Israel and should have been on the aircraft. Related Article Updated

Aviation Five passengers to be awarded for heroism during apparent attempt to crash plane Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev suspended flydubai operations to Israel while ordering a formal inquiry into potential breaches of aviation treaties. One colleague who knew the Omani co-pilot described him as a religious extremist in an article published by The Times of Israel. The colleague, who is also a pilot, told Israel’s Channel 16 that the Omani national joined flydubai eight months ago.



“He prayed excessively throughout the day and refused to shake hands with women,” the pilot said. Netanyahu expressed amazement at the way the passengers subdued the co-pilot and said one of them, Hayoun, a plumber, had told him he watched aircraft crash investigation documentaries on television. This helped the passenger know how to bring the aircraft out of its dive. “I asked him, ’How did you know how to do that? And he said, ‘Well, I watched these air disaster films’,” Netanyahu told Fox News. “This is Hollywood on steroids. You can’t make this up. You can’t believe that it actually happens in real life, but it did.” Two Australians on board, Steven and Carol Moss, are yet to comment on the events.

World.title: ASX eyes gains after rocky night on markets; Oil prices climb
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX eyes gains after rocky night on markets; Oil prices climb Stan Choe October 2, 2026 — 5:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More swings in the bond market are rattling stock markets around the world. On Wall Street, the moves were relatively modest after US bond yields cranked higher but then gave back the gains later in the day. The S&P 500 rose 0.3 per cent and was on track to break a three-day losing streak. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was virtually unchanged in mid-afternoon trade and the Nasdaq composite was 0.3 per cent higher. It has been a rollercoaster ride on global markets overnight. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to climb, with futures at 5.01am AEST pointing to a rise of 40 points or 0.5 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 2 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.24¢. The moves were more dramatic in Europe, where stock indexes tumbled 1.7 per cent in London, 1.6 per cent in Paris and 1 per cent in Frankfurt. They were hurt by sharp moves for bond yields on that side of the Atlantic. The yield on the 10-year French government bond, for example, shot to nearly 4.95 per cent and then veered toward 4.80 per cent and back up to 4.90 per cent.



Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Donald Trump’s war on the world faces a lethal blow Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist That is a punishing swing for the bond market, where moves get measured in hundredths of a percentage point. High yields slow the economy by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money, while undercutting prices for stocks and other investments. Yields are on the rise for a range of reasons, including worries about high inflation and oil prices, signals that the US economy remains solid and governments’ insistence to continue to spend much more money than they bring in. Those worries don’t look to be going away anytime soon, and oil prices climbed again Thursday to keep the pressure up on inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude leaped 4.3 per cent to $US102.24 for its latest yo-yo move on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global oil industry to return to normal.



Further reports also signalled the US economy is powering through its many challenges. Fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could mean companies are laying off fewer workers. A separate report on Thursday said growth for US manufacturing also continued in September. Potentially more concerning in that report from the Institute for Supply Management was that increases in prices accelerated, which could mean further pressure on inflation. It all sent the yield on the 10-year US Treasury briefly toward 5.34 per cent and its highest level since 2002. But the 10-year yield relented later in the day and pulled back to 5.23 per cent from 5.29 per cent late Wednesday. That helped stocks on Wall Street recover their losses and turn higher. Still, the 10-year yield remains much higher than it was last week, when it was below 5 per cent, and from before the war with Iran began, when it was below 4 per cent. High yields can hurt real-estate owners in particular. Not only do they raise the cost of borrowing, they can also make investors looking for income leave real-estate stocks and their dividends for bonds.



BXP, which owns office buildings around the country, sank 1.6 per cent. Alexandria Real Estate Equities, which owns campuses for life sciences companies, fell 2.2 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Employment Unemployment probably does need to climb … for now Millie Muroi Economics Writer Helping to counteract such losses were gains for stocks benefiting from the boom around artificial-intelligence technology. Optimism rose after Micron Technology delivered a stronger profit report for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Micron also said growth is strengthening, and it gave forecasts for upcoming profit and revenue that topped analysts’ estimates because of the AI boom. Micron’s stock rose 1.7 per cent to bring its stellar gain for the year so far to nearly 280 per cent. Elsewhere in AI, Nvidia added 1.6 per cent and was the single strongest force lifting the S&P 500, while Applied Materials rose 3.8 per cent.



Outside of tech, Accenture leaped 17 per cent after the consulting and services company reported stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It saw growth around the world, from the Americas to Asia. In stock markets abroad, Asian indexes did better than the rest of the world thanks to optimism around AI following Micron’s profit report. Japan’s Nikkei 225 jumped 3.3 per cent, and South Korea’s Kospi climbed 1.9 per cent. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ‘Seriously bonkers’: Inside the Knights-mania sweeping Newcastle
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘Seriously bonkers’: Inside the Knights-mania sweeping Newcastle Tom Decent October 2, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Electric Pantera Tattoo Parlour in Newcastle is buzzing. It’s been a big few weeks for body art of a certain motif in a town gearing up for Sunday’s NRL grand final. On Thursday afternoon, when most Novocastrians are hard at work, three men are sprawled across tattoo beds getting Newcastle Knights ink. Mick Sharp gets a Newcastle Knights tattoo from artist Dave Ross at Electric Pantera Tattoo Parlour in Newcastle on Thursday. Sitthixay Ditthavong One is already wearing a Knights jersey. Some tattoos are large. Others are small. The passion for the Knights is extra large.



Mick Sharp found time before his 12-hour night shift at a chemical plant to get the Knights logo that he’s wanted for years tattooed on his upper arm. He is such a Newcastle tragic that he named his first son Joey after Andrew “Joey” Johns. Loading “I was at the game on Sunday and have tickets for this Sunday, so thought why not get amongst it,” Sharp says. “It was the best rugby league moment of my life. “We talk about the Knights pretty much every time I get my tattoos. I can’t believe the way the town lifts from it.”



The first thing you see upon entering the parlour is a red and blue book on the reception desk. Our Town, Our Team: The Story of the Newcastle Knights. Newcastle Knights fans take selfies in front of a Knights mural at The Goodfriends Eatery at The Junction, Newcastle on Thursday. Sitthixay Ditthavong Owner Dave Ross has been completing about “six to seven” Knights tattoos a day of late. There were dozens in September as the team went through finals, beating the Rabbitohs, Warriors and Panthers to qualify for a grand final few expected them to make. Things got so busy Ross had to call in extra staff. The moment Newcastle edged out Penrith on Sunday in a stunning preliminary final upset, Ross heard his phone vibrating in his pocket. They were messages from prospective clients.



Beside his tattoo machine are VHS tapes of the 1997 and 2001 grand finals, Newcastle’s two premiership triumphs. Ross is wearing a corduroy hat emblazoned with an image of a shirtless Andrew Johns riding a skateboard down King Street – the famous scene after the Knights’ triumph over Manly 29 years ago. Newcastle Knights fans pose for photos with cheerleaders at a training session at McDonald Jones Stadium. Sitthixay Ditthavong After Wednesday’s open training session at McDonald Jones Stadium, where 12,000 fans turned out to watch their heroes, Thursday was supposed to be a quieter day as everyone began mentally preparing for the game ahead. It didn’t turn out that way. The young men in the tattoo parlour chat away to the artists. At times, it feels more like a therapy session – black leather couch and all – as they recall their fondest memories of Knights games from years gone by. There have been some seriously lean years along the way, too, which makes this week all the more special.



“Newcastle feels like the centre of the universe at the moment,” Ross says. “It’s truly like nothing we’ve ever experienced. “It’s never been busier. I never thought it would ever take off like this. Last week was pretty bonkers, but since the win on Sunday it’s gone seriously bonkers.” A banner supporting the Newcastle Knights is strung across the scaffolding of a house under construction at the start of the Newcastle Memorial Walk. Sitthixay Ditthavong As much as Ross would probably love the extra business, Sunday will remain sacred. No tattoos. “I need the morning and the day to mentally prepare for the Knights,” he says with a laugh.



“Everyone is the happiest I’ve seen. You can’t walk on the street without seeing a Knights shirt. It’s just the most incredible time.” To understand the Knights-mania sweeping through Newcastle, consider this: 22,000 free tickets for a grand final watch party at McDonald Jones Stadium on Sunday sold out in three minutes. Newcastle fans pack out McDonald Jones Stadium. Sitthixay Ditthavong That’s 122 a second. On Saturday, fans will line the streets of Newcastle to farewell the players as they depart for Sydney. The team bus will leave the Knights Centre of Excellence at 9.30am, travelling through the city before heading towards the M1.

World.title: The sub-tropical islands of Japan are a world away from Tokyo and Kyoto
World.content:
InspirationAsia The sub-tropical islands of Japan are a world away from Tokyo and Kyoto Catherine Marshall October 2, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The first typhoon of the season is scheduled to arrive at midday. If all goes according to plan, we will sail into its eye somewhere along Shikoku’s southern seaboard. “My question: how are your sea legs?” asks Captain Pierre-Marie Ducournau. Ponant’s Odyssey in the Heart of Japan’s Subtropical Islands alternates departures between Osaka, Japan, and Keelung, Taiwan (pictured). A nervous titter washes through Le Soleal’s auditorium, where we’ve gathered for a pre-departure briefing. But Ducournau is just teasing. Instead of sailing headfirst from Osaka into the capricious Pacific Ocean, he will instead detour through the truly pacific Seto Inland Sea. It won’t be the last calamity we thwart on this trip. “We can see Typhoon Jangmi will go fast [up] the east of Japan,” he says. “That will clear our path on the west coast of Kyushu, and thanks to this, we will be able to resume our itinerary in Kagoshima.”



We glide westwards through the night, and dock next morning at Imabari on Shikoku’s northern shore. The world outside the windows of my deluxe suite is ice blue: the millpond sea; the bridges threading together islets on their journey from Honshu; Shikoku’s mountains stacked like frozen waves against the sky. It’s hard to believe a typhoon is about to shred the coast beyond those resolute ridges. 



The sea is polished as we drift forth overnight. At dawn, the ship slips through the narrow strait separating Honshu and Kyushu and pops like a cork into the Korea Strait. Rain smudges the windows of the observation lounge. “Ah yes – the rain, the rain,” laments Yamamoto. Kurushima Kaikyo bridge in Ehime, Japan. iStock But our entreaties to the mountain god will pay multiple dividends by the end of this trip. We bump along Kyushu’s western seaboard, take refuge in Hakata Bay and make our second hastily planned stop at Fukuoka. Cherry blossom-pink buses ferry us to Kyushu National Museum in Dazaifu. “Thank you for coming in the typhoon – the typhoon!” says guide Yuko Ehara. “Usually, the typhoon season is summer time, but this [springtime] rainy season is very important for growing rice.”



Rice sprouts tremble in the flooded fields, and the glass-encased museum is spattered with raindrops. History is sealed safely inside it: earthenware vessels, sutra containers, fragile scrolls and the fossilised jaw of a Naumann’s elephant, an extinct species from the Pleistocene era. The exhibit was dredged from the Seto Inland Sea in the 19th century. “We’re just in time to see the typhoon passing,” says Ducournau, as he eases Le Soleal out of Hakata Bay and towards the East China Sea. The active volcano Sakurajima is in Kagoshima Bay on the island of Kyushu. Kagoshima Bay comes into sight right on schedule. Sakurajima, an active volcano, squats at its centre, its vent capped not with steam but with white cloud. Once an island, it’s now fastened with a collar of lava to the mainland opposite Kagoshima, from which an around-the-clock ferry service transports the residents still living in the shadow of this volatile formation named, curiously, for the graceful cherry blossom. “You want to know how many times this year it erupted?” asks guide Mayumi Uchiyama. “So far, around 30 times.”



Most eruptions are insubstantial, but some reshape the landscape: Sakurajima Visitor Centre stands on a lava field formed after an eruption in 1914. A trail skirts the volcano’s flanks; up close, it looks innocuous with its cloudy scarf and skirt of spruce. But in five days’ time it will erupt violently, blackening the sky and spewing effluvium. Mercifully, there will be no casualties. The UNESCO World Heritage-listed island of Yakushima is layered with subtropical shores, temperate slopes and sub-Arctic peaks. But we’re long gone by then, weaving our way through the Ryukyu Archipelago, which arches like a dislocated spine towards Taiwan. Until 1879, these scattered islands were part of the Ryukyu Kingdom. On their northern tip is the UNESCO World Heritage-listed Yakushima, a cupcake of an island layered with subtropical shores, temperate slopes and sub-Arctic peaks. “Botanists from all over the world come here,” says guide Yuko Ehara. “It’s a miracle island.”



Somewhere in its mountainous middle stands the 1000-plus-year-old Jomonsugi, a sugi (cedar) said to be Japan’s oldest tree. Sugis were once used to make shingles. Now protected, they provide shelter as we move through the forest’s damp, spongy epiphyte-ribbed understorey. Okinawa begins far south-west of here, a string of 160 isles anchored by the slender, elongated Okinawa Island. By the time we reach it, we’ve managed to shake off Typhoon Jangmi’s residual wisps, but the sky is still chalky, the typically radiant bays a dull turquoise. The subtropical Kerama Islands in Okinawa, Japan. iStock The ruins of Nakijin Castle at Motobu in the north seem anachronistic amid the sugar cane and pineapple plantations, the powdery beaches and shallow oyster beds. Okinawa feels more Polynesian than Japanese, like a sliver of land that’s dislodged from Hawaii and drifted into foreign waters. After Japan took over the Ryukyu Kingdom, the indigenous Okinawan language “was like a symbol of a punishment or embarrassment”, says guide Shoko Gushiken Lamb. “Okinawan language is very different to Japanese but is in danger of extinction.”



Today, an American lilt can be heard in some Okinawans’ English, a legacy of 27 years of military occupation by the US following the 1945 Battle of Okinawa, in which at least 100,000 civilians were killed. The islands were returned to Japan in 1972, but US military bases are still scattered across the island. The 50,000-odd Americans living here contribute to Okinawa’s rich cultural brew, known as champuru. “Champuru means stir fry,” says Lamb. “You know, you use some kind of meat or fish, and cook it with several vegetables, and that makes it a nice, good dish? Okinawan culture is like that.” In Naha, the island’s main city, Spam and Campbell’s soup are sold in the grocery stores beside Okinawan specialities such as beni imo, pastry shells filled with the purple sweet potato that grows plump and sticky in the subtropical heat. All night, we plough onwards through the Okinawa Trough, and in the morning find a paradise of translucent bays lapping the Miyako islands. Miyakojima’s northern spit is famed for yukishio (snow salt), so named for its powdery softness.



To the west, Irabu Ohashi, Japan’s longest non-toll bridge, rises to a pinched point before spindling downwards to tiny Irabujima and the Makiyama Observation Deck. Perched at the island’s highest point, 80 metres, it’s shaped like the open wings of the grey-faced buzzards that flock here in autumn. On the crossing, I see turtles paddling beneath the bridge in water of such an improbable hue it gave rise to the term “Miyako blue”. Related Article Japan People here live longer than anyone, but my visit shortened my lifespan “When I first visited Miyako Island, I was so surprised how beautiful the ocean is,” Lamb says. This heavenly snapshot dissolves behind us as we slide onwards to Ishigaki, our final stop before reaching Taiwan. Next morning, as I wait to join my shore excursion, an alarm shrieks through the lounge. Everyone’s phone has pinged simultaneously with an emergency alert. “Get out of the water and leave coastal regions immediately,” it says.



Ducournau’s calm voice comes over the intercom: “An 8.2-magnitude earthquake has occurred off the Philippines’ coast, and the entire Japanese archipelago is under a tsunami alert.” We sail to deeper waters; fishing vessels, small cargo ships and the coastguard follow in our wake. For hours, we anchor out there, reading, attending lectures, enjoying the fine food served in the ship’s two restaurants. Finally, we’re approved to return to shore to complete immigration procedures. Despite a slight ocean surge, Ishigaki is unscathed. Ducournau, and perhaps the mountain god, has excelled. We’ve avoided a typhoon, a volcanic eruption and a tsunami. But then, who said getting to paradise was plain sailing? DETAILS FLY

Cathay Pacific flies from Sydney and Melbourne to Osaka via Hong Kong, and return from Taipei via Hong Kong. See cathaypacific.com



CRUISE

Ponant’s 10-day Odyssey in the Heart of Japan’s Subtropical Islands alternates departures between Osaka, Japan, and Keelung, Taiwan. The next sailing departs on September 20, 2027, from $12,290 a person. See au.ponant.com The writer was a guest of Ponant.

World.title: We looked at staff salaries at Brisbane’s private schools. These pay the most
World.content:
NationalQueenslandTeaching We looked at staff salaries at Brisbane’s private schools. These pay the most Catherine Strohfeldt October 2, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of Brisbane’s most prestigious schools has inked a new pay deal for teachers, as Queensland’s private institutions set the state standard for teachers’ wages. Among the first Brisbane private schools to negotiate new deals was Brisbane Grammar School, which sent a new agreement to the Fair Work Commission for final approvals in mid-September. It would pay senior teaching staff as much as $140,000 by January next year, which Independent Education Union Queensland branch secretary Terry Burke said would match Brisbane Girls Grammar School salaries. Brisbane Grammar School is expected to finalise a new wage deal that would boost the upper limit on base salaries to $140,000. Catherine Strohfeldt “They saw the school over the other side of the lane, getting particular rates and thought that as a staff they should be getting paid those rates too,” Burke said.





The school declined to comment when contacted by this masthead. The latest Commonwealth data from the Workplace Gender Equality Agency showed the average wage for all staff across almost 40 eligible Brisbane private secondary schools sat at about $117,000 in the 2024-25 financial year. This number, which included non-teaching staff, increased from the previous year by about $4000 across all Brisbane private schools. Among the schools with the highest averages on its list was Anglican Church Grammar School (Churchie), which paid teaching and non-teaching staff an average of $149,000 across the 2024-25 financial year.



However, in 2026, the highest base salary for a teacher sat at $130,996, although teachers with additional qualifications, such as highly accomplished and lead teachers, could add another $16,000. Burke said across private institutions, independent-sector schools had an “energetic promotion” of staff to specialised roles, such as highly accomplished and lead teacher roles, which come with a several-thousand-dollar bonus. Teachers in the highest pay brackets at Brisbane Girls’ Grammar School could earn up to $135,206 this year. Catherine Strohfeldt Catholic schools, he said, were generally employing more graduate teachers, driving down salary average figures. “Even more so, the pattern of doing internships in the last year of the four-year degree – that continues to rise,” Burke said.



At the lower end of the figures, Brisbane Adventist College and Brisbane Boys’ College (BBC) paid staff, on average, less than $100,000. However, BBC’s current wage deal stipulated the school would pay its non-specialised teachers a base salary of up to $131,000 this year. Burke said the state’s public sector generally set the precedent for teachers’ pay, and private schools were “the next cab off the ranks”. “The last little while we’ve been so-so, but the big increases should have occurred in July last year for the Queensland Teachers’ Union,” he said.



The union was instead fronting arbitration in April next year, leaving the private sector to eke out its own pay deals ahead of public school teachers, Burke said. Related Article Updated

Schools State school teachers secure interim pay rise The Education Department told this masthead the current average for state school teachers – falling in the 2026-27 financial year – was about $117,000. A spokesperson said the September interim wage order bumped teachers up to base salaries between $86,600 and about $126,700. The department also offered “valuable initiates” to teachers, the spokesperson said, including incentive programs, relocation packages, and retention payments.



The Catholic sector was next to negotiate fresh pay deals. These included six agreements with Queensland’s five dioceses, and one covering religious institute schools – a group which includes St Joseph’s College Gregory Terrace (Terrace), Marist College Ashgrove and All Hallows’ School. World.title: ‘A privilege and a pleasure’: What life’s like in an award-worthy house
World.content:
PropertyNewsArchitecture ‘A privilege and a pleasure’: What life’s like in an award-worthy house Carmen Forward October 2, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When they walked into their home for the first time, Roberta Easton turned to her husband and said, “Patrick, this is it.” During her house hunt, Roberta, an interior designer, had a request. “I kept saying to the real estate agents, I have to have a wow factor… You have to show me something that is amazing … not cookie cutter,” she said. Roberta and Patrick Easton with their dog Teddy. James Brickwood In 2016, the couple bought Reeves House, designed by architects Peter Stutchbury and Sue Harper. It was commended for the Robin Boyd Award for Residential Architecture – the Australian Institute of Architects’ top award for new homes – in 2000. The tri-level property is nestled in the treetops of Clareville on Sydney’s northern beaches, with views to Pittwater, and features open spaces that maximise sun but offer shelter from the weather.



After 10 years living at 91 Hudson Parade, Roberta and Patrick, both aged 65, have decided to sell the home and make a tree change. The property is listed for sale with a $6 million price guide by private treaty. Before moving to the northern beaches, the couple were in the inner west for almost a decade and had renovated a Victorian terrace house. Patrick, a business consultant, said the difference between their current home and their prior inner west terrace was that they had felt “all enclosed.”



Roberta explained, “You walk through the front door, past the great rooms, staircase going up, and it’s not till you actually… get to the back of the house where it opens up.” “We always thought, gee, we would love to see more of the outdoors,” Patrick said. The home is set in the treetops. James Brickwood As soon as they walked into the Clareville property the empty nesters could see trees everywhere they looked. “Because I’m so interested in design and interiors … The house just stood out,” Roberta said.



She said there are “so many magnificent features, and everywhere you look in the house, it’s just another interesting moment.” They purchased the house for $2,925,000 and lived there for a while to see if they needed any changes. Residents can enjoy the outdoors. James Brickwood They added a swimming pool five years ago. “The pool is one spectacular feature. There’s no fence around the pool,” Roberta said. It was also designed by Peter Stutchbury, with edges that can’t be walked on. Updates have been minimal. Roberta added green to the colour palette to reflect more of the nature outside on the inside.



They refurbished the bathroom tiles and the splashback in the kitchen. The garden matured with the house. The use of green in the colour palette inside connects with the treetops outside. James Brickwood Day to day, they notice the impact of the architectural design detail. Patrick appreciates the house’s thoughtful orientation. “It really catches the northern sun as well as handles the western sun as well,” he said. “It’s really nestled into a little nook too, so it’s very well protected from the weather … So you might have a howling southwesterly, but you [can] still sit outside because there’ll be a deck that you can sit on that’s sheltered from that.”



The entire layout is open plan yet feels private at the same time. And while the design is primarily doorless, other than two downstairs doors, the couple didn’t mind the lack of door to their en suite. It was just the two of them. Because of the flow of the home, they haven’t felt the need to overfill the space with furniture. Each piece, Roberta said, is “limited but very considered”. The home is open plan. James Brickwood “You don’t need a lot of decor in a house like Peter Stutchbury’s house because the house is the decor, the angles, the materials,” she said. “We sit and watch the clouds roll by,” she added. They also watch the sunsets and how the light changes through the day.



A highlight of the past decade has been having Pittwater on their doorstep. They moor their Beneteau across the road. “It’s a sailors’ playground,” Roberta said, adding that Patrick is a very “keen, great sailor.” Roberta and Patrick are preparing for their next move. James Brickwood Within five minutes, they can be across the water, having lunch at Morning Bay, or sleep a few nights on the Hawkesbury River or in four hours be in Sydney Harbour. “It’s been a privilege and an absolute pleasure,” she said.



The couple will miss Clareville but are looking forward to a different experience in the Hunter Valley. Related Article Construction How Vickii transformed a higgledy-piggledy home into an entertainer’s dream “It’s a time in our life where we need to stretch out and have another adventure,” Roberta said. Roberta is going to have a pottery studio, and Patrick will continue to sail from Sydney. And their adult children look forward to visiting them in the next spot. Selling agent Marcus Lloyd-Jones from Modern House says the home stands out due to its architecture and location.



“There is a certain part of the market that truly understands great design, fantastic engineering and building,” he said. “A property of this quality is rare. It really is.”
