World.title: The quiet cul-de-sac at the centre of Sydney’s newest housing debate
World.content:
NationalNSWPublic housing The quiet cul-de-sac at the centre of Sydney’s newest housing debate Anthony Segaert October 2, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There are many things that concern Louise Marchant and her son, Gary, about being forced out of their home after more than 30 years. Where will they go? How do they pack up the dozens of family photos and memories? And what do they do about the sheds overflowing with Christmas decorations in their backyard? Louise, 67, and Gary, 39, have worked with neighbours and friends to light up the quiet cul-de-sac of Indigo Way, Blacktown, in Sydney’s west, with a show-stopping display of lights and decorations ranging from snow-capped model towns to rooftop reindeer. Gary Marchant is responsible for turning Indigo Way into a Christmas wonderland. Sitthixay Ditthavong Last Christmas was their final display. Homes NSW is relocating Indigo Way’s public housing tenants, with plans to demolish 16 freestanding homes and replace them with 134 apartment blocks up to six storeys high. In being forced out, residents on the quiet cul-de-sac have found themselves at the centre of a new housing battle, stretching from the public housing centre of Waterloo to Blacktown: how, exactly, should the government increase the public supply of homes?



Homes NSW, the government agency responsible for delivering and managing public housing, is pushing in some areas to demolish and replace ageing or lower-density homes with modern and more densely packed apartments. But the Greens and other housing advocates are pushing the government to build new homes on vacant, government-owned land – and not demolish existing housing. “The delivery of these new homes could take up to 10 years,” said Greens MP Jenny Leong, the party’s housing spokesperson, who said the net effect would be a reduction in public housing numbers before construction finished. Louise Marchant has lived in her home for more than 40 years. Sitthixay Ditthavong Louise and her neighbours, most of whom declined to be interviewed, were contacted by Homes NSW on July 20 with a letter saying its staff is surveying the area for potential development and that residents may be moved in the future. Nine days later, a second letter arrived. All residents would be relocated. “We were told that they would come out here to us, to have an interview in our house, to see what we need. Not one person has had anyone come out,” Gary said. “I would have expected that within a week, you’d have a knock on the door, or a text message.



“At the end of the day, we’re happy to do it, but the way it’s being handled, the way we’re being treated – it’s not right. And we’re not standing for it.” Louise is concerned about where Homes NSW will move her, given much of her community and social life exists up and down the street. She regularly cares for her six-year-old granddaughter, who has cerebral palsy and uses her home for therapy. “We have to make it safe for her as well,” she said. Some residents of Indigo Way have already moved out of the quiet cul-de-sac. Sitthixay Ditthavong “What I can’t understand is, if they’ve got 16 empty places out there [for the residents of Indigo Way to move into], why aren’t people living [in them]? Why are they taking us out and putting us into those 16 houses … Why destroy homes that are all right and have a good community?” A similar debate has been raging in Waterloo, in inner Sydney, since the government in May announced plans to bulldoze 750 apartments built in the 1970s and put 3300 new apartments up to 33 storeys high in their place. Leong is calling on the government to build public housing on unused state-owned land.



“[The government has] confirmed under their land audit that they’ve identified unused sites that are publicly owned already that are capable of delivering 13,000 homes,” she said. “But less than 15 per cent of those are being used by the government and, of those, less than 30 per cent will be social housing.” Related Article Exclusive

City life Hundreds of inner Sydney homes to be bulldozed for 3300 units NSW Housing Minister Rose Jackson said the cost of land was a major issue in delivering housing, and “large-scale renewals on our own under-utilised land” was one method of avoiding buying more land. “I acknowledge that some families would rather stay in their existing homes and we don’t take these decisions lightly. But I have an obligation to every person on the social housing waitlist to do everything in my power to build more homes and that’s what we’re doing,” she said. “Every resident that relocates is always given a right of return, and overwhelmingly the feedback I get from residents is that they love their new homes.”



The street has garnered more than 750 signatures on a petition to the government, but hopes are fading for a Christmas display this year. “It’s going to be the worst feeling, not to be able to come and look at this house at Christmas,” Gary said. “It’s such a good little community.”

World.title: The world’s 20 last great free attractions (plus five close to home)
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As of this month, visitors to Cologne Cathedral in Germany must pay an entry fee. The colossal Gothic masterpiece has been free to visit for centuries, but that privilege ended on July 1, with tourists wanting to admire its cavernous interior now required to cough up €12 ($19.50). It is the latest in a string of attractions around the world that have introduced admission charges in recent times. The Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, for example, went from being free to costing €25 ($40) in 2024, while Rome brought in charges for both the Pantheon (in 2023) and the Trevi Fountain (in 2025). Even the great outdoors is not immune to the trend, with hikers tackling Japan’s Mount Fuji now subject to a fee. So, which of the world’s great landmarks are, for now, still completely free to visit? East Side Gallery, Berlin The famous Berlin mural depicting Leonid Brezhnev and Erich Honecker. iStock This surviving section of the Berlin Wall now stands as the world’s longest open-air gallery, featuring more than 100 paintings across almost two kilometres. The East Side Gallery has official “Denkmal” (heritage-protected) status and is open 24 hours a day, attracting more than three million visitors annually. Keep an eye out for one of its most well-known murals: the “Fraternal Kiss” depicts Erich Honecker, the East German chairman, and Leonid Brezhnev, the Soviet leader, locking lips. 



The Giant’s Causeway’s hexagonal basalt columns formed by ancient volcanic activity. iStock According to science, Northern Ireland’s first World Heritage Site owes its existence to volcanic activity and continental drift. According to legend, it owes it to a rivalry between giants. Whatever its origin story, the result was 40,000 hexagonal basalt columns and one of the UK’s most spectacular views. Book a paid visitor experience through the National Trust if you’d like to be accompanied by a storyteller, but otherwise, simply walk down to the stones on the Atlantic shore at no cost. Plaza de Espana, Seville See Seville’s charming Plaza De Espana while it’s still free. iStock With its azulejo-adorned benches and a charming canal dotted with rowing boats, the semicircle-shaped Plaza de Espana is one of Seville’s numerous architectural delights. It is also one of the few that remain free; the Royal Alcazar, the cathedral and the Giralda, as well as the Setas de Sevilla, all charge. This might change. Jose Luis Sanz, the mayor of the city, announced plans to introduce an entry fee in 2024, and it would appear that the project is still in motion despite delays. The plaza could therefore follow in the footsteps of other ticketed open-air spaces in Spain, such as Barcelona’s Park Guell, which is priced at €18 ($29). As it stands, however, the Plaza de Espana is free, even if not for much longer. Notre-Dame, Paris



You might have to queue up but visiting Notre-Dame is worth it. iStock The Parisian cathedral of Notre-Dame, overlooking the Seine, charges a fee to climb the 424 steps of one of its towers, but tourists are still able to visit the rest of the building free of charge. As with the British Museum, reserving an entry time is advised, but this is also free. The cathedral is older than Cologne’s and underwent extensive restoration following the 2019 fire that forced it to close for five years. Now, visitors can once again see its 13th-century rose windows and the Crown of Thorns relic in all their glory. The British Museum, London The British Museum’s Great Court is enclosed by a spectacular glass roof and was designed by Foster and Partners. More than 6.4 million people visited the British Museum last year, many of them probably eager to catch a glimpse of the Rosetta Stone, the treasures of Sutton Hoo or the Elgin Marbles. And if that wasn’t enough of a reason to go, viewing its impressive collection costs precisely nothing. Some temporary exhibitions do charge an entry fee; for example, standard tickets for the forthcoming loan of the Bayeux Tapestry carry a hefty price tag of £33 ($62). But fees do not apply to standard admission. That said, it is advised to book a timed slot to avoid the queues. Of course, it is just one of many excellent and free museums in London. The Natural History Museum overtook the British Museum as the UK’s premier visitor attraction last year, while the Tate Modern, the V&A and the National Gallery are home to world-class artistic collections.



St Peter’s Basilica, Vatican City Michelangelo’s Pieta can be seen free of charge at St Peter’s in Rome. iStock Although you’ll pay to see some parts of St Peter’s Basilica, such as the dome above or necropolis beneath, a general visit is free providing you’re willing to take your chances in often long queues. If you want to book a time slot, a €7 ($11) fee will apply – though you get a digital audio guide with it. The basilica is crammed with artworks; Michelangelo’s great masterpiece, Pieta, is alone worth the visit. Everywhere you look there’s something remarkable: gilded cherubs, mosaics, statues of saints, popes’ tombs, memorial tablets. Everything is on a colossal scale. Be aware that dress codes are strictly enforced, so avoid shorts, bare shoulders and skirts above the knee. Papal audiences in the square outside, held every Wednesday morning whenever the pope is in Rome, are also free. Jemaa el-Fnaa, Marrakesh Bustling Jemaa el-Fnaa square at sunset in Marrakesh, Morocco. iStock



The beating heart of Marrakesh’s medina has been drawing the city’s visitors since the 11th century, and today the square is an unmissable entry on any traveller’s itinerary. Mornings are filled with the sound of snake charmers’ pungi flutes and the smell of freshly squeezed orange juice, while evenings see it transform into a labyrinthine, lantern-lit set-up filled with food stands and fortune tellers. The Golden Temple, Amritsar The Golden Temple, in Amritsar, feeds 150,000 people daily, free of charge. iStock The Sri Harmandir Sahib complex, which houses the Golden Temple, feeds 150,000 people daily, free of charge, as a manifestation of the Sikh belief that its places of worship are open to all. Head coverings are mandatory for all visitors, but these are provided, as are foot-washing stations and shoe storage. A fee of any sort would jar with its entire ethos. The temple seems to float on the waters of the Amrit Sarovar pool and is surrounded by marble walkways where gurus read scripture and visitors rest in the shade. Dawn is often said to be the best time to visit, when the building reflects in the tranquil waters while the morning light catches on its gilded domes. Fushimi Inari Taisha, Kyoto There are 10,000 torii gates at the Fushimi Inari Shrine in Kyoto. iStock Japan’s ancient capital has no shortage of captivating Shinto shrines, but this one at the base of Mount Inari has become one of the country’s most emblematic sites. Dedicated to the harvest deity, Fushimi Inari Taisha is best known for its 10,000 densely packed torii gates.

World.title: Three people dead, body seen laying on porch of home in Auckland's Papatoetoe
World.content:
Three people are dead following a "serious incident" in Auckland's Papatoetoe.

It comes after a man told RNZ he saw a body lying on the front porch of his neighbour's home as police and ambulances arrived at the scene.

Police responded to the scene on Cambridge Terrace after receiving a call at 6.40pm on Thursday about a dead person at an address, Detective Inspector Karen Bright said.

Do you know more? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz

On arrival, Bright said police located the person and two others who were found dead in the home.

"While our investigation is in the early stages, we are not currently looking for anyone else in connection to what has occurred."

Bright said police didn't believe there was any risk to the wider public.

"We are waiting for the completion of the scene examination, which will help us piece together the circumstances that led to this tragic event," Bright said.

"Police recognise events like this hit at the hearts of our communities, and we are doing everything we can to answer the many questions around this devastating incident."

RNZ / Felix Walton

Quentin Fenton told RNZ he saw ambulances and police start showing up before seeing a body lying on a front porch and "blood everywhere".

Ten minutes earlier, Fenton had sent his children up to the shops. They walked past the neighbour's house and waved to a man outside, who smiled back at them.

Fenton said those who live in the house are "good people" who have helped him jump start his car.

He said the incident was a "big shock" and "too close to home".

RNZ / Felix Walton

"I've got four kids myself, just a bit freaked out by this."

Fenton said it was "all a bit surreal" and "too much".

Bright said police were providing wraparound care to the whanāu of those who had died as well as neighbours.

World.title: Minor parties keep calm and carry on in tepid kingmakers debate
World.content:
Existing policy and reasonableness reigned in a debate excluding the two Chrises, and which Winston Peters seemed to think was a waste of his time.

The NZ First leader dismissed both Christopher Luxon and Chris Hipkins as "not in the same league" as other prime minister he had worked with.

See how the day unfolded in our Thursday election blog.

Not long after, he was seen checking his watch on stage.

"You said 8.30," he told the moderators Andrea Vance and Jenna Lynch, and when they asked if he had somewhere else to be he responded "yes I have".

And despite saying he would not have any kneejerk reactions, Peters was the only one to make substantive policy commitments: a $120 increase in weekly Working for Families benefit payments.

The Post editor Matthew Hooton observed in the panel afterwards that it was Christopher Luxon and Chris Hipkins who were the losers of the debate, saying "any one of these people would be a better prime minister than them".

With National and Labour down to just 28 percent each on TVNZ's latest poll, the minor parties have never been more central to New Zealand's political future, but the proverbial greater power comes with greater responsibility.

National's Christopher Luxon (L) and Labour's Chris Hipkins. RNZ/NZME

That could be what led to greater restraint than would be expected in the debating chamber, or it could be that none of them wanted to put their polling gains at risk.

All five of the participants - David Seymour, Chloe Swarbrick, Peters, Qiulae Wong and Rawiri Waititi - kept the debate mostly civil, with Wong and Seymour especially cordial.

"I was a bit surprised, to be honest", Wong told reporters afterwards. "I was expecting a little bit more bickering as we've been used to seeing on TV and in Parliament. But maybe that's the influence that Opportunity is having on politics already."

Seymour even said he trusted Peters, a reversal of his position three years earlier, and which Peters did not return in kind.

Perhaps expecting a more boisterous affair, Swarbrick seemed to take the most jabs at her opponents, particularly Peters, like when she sarcastically said he "loves migrants", to which he shot back "the right migrant, not everybody, like you".

But Peters' main target was the moderators and the media, as he made clear when answering reporters questions afterwards, saying he thought the questions did not get to the point and lambasting the lack of reporters at his public meetings.

Wong soaked up the most support on the "vibe tracker", an interactive live reflection of audience opinion following in the footsteps of the "worm" from the 2002 debate that saw a huge spike in support for United Future's Peter Dunne.

She won 35 percent support, Swarbrick 29 percent, Seymour 23 percent, Peters 9 percent, and Waititi 4 percent.

Cost of living and health were major topics, with support for business, regulation of AI, and funding for superannuation also canvassed, but the responses were largely as would be expected based on policies the parties had already unveiled.

Seymour was the only one willing to share his salary - $515,060 - and the only one willing say he believed Health Minister Simeon Brown that there was no freeze on hiring nurses.

World.title: Flydubai attack 'shocking' given strict character checks pilots undergo, aviation expert says
World.content:
Audio player for " Ashok Poduva discusses FlyDubai hijacking incident " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/world/1676909%2Fflydubai-attack-shocking-given-strict-character-checks-pilots-undergo-aviation-expert-says

Ashok Poduva discusses FlyDubai hijacking incident Morning Report Download MP3 6m

An alleged attempt to crash a Flydubai flight by a pilot is "shocking" to hear, a former airline pilot says, due to strict character and competency checks.

Passengers on the flight reached Israel safely on Wednesday after customers and crew foiled the co-pilot's attempt to crash the aircraft, Israeli officials said.

The struggle began when the man stabbed his colleague and sent the jet plunging nearly 14,000 feet (4267 metres) in less than 30 seconds while enroute from Dubai to Tel Aviv.

Massey University's school of aviation chief executive and former airline pilot Ashok Poduval told Morning Report pilots have to be classified as fit and proper persons before getting a pilot's licence, and airlines do regular background checks.

He said after 9/11 many safety changes were made to strengthen both the doors and the frames of the cockpit, along with locks.

"It's quite shocking and most unexpected," Poduval said.

The locks on the doors were strong enough to be protected by ballistic penetration, he said, but this was to prevent threats from the outside.

He said when someone became a pilot they were monitored right through on their competency and he couldn't see what more could be done to prevent a situation like what happened on the flight.

World.title: Cocaine-for-flour swap could threaten drug prosecution, Fiji lawyer says
World.content:
Audio player for " Fiji lawyer raises questions after cocaine goes missing " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/pacific/1676923%2Fcocaine-for-flour-swap-could-threaten-drug-prosecution-fiji-lawyer-says

Fiji lawyer raises questions after cocaine goes missing Pacific Waves Download MP3 6m

A Fijian lawyer says the disappearance of cocaine from the Suva High Court could complicate the criminal case for which the drugs were seized.

The cocaine, weighing nearly 40kg with an estimated street value about US$14 million, was being held in the court's exhibit room as evidence in the high-profile case involving Fiji-Canadian national Joshua Aziz Rahman.

The drugs were discovered missing after forensic testing found that what was believed to be cocaine had been replaced with flour.

Rahman was convicted in Fiji of unlawful possession of illicit drugs - 39.5kg of cocaine - and originally sentenced to 23 years' imprisonment with a non-parole period of 14 years. His conviction was quashed by the Fiji Court of Appeal in February. The court ordered a retrial, resulting in his release.

However, in August 2026, the Supreme Court restored the original conviction and sentence, allowing the State's appeal and overturning the Court of Appeal's ruling.

Roopesh Singh from Patel and Sharma Law Firm in Nadi told Pacific Waves that the cocaine would have been important in proving Rahman was in possession of the drugs.

"That'll be one of the most important evidence at the end of the day to be tendered to prove any accused's guilt of what was found, what was in fact seized and found in possession of the accused," Singh said.

However, he said the disappearance does not necessarily mean prosecutors have no other options.

"There could be circumstantial evidence that could be used," he said, adding that it would be up to the court to consider the evidence presented by the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP).

Singh also raised concerns about how individual court officers were able to access security systems at the High Court.

He said the amount of cocaine involved and how it was tampered with should prompt the Fijian government to do more to secure drug exhibits.

"It's not something that you go in and take. Someone had a lot of time to do that."

Fiji Police confirmed on Wednesday that CCTV covering the evidence room was not working and the biometric security was faulty when the drugs went missing.

Police have also confirmed that six people of interest are now being investigated.

Singh said access to drug exhibits should be more restricted, with only a small number of senior officials knowing where they were stored.

The ODPP defended its drug-disposal protocols, saying its policies changed after the establishment of the Anti-Narcotics Division in 2024 and that it is now prioritising applications to destroy drug exhibits.

World.title: Winston Peters wins the airtime battle in first leaders debate, but who won the war?
World.content:
In a debate where Winston Peters and David Seymour flexed their political muscle, newcomer Qiulae Wong struggled for airtime but stood out in different ways.

Analysis: Since polls started regularly suggesting Opportunity may have a kingmaking position after the November 7 election, leader Qiulae Wong has had a good chunk of airtime in interviews across all the major media outlets.

The first televised leaders debate of the campaign last night, however, was a whole different affair.

Wong was on stage for the The Press Kingmakers' debate directly alongside political veteran and NZ First leader Winston Peters, who she has directly challenged for the kingmaker role. ACT's David Seymour, Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick, and Te Pāti Māori co-leader Rawiri Waititi, were also there and all experienced in the format.

Peters appeared to relish his status as the old hand, even leaning into it as part of his pitch that experience is so important in politics. He had knowing exchanges with the moderators, lots of lessons to share from decades past and got the most words in. Wong, on the other hand, was the only person to mention words like 'climate' or 'environment' and RNZ's analysis found she used the highest proportion of positive words and the lowest proportion of negative.

Who talked the most?

Peters chalked up 3013 discernable words during the debate compared to second place Seymour's 2781.

Waititi said 2122 words and Swarbrick and Wong both fewer than 2000. At just 1045 words, Wong spoke roughly a third of the words as Peters.

The percentage of words Peters spoke was in line with his performances in debates in 2020 and 2023.

The length of answers varied among speakers, with Seymour giving the longest uninterrupted answer of the night of 239 words against policies to buy or break up supermarkets.

Issues with the health system were the topic of Swarbrick's longest answer, where she talked about the lack of hospital beds and ambulance "ramping".

The longest answer from Peters was in response to modertor Andrea Vance's question on whether the prime minister should have more license to sack coalition ministers. He pointed to the Greens and Te Pāti Māori losing MPs and said the responsibility was to provide a stable government, and he referenced time spent in government with Helen Clark.

"I think that was a no," was Vance's interpretation of his 171 word answer.

Waititi's longest answer related to opportunities for Māori in small business, and Wong's longest answer was 124 words related to artificial intelligence.

Peters dominated speaking turns as well as overall wordcount. A 'speaking turn' is counted as each time six words or more were spoken in a row by one of the leaders.

Peters was way out in front on this measure, taking nearly double the next highest, Seymour and almost triple Wong's tally.

On average, however, Peters' turns ran to 46 words, compared with 77 for Seymour.

What was said

There were words the leaders said over and over again. "Well" was the top word for Peters and Wong. "People" was Seymour's top word, followed by "going", then "well". Waititi's most used word was Māori.

Of the leaders, Peters said the highest number of unique words (936), followed by Seymour (919). Wong and Waititi said the fewest, with 417 and 606 respectively.

RNZ counted how many times each leader used certain words which relate to key topics. Māori, health and tax were mentioned the most, at 23 times each. The economy was mentioned 18 times.

Wong was the only leader to mention climate, environment and emissions - all once each. She was also the only one to mention Kiwisaver.

The word "treaty" was mentioned once by Waititi.

What was the vibe?

According to a language sentiment data dictionary, which rates words as either positive, neutral or negative, Wong came out on top for positive language, with 6 percent of words she used classed as positive. She scored the lowest of all the leaders for negative words.

Waititi used the lowest percentage for positive words and Seymour used the highest percentage of negative words.
